cadence: one lesson per US weekday, strictly in this order; a Systems Case closes each block
target_length: about 15 minutes (~3,100 words); one concept; opens with a real story
note: Logan's Connected Path, restarted at Day 1 on 2026-10-15 (docs/SPEC.md Sec.0d): sixteen fields, Mathematics first with applications from day 1, statistics and causal inference early, Systems Thinking early, and a Systems Case closing each block that traces one real system through his chain (need, invention, physical constraints, engineering, financing and production, regulation, adoption, consequences, feedback) as a loop. Each lesson opens with a real story, explains one concept, links back and across, recommends one resource checked by web search when this plan was written, and ends with one application question. No Economics/Finance blocks: Logan is studying for the CFA.
rationale:
PROPOSAL FOR LOGAN'S APPROVAL, revised after an adversarial review. He wrote "lmk before you put in", so nothing goes into curriculum/ until he confirms the three replacement fields and this shape.

SHAPE. 293 weekday lessons: 275 lessons plus 18 Systems Cases, in 18 blocks over his 16 fields. History and Philosophy are each split in two. Day 1 is Thu 15 Oct 2026. At one lesson per weekday (market holidays included), the first case falls on Day 24 (Tue 17 Nov 2026) and Day 293 on Mon 29 Nov 2027.

WHY 293 AND NOT 300. Each block was sized from what later blocks and the book need, then summed. The review added four lessons that closed real gaps, and nothing else:
- the solar system, which Logan's own scope for Space & Astronomy names and the draft left out;
- metaethics (can a moral claim be true at all?), which every later argument about moral progress presupposes;
- the Age of Revolutions and where rights talk came from, the one gap in the book's history of moral progress;
- motivated reasoning, the bias an author with a worldview most needs to see, in himself and in his critics.
Padding to 300 would only add filler, and the procedure reads total_days (T), so nothing depends on 300. The weight goes to the book's spines:
- History: 35 lessons, including the Great Enrichment economic history that the dropped Economics block would have carried.
- Philosophy: 29.
- How We Know: 9, inside Mathematics.
- Biology, Medicine & Health: 21 (the mortality revolution).
- Energy, Chemistry & Materials: 20 (energy at civilizational scale).
Lean blocks are Systems Thinking (12, a toolkit taught with its limits), Computing (13) and Space (15).

ORDER (a "how the world works" ladder):
1. Mathematics with How We Know (1-24)
2. Systems Thinking (25-36)
3. Philosophy I: knowledge, evidence, values (37-49)
4. Physics (50-66)
5. Energy, Chemistry & Materials (67-86)
6. Engineering (87-103)
7. Computing (104-116)
8. Space & Astronomy (117-131)
9. Biology, Medicine & Health (132-152)
10. Psychology (153-169)
11. AI (170-184)
12. History I (185-200)
13. Sociology (201-216)
14. History II (217-235)
15. Government (236-249)
16. Law (250-263)
17. International Relations (264-277)
18. Philosophy II (278-293)
The arc runs: tools; the connective toolkit; how we know and what is good; matter and energy; materials and power; building; information machines; space as infrastructure; life and health; minds; machine minds; the deep past; societies; the modern world; states; law; world order; and last, the questions about persons, God and progress that the book must answer.

PREREQUISITES. A script checked every back-link (D-number) in the skeleton; each one points to an earlier day, with no forward links, and every case's Preview names a block still to come (the review moved four "previews" of blocks already taught into Deep).
- Mathematics feeds the sciences: calculus, logs, differential equations and S-curves come before Physics, Systems and Biology; vectors before forces, GPS and neural nets; probability and Bayes before epistemology, perception, reliability and reinforcement learning.
- The physical sciences feed each other in order:
  - Physics (circuits, induction, the quantum atom, E=mc²) comes before batteries, silicon, the grid and fission.
  - Physics and materials come before Engineering (engines, steel, plastics).
  - Physics and materials also come before Space: the rocket equation needs momentum and logs, and the GPS case needs relativity.
  - Silicon comes before the transistor.
- Minds and machines: Computing precedes AI. Biology (neurons, dopamine) precedes Psychology, and Psychology (reinforcement, calibration) precedes AI.
- Ethics before cases: Philosophy I (is-ought, metaethics and the four frameworks) comes before every case's Evidence check.
- History and Sociology interleave:
  - History I (the Reformation) comes before Sociology (secularization, Durkheim re-tested).
  - Sociology (the demographic transition, diffusion) comes before History II (Malthus, the Great Enrichment).
  - Both History parts come before Government, Law and IR.
- The institutional blocks build on each other:
  - Government (legitimacy, capacity, capture) comes before Law's administrative law and IR's state-building.
  - Game theory comes before IR's bargaining and deterrence lessons.
  - Natural law (Philosophy I) comes before the origins-of-rights debate (History II) and Hart against Fuller (Law).
  - LLMs (AI) come before the consciousness lesson in Philosophy II.
- Earlier cases preview later fields in a sentence, never teaching them early. IR's just-war lesson carries Augustine's just-war teaching; Philosophy II later teaches a different Augustinian concept, the two cities.

APPLICATIONS EARLY. Day 1 is Fermi's Trinity estimate, applied at once to the car's energy budget (gasoline against batteries, before and after efficiency). Every maths lesson has a real application, several on Logan's car chain:
- the 55-mph limit and what a flat optimum implies about the fuel it saved;
- IIHS death rates and confounding;
- the speed-limit repeal as a natural experiment;
- speed cameras and regression to the mean;
- Volkswagen and Goodhart's law;
- the SUV game.
Car I is Day 24 and Systems Thinking starts on Day 25.

WHERE THE BOOK'S NEEDS LIVE:
- How We Know: Bayes and base rates 15, sampling 16, significance 17, confounding 18, regression to the mean 19, randomized trials 20, natural experiments 21, replication 22, Goodhart 23.
- Ethics foundations: is-ought 43; metaethics (Euthyphro, divine command, evolutionary debunking) 44; the four frameworks 45-48 (natural law and Aquinas 48).
- Christian thought: Augustine 283; Aquinas's Five Ways 280; Catholic social teaching 285; Protestant social ethics 286; dignity 287.
- Progress: moral progress 288; the idea of progress 289; philosophy of technology 290.
- Christianity in history: the Reformation 197 (with Cantoni's null result beside Becker & Woessmann); the Christianity-and-science historiography 199 (Draper and White against Brooke, Numbers and Harrison; Stark and Hannam with their critics; the conflict view's remaining defenders), with Stark 189 and Holland 190; Christian anti-Judaism and Christian resistance in 232; the papal bulls that licensed enslavement in 196.
- The Great Enrichment debate: 217-224 (Malthus, measurement, Allen, Mokyr, McCloskey, Acemoglu and Robinson, Pomeranz, the invention of invention).
- Rights and abolition: the Age of Revolutions and the origins of rights (Tierney, Hunt, Moyn) 225; Williams against Drescher 226; Christian arguments on both sides from Anstey, Davis, Brown and Noll, with the enslaved's own revolts and Enlightenment critics 227; case 235.
- Measuring progress and its critiques: 218 and 234, plus well-being 168.
- The mortality revolution: 145.
- Law: property 252, contract 253, tort 254, the corporation 255, international law 261.
- Regulation and public choice: 243-244.
- Bioethics: 149 and 287.
- The author's own discipline: motivated reasoning 163, calibration 167, arguing fairly 292.

ONE HOME PER CONCEPT:
- Ohm's law is taught only in Physics.
- Gravity, orbits, the solar system, rockets and stellar fusion belong to Space; nuclear physics to Physics; nuclear power to Energy, Chemistry & Materials (ECM).
- The greenhouse effect is taught once, at ECM 85.
- Medical evidence is split three ways: the logic of trials (Math 20), observational epidemiology (Biology 143) and drug regulation (the Government case, 249).
- Snow's natural experiment is the Math 21 story; germ theory is told through Semmelweis (Biology 140).
- Computing and AI: matrices and the dot product are taught in AI 172; Boolean logic and Gödel/Turing in Computing.
- Social contract theory is Government 236; just war is IR 270.
- Grounding human rights is Philosophy I 48; their historical origins are History II 225; their enforcement is IR 274.
- Stock-flow modelling is Systems 25, built on the integral (Math 5).
- Learning curves are Engineering 97; earlier lessons only read prices on a log scale.

STORIES. Every lesson names a real, specific, dated story. Legendary details are flagged as legend: Joule's honeymoon thermometer, Iron Ring steel, Fleming's open window, "eppur si muove", Luther's hammer, the Prague dung heap, the misprinted log table in the honeycomb story.
None of the opening stories Logan already read in the earlier tracks is reused. That excludes the root-2 cult, al-Khwarizmi, Eratosthenes, Zeno, Bolt, the Greenbird land yacht, DART, the falling cat and Caterpillar - and, after the review checked all 43 taught pages, Kepler's wine barrel (told in an old integrals lesson) and Halley's 1684 visit to Newton (told in the old Newton's-laws lesson), which the draft had reused. No story is used twice inside the path either (the draft told Richardson's deadly quarrels, Carnot's 1824 book and the Domesday survey twice each).
The restart does re-cover the 13 maths lessons taught from 28 Sep to 14 Oct, now as 14 plus 9 lessons with new stories and applications.

NO ECONOMICS OR FINANCE. There is no economics or finance block, because Logan is studying for the CFA. Where a field needs a mechanism, a clause names it at CFA level: installment credit and GMAC 1919, Fust's loans to Gutenberg, PDUFA user fees, subsidies, hyperscaler capex, Vogtle's cost. The economic history the book needs lives in History II.

CHALLENGES BUILT IN:
- The car chain is taught as a loop with documented reversals: the 1865 Red Flag Act came before the car, the Good Roads movement before the car, credit and street law before demand, and the cotton gin as "invention the mother of necessity".
- "Human needs" is tested with Tay and Diener (159).
- Systems Thinking is taught with its failures (34, where neither Simon nor Ehrlich gets a free victory lap), and the linear model of innovation is challenged (35).
- Lessons ask "progress toward what, and for whom?" (234, 289), and whether moral claims can be true at all (44).
- Claims that flatter Christianity and claims that indict it meet one evidence standard (41, 190, 197, 199, 227, 229, 232, 291); so do claims that flatter a secular reading (Hume on miracles meets Earman; the conflict thesis meets its historians; secularization meets Voas and Chaves and Stark and Finke).
- Motivated reasoning (163) is taught before AI and long before the book chapters, so Logan meets the bias in his own camp and in his critics'.
cases_plan:
EIGHTEEN SYSTEMS CASES. One closes each block; 16 fields with History and Philosophy split give 18.
- D24 Car I: the car by the numbers (spiral visit)
- D36 The Grand Banks cod collapse (and its disputed 2024 reopening)
- D49 Leaded gasoline and the burden of proof
- D66 The electric grid: why the world runs on AC
- D86 Haber-Bosch: bread from air
- D103 Car II: building the car, from Highland Park to the gigafactory
- D116 The internet
- D131 GPS: the invisible utility
- D152 Antibiotics: from mould to resistance
- D169 Social media and teenage mental health
- D184 Large language models
- D200 The printing press
- D216 Car III: the car remakes society
- D235 The cotton gin, slavery and abolition
- D249 The FDA: drug regulation built by disasters
- D263 Tobacco and manufactured doubt
- D277 Nuclear power: Atoms for Peace
- D293 Car IV: the full loop, and was the car progress?

THE CAR SPIRAL. Four visits, each deep on different links.
- Car I (D24, built from Mathematics only): physical constraints (energy density), production prices read on a log scale (why they fell is left to Engineering), regulation evidence (the 55-mph limit, the repeal as a natural experiment, Volkswagen and Goodhart), adoption as an S-curve, and consequences read as rates with confounding.
- Car II (D103): engineering, production (including learning curves, now taught), materials and emissions, and the EV battery learning curve.
- Car III (D216): needs and status, the invented offence of jaywalking, norms, diffusion, suburbs, social capital and induced demand.
- Car IV (D293): every link deep, followed by the moral evaluation across frameworks, with metaethics (44) behind the question of whether "beneficial" can be true. This is the book's own question.
The spiral and Day 1 (Fermi plus the car's energy budget) bracket the path.

DEPTH RULE. Each case's one_line lists:
- "Deep" links, with the taught days they draw on (all earlier; machine-checked).
- "Preview" links: one or two sentences naming a block still to come. A link whose block is already taught is never a preview (the review moved four: Haber's scale-up became an Engineering preview of the next block, and penicillin's mass production, the printing press's movable type and tobacco's nicotine became Deep links to Engineering and Biology).
Depth grows along the path: Car I is mostly preview, nuclear power (D277) is the first case with no preview links, and Car IV is deep on every link.
The financing link names the real mechanism and numbers at CFA level and never teaches finance. Examples: GMAC 1919 credit, Fust's roughly 2,026 guilders, PDUFA user fees, subsidies, hyperscaler capex, Vogtle's roughly $35 billion.

LOOP RULE. Each case is taught as a loop, not a pipeline, with documented reversals:
- Regulation before invention: the 1865 Red Flag Act; Insull asking for regulation; Kehoe's rule.
- Invention before need: the cotton gin (Kranzberg), ARPANET e-mail, Bonsack's 1881 machine, LLM capability before uses.
- Consequences before evidence: social media.
- Disasters writing rules: the FDA, Bayway lead, KAL 007 opening GPS.
- War driving scale-up: Haber-Bosch at Leuna, the bomb before the reactor.
- Success breeding failure: antibiotic resistance; the cod fishery, whose catch rates hid the collapse.
- Models moving policy: the cod moratorium ended in 2024 after a model revision, not a surge of fish.
- Credit and street law building demand: the car.

BALANCE. The book should not be built only from successes:
- Benefit-led: the grid, GPS, the internet.
- Mixed: Car I-IV, Haber-Bosch, antibiotics, the printing press, LLMs, the FDA, nuclear power.
- Harm-and-repair: cod, leaded gasoline, social media (contested, with Haidt and Twenge against Odgers, Orben and Przybylski named), the cotton gin, tobacco.

EVERY CASE ends Why It Matters with the Evidence check:
- settled;
- debated, naming the sides;
- value judgment: who gained, who paid, who consented.
On the value side it names at least one framework besides the Christian one, keeps the counterfactual marked as unknowable, and uses only claims the run verifies.

phases.name: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
phases.mission: After this block Logan can estimate any quantity to a power of ten, read growth on a log scale, think in rates and accumulations, write a rule for change as a differential equation, see S-curves, optima, vectors, proof, probability, fat tails, networks and games at work in real systems, and then (How We Know, from the Bayes lesson on) judge evidence: base rates, sampling, significance, confounding, regression to the mean, randomized trials, natural experiments, replication and Goodhart's law. Every lesson is anchored to a real application, and the block closes with the first car case. Scope: no stock-flow or loop modelling (Systems Thinking), no Boolean logic, computability or Gödel (Computing), no matrices (taught where neural networks need them in AI), no calibration or forecasting (Psychology), no finance mathematics (Logan's CFA).
phases.folded_in: Re-covers the 13 academy-300 maths lessons already taught (numbers to vectors) with new stories and applications; the Pythagorean root-2 and al-Khwarizmi stories are not reused, and neither is Kepler's wine barrel, which an old integrals lesson told. Complex numbers, series, trigonometry, combinatorics and set theory are cut or folded (sine and cosine inside vectors; counting inside probability). Adds the How We Know sequence all five audits found missing (Bayes, sampling, significance, confounding, regression to the mean, RCTs, natural experiments, replication, Goodhart), placed here so every later block can use it.

phases.name: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
phases.mission: After this block Logan can draw any system as stocks, flows and reinforcing and balancing loops, spot delays, thresholds, unintended consequences, commons problems, lock-in and emergence, find leverage points, and - just as important - say when a systems model is overreaching. It is the connective toolkit every later Systems Case uses, and it challenges his linear chain directly (innovation as a coupled system, not a pipeline). Scope: uses the maths already taught (integrals, differential equations, S-curves, networks) without re-teaching it; leaves control engineering to Engineering, ecology to Biology and economics named at CFA level only.
phases.folded_in: New: no lesson in the old track taught stocks and flows, loops, delays, Goodhart-style feedback, path dependence or model limits (audits 0, 1 and 2). Folds the old engineering feedback lessons' systems ideas in here and turns the old 'graph theory' and 'Limits to Growth' fragments into tools with their failure modes.

phases.name: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
phases.mission: After this block Logan can test an argument's validity and soundness, state the problem of induction, use falsification and paradigms properly (and their limits), weigh testimony and extraordinary claims with one standard, see where values legitimately enter science (inductive risk), keep 'is' and 'ought' apart, say what it would take for a moral claim to be true (realism, anti-realism, divine command and the evolutionary debunking challenge), and name what consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and natural law each say about a case. This is the vocabulary of every later Evidence check and of his book's empirical-versus-moral discipline. Scope: philosophy of mind, free will, God's existence, political philosophy, Augustine, Catholic and Protestant social ethics, moral progress and philosophy of technology are Philosophy II; just war is International Relations.
phases.folded_in: Draws the old track's Philosophy lessons on logic, knowledge, Popper and Kuhn, utilitarianism, Kant, virtue and is-ought forward to the start, where audits 1 and 2 said the book's empirical-versus-moral split needs them. Adds what the old track lacked: natural law (Aquinas), metaethics (Euthyphro, divine command, evolutionary debunking), testimony and miracles, values in science.

phases.name: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain the laws that bound everything built: force and inertia, momentum and impulse, energy and its conservation, power, heat engines and the Carnot limit, entropy, pressure and buoyancy, drag and lift, waves, circuits, induction, the electromagnetic spectrum, relativity, the quantum atom, mass-energy and radiation dose. Scope: gravity, orbits and rockets are Space & Astronomy; chemistry of fuels and batteries, nuclear power and grid operations are Energy, Chemistry & Materials; structures and control are Engineering; stellar physics is Space.
phases.folded_in: Replaces the old Physics block (21-40). Ohm's law gets one home here (the old day 173 duplicate is gone). Projectile motion is cut for fluids, drag and lift, which audits 0 and 1 found missing. Stories are new (the falling cat, DART and Usain Bolt stories Logan already read are not reused).

phases.name: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain, at the level of atoms and bonds where needed, why fuels burn, batteries store, steel, concrete, plastics and silicon behave as they do, how ammonia is made, what fossil fuels, reactors, solar, wind and the grid can and cannot do, why energy transitions are slow and land-hungry, and how CO2 warms the planet and acidifies the sea - with Smil-style numbers. Scope: nuclear physics and radiation are Physics; machines and structures are Engineering; biology of nitrogen and food is Biology; climate policy is International Relations.
phases.folded_in: Logan's choice to replace Economics and Finance & Accounting. Compresses the old Chemistry block (121-140) to what energy, materials and the car need (cuts the mole, VSEPR, gas laws and solutions as standalone lessons), and adds what audits 0-2 found absent: Haber-Bosch, the materials of modernity, the grid, power density and energy at civilizational scale (Smil). The greenhouse effect gets one home here (the old track taught it three times).

phases.name: Engineering: Designing, Building and Making It Safe
phases.mission: After this block Logan can think like an engineer about trade-offs, loads, fatigue, resonance, engines, feedback control, redundancy, system accidents, interfaces, mass production, learning curves, lean quality, standards, infrastructure wear, crashworthiness and professional duty - and walk the car from Highland Park to the EV. Scope: materials chemistry is Energy, Chemistry & Materials; rockets are Space & Astronomy; computers are Computing; the grid's physics is Physics.
phases.folded_in: Moves Engineering up from the old day 161 (May 2027) to straight after Physics and materials, as audit 1 urged. Drops the old Ohm's-law duplicate (173). Adds the internal-combustion engine, learning curves, lean production, containerization and road wear, and makes the old 'automobile as a system' capstone into Car II.

phases.name: Computing: Information Machines
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain what information is, how logic becomes circuits and circuits become computers, why some problems are hard and some unsolvable, why software fails differently from hardware, how packets, encryption and data centres work, and why security is adversarial. Scope: machine learning and AI are the AI block; social media's effects are Psychology; intermediary liability is Law; chip geopolitics is International Relations.
phases.folded_in: Keeps the old Computing core (61-69, 78-79) in fewer lessons, moves Shannon's information here from the old Communication block, and takes Turing and Gödel from the old math day 20. Adds software failure, data centres' physical footprint and open source as a commons.

phases.name: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain gravity and orbits, how the solar system formed and why impacts still matter, the rocket equation and why reusability changed launch, Apollo as politics, satellites as everyday infrastructure, debris and space weather as risks, how stars shine and forge elements, how we measure the cosmos, the Big Bang evidence and the search for other worlds - and trace GPS as a system. Scope: relativity and the electromagnetic spectrum are Physics; propellant chemistry is Energy, Chemistry & Materials; systems engineering is Engineering; space law is named, not taught.
phases.folded_in: Logan's choice to replace Economics and Finance & Accounting; it uses the old Rockets & Space block (41-60) compressed and reframed toward space as infrastructure, as audits 0 and 2 suggested. Specialist orbital-mechanics and spacecraft-subsystem lessons are cut; satellites, debris, space weather and the solar system (formation and impacts, a scope Logan's field list names) are added. The DART story and Halley's 1684 visit to Newton, which Logan already read, are not reused.

phases.name: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain cells, metabolism, evolution, DNA, heredity and gene editing, ecosystems and extinction, germ theory, immunity and vaccines, pandemics, epidemiology, sanitation, the mortality revolution, the Green Revolution, nutrition science's evidence problems, chronic disease, research ethics, and the brain's basics - neurons and reward - before Psychology. Scope: trial statistics were taught in Mathematics (How We Know); drug regulation as an institution is the Government case; psychology of behaviour is Psychology; bioethics at the edges of life is Philosophy II.
phases.folded_in: Logan's choice to replace Economics and Finance & Accounting. Compresses the old Biology block (141-160) and adds what audits 0-3 found absent and the book needs: germ theory, sanitation, epidemiology, the mortality revolution (McKeown versus Preston), the Green Revolution and nutrition science. The brain's basics come here, just before Psychology, so the old neuron overlap (83/156) disappears.

phases.name: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain perception as inference, reconstructive memory, reinforcement, heuristics and biases (and their critics), prospect theory, risk perception, motivation (and why Maslow's pyramid is not what Maslow said), conformity and obedience with their replication status, moral psychology, motivated reasoning, development, intelligence and heritability, mental-health evidence, calibration, and well-being - labelled for evidence strength throughout. Scope: neurons and dopamine are Biology; groups and institutions are Sociology; AI is the next block.
phases.folded_in: Keeps the old Psychology block (81-100) in 16 lessons, adds prospect theory, motivated reasoning (Kahan), calibration (Tetlock) and well-being research, and labels fragile classics (Milgram, Zimbardo, Rosenhan) as the audits asked. Maslow is taught with Tay & Diener's evidence, which challenges the 'human needs' link of Logan's chain.

phases.name: AI: Machines That Learn
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain how modern AI learns from data, why models overfit and fail under shift, what a neural network computes (matrix multiplication taught here), how gradient descent trains it, why deep learning took off in 2012, embeddings, reinforcement learning, transformers and scaling laws, alignment and specification gaming, hallucination and evaluation, the self-driving long tail, AI and work, and the governance debate - and trace large language models as a system. Scope: computer hardware and data centres are Computing; consciousness and the Chinese Room are Philosophy II; liability law is Law.
phases.folded_in: Keeps the old AI core (70-77, 80) and adds what audits 0 and 1 found missing: alignment, evaluation, labour effects and governance, plus self-driving cars as AI's car lesson. Matrices, cut from Mathematics, are taught where neural networks need them.

phases.name: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
phases.mission: After this block Logan can use historians' methods (source criticism, the Whig warning), and explain the agricultural revolution's trade-offs, writing and the state, ancient growth and its ceiling, Christianity's rise and its effect on moral norms (with the evidence standard applied both ways), the Islamic transmission of learning, the medieval Church as an institution-builder, medieval technology, the Black Death, the Columbian exchange, the Atlantic slave trade, the Reformation, Westphalia, and the Christianity-and-science historiography - then trace the printing press as a system. Scope: philosophy is Philosophy; modern economic history and abolition are History II; sociology of religion is Sociology.
phases.folded_in: Replaces the first half of the old History block (181-200) and adds what audit 2 found missing for the book: the Reformation, Christianity and human dignity in late antiquity (Holland and his critics), Stark's growth estimates, Christianity and science (Draper/White against Brooke, Numbers, Harrison; Stark and Hannam and their critics), Westphalia, and the slave trade. Contested causal claims in the old descriptions (printing caused the Reformation; farming caused hierarchy) are taught as contested.

phases.name: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain social facts, norms and how they flip, weak ties, social capital and trust, mobility and neighbourhood effects, how discrimination is measured, religion and secularization, the demographic transition, immigration and assimilation, cities, organizational failure (normalization of deviance), social movements, diffusion of innovations (the adoption link of his chain), media effects and crime trends - and trace how the car remade society. Scope: individual minds are Psychology; the state is Government; inequality's economics is named at CFA level.
phases.folded_in: Keeps the old Sociology block's strongest lessons (261-279) and folds in the old Communication block's diffusion and media lessons (295-299), which audit 3 found the cases depend on. Adds demography, immigration and cities (audits 0 and 2). The old Neolithic and bureaucracy duplicates are gone.

phases.name: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
phases.mission: After this block Logan can lay out the Malthusian world and its escape, how the Great Enrichment is measured, the competing explanations (Allen's wages and coal, Mokyr's Industrial Enlightenment, McCloskey's bourgeois dignity, Acemoglu and Robinson's institutions, Pomeranz's Great Divergence), the invention of invention, the Age of Revolutions and where rights talk came from, the slavery-and-capitalism debate, abolition with Christian arguments on both sides, nationalism, empire and its legacies, industrial war, totalitarian famine, the Holocaust, the Cold War, and how progress is measured and contested - then trace the cotton gin to abolition as a system. Scope: economics is named at CFA level, never taught; war theory is International Relations; moral progress as philosophy is Philosophy II.
phases.folded_in: Replaces the second half of the old History block and carries the economic history the book needs, which the dropped Economics block would have held (Logan is studying for the CFA): the Great Enrichment debate (audit 2's 'book backbone'), measuring progress, slavery and capitalism (Williams, Drescher, Baptist, Olmstead & Rhode), abolition (Davis, Anstey, Brown, Noll), empire (Nunn, Dell, Woodberry and its re-analysis). Adds the Age of Revolutions (the Haitian Revolution and the origins-of-rights debate: Tierney, Hunt, Moyn). WWI gets its own lesson; WWII is taught through the Holocaust, the bomb (Physics, ECM) and just war (IR) rather than as campaign history; the Great Leap famine is added.

phases.name: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain why states are obeyed, what state capacity is, how constitutions check power, why no voting rule is perfect, how democracies break down, federalism and subsidiarity, bureaucracy, the regulatory toolkit, capture and public choice, evidence-based policy, corruption, how modern autocracies survive, church-state models - and trace US drug regulation as a loop of disasters and reforms. Scope: courts and legal doctrine are Law; relations among states are International Relations; economics of regulation is named at CFA level (externalities, public goods) and never taught.
phases.folded_in: Compresses the old Government block (221-231, 237-240), moves social contract theory here as the first lesson (from the old Philosophy 116), and adds what audits 0-3 found missing: regulation and capture (Stigler, Olson), evidence-based policy, subsidiarity (Catholic social teaching's contribution) and church-state models.

phases.name: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
phases.mission: After this block Logan can explain what law is (positivism versus natural law), how common law grows by precedent, and what property, contract, tort and product liability, the corporation, intellectual property, criminal law, burdens of proof, judicial review, administrative law, international law and intermediary liability each do - and trace tobacco through law's whole toolkit. Scope: the state and regulation as policy are Government; the UN, human rights enforcement and war are International Relations; securities and finance law are excluded (CFA).
phases.folded_in: Replaces the old Law lessons (232-236, 239), which covered how law is organized but not its content. Adds property, contract, tort, corporate law, IP, international law, administrative law and Hart against Fuller, as audits 0-2 asked.

phases.name: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
phases.mission: After this block Logan can use realism, liberalism and constructivism as lenses, explain war as bargaining failure, nuclear deterrence, the debate over whether war has declined, just war theory and double effect, economic statecraft, power transitions, the UN, the human-rights regime, collective action on global commons, and outside state-building - then trace nuclear power through every field. Scope: international law's sources are Law; trade and sanctions economics are named at CFA level; history of the world wars and Cold War is History II.
phases.folded_in: Compresses the old IR block (241-260). Game theory and expected value now come before it (Mathematics), as audit 1 required for Fearon and Schelling. Adds just war (Augustine, Aquinas, Anscombe, Walzer, and the Christian pacifist dissent of Yoder), the decline-of-war debate and the Montreal Protocol.

phases.name: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
phases.mission: After this block Logan can state the hard problem of consciousness, the free-will positions, the main arguments for God's existence and the problem of evil with the strongest replies on each side, evidentialism against Reformed epistemology, Augustine's two cities, Rawls against Nozick, Catholic social teaching, Protestant social ethics, human dignity and its critics, moral progress and its critics, the history of the idea of progress, philosophy of technology, Christian thought on ecology, and how to argue fairly - and judge the car as a whole. These are the questions his book on morally beneficial progress must answer. Scope: the epistemology and ethics toolkit is Philosophy I; just war is International Relations.
phases.folded_in: Replaces the old Philosophy II material (108-120) and adds what audit 2 found the book needs: Augustine, Catholic social teaching (Rerum Novarum to Antiqua et nova), Protestant social ethics (Kuyper, Niebuhr, Hauerwas, O'Donovan), human dignity, moral progress (Buchanan & Powell), the idea of progress (Bury, Löwith, Blumenberg, Nisbet, Lasch), philosophy of technology (Winner, Ellul, Lewis) and Lynn White's ecology thesis. Christian positions are presented among others, accurately and attributed.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Orders of magnitude: estimating the world in powers of ten
days.headline_hint: Fermi Sized the First Atomic Bomb With a Handful of Torn Paper. His Answer Was About Half the Real Yield, and That Counted as Right.
days.concept: You can reach a usable estimate of almost any quantity by breaking it into rough factors you can guess, multiplying them while tracking units and powers of ten, and aiming to be right within a factor of a few rather than exactly.
days.focus: Teaches Fermi estimation as a disciplined method: decompose the quantity, estimate each factor to the nearest power of ten, carry the units through, and sanity-check the order of magnitude. It also shows why errors in several independent factors partly cancel. The anchor is the car's physical-constraint link: the energy-per-kilogram gap between gasoline and lithium-ion batteries, and how drivetrain efficiency narrows it.
days.model_or_equation: Q ≈ f1 × f2 × … × fn, so log10 Q = log10 f1 + … + log10 fn: an estimate is a sum of logarithms. If each of n independent factors could be off by a factor of about k either way, over- and under-estimates partly cancel, so the product is typically off by about k^√n rather than k^n. State this as a rule of thumb: the square-root rule for independent errors is explained with sampling on Day 16.

story.title: Ten miles from the first atomic bomb, a physicist tears up a sheet of paper
story.hook: At 5:29 a.m. on 16 July 1945 the first atomic bomb exploded at the Trinity site in the New Mexico desert. Enrico Fermi was at base camp, about 10 miles (16 km) away. By his own memo, the air blast reached him about 40 seconds after the flash. He dropped small scraps of paper from about six feet up, before, during and after the blast wave passed, and measured how far they were carried: about 2½ meters. From that one observation he wrote that the blast corresponded to roughly ten thousand tons of TNT. Measurements made in 1945 put the yield at about 18.6 kilotons; the long-standing official figure later became about 21 kilotons; and a 2021 reassessment (Selby et al.) found 24.8 ± 2 kilotons.
story.puzzle: How can a few falling scraps of paper and no instruments give the energy of an atomic bomb to within a factor of two or so, and what kind of 'right' is that?
story.payoff: Fermi was not measuring the bomb. He was chaining rough physical factors (how far the air moved, how far away he stood, how a blast's push falls off with distance and scales with energy) to land on the right power of ten. A Fermi estimate aims at the order of magnitude. Coming within a factor of about two to two and a half of a 20-odd-kiloton yield, rather than guessing 200 tons or 2 megatons, is the kind of right that lets you decide things. Part of the shortfall may be physical as well: a nuclear explosion sends much of its energy out as heat and light rather than air blast, which is what the paper scraps responded to (see Katz 2021).
sources: Enrico Fermi, 'My Observations During the Explosion at Trinity on July 16, 1945' (Los Alamos memo, 1945; widely reproduced)
J. I. Katz, 'Fermi at Trinity', arXiv:2103.05784 (2021)
H. D. Selby et al., 'A New Yield Assessment for the Trinity Nuclear Test, 75 Years Later', Nuclear Technology (2021): 24.8 ± 2 kt, versus 18.6 kt (1945) and the long-standing 21 kt

days.application: The car's physical-constraint link. Gasoline holds about 33.7 kWh per gallon (the EPA's MPGe benchmark). At roughly 2.8 kg per gallon that is about 12 kWh per kilogram. A lithium-ion pack stores about 0.15-0.25 kWh per kilogram (pack level, mid-2020s), a gap of roughly 50-80 times by weight. Counting efficiency, the useful-energy gap shrinks to roughly 10-25 times, about 15-20 for typical values. Fueleconomy.gov puts a gasoline car at roughly 12-30% of its fuel energy reaching the wheels and an EV at well over three-quarters of its electrical energy; the routine must confirm the site's current wording for both before quoting them. This is the worked example, with every unit carried.

across.link: Frank Drake's equation, written for a November 1961 meeting at Green Bank, West Virginia, estimates the number of communicating civilizations in the galaxy as a product of factors. It is a Fermi chain. It also shows the method's breaking point: several of its factors are uncertain by many powers of ten, so honest estimates of the product span many orders of magnitude.

days.apply_question: A short-haul airliner burns roughly 5 tonnes of jet fuel, which stores about as much energy per kilogram as gasoline, on a two-hour flight: using today's roughly 60-fold energy-per-kilogram gap between fuel and battery packs, why are city buses and cars electrifying long before such an airliner can?
days.evidence_note: The method is settled. The Trinity yield has more than one published value: about 18.6 kt (1945), about 21 kt (the long-standing official figure) and 24.8 ± 2 kt (Selby et al. 2021 reassessment). Give the range rather than one number. Battery energy density is a moving target, and pack-level figures are lower than cell-level ones, so state the year and level of any figure.

resource.title: Powers of Ten (1977)
resource.creator: Charles and Ray Eames (Eames Office), narrated by Philip Morrison
resource.why: The film starts from a picnic in a park beside Lake Michigan in Chicago. The camera pulls back by a factor of ten at regular intervals out to the scale of galaxies, then dives inward to subatomic scale. It gives the felt sense of powers of ten that prose cannot. days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: In 1965 Gordon Moore Drew a Straight Line Through a Few Dots and Called 65,000. A Decade Later the Chips Were Roughly There.
days.concept: When something grows by a constant percentage per period it compounds. A logarithmic scale turns that compounding into a straight line whose slope is the growth rate, which is the quickest way to read, compare and (cautiously) extrapolate growth.
days.focus: Teaches exponential growth, doubling time (the rule of 70) and the logarithm as the inverse of exponentiation. It then treats the log-scale chart as a reading instrument: equal vertical steps are equal ratios, a straight line means constant percentage growth, and a bend means the rate itself is changing. Ends on the limit: a straight line on a log plot describes the past, not a law of nature.
key_concepts: doubling time and the rule of 70
days.model_or_equation: N(t) = N0 × 2^(t/Td), so log N = log N0 + (t/Td) × log 2, which is a straight line in t on a log scale. Doubling time Td ≈ 70 / (percent growth per period). Moore's case: 64 components × 2^10 ≈ 65,536 after ten annual doublings.

story.title: A few dots on a log scale, extended ten years
story.hook: The 19 April 1965 issue of Electronics carried an article by Gordon Moore, a chemist by training and then director of research and development at Fairchild Semiconductor. He plotted the number of components on the most cost-effective integrated circuits for a handful of years from 1959 to 1965, rising from a single component to about 64. On a logarithmic vertical axis the points fell close to a straight line, doubling about every year. He extended the line a full decade and wrote that by 1975 a chip would hold about 65,000 components. He later called it 'a wild extrapolation.' In 1975 he reported that complexity had kept roughly to the annual doubling, pointing to a 16,384-bit charge-coupled-device memory chip. He then slowed his forecast to a doubling about every two years.
story.puzzle: Why would anyone trust a straight line through a handful of points to forecast a thousand-fold increase, and why did drawing it on a log scale make the forecast look so reasonable?
story.payoff: On a logarithmic axis constant-percentage growth is a straight line. Moore's few points made the pattern visible, and the decade-ahead number became a matter of ten doublings: 64 × 2^10 ≈ 65,000. The log scale made the extrapolation easy to see, and it also hid its fragility. A straight line on a log plot describes the past rate. It held for Moore partly, many historians of technology argue, because the industry planned around it, and the rate itself changed in 1975.
sources: Gordon E. Moore, 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits', Electronics, 19 Apr 1965
Gordon E. Moore, 'Progress in Digital Integrated Electronics', IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting, 1975
Computer History Museum, '1965: Moore's Law Predicts the Future of Integrated Circuits' (Silicon Engine timeline)

days.application: Early COVID-19 case counts in March 2020. In many countries confirmed cases were then growing by roughly 15-30% a day, and the Financial Times' John Burn-Murdoch popularized log-scale charts comparing countries' cases and deaths. Worked example: a daily factor of 1.15 gives a doubling time of ln 2 / ln 1.15 ≈ 5 days, and 1.25 gives ≈ 3.1 days. When the growth rate slows, the line of cumulative cases on a log plot bends flatter while the same curve on a linear plot still curves upward. That is why the turn showed on log charts days before daily new cases peaked.

builds_on.why: A log scale is an axis marked in orders of magnitude, so reading one is Day 1's powers-of-ten bookkeeping made visual.

across.link: OpenAI's 2018 analysis 'AI and Compute' (Dario Amodei and Danny Hernandez) found that the computing used in the largest AI training runs had grown about 300,000-fold since 2012, doubling roughly every 3.4 months against Moore's two years. It reads that growth with the same straight-line-on-a-log-plot method, applied to a much faster process.

days.apply_question: World population grew a little over 2 percent a year at its 1960s peak and under 1 percent a year in the early 2020s: given the doubling time each rate implies, how would that slowdown show on a log-scale chart of world population since 1800?
days.evidence_note: The mathematics is settled. Moore's law is an empirical trend, not a law of nature, and engineers debate whether and when it ended: transistor density and cost per transistor tell different stories, and Dennard scaling broke down in the mid-2000s. Say which measure is meant. Early-COVID doubling times varied by country and between cases and deaths, and changes in testing distorted case curves.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Scaling and power laws: the square-cube law
days.headline_hint: Drop a Mouse Down a Thousand-Yard Mine Shaft and It Walks Away. A Horse Splashes. Size Alone Explains Why.
days.concept: When an object is scaled up by a factor L, its areas grow as L² while its volume and weight grow as L³. Any property that depends on the ratio of the two therefore changes with size, and such power-law relationships appear as straight lines on log-log plots.
days.focus: Teaches the square-cube law (Galileo's insight, made famous by Haldane's essay) and power laws y = a·x^b, read as straight lines with slope b on log-log axes. Uses them to explain falling, strength, heat loss and metabolism. Introduces Kleiber's 3/4 exponent as an empirical power law whose exact value and explanation are debated.
key_concepts: log-log plot (the exponent is the slope)
days.model_or_equation: Area ∝ L² and volume (and weight) ∝ L³. So weight per unit of bone cross-section ∝ L, and surface per unit of volume ∝ 1/L. A power law Y = a·M^b becomes log Y = log a + b·log M, a straight line of slope b. Kleiber: metabolic rate B ∝ M^(3/4), so B/M ∝ M^(−1/4) per kilogram.

story.title: A biologist drops animals down a mine shaft, on paper
story.hook: In March 1926 the British biologist J. B. S. Haldane published 'On Being the Right Size' in Harper's Magazine; it was collected the next year in Possible Worlds. It contains one of the most quoted thought experiments in science writing: 'You can drop a mouse down a thousand-yard mine shaft; and, on arriving at the bottom, it gets a slight shock and walks away, provided that the ground is fairly soft. A rat is killed, a man is broken, a horse splashes.' Nobody dropped any animals; Haldane was reasoning from geometry. The same essay explains why the sixty-foot giants of Pilgrim's Progress would have broken their thighbones at every step, and why an insect, breathing by diffusion through tubes, cannot grow very large.
story.puzzle: Why should the same fall be harmless to a mouse and fatal to a horse when both obey the same law of gravity?
story.payoff: Scale every length by L and weight grows as L³, while the area that air resistance acts on grows only as L². Drag per unit of weight therefore falls as 1/L: the mouse reaches a low terminal speed, while a horse keeps accelerating. The bones and tissues that must absorb the landing have cross-sections that grow as L² while the load grows as L³. Gravity is the same for both animals; what differs is the geometry of size.
sources: J. B. S. Haldane, 'On Being the Right Size', Harper's Magazine, March 1926; reprinted in Possible Worlds and Other Essays (Chatto & Windus, 1927)

days.application: Kleiber's law. Across mammals from mice to elephants, resting metabolic rate rises roughly as body mass to the 3/4 power (Max Kleiber, 1932), a straight line on a log-log plot. Worked example: a million-fold difference in mass (a few grams against a few tonnes) means about a 31,600-fold difference in total metabolic rate. Per kilogram, though, the small animal burns about 32 times faster. That is why tiny shrews must feed almost continuously. It also explains why an elephant, with too little surface for the heat its bulk makes, has sparse hair and sheds heat through its huge ears.

builds_on.why: Day 2's log scale becomes a log-log plot. Taking logs of both axes turns a power law into a straight line, just as one log axis straightened exponential growth.
Scaling arguments are order-of-magnitude reasoning: a factor of 10 in length is a factor of 100 in area and 1,000 in weight.

across.link: Galileo's Two New Sciences (1638) used the square-cube law to argue that ships, buildings and animals cannot simply be enlarged. He drew a giant's bone that must be disproportionately thick. Engineering uses the same reasoning: when shape is kept fixed, the stress from a structure's own weight grows in proportion to its size.

days.apply_question: If a wind-turbine maker lengthens its blades by half while keeping their shape, why does the square-cube law push it toward stiffer, lighter blade materials?
days.evidence_note: The square-cube law is settled geometry. Kleiber's 3/4 exponent is an empirical fit whose exact value and explanation are debated. West, Brown & Enquist (1997) derive 3/4 from branching supply networks. White & Seymour (PNAS 2003) and others find mammalian basal metabolic rate closer to 2/3, and exponents vary across groups and conditions. Teach 'roughly 2/3 to 3/4' and name the debate.

resource.creator: Geoffrey West, TED (TEDGlobal, July 2011)

It puts today's log-log reasoning to work on systems Logan will meet later. It presents one researcher's own theory: the exact exponents and the extension to cities are debated.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: The CO2 Over Mauna Loa Falls Every Summer. Charles Keeling's Curve Is Still Getting Steeper.
days.concept: The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change of a quantity: the slope of its graph at a point. The second derivative, the rate of change of that rate, tells you whether growth is speeding up or slowing down.
days.focus: Teaches the derivative as the limit of average rates over shrinking intervals and separates a quantity, its rate and the rate's own change. Shows how to tell a short-term wiggle from a long-term trend. The Keeling curve, with its seasonal dips and accelerating trend, needs both the first and second derivatives to be read honestly.
days.model_or_equation: f′(t) = lim (h→0) [f(t+h) − f(t)] / h, and f″(t) is the derivative of f′(t). For the Keeling record, comparing each month with the same month a year earlier, [C(t + 1 yr) − C(t)] / 1 yr, removes the seasonal cycle and estimates the trend's rate. If that rate keeps rising, f″ > 0.

story.title: A young chemist's instrument on a Hawaiian volcano
story.hook: In March 1958 Charles David Keeling, a 29-year-old geochemist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, began continuous carbon dioxide measurements at a new observatory high on Mauna Loa in Hawaii, far from cities and forests. The first readings were about 313-316 parts per million (sources differ). Within a couple of years his record showed something odd. CO2 rose through the northern winter, peaked around May, then fell for months as the Northern Hemisphere's plants grew: a swing of several ppm every year. Funding was precarious, and in 1964 budget cuts interrupted the record for a few months. Underneath the sawtooth the line kept climbing: by about 0.9 ppm a year in the 1960s and about 2.4 ppm a year in the 2010s. Scripps reported a record 4.7 ppm jump between March 2023 and March 2024.
story.puzzle: If the reading goes down for months every year, in what sense is CO2 rising, and how could anyone tell from a wiggling line that the rise is speeding up?
story.payoff: The derivative separates the questions. Each northern summer the instantaneous rate is negative, because plants are drawing CO2 down. The trend's rate, measured month against the same month a year earlier, has been positive throughout the record. That rate has itself grown, from under 1 to over 2 ppm a year, so the second derivative is positive. 'Rising' and 'steepening' are two different claims, and each can be measured separately.
sources: Scripps Institution of Oceanography, The Keeling Curve (keelingcurve.ucsd.edu), including its 2024 report of the largest 12-month gain on record
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa CO2 annual mean growth rates
C. D. Keeling, 'The concentration and isotopic abundances of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere', Tellus 12 (1960)
APS News, 'This Month in Physics History' on Keeling's Mauna Loa measurements (2025)

days.application: An airbag fires on the derivative of speed, at the car chain's engineering link. A micromachined accelerometer continuously measures deceleration, the rate of change of velocity. Analog Devices announced the ADXL50, an early mass-produced micromachined accelerometer built for exactly this job, in 1991; such chips replaced bulky mechanical ball-in-tube crash sensors. Typical engineering accounts of a 30 mph barrier crash give the bag about 30 ms to fill, leaving roughly 20 ms for the controller to tell a crash pulse (sustained deceleration) from a pothole (a sharp, brief spike); the routine should quote these as typical figures, not a standard.

builds_on.why: Day 2's growth rate, change per period relative to size, was already a derivative in disguise. Today defines the rate itself, and the rate of that rate.

across.link: The derivative term of a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) controller acts on how fast an error is changing, which damps overshoot before it happens. Nicolas Minorsky's 1922 analysis of automatic ship steering, 'Directional Stability of Automatically Steered Bodies', is the classic early statement of three-term control.

days.apply_question: NASA reports that the yearly rise in global sea level measured by satellites has roughly doubled since 1993: why would a planner of 50-year coastal infrastructure care more about the second derivative of sea level than a homeowner reading this year's tide gauge?
days.evidence_note: The mathematics is settled. That CO2 is rising, and that the rise has accelerated, are direct measurements. That the rise comes mainly from burning fossil fuels is settled science, resting on isotopic and carbon-budget evidence (IPCC AR6). Single-year jumps such as 2023-24 are amplified by El Niño, so judge acceleration on multi-year averages.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: Nobody Could Measure How Fast BP's Well Was Gushing. A Federal Court Still Had to Add Up 87 Days of It.
days.concept: An integral adds up a rate multiplied by tiny slices of time (or space) to get a total. The fundamental theorem of calculus says that accumulating a rate and taking the rate of an accumulation undo each other.
days.focus: Teaches accumulation as the area under a rate curve, approximated by rectangles and trapezoids and made exact as the slices shrink. The fundamental theorem ties it back to Day 4's derivative. The Deepwater Horizon total shows that uncertainty in a total comes from uncertainty in the rate, not from the arithmetic.
days.model_or_equation: Total = ∫ from a to b of r(t) dt ≈ Σ r(t_i) Δt. Fundamental theorem: if A(t) = ∫ from a to t of r(s) ds, then A′(t) = r(t). Spill check: a flow falling roughly steadily from 62,000 to 53,000 barrels a day over 87 days averages about 57,500, so the total ≈ 57,500 × 87 ≈ 5.0 million barrels.

story.title: A leak a mile down, and a number nobody could see
story.hook: On 20 April 2010 the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers. The Macondo well, about a mile below the surface, gushed oil until it was capped on 15 July, 87 days later, and its flow was never metered. The first official estimate, given with BP, was 1,000 barrels a day; on 28 April the Coast Guard and NOAA raised it to 5,000. Independent scientists working from video of the plume put it far higher. On 2 August the government's Flow Rate Technical Group estimated about 62,000 barrels a day at the start, falling to about 53,000 before capping: some 4.9 million barrels in all, ±10%. BP's experts argued for about 2.45 million. Clean Water Act penalties ran up to $4,300 a barrel, so the court needed one number. In January 2015 Judge Carl Barbier found that about 4 million barrels had left the well. After subtracting oil captured at the wellhead (about 0.8 million barrels), he set the discharge at 3.19 million barrels.
story.puzzle: How do you total 87 days of a flow that no one could measure directly, that changed from day to day, and whose daily rate estimates differed by more than a factor of fifty?
story.payoff: The total is the integral of the flow rate over time: the area under the rate curve. Once experts agreed on that curve's shape (falling as reservoir pressure dropped), the arithmetic was easy: 87 days at an average near 57,500 barrels a day gives about 5 million. The dispute was never about integration. Every contested barrel came from the rate, which is why the court's finding landed between the two sides' totals.
sources: US Department of the Interior, 'U.S. Scientific Teams Refine Estimates of Oil Flow from BP's Well Prior to Capping' (2 Aug 2010)
Office of Rep. Edward Markey, press releases on BP's flow-rate estimates (2010)
In re: Oil Spill by the Oil Rig 'Deepwater Horizon', Phase Two findings of fact and conclusions of law (E.D. La., 15 Jan 2015), as reported by AP and others

days.application: An electric car's trip energy is its power draw integrated over time, at the car chain's physical-constraint link. Power swings from tens of kilowatts on a climb to negative values when regenerative braking returns energy, so the battery's kWh used is the signed area under the power curve. A dashboard reading in kW (a rate) and a battery gauge in kWh (an accumulation) are a derivative-and-integral pair, and the EPA label's kWh per 100 miles is that accumulated energy divided by distance. Worked example: 20 minutes at 15 kW, 10 minutes at 40 kW up a pass, and 10 minutes at −10 kW coming down give 5 + 6.67 − 1.67 = 10 kWh.

builds_on.why: The integral is the derivative run backwards. Day 4 took a rate from a total; the fundamental theorem says accumulating that rate rebuilds the total.

across.link: Drug regulators judge a generic medicine by an integral. The FDA's bioequivalence standard compares the area under the blood-concentration-versus-time curve (AUC), and requires the 90% confidence interval for the generic-to-brand ratio to fall within 80-125%.

days.apply_question: During a flood, a US Geological Survey streamgage records a river's flow in cubic feet per second every 15 minutes: if two experts give different totals for the volume of water that passed the gage, which part of the calculation is their disagreement almost certainly about?
days.evidence_note: The mathematics is settled. The Deepwater Horizon totals were contested evidence: the government's 4.9 million barrels (±10%), BP's roughly 2.45 million, and the court's 3.19 million discharged after about 0.8 million captured. The court's figure is a legal finding, not a measurement. Present all three.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: Willard Libby Checked His Atomic Clock Against Timber From a Pharaoh's Tomb. Within a Few Centuries, It Kept Time.
days.concept: A differential equation states how a quantity changes in terms of its current value. For example, dN/dt = −kN says 'the decay rate is proportional to what is left.' Together with a starting value, such a rule fixes the quantity's entire future and past, including a constant half-life.
days.focus: Teaches the differential equation as a rule for change. Solves dN/dt = −kN to get exponential decay, derives the half-life (ln 2 / k) and shows how the same rule run backwards becomes a clock. Names the rule's assumptions, a constant k and a known starting amount, which is why radiocarbon dates need calibration.
days.model_or_equation: dN/dt = −kN gives N(t) = N0·e^(−kt), with half-life t½ = ln 2 / k. Age from a measured fraction: t = (t½ / ln 2) × ln(N0 / N). With t½ = 5,730 years, wood keeping half its original carbon-14 activity is about 5,730 years old, and wood keeping a quarter is about 11,460.

story.title: A chemist's clock, checked against a pharaoh
story.hook: In the late 1940s at the University of Chicago, Willard Libby and his colleagues worked out a new clock. Every living thing takes in a little radioactive carbon-14 from the air, and after death that carbon-14 decays away with a fixed half-life. Libby used about 5,568 years; today's value is 5,730. If that was right, measuring what was left would date the dead, but no one had ever checked such a clock. So Libby and James Arnold gathered wood whose ages were already known: tree-ring-dated timber from the American West, and wood from ancient Egypt supplied by museum collections. One sample was timber from the tomb of the pharaoh Djoser, about 4,650 years old. They measured its faint radioactivity with shielded Geiger counters. Their December 1949 paper in Science reported radiocarbon ages that came out within a few centuries of the known ages, about what the method's precision allowed, and judged the agreement satisfactory. The plot of known age against measured activity became Libby's 'Curve of Knowns.' He received the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
story.puzzle: How can a rule about how fast atoms disappear tell you how long ago something died, and how could Libby trust it before he had checked it?
story.payoff: Carbon-14 decay obeys a differential equation, dN/dt = −kN: the rate of loss is proportional to what remains. Its solution is exponential decay with a fixed half-life, so the fraction left fixes the elapsed time; it is the rule run backwards. The Curve of Knowns tested the two assumptions the clock depended on: a constant decay rate, and a roughly constant starting level of carbon-14 in the air. The first held. The second held only approximately, which is why modern dates are calibrated against tree rings.
sources: J. R. Arnold and W. F. Libby, 'Age Determinations by Radiocarbon Content: Checks with Samples of Known Age', Science 110 (Dec 1949): 678-680
American Chemical Society, National Historic Chemical Landmark 'Discovery of Radiocarbon Dating' (2016)
Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day: Willard Libby' (names the Zoser/Djoser timber)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1960, nobelprize.org

days.application: Drug elimination. Many drugs leave the blood at a rate proportional to the amount present, which is the same equation. A National Academies (Institute of Medicine, 2001) review puts caffeine's half-life in healthy adults at about five hours on average, ranging from about 1.5 to 9.5 hours. Pregnancy and some medicines lengthen it; smoking shortens it. Worked example: 200 mg at 8 a.m. leaves about 100 mg at 1 p.m., 50 mg at 6 p.m. and 25 mg at 11 p.m. With repeated doses, the drug builds toward a steady level reached after about four to five half-lives. That is why dosing intervals are set relative to a drug's half-life.

builds_on.why: Exponential decay is Day 2's exponential growth with a negative rate. The half-life is the doubling time run in reverse, computed with the same logarithm.
A differential equation is a statement about Day 4's derivative: the rate of change, set equal to a rule about the current amount.

across.link: Calibrated radiocarbon dates overturned the chronology of European prehistory. Colin Renfrew's Before Civilization (1973) argued that the corrected dates made Malta's temples older than Egypt's pyramids, and Stonehenge older than the Mycenaean civilization once thought to have inspired it. That undercut the view that civilization simply diffused outward from the Near East.

days.apply_question: After the Chernobyl accident in April 1986, why did health authorities worry about iodine-131 (half-life about 8 days) for weeks but about cesium-137 (half-life about 30 years) for decades, judging by how much of each the decay rule leaves after one year?
days.evidence_note: The physics and mathematics are settled. Radiocarbon dating assumes a constant level of carbon-14 in the atmosphere, which is only approximately true. Since the 1960s dates have been calibrated against tree rings and other records (today the IntCal curves), and 'radiocarbon years' differ from calendar years. The brief should say so rather than present raw dates as exact; it should not claim that each 1949 sample matched exactly.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.headline_hint: In 1920 Two Scientists Fit a Near-Perfect Curve to America and Capped It at 197 Million. The Country Passed 200 Million in 1967.
days.concept: Growth that is limited by a ceiling follows an S-shaped (logistic) curve: nearly exponential at first, fastest at the midpoint, then flattening. The ceiling is an assumption fed into the model, and early data cannot reveal it.
days.focus: Teaches the logistic differential equation dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), its S-shaped solution and the meaning of the midpoint (inflection point). Draws the hard lesson that before the inflection the data cannot pin down K. Pearl and Reed's population forecast is the cautionary story, and technology adoption curves are the working application.
key_concepts: identifiability (why early data cannot fix the ceiling)
days.model_or_equation: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), whose solution is N(t) = K / (1 + e^(−r(t − t0))). Growth is fastest at N = K/2, the inflection point at time t0. Before t0, curves with very different values of K fit the same data almost equally well.

story.title: A near-perfect fit to 120 years of census data
story.hook: In June 1920 two Johns Hopkins scientists, the biologist Raymond Pearl and the statistician Lowell Reed, published a curve in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. It was fitted to every US census from 1790 to 1910. It was the logistic, a curve the Belgian mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst had proposed for populations in 1838, and it fit beautifully. It said American growth had passed its fastest point around 1914 and would level off at a ceiling of about 197 million people. Pearl went on to fit the same curve to fruit flies in bottles and to yeast, convinced he had found a law of population growth. In November 1967 the Census Bureau's population clock passed 200 million. The 2020 census counted about 331 million.
story.puzzle: If the curve fit 120 years of data so well, how could its ceiling be off by more than 100 million people?
story.payoff: Before a logistic curve reaches its midpoint, the ceiling K is almost unconstrained. In 1920 the US data had barely reached it, and curves with very different ceilings fit the past nearly equally well. Pearl and Reed's 197 million was an extrapolation of an assumed form, not a measurement. Immigration, fertility, medicine and agriculture then moved the real ceiling. The S-shape is real for bounded processes, but the level where it flattens is a model input.
sources: R. Pearl and L. J. Reed, 'On the Rate of Growth of the Population of the United States since 1790 and Its Mathematical Representation', PNAS 6 (1920): 275-288
US Census Bureau: the 200-million milestone (November 1967) and 2020 Census results
P.-F. Verhulst, 'Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son accroissement' (1838)

days.application: Technology diffusion. The share of US households with electricity, cars, telephones, computers and smartphones traces S-curves. Diego Comin and Bart Hobijn's cross-country dataset ('An Exploration of Technology Diffusion', American Economic Review, 2010) shows adoption lags differing by decades between countries. To read where a technology sits on its S, look at the annual gain: it peaks at the midpoint, so a gain that is still rising means you are below it. A ceiling for 'share of households' is capped at 100%, but a ceiling for 'units per person' is not. This is how to read the adoption link of the car chain.

builds_on.why: The logistic is a differential equation like Day 6's decay rule, with a braking term (1 − N/K) that slows growth as the ceiling nears.
Its early phase is Day 2's exponential growth. That is why an S-curve looks exponential until it doesn't, and why a log plot shows the bend first.

across.link: Kermack and McKendrick's 1927 epidemic model gives an S-shaped cumulative case curve that stops before everyone is infected. Its ceiling, the final epidemic size, is set by transmissibility and immunity rather than by population size alone. The ceiling is an output of the mechanism, not a fixed cap.

days.apply_question: Why can you trust the ceiling of the S-curve traced by yeast in a sealed flask of sugar water, which levels off as the sugar runs out and alcohol builds up, far more than Pearl and Reed's ceiling for the United States?
days.evidence_note: Settled: bounded growth processes trace S-curves, and fitting a logistic before the inflection point leaves the ceiling poorly determined. Whether a given technology or market is near saturation is an empirical judgment that often goes wrong. Pearl's claim to have found a general 'law of population growth' was not accepted by later demographers.

resource.title: Growth: From Microorganisms to Megacities, Chapter 1 ('Trajectories: or Common Patterns of Growth')
resource.creator: Vaclav Smil (MIT Press, 2019)
resource.length: the chapter's part on bounded, S-shaped growth (logistic and related curves), about 30 minutes
resource.why: Smil, the energy scientist the later Energy block draws on, opens by surveying the common shapes of growth (linear, exponential and bounded, including the logistic) across organisms, machines and societies. It gives many more real S-curves than one lesson can.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Optimization: why the best point is flat
days.headline_hint: In 1739 a Calculation Said the Bees Had Their Angles Wrong by Two Minutes of Arc. The Calculation Was Wrong, and It Hardly Mattered.
days.concept: At the best point of a smooth trade-off the derivative is zero, so the curve is flat there. Small errors in the choice cost almost nothing, because the loss grows only as the square of the error, while constraints can move the best point itself.
days.focus: Teaches optimization with calculus: set the derivative to zero, check the second derivative, and use the flatness of a smooth optimum to judge how much precision matters. The honeybee cell shows a flat optimum. The 1974 55-mph limit shows a regulation imposed near, though not exactly at, a technical optimum, and why the gain was modest.
key_concepts: flatness: quadratic loss near the optimum
days.model_or_equation: At an optimum x*, f′(x*) = 0, so f(x* + δ) ≈ f(x*) + ½ f″(x*) δ². The penalty for missing by δ grows as δ², not δ. For the bee's cell, the wax-minimizing rhombus angle is arccos(−1/3) ≈ 109°28′16″. Missing it by 2′ changes the cell's wax by less than one part in a million.

story.title: The bees, the academician and two minutes of arc
story.hook: In 1712 Giacomo Filippo Maraldi, an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, studied the three rhombus-shaped faces that close the bottom of a honeybee's cell and reported their angles as about 109°28′ and 70°32′. Decades later René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur, who suspected the bees were saving wax, asked the young mathematician Samuel König which angles would enclose a cell with the least wax. König's answer, around 1739, was 109°26′ and 70°34′, so the bees seemed to be off by two minutes of arc. In 1743 the Scottish mathematician Colin Maclaurin showed geometrically that the bees' angles were the true optimum and that the calculation had erred. Later tradition blames a misprinted logarithm table, but that is not established. Then, in 1964, the Hungarian mathematician László Fejes Tóth found a cell bottom of two hexagons and two small rhombi that uses less wax than the bees' design, saving less than 0.35% of the area of the cell's opening.
story.puzzle: If the bees were 'wrong' by two minutes of arc in 1739 and a mathematician beat their design in 1964, how much wax were they actually wasting, and why does the answer hardly depend on getting the angle exactly right?
story.payoff: At the wax-minimizing angle the derivative of the wax cost is zero, so the cost curve is flat. A two-minute error changes the wax by less than one part in a million, because the loss grows with the square of the error. König's discrepancy mattered as mathematics, not as beekeeping. Fejes Tóth's better design is a different shape, not a better angle, and even it saves only a fraction of a percent. Near a smooth optimum there is little left to gain.
sources: L. Fejes Tóth, 'What the bees know and what they do not know', Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 70 (1964): 468-481
C. Maclaurin, 'Of the bases of the cells wherein the bees deposit their honey', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 42 (1743)
G. F. Maraldi, 'Observations sur les abeilles', Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences (1712)

days.application: The 1974 national 55-mph speed limit, imposed after the Arab oil embargo by the Emergency Highway Energy Conservation Act (signed 2 January 1974), at the regulation link of the car chain. A car's fuel economy is a smooth curve in speed. DOE/Oak Ridge National Laboratory tests find it peaking at moderate speeds, and fueleconomy.gov notes that mileage usually falls off rapidly above about 50 mph. Because the peak is flat, nudging cars that were already near it gains little; the savings came from slowing the high-speed driving far out on the falling side of the curve. The Transportation Research Board's 1984 review, '55: A Decade of Experience' (Special Report 204), judged the fuel saving modest; the routine must confirm TRB's exact estimates before quoting a number.

builds_on.why: An optimum is where Day 4's derivative is zero. The second derivative says whether it is a minimum or a maximum and how sharply the cost rises away from it.
The bee's problem is Day 3's surface-versus-volume trade-off: enclose the most honey with the least wax.

across.link: Murray's law (Cecil D. Murray, PNAS, 1926) treats a blood vessel's radius as an optimum. A wider vessel cuts the power needed to push blood through it, which falls as the fourth power of the radius, but holds more blood that the body must maintain, which rises as the square. Setting the derivative of the total cost to zero predicts that flow is proportional to radius cubed, so at a branch the parent's radius cubed equals the sum of its daughters'. Measured vessels follow it roughly rather than exactly (T. F. Sherman, Journal of General Physiology, 1981).

days.apply_question: Airlines set a 'cost index' in their flight-management computers that trades fuel cost against time-related costs such as crew and maintenance, and the computer uses it to choose cruise speed: if fuel prices jump 20 percent, why does the flat-optimum idea suggest an airline loses little by updating its index a few weeks late?
days.evidence_note: The mathematics is settled. How bees build is debated: Karihaloo and colleagues (2013) argue that the hexagons form partly as warm wax flows, while Bauer and Bienefeld (2013) argue the bees shape them actively. 'Bees optimize' is therefore shorthand, not a finding about intent. Whether Maraldi measured his angles to the minute or partly derived them is unclear, so the brief should say he 'reported' them. The 55-mph limit's fuel and safety effects were estimated rather than measured directly and remain contested; Day 21 (natural experiments) uses the 1995 repeal.

resource.title: Infinite Powers: How Calculus Reveals the Secrets of the Universe, Chapter 4 ('The Dawn of Differential Calculus')
resource.creator: Steven Strogatz (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2019)
resource.why: A leading applied mathematician tells how Fermat found maxima and minima by noticing that a curve goes flat at its peak, and how the same idea gave the law of refraction. It supplies the history and intuition behind setting a derivative to zero.
