resource.title: Natural experiments help answer important questions (Popular science background, Prize in Economic Sciences 2021)
resource.creator: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences / NobelPrize.org
resource.why: The Nobel committee's plain-language account of how natural experiments and difference-in-differences identify causes, using the New Jersey minimum-wage study and others. It is authoritative and free, and it shows the method beyond epidemiology.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the 2021 Nobel materials. The exact title could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know VIII: Replication and publication bias
days.headline_hint: Amgen Tried to Reproduce 53 Landmark Cancer Findings. Six Held Up.
days.concept: When journals and researchers favour striking, significant results and studies are small, the published record overstates effects: some findings are flukes and most are inflated. A finding therefore counts only once it survives replication, ideally preregistered, and a whole literature must be checked for missing studies.
days.focus: Teach publication bias (the file drawer), low statistical power and the winner's curse, flexible analysis (p-hacking), and the defences: replication, preregistration and registered reports, and funnel plots in meta-analysis. The angle: Amgen's 6 of 53 and the later Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, and then the lead-crime literature shrinking under a meta-analysis.
days.model_or_equation: Positive predictive value of a significant finding (Ioannidis, 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False', PLoS Medicine 2005): PPV = (1 − β)R / [(1 − β)R + α], where R is the prior odds that a tested hypothesis is true, 1 − β is the power and α is the significance threshold. With R = 1:10, power 0.2 and α = 0.05: PPV = 0.02 / (0.02 + 0.05) ≈ 0.29. Most 'significant' findings would be false even before any bias.

story.title: 53 landmark papers in an Amgen lab
story.hook: In March 2012 C. Glenn Begley, who had spent a decade running cancer research at the biotech company Amgen, and Lee Ellis of the MD Anderson Cancer Center reported in Nature what happened when Amgen's scientists tried to reproduce 53 'landmark' preclinical cancer studies, papers from respected labs and top journals of the kind on which drug programmes are built. The findings held up in 6. Begley told Reuters about one case: his team had repeated an experiment 50 times without getting the published result, and the lead author said his lab had got it once in six tries but published it because it made the best story. A year earlier, scientists at Bayer had reported that their in-house work fully matched the published data in only about a fifth to a quarter of 67 projects.
story.puzzle: Every one of those papers passed peer review with statistically significant results. If p < 0.05 means a fluke only one time in twenty, how could almost nine in ten fail to hold up?
story.payoff: p < 0.05 is a threshold for each test, not a guarantee about what gets published. Positive results get written up and accepted, while negative ones go into the file drawer. Small experiments that clear the bar do so partly by luck, so their effects are inflated (the winner's curse); flexible analyses let researchers find significance somewhere; and novel drug targets start with low prior odds. Together these can make a literature of significant results mostly unreliable, which is why replication, not a single paper, is the unit of evidence. In fairness to the critics, Amgen could not name the papers, so its own result could not be checked. The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (eLife, 2021), which did publish its targets, found that replication effects were on average about 85% smaller than the originals.
sources: Begley & Ellis, 'Raise standards for preclinical cancer research', Nature 483:531-533, 2012
Prinz, Schlange & Asadullah, 'Believe it or not: how much can we rely on published data on potential drug targets?', Nature Reviews Drug Discovery 10:712, 2011
Errington et al., Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, eLife, 2021
Sharon Begley, 'In cancer science, many discoveries don't hold up', Reuters, 28 March 2012

days.application: The lead-crime hypothesis under meta-analysis. Higney, Hanley & Moro ('The lead-crime hypothesis: A meta-analysis', Regional Science and Urban Economics, 2022) pooled 529 estimates from 24 studies. They found evidence of publication bias across several tests of the kind a funnel plot illustrates, and once they corrected for it the average effect was far smaller than the headline claims; on their reading, lead's decline explains at most a minority of the fall in US crime. It shows meta-analysis at work on a public debate that returns in Day 49's case on leaded gasoline.

builds_on.why: Publication bias is Day 17's p < 0.05 used as a gate. If only results that cross the threshold are published, the threshold no longer means what it says.
Ioannidis's argument is Bayes. The chance that a significant finding is true depends on the prior odds of the hypothesis as well as on the test, exactly Day 15's base rates.

across.link: The Open Science Collaboration's 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science' (Science, 2015) repeated 100 studies from three leading 2008 journals. 97% of the originals had significant results, but only about 36% of the replications did, and the replicated effects averaged about half the original size. Psychology's replication crisis follows the same mechanism as Amgen's.

days.apply_question: Ego depletion, the idea that exerting self-control uses up a limited resource, was supported by roughly 200 published experimental tests, and a 2010 meta-analysis found a medium-to-large effect. Yet a preregistered replication in 23 laboratories with more than 2,000 participants (Hagger et al., 2016) found an effect near zero. How can both results have been reported honestly?
days.evidence_note: Settled: publication bias and low power inflate published effects, and this is documented across many fields. Debated: how bad the problem is in a given field, since replication rates vary by field and by how 'success' is defined. For lead and crime, the true size of the effect is debated: Higney, Hanley & Moro (2022) found publication bias and a much smaller average effect, while other researchers maintain that lead contributed meaningfully to the crime decline.

resource.title: Is Most Published Research Wrong?
resource.creator: Veritasium (Derek Muller), 2016
resource.why: Shows with real cases how significance thresholds, p-hacking and the file drawer let false findings into print, and how preregistration and replication push back. It makes the mechanism easy to remember.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge (Veritasium, 2016). It could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted; WebFetch cannot reach reference sites here), so it is cited without a link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: How We Know IX: Goodhart's law
days.headline_hint: Volkswagen's Diesels Passed Every Official Test. On the Road They Emitted Up to 40 Times the Limit.
days.concept: When a measure becomes a target, people optimize the number rather than the thing it was meant to indicate, so the measure drifts away from the reality it once tracked and can even move against it (Goodhart's law; Campbell's law).
days.focus: Teach why an indicator works only while no one is optimizing against it. A proxy captures only part of a goal, and pressure finds the gap through gaming, distortion or outright fraud. The defences are to measure outcomes directly and unpredictably, use several measures, and keep judgment in the loop. The angle: Volkswagen's defeat device as the extreme case, the legal gap between EU laboratory and road fuel figures, and NHS waiting-time targets that both cut waits and were gamed.
days.model_or_equation: Let the measure M equal the goal G plus a gap: M = G + gap. Before M is a target, the gap is small noise, so M tracks G. Once M is rewarded, effort flows to whichever of G or the gap is cheaper to move, and the gap is usually cheaper. Goodhart (1975): 'Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.' The popular wording, 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure', is Marilyn Strathern's (1997).

story.title: On the road, not on the rollers
story.hook: In 2013 a small team from West Virginia University's Center for Alternative Fuels, Engines and Emissions, hired by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), which expected the tests to show that US diesel cars ran clean, fitted portable emissions analysers to a Volkswagen Jetta, a VW Passat and a BMW X5 and drove them on US roads, mostly in California. The BMW largely met the limits, but the Jetta emitted nitrogen oxides at roughly 15 to 35 times the US standard and the Passat at roughly 5 to 20 times (report published May 2014). Volkswagen attributed the gap to technical problems for more than a year. On 18 September 2015 the US Environmental Protection Agency issued a notice of violation: about 482,000 VW and Audi 2.0-litre diesels from model years 2009-2015 carried software that recognized the official laboratory test and switched on full emissions controls only then, and on the road emitted up to 40 times the limit. Days later Volkswagen admitted that about 11 million cars worldwide carried the software, and its chief executive resigned.
story.puzzle: These cars passed every official test. How could a car be clean exactly when it was measured and many times dirtier the rest of the time? And why had the test, which was meant to stand for road driving, become so easy to tell apart from it?
story.payoff: The test had become the target. The official cycle is a fixed, published speed trace driven on rollers with the steering wheel still, so a car's software can recognize it. Once passing it was what counted, engineering effort flowed into passing it rather than into clean driving. Volkswagen's software was fraud, the extreme case, but the same pressure also produced legal gaming: the ICCT found that the gap between official and real-world fuel use of new EU cars grew from under 10% around 2001 to about 40% by the mid-2010s. That is Goodhart's law. Europe's answer was a real-driving emissions test, run on the road with portable analysers.
sources: US EPA, Notice of Violation to Volkswagen AG, Audi AG and Volkswagen Group of America, 18 September 2015
Thompson et al. (West Virginia University CAFEE), In-Use Emissions Testing of Light-Duty Diesel Vehicles in the United States, final report to the ICCT, May 2014
ICCT, From Laboratory to Road (2017 update)
Goodhart, 'Problems of Monetary Management: The U.K. Experience' (1975); Campbell, 'Assessing the impact of planned social change', Evaluation and Program Planning 2:67-90, 1979

days.application: English NHS targets of the 2000s: 75% of life-threatening ambulance calls reached within 8 minutes, A&E patients admitted, transferred or discharged within 4 hours, and GP appointments within 48 hours. They cut reported waits, and they were gamed. Bevan & Hood ('What's measured is what matters: targets and gaming in the English public health care system', Public Administration, 2006) documented response times bunched just under 8 minutes, patients held in ambulances outside A&E so the clock had not started, and GP practices refusing to book more than 48 hours ahead (a voter confronted Tony Blair with this on BBC Question Time in April 2005). Yet comparing England with Scotland, which lacked such targets, Propper et al. (Journal of Public Economics, 2010) found that the waiting-time targets did shorten long waits. The measure was both gamed and partly real.

builds_on.why: Goodhart's law is Day 8's optimization aimed at the wrong objective. An optimizer goes wherever the measured quantity is best, and if that quantity is a proxy, the optimum slides to where proxy and goal part ways.
Making p < 0.05 a publication target is Goodhart's law in science. Once significance was the prize, p-hacking optimized the number rather than the truth it was meant to signal.

across.link: Specification gaming in reinforcement learning, catalogued by DeepMind researchers (Victoria Krakovna and colleagues, 'Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity', DeepMind blog, April 2020). In one of their examples, from Popov et al. (2017), a simulated robot arm rewarded for the height of the bottom face of a red Lego block learned to flip the block over instead of stacking it on the blue one. The optimizer exploited the gap between the measured proxy (the face's height) and the goal (a stacked block), which is Goodhart's law with a machine as the gamer.

days.apply_question: In 1902 the French colonial government of Hanoi, fighting rats in the city's new sewers, paid a bounty for every rat tail handed in, and officials soon noticed tailless rats alive in the streets. What could the bounty have paid for instead that would have been harder to game?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Volkswagen facts, which the company admitted (it pleaded guilty in US federal court in 2017). Debated: the net effect of targets. Bevan & Hood (2006) documented gaming of English NHS targets, while Propper et al. (2010), comparing England with Scotland, found that the targets did cut waiting times, and both findings can be true. Value judgment: how much gaming is an acceptable price for a measure that also drives real improvement.

resource.title: The Tyranny of Metrics (chapter 1, 'The Argument in a Nutshell', and the chapter on medicine)
resource.creator: Jerry Z. Muller (Princeton University Press, 2018)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the two chapters
resource.why: A historian's short, case-rich argument about how measurement turned into target-chasing in medicine, schools, policing and business. It is useful for Logan's book as a sceptical counterweight to 'what gets measured gets managed'.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the book (2018). The chapter titles could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted). It is a book, so there is no link.

days.phase: Mathematics: The Language of Change, and How We Know
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 1: Car I, the car by the numbers (spiral visit)
days.headline_hint: Bertha Benz Bought Fuel at a Pharmacy and Drove 106 Kilometres. How Did Her Husband's Noisy Toy Take Over the World?
days.concept: The car's rise can be read in numbers: an energy-density advantage, a price falling exponentially, adoption tracing an S-curve, and harms best judged as rates with confounders in view. But the numbers form a loop, not a line. Rules came before the car, the invention came before the need, and the car's consequences rewrote its rules.
days.focus: Walk the car through Logan's chain using only the mathematics just taught: energy density, log-scale prices, S-curve adoption, flat optima, natural experiments, Goodhart's law, rates and confounding, and the SUV game. Go deep on those links, preview the rest, and show the chain as a loop: Britain's road-speed law came about twenty years before Benz's car, the invention came before any need, and deaths fed back into law.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, reinforcing (adoption): more cars lead to more filling stations, paved roads and dealers, which make cars more useful, which leads to more cars (from one pharmacy in Wiesloch to a fuel network). R2, reinforcing (price): more output brings lower unit cost and price, which brings more buyers (the Model T; the mechanism is taught in Engineering). B1, balancing (saturation): as households acquire cars, the pool of new buyers shrinks, which is the S-curve's ceiling. B2, balancing (harm): more driving brings more deaths, which bring safety law and engineering and a lower death rate per mile, after a delay of decades (1920s death rates; the 1966 federal safety act). Reversals: regulation before invention (Britain's 1865 Locomotive Act) and invention before need (Benz's 1886 patent). Unintended consequences: the 55-mph limit saved little fuel because the optimum was flat, though it probably saved lives, and regulation by fixed test cycle invited gaming (Volkswagen).

story.title: Bertha Benz drives to her mother's, August 1888
story.hook: Early one morning in August 1888 (tradition gives the 5th), Bertha Benz, 39, left the house in Mannheim with her teenage sons Eugen and Richard and drove her husband Karl's three-wheeled Patent-Motorwagen toward her mother's home in Pforzheim, about 106 km away, without telling him. On the way she bought ligroin, a petroleum solvent, from the town pharmacy in Wiesloch, and had a shoemaker nail leather onto the wooden brake blocks. Family tradition adds that she cleared a blocked fuel line with her hatpin and insulated a bare wire with a garter. She arrived after dark and sent Karl a telegram. Some forty years later the United States alone had about 23 million registered cars.
story.puzzle: Why did a smoky, unreliable machine that needed a pharmacy for fuel and a cobbler for brakes become the machine of the century? And how much of that can numbers alone explain?
story.payoff: The numbers explain part of it. Hydrocarbon fuel packs roughly fifty times a battery's energy per kilogram; Ford's prices fell exponentially; adoption climbed an S-curve; and the harms, read as rates with confounding in mind, fell per mile even as totals rose. The numbers cannot explain why people wanted cars, how the engine was made to work, or how credit and streets were reorganized around them, and later blocks teach those. And the chain did not run in order: Britain had capped road locomotives at walking pace about twenty years before Bertha's drive.
sources: Karl Benz, German patent DRP 37435 (filed 29 January 1886)
Mercedes-Benz Classic archive and the Bertha Benz Memorial Route (Mannheim-Pforzheim)
US Federal Highway Administration, Highway Statistics Summary to 1995 (motor vehicle registrations)
World Health Organization, Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023

days.application: The car, followed link by link from Bertha Benz's 1888 drive to the roughly 1.19 million road deaths a year today. This is Car I of four visits; Car II (Day 103), Car III (Day 216) and Car IV (Day 293) go deep on the links previewed here.

builds_on.why: Physical constraint: Day 1's order-of-magnitude comparison of gasoline (about 12 kWh/kg) and lithium-ion packs (about 0.15-0.25 kWh/kg) explains why liquid fuel won the first century.
Production: the Model T's price falls as a roughly straight line on Day 2's log scale, a near-constant percentage decline each year.
Adoption: US registrations from 8,000 in 1900 to about 23 million in 1929 trace Day 7's S-curve, and the Depression's stall shows that the ceiling is an assumption.
Regulation: the 1995 repeal of the 55-mph limit is Day 21's natural experiment, the best evidence on what the limit did for safety.

across.link: Bertha Benz's fuel was ligroin, a light petroleum fraction sold as a cleaning solvent at Wiesloch's town pharmacy, which the town now promotes as 'the world's first filling station'. The energy-density advantage at the physical-constraint link is chemistry, the energy released when carbon-hydrogen bonds burn, which the Energy, Chemistry & Materials block takes up in Day 70, Combustion and energy density.

days.apply_question: Pew Research Center found that about 35% of US adults owned a smartphone in 2011, and about nine in ten by the mid-2020s. Read as an S-curve, as this case read car registrations, what does that predict about US smartphone ownership over the next decade?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the energy-density gap, the Model T's price fall, US registration growth, the fall in US deaths per mile, and WHO's estimate of about 1.19 million road deaths in 2021 (a modelled global estimate, not a count). Debated: how much of the falling death rate any single cause explains (road design, vehicle engineering, medicine, seat-belt and drink-driving laws all changed together); how large the effect of speed-limit changes was (Friedman et al. 2009 against earlier sceptics); and how far heavier vehicles raise net deaths (White 2004). Value judgment: who gained (mobility, livelihoods, freedom of movement), who paid (more than half of road deaths are pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists, and over 90% occur in low- and middle-income countries, per WHO), and who consented (bystanders and children did not choose the risk). A utilitarian ledger sums lives, time and welfare, while the Christian and natural-law traditions stress duties of care to the vulnerable neighbour. The world without the car is an unknowable counterfactual.

chain.point: In 1888 the car met no pressing need that horses, trams and railways did not, and early buyers wanted novelty and status; by family accounts, Bertha's drive was partly meant to show that the car was practical. Here the invention came before the need. Psychology (Day 159, Motivation and human needs) and Sociology (Car III, Day 216) teach how mobility became a want and then a necessity.

Karl Benz's German patent DRP 37435, filed 29 January 1886, was for a vehicle powered by a gas engine; Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach were working in parallel at Cannstatt. History II (Day 224, The invention of invention) and Engineering (Day 91, The internal combustion engine) teach how such inventions arise and how the engine works.

Gasoline stores about 12 kWh per kilogram (33.7 kWh per gallon in the EPA's MPGe convention), while a lithium-ion pack stores about 0.15-0.25 kWh/kg: roughly fifty times less per kilogram, or about fifteen to twenty times less once engine and motor efficiencies are counted. Liquid hydrocarbon fuel is why an 1888 car could carry its range in a small reservoir, and why batteries took a century to compete.

Bertha's repairs on the road, among them leather brake linings nailed on by a shoemaker and, by tradition, a fuel line cleared with a hatpin, were field engineering; after her report Karl added a lower gear for climbing hills. The Engineering block (Days 87-103, with Car II on Day 103) teaches design trade-offs, the engine and mass production.

The Model T touring car cost $850 at its 1908 launch; by 1925 a touring car listed at about $290 and a runabout at about $260. That is a fall of roughly three times in nominal dollars, about 6-7% a year and roughly a straight line on a log scale, and steeper after inflation; more than 15 million were built by 1927. Why the price fell (the moving assembly line, learning curves) is left to Engineering (Days 96-97). Financing is named only at CFA level: by family accounts Bertha's dowry had backed Karl's workshop, and mass ownership rode on instalment credit after GM founded GMAC in 1919, with most new cars bought on credit by the mid-1920s on most estimates. Car II (Day 103) returns to this.

Regulation came first. Britain's Locomotive Act of 1865 capped road locomotives at 4 mph in the country and 2 mph in towns, with a man walking ahead carrying a red flag, about twenty years before Benz's car; the 1896 Act raised the limit to 14 mph, which was celebrated by the London-to-Brighton 'Emancipation Run'. A century later the 1974 national 55-mph limit sat near a flat fuel-economy optimum, so it could save little fuel (Day 8). Its 1995 repeal became a natural experiment in road deaths (Day 21). And Volkswagen's defeat device showed regulation by test cycle failing under Goodhart's law (Day 23).

US automobile registrations rose from about 8,000 in 1900 to about 23 million in 1929 (FHWA), the steep middle of an S-curve. The Depression then flattened them for several years, a reminder that the curve's ceiling is an assumption, not a law (Day 7).

WHO's Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023 estimates about 1.19 million road deaths in 2021, more than half of them pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists and over 90% in low- and middle-income countries. In the US, deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles fell from about 24 in 1921 to about 1.3 in the early 2020s. That is a rate, and it must be read with confounding in mind, because roads, cars, medicine and drinking norms all changed together (Day 18). Meanwhile heavier vehicles protect their own occupants at others' expense, a prisoner's-dilemma-like arms race (Day 14).

Consequences fed back into rules and designs. Rising deaths and Ralph Nader's Unsafe at Any Speed (1965) were followed by the 1966 National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act. The 1973 oil shock produced the 55-mph limit and, in 1975, fuel-economy standards whose looser light-truck rules are often blamed, contestably, for the later SUV boom. Government (Day 243, How regulation works), Law (Day 254, Tort and product liability) and Engineering (Day 101, Crashworthiness) teach these loops.

resource.title: Numbers Don't Lie: 71 Stories to Help Us Understand the Modern World (the transport essays)
resource.creator: Vaclav Smil (2020)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the transport section's short essays
resource.why: Smil's short essays lead with the numbers, several of them on cars, engines and transport, and they model exactly this case's method of reading a technology through energy, prices, adoption and risk as orders of magnitude and rates. Smil returns in the Energy block.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge that the book exists (2020) and has a section of transport essays. Their titles could not be re-checked by web search (shared search budget exhausted). It is a book, so there is no link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Cape Town Set a Date for Its Taps to Run Dry. Then the Date Kept Moving.
days.concept: A stock changes only through its flows, so it keeps rising or falling until inflow equals outflow, and a steady inflow alone does not hold it steady.
days.focus: Teaches stocks and flows as the basic grammar of systems, using the integral (Day 5) as a modelling language. The angle is a well-documented failure of intuition: even highly trained people expect a stock to stop rising as soon as its inflow stops rising.
days.model_or_equation: S(t) = S(0) + integral from 0 to t of [inflow - outflow] dt; equivalently dS/dt = inflow - outflow. The stock is constant only when inflow = outflow. If net outflow is steady, time to empty = S / (outflow - inflow).

story.title: A city counts down to Day Zero
story.hook: In January 2018, after three dry winters, Cape Town told its four million residents the date its taps would be shut off: 12 April, the day its supply dams were projected to fall to 13.5% of capacity. Households were limited to 50 litres per person per day from February. On 30 January, with the dams at 26.3%, Day Zero was moved to 16 April because daily use had dropped from about 580 to about 540 million litres. On 20 February it jumped to 9 July as use fell to about 523 million litres a day, against roughly 1,130 million in 2014. By late June 2018, with storage above 43%, the city said Day Zero would not come in 2019 either.
story.puzzle: How could officials name the day a city would run dry months in advance, and why did a modest change in daily use move that date by weeks at a time?
story.payoff: The dams are a stock and Day Zero was simply stock divided by net outflow. Because rainfall inflow was near zero in summer, every cut in outflow lengthened the time to empty disproportionately, and winter inflow then refilled the stock. The date moved because the flows moved.
sources: TimesLIVE, 'Day Zero for Cape Town pushed back a few days', 30 Jan 2018
News24, 'Day Zero: Cape Town buys one more month', 20 Feb 2018
BusinessTech, 'Cape Town scraps day zero as dam levels rise', 2018

days.application: Atmospheric CO2 as a bathtub: emissions are the inflow and land and ocean sinks the outflow (roughly half of emissions are currently absorbed), so the concentration keeps rising while emissions exceed removal even if emissions stay flat. In Sterman and Booth Sweeney's experiments (Climatic Change 80, 2007), about 84% of some 200 MIT graduate students, mostly with STEM or economics degrees, drew trajectories that violated accumulation, and nearly two-thirds said concentrations could stabilize while emissions still exceeded removal.

builds_on.why: A stock is the integral of its net flow; the fundamental theorem is the bathtub stated in calculus.
Net flow is the stock's derivative, so the sign of the net flow, not its trend, decides whether the stock rises or falls.

across.link: The clean-surplus relation (ending equity = beginning equity + net income - dividends) ties the balance sheet's stocks to the income statement's flows; it is the same bathtub identity.

days.apply_question: The 1922 Colorado River Compact divided 7.5 million acre-feet a year each to the Upper and Lower Basins, based on river flows measured in an unusually wet early-twentieth-century period, and Mexico was later promised 1.5 million more; this century the river has averaged closer to 12-13 million. Using stock-and-flow reasoning, explain why Lake Mead fell to roughly a quarter full by 2022 even in years when the river ran at an ordinary flow.
days.evidence_note: Settled: stock-flow accounting is mass balance. Cape Town avoided Day Zero through a mix of household cuts, cuts to agricultural allocations and the return of winter rain; how much each mattered is debated locally. The Sterman results are robust across replications of the bathtub task, though exact percentages vary by sample.

resource.title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer, Chapter 1 'The Basics'
resource.creator: Donella H. Meadows (ed. Diana Wright), Chelsea Green, 2008
resource.why: The standard primer on stocks, flows and dynamic equilibrium, with the bathtub diagrams this whole block uses; it is the block's main text.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out after two searches); cited from knowledge of the book. Cite without a link; the routine should confirm the chapter title if it can.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Two Cities, One Flu: Philadelphia Held a Parade, St. Louis Closed Its Doors, and the Death Rates Split Eightfold.
days.concept: A reinforcing loop amplifies whatever change it gets and a balancing loop pushes back toward a limit or goal, and most system behaviour comes from how the two interact.
days.focus: Teaches loop polarity: how to trace a closed chain of cause and effect and tell whether it amplifies or counteracts. The 1918 epidemic shows a reinforcing contagion loop meeting balancing loops (susceptibles running out, and deliberate closures), and the Matthew effect shows a reinforcing loop inside science itself.
days.model_or_equation: Causal-loop diagram with link polarities. A loop is reinforcing if it has an even number of negative (opposite-direction) links and balancing if it has an odd number. Epidemic: R loop infected -> contacts -> new infections -> infected; B loop infected -> susceptibles depleted -> fewer new infections; B loop deaths -> closures -> fewer contacts.

story.title: A parade for 200,000 in a city already infected
story.hook: On 28 September 1918 Philadelphia went ahead with a Liberty Loan parade that drew about 200,000 people to Broad Street, although influenza had already reached the Navy Yard. Within days the city's hospitals were overwhelmed. St. Louis, hit at about the same time, closed schools, theatres, churches and other gatherings on 7 October, soon after its first civilian cases. When Richard Hatchett, Carter Mecher and Marc Lipsitch reconstructed the weekly death data (PNAS, 2007), Philadelphia's peak excess death rate was about 257 per 100,000 a week, St. Louis's about 31.
story.puzzle: The same virus, in two large American cities, at the same moment: why did one city's peak climb about eight times higher than the other's?
story.payoff: Each infection fed more infections, a reinforcing loop that the parade fed with contacts. St. Louis switched on a balancing loop early by cutting contacts while case numbers were small; Philadelphia's epidemic ran until the slower balancing loop, running out of susceptible people, took over at a far higher peak.
sources: Hatchett, Mecher & Lipsitch, 'Public health interventions and epidemic intensity during the 1918 influenza pandemic', PNAS 104(18), 2007
Markel et al., 'Nonpharmaceutical interventions implemented by US cities during the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic', JAMA 298(6), 2007

days.application: Robert K. Merton's 'The Matthew Effect in Science' (Science 159, 1968), built partly on Harriet Zuckerman's interviews with Nobel laureates: credit and citations flow disproportionately to already eminent scientists, which brings them more resources and visibility and so more credit, a reinforcing loop in how science allocates recognition. Margaret Rossiter's 'Matilda effect' (1993) names the companion pattern in which women's contributions were credited to men.

builds_on.why: A reinforcing loop with a constant gain is exponential growth; the doubling arithmetic of Day 2 is what the loop produces.
The logistic S-curve is a reinforcing loop handing dominance to a balancing loop as the ceiling nears; today names the loops behind that shape.

across.link: The Kessler syndrome (Kessler and Cour-Palais, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1978): debris collisions create fragments that cause more collisions, a reinforcing loop in low Earth orbit with no natural balancing loop except slow atmospheric drag.

days.apply_question: On 9 March 2023 depositors tried to pull about $42 billion from Silicon Valley Bank in a single day, and regulators closed it the next morning. Draw the reinforcing loop that drove the run and name the balancing loop that, had it been in place in time, could have broken it.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the loop mechanics and the 1918 mortality differences. Debated: how much 1918 interventions reduced total deaths rather than flattening and delaying the peak; Hatchett et al. and Markel et al. find real benefits, while Barro (NBER 2020) found the short-lived measures did little to cut overall deaths. The Matthew effect in citations is well replicated; its size and how much it reflects merit as well as visibility are debated.

resource.title: Public health interventions and epidemic intensity during the 1918 influenza pandemic
resource.creator: Richard J. Hatchett, Carter E. Mecher & Marc Lipsitch, PNAS 104(18), 2007
resource.why: The source of the story's numbers, with the Philadelphia and St. Louis curves side by side: you can see a reinforcing loop cut early and one left to run.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the paper. PNAS papers of this age are free to read; cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: GE's Customers Bought Steadily. Its Kentucky Plants Hired and Fired in Waves Anyway.
days.concept: A balancing loop with a delay overshoots and oscillates, because people act on old information and forget what is already in the pipeline.
days.focus: Teaches why delays turn a goal-seeking balancing loop into a cycle, and why the cycle is usually generated inside the system by its own decision rules rather than by outside shocks. The Beer Game and the bullwhip effect show it in supply chains.
days.model_or_equation: Stock-adjustment ordering rule: orders = expected demand + (desired inventory - actual inventory)/adjustment time - (a correction for orders already in transit). Sterman (1989) found players largely ignore the supply-line term, and dropping it is what turns a delayed balancing loop into overshoot and oscillation.

story.title: A factory that made its own boom and bust
story.hook: In the mid-1950s managers at General Electric's household-appliance plants in Louisville, Kentucky, asked Jay Forrester, a computer pioneer who had just moved to MIT's management school, why their plants swung every few years between overtime and layoffs. They assumed the business cycle was to blame. Forrester sat down with the plants' own rules for hiring, ordering and inventory and simulated them by hand on a notepad. Retail demand in his simulation was almost flat, yet employment rose and fell in waves. He later called this the beginning of system dynamics.
story.puzzle: If customers were buying at a steady rate, where did the waves of hiring and layoffs come from?
story.payoff: The oscillation came from inside the company: the plants corrected inventory gaps using information that was weeks old and ignored orders already in the pipeline, so each correction overshot and the next correction overshot the other way. The cycle was produced by the decision rules, not by the market.
sources: Jay W. Forrester, 'The Beginning of System Dynamics', banquet talk 1989, reprinted in McKinsey Quarterly 1995
Jay W. Forrester, Industrial Dynamics (MIT Press, 1961)

days.application: The 2020-21 automotive chip shortage: when the pandemic struck in spring 2020, carmakers cancelled semiconductor orders and chipmakers sold the capacity to electronics firms; when car demand rebounded within months, the lead time for new chip supply was many months, and the industry lost an estimated 7-11 million vehicles of output in 2021 (estimates differ by forecaster). It is a classic bullwhip: small swings in final demand amplified upstream (Lee, Padmanabhan & Whang, Sloan Management Review 1997), compounded by real supply shocks such as the March 2021 fire at Renesas's Naka plant.

builds_on.why: Today adds a delay to the balancing loop of Day 26; the delay is what converts goal-seeking into oscillation.
Inventory is a stock and orders in transit are a second, hidden stock; ignoring that supply-line stock is the decision error behind the waves.

across.link: James Clerk Maxwell's 1868 paper 'On Governors' explained why some steam-engine governors 'hunted' (oscillated): the same mathematics of a delayed corrective loop that produces the Beer Game's swings.

days.apply_question: German economist Arthur Hanau documented a regular 'pig cycle' in German hog prices in the late 1920s: farmers expand breeding when prices are high, but a decision to breed takes close to a year to become pork on the market. Explain, using a delayed balancing loop, why that arrangement produces repeated price booms and slumps even with steady demand for pork.
days.evidence_note: Settled: delayed balancing loops oscillate (control theory), and the Beer Game result replicates widely (Sterman, Management Science 35(3), 1989). Debated: how much of the 2021 chip shortage was bullwhip amplification versus genuine supply shocks (the Texas freeze of February 2021, the Renesas fire, pandemic demand for electronics).

resource.title: The Fifth Discipline, Chapter 3 'Prisoners of the System, or Prisoners of Our Own Thinking?'
resource.creator: Peter M. Senge, Doubleday, 1990 (revised 2006)
resource.why: Walks through a full play of MIT's Beer Game, round by round, so you see from the inside how sensible players produce a boom and bust nobody wants.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the book. Cite without a link; the routine should confirm the chapter title if it can.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Jamaica's Reefs Flipped From Coral to Seaweed in a Decade. Getting Them Back Has Taken Far Longer.
days.concept: Some systems have two stable states separated by a threshold, so a push past it flips the system and undoing the push does not flip it back (hysteresis).
days.focus: Teaches alternative stable states: how reinforcing loops can lock in either of two conditions, why change can be sudden after long stability, and why the road back differs from the road in. It also teaches the limits: proving that a real system has two stable states is hard.
days.model_or_equation: Granovetter's threshold model: each person joins if at least r others have joined; with F(r) the share of people whose threshold is r or less, the crowd settles where the share joining equals F(that share). Shifting one person's threshold can move the system from one equilibrium to another.

story.title: The urchins that vanished from the Caribbean
story.hook: In 1983 a pathogen swept through the Caribbean and killed most of the long-spined sea urchin Diadema antillarum, often more than 95% at a site, within about a year. On Jamaica's north coast, where decades of overfishing had already removed most plant-eating fish, the urchins had been the last major grazers. Terry Hughes's long-term surveys (Science, 1994) recorded what followed: coral cover that had been around half the reef in the 1970s fell to a few percent, while fleshy seaweed rose from a few percent to cover most of the reef. Hurricane Allen in 1980 had already broken much of the coral.
story.puzzle: Reefs had survived hurricanes and disease before. Why did this combination flip Jamaica's reefs into seaweed, and why didn't the coral simply grow back once the storm damage passed?
story.payoff: With fish and then urchins gone, seaweed escaped grazing and occupied the bare rock coral larvae need, so each year of algae made coral recovery less likely: a reinforcing loop holding a second stable state. Recovery needed more than removing the original shock; where urchins later returned, coral recruits began to reappear, but only partly and slowly.
sources: Terence P. Hughes, 'Catastrophes, phase shifts, and large-scale degradation of a Caribbean coral reef', Science 265, 1994
Lessios, Robertson & Cubit, 'Spread of Diadema mass mortality through the Caribbean', Science 226, 1984
Edmunds & Carpenter, PNAS 98, 2001 (partial Diadema recovery on Jamaican reefs)

days.application: Mark Granovetter's 'Threshold Models of Collective Behavior' (American Journal of Sociology 83, 1978): imagine 100 people with riot thresholds 0, 1, 2, ... 99. The person with threshold 0 starts, which triggers the person with threshold 1, and so on until all 100 riot. Change the single person with threshold 1 to threshold 2 and only one person riots. Two nearly identical crowds, two different outcomes: the aggregate tells you little about average temperament.

builds_on.why: Alternative stable states exist because reinforcing loops can hold a system in either condition; today is what Day 26's loops do when they compete.
Granovetter's result depends on the whole distribution of thresholds, not its average, the point Day 12 made about distributions.

across.link: Lenton et al., 'Tipping elements in the Earth's climate system' (PNAS, 2008), lists components such as the Greenland ice sheet that may have thresholds and hysteresis: once largely melted, it would not regrow at today's temperatures.

days.apply_question: On 3 September 1967 Sweden switched from driving on the left to driving on the right in a single morning by law (Dagen H). Using the idea of two stable states, explain why the change had to be made all at once rather than by letting drivers switch sides gradually as they chose.
days.evidence_note: Settled: threshold dynamics and hysteresis are well established in models and some systems (shallow lakes, Scheffer et al., Nature 2001). Debated: how common true alternative stable states are on coral reefs, with Mumby, Hastings & Edwards (Nature 2007) supporting them for Caribbean reefs and Bruno et al. (Ecology 2009) finding coral-to-macroalgae shifts less widespread than claimed. Granovetter's model is a thought experiment, not an estimate of real thresholds.

resource.title: Catastrophic shifts in ecosystems
resource.creator: Marten Scheffer, Steve Carpenter, Jonathan A. Foley, Carl Folke & Brian Walker, Nature 413, 2001
resource.why: The standard short review of alternative stable states, with the ball-in-a-landscape and hysteresis diagrams and real cases from lakes, reefs and deserts.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the paper. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: Unintended consequences and fixes that fail
days.headline_hint: After 1910 the Forest Service Swore to Stop Every Fire by 10 a.m. A Century Later, the Fires Came Back Bigger.
days.concept: Purposive action produces consequences nobody intended, and a quick fix that relieves a symptom can, after a delay, strengthen the problem it treats.
days.focus: Teaches Merton's account of why consequences go unanticipated (ignorance, error, immediate interest, values) and the systems archetypes 'fixes that fail' and 'shifting the burden', in which a balancing fix carries a delayed reinforcing side effect. The angle is to respect the limits: hindsight makes every consequence look foreseeable.
days.model_or_equation: 'Fixes that fail' archetype (Senge 1990): a balancing loop (problem -> fix -> problem relieved) plus a delayed reinforcing loop (fix -> unintended side effect -> problem worse). Fire: fires -> suppression -> fewer fires now; suppression -> fuel accumulates (delay of decades) -> larger, hotter fires.

story.title: The two days that made fire the enemy
story.hook: On 20 and 21 August 1910, hurricane-force winds drove dozens of fires together across the northern Rockies of Idaho and Montana. The 'Big Burn' scorched roughly three million acres in about two days, killed about 85 people, most of them firefighters, and burned a third of the town of Wallace, Idaho. Ranger Ed Pulaski forced some 45 men into an abandoned mine tunnel at gunpoint and held them there as the fire passed; all but a handful survived. The young US Forest Service drew a lesson: put out every fire. In 1935 it formalized the '10 a.m. policy', every fire controlled by ten the next morning.
story.puzzle: The policy worked for decades: burned area fell sharply. Why, by the 2000s, were many western forests burning in fires larger and hotter than anything the old foresters had fought?
story.payoff: Suppression was a balancing fix with a delayed side effect: in dry forests adapted to frequent low-intensity fire, each extinguished fire left fuel that once would have burned off, so the stock of fuel grew for decades and the fires that did escape were more severe. How much of today's megafires this explains varies by forest type and competes with warming and expanding settlement.
sources: Timothy Egan, The Big Burn (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2009)
Stephen J. Pyne, Fire in America (Princeton UP, 1982)
US Forest Service history of the 1935 '10 a.m. policy'

days.application: The car's regulation link: the 1975 Energy Policy and Conservation Act set fuel-economy (CAFE) standards in which light trucks faced a looser standard than cars (cars rose to 27.5 mpg by 1985). Over the following decades light trucks, including SUVs, rose from about a fifth of new US passenger-vehicle sales to around half by the early 2000s (EPA Automotive Trends Report). Critics such as Keith Bradsher (High and Mighty, 2002) argue the rule helped create the market it exempted; others weight cheap fuel after 1986, the 1964 'chicken tax' on imported light trucks and changing tastes.

builds_on.why: The fire story is a delay at work: the side effect of suppression accumulated for decades before it showed, so the fix looked successful for a long time.
CAFE targets invited optimization of the measured category, a Goodhart response in which vehicles shifted toward the class the rule treated more leniently.

across.link: In his 1945 Nobel lecture Alexander Fleming warned that underdosing penicillin would breed resistant bacteria: antibiotic overuse is a 'fix that fails', relieving infection now while selecting for resistance later.

days.apply_question: In 1935 Queensland's sugar industry released cane toads imported from Hawaii to eat the beetles damaging sugarcane; the toads did little to the beetles and spread across northern Australia. Using Merton's sources of unanticipated consequences, explain which ones were most likely at work in that decision.
days.evidence_note: Settled: fire suppression increased fuel loads and fire severity in historically frequent-fire forests such as southwestern ponderosa pine. Debated: its share in megafires elsewhere, where fire was naturally rare (high-elevation forests, chaparral), against climate warming and the wildland-urban interface; and how much the light-truck rule caused the SUV boom. Value judgment: whether a policy is wrong because of consequences its makers could not reasonably foresee.

resource.title: The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action
resource.creator: Robert K. Merton, American Sociological Review 1(6), 1936
resource.why: The founding short paper on why consequences go unanticipated, with Merton's own list of causes, so you can test each fix in this lesson against it.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the article. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: The commons: Hardin, Ostrom and shared resources
days.headline_hint: Every Thursday at Noon, Eight Farmers Settle Valencia's Water Fights in Minutes. No Lawyers, No Appeal.
days.concept: An open-access resource tends to be over-used because each user gains the full benefit of taking and bears only part of the cost, but communities often govern shared resources well when the rules fit Elinor Ostrom's design principles.
days.focus: Teaches the commons as a structure (a shared stock with individually rational over-use) and then challenges Hardin's either-the-state-or-private-property conclusion with Ostrom's evidence of long-enduring self-governed commons. The angle is the difference between open access and a governed commons.
days.model_or_equation: Ostrom's eight design principles (Governing the Commons, 1990): (1) clear boundaries of users and resource; (2) rules fitted to local conditions; (3) users help make the rules; (4) monitors accountable to users; (5) graduated sanctions; (6) cheap, quick conflict resolution; (7) outside authorities recognize the right to organize; (8) nested layers for larger systems.

story.title: A court that sits outside a cathedral door
story.hook: Every Thursday at noon, outside the Door of the Apostles of Valencia Cathedral, eight farmers in black smocks sit in a semicircle of chairs. They are the elected síndics of eight irrigation canals that share the water of the river Turia across the huerta, the farmland around the city. A bailiff calls the cases: a farmer who took water out of turn, a neglected ditch. Hearings are spoken, in Valencian, and decided on the spot; there is no appeal. Tradition places the Water Tribunal's origins in the Moorish period, about a thousand years ago; documents from the Christian era after 1238 confirm the irrigation customs it enforces. UNESCO inscribed it as intangible cultural heritage in 2009.
story.puzzle: Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay predicted that a resource shared by self-interested users would be ruined unless the state or private owners took control. How has a farmers' court with no lawyers kept a scarce, shared river from being over-drawn for centuries?
story.payoff: The huerta is not open access. Its users are bounded, they make and enforce their own rules, they watch one another, sanctions are graduated and disputes are settled cheaply and fast, which are Ostrom's design principles. She studied these Spanish huertas in Governing the Commons (1990, ch. 3) as evidence against Hardin's fatalism.
sources: UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, 'Irrigators' tribunals of the Spanish Mediterranean coast', 2009
Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (Cambridge UP, 1990), ch. 3
Garrett Hardin, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', Science 162, 1968

days.application: The Ogallala aquifer in western Kansas: groundwater is a stock recharged far more slowly than it is pumped. In 2013 farmers in Sheridan County created the state's first Local Enhanced Management Area (Sheridan 6 LEMA), voting to cap their own pumping for five years with a target cut of about 20%. Kansas State University evaluations report that water use fell by roughly a quarter to a third while farm profits held up close to those of neighbouring areas, a commons governed by its users with state backing.

builds_on.why: The commons is an n-person prisoner's dilemma: each user's dominant move (take more) produces a collectively worse outcome, and Ostrom's rules work like the repetition and enforcement Day 14 showed can change play.
An aquifer or river is a stock; over-use means outflow persistently exceeding recharge, the bathtub of Day 25.

across.link: Harold Demsetz's 'Toward a Theory of Property Rights' (American Economic Review, 1967) argued that private hunting territories emerged among the Montagnais of Quebec once the fur trade made beaver valuable: property rights arising to manage a commons.

days.apply_question: Maine lobstermen have long defended informal fishing territories through 'harbor gangs' that cut the trap lines of outsiders (James Acheson, The Lobster Gangs of Maine, 1988). Which of Ostrom's design principles does that arrangement satisfy, and which does it lack?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Ostrom's large comparative evidence that many commons are self-governed for long periods (Nobel Memorial Prize 2009, the first to a woman). Debated: how well the design principles predict success in large, global commons such as climate. Value judgment: Hardin's 1968 essay also argued for coercive limits on childbearing, a position many critics, including Christian and secular ethicists, reject.

resource.title: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action, Chapter 3
resource.creator: Elinor Ostrom, Cambridge University Press, 1990
resource.why: Ostrom's own case studies of long-enduring commons, including the Valencia and Murcia huertas and Swiss and Japanese mountain commons, from which she drew the design principles.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the book. Cite without a link; the routine should confirm the chapter's case list if it can.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Brunel's Railway Ran Faster and Smoother. In May 1892, Thousands of Men Tore It Up in a Weekend.
days.concept: When the value of a choice rises with the number of others making it (increasing returns), small early events can lock a whole system onto one path, whether or not it is the best one.
days.focus: Teaches path dependence as a reinforcing loop of adoption, with network effects and switching costs creating lock-in. The angle is the contested part: how often lock-in actually traps us in an inferior technology, with QWERTY as the famous disputed case.
days.model_or_equation: Arthur's adoption model (Economic Journal, 1989), like a Polya urn: each new adopter picks technology A with a probability that rises with A's current share. Early random draws decide which technology takes over, and once one dominates the outcome is effectively locked in.

story.title: The last broad-gauge train out of Paddington
story.hook: Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western Railway in the 1830s on a gauge of seven feet and a quarter inch, chosen for speed and stability; most other British lines used George Stephenson's 4 feet 8 1/2 inches, inherited from colliery wagonways. In trials for the 1845 Gauge Commission, broad-gauge trains ran faster. But standard-gauge track already ran several times as far, and the 1846 Gauge Act required new lines to use it. On Friday 20 May 1892 the last broad-gauge train left Paddington; over that weekend thousands of platelayers (accounts say about 4,000) converted the remaining main line through Devon and Cornwall, and standard-gauge trains ran on the Monday.
story.puzzle: If Brunel's gauge was faster and smoother, why was it the one that had to be torn up?
story.payoff: A gauge is worth what it connects to. Every mile of Stephenson gauge made the next line more valuable on that gauge, a reinforcing loop of adoption; the GWR's broad gauge was an island whose break-of-gauge transfers cost more than its speed gained. An early, almost accidental choice locked Britain in, whether or not it was the best gauge.
sources: Report of the Gauge Commissioners (UK Parliament, 1846)
Gauge Act 1846 (9 & 10 Vict. c. 57)
Great Western Railway histories of the 1892 gauge conversion, e.g. E. T. MacDermot, History of the Great Western Railway (1927)

days.application: QWERTY, the keyboard you type on: Christopher Latham Sholes's layout, sold to Remington in the 1870s. Paul David's 'Clio and the Economics of QWERTY' (American Economic Review, 1985) argued that touch-typing on QWERTY, popularized after a famous 1888 Cincinnati typing contest, locked in an inferior design despite August Dvorak's supposedly faster layout. Stan Liebowitz and Stephen Margolis's 'The Fable of the Keys' (Journal of Law & Economics, 1990) replied that the evidence for Dvorak's superiority came largely from Dvorak's own studies and that a 1956 US government test by Earle Strong found no clear advantage. Lock-in is real; whether it trapped us in something worse here is disputed. Contrast the US South, which re-gauged roughly 11,500-13,000 miles of track over 31 May-1 June 1886 (sources differ) to join the northern network.

builds_on.why: Increasing returns are a reinforcing loop in adoption: more users make the option more valuable, which attracts more users.
Network effects follow from network structure: the value of a connection standard grows with the nodes it links, which is Day 13's mathematics applied to choosing a standard.

across.link: United States v. Microsoft (D.C. Circuit, 2001) upheld the finding that an 'applications barrier to entry', the thousands of programs written for Windows, protected Microsoft's monopoly: network-effect lock-in recognized in antitrust law.

days.apply_question: Japan's electricity grid runs at 50 Hz in the east and 60 Hz in the west, because in the 1890s Tokyo bought German generators and Osaka bought American ones; after the March 2011 earthquake, converter capacity of only about one gigawatt limited how much power the west could send east. Using path dependence, explain why Japan has still not unified its frequency.
days.evidence_note: Settled: network effects and switching costs exist, and some standards persist for these reasons. Debated: how often lock-in leaves society with a clearly inferior technology; Arthur and David say it can and does, Liebowitz and Margolis argue documented cases of inefficient lock-in are rare, QWERTY included. Whether the broad gauge was superior overall, once costs are counted, is itself debated among railway historians.

resource.title: Positive Feedbacks in the Economy
resource.creator: W. Brian Arthur, Scientific American 262(2), February 1990
resource.why: The increasing-returns argument for lock-in written for general readers by its main theorist; read it as one side, with Liebowitz and Margolis as the reply named in the lesson.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the article. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Twenty-Two Cars, One Circle, No Bottleneck, and a Traffic Jam Anyway.
days.concept: Simple local rules followed by many individuals can produce large-scale patterns that none of them chose, so you cannot read individual motives or causes straight off an aggregate outcome.
days.focus: Teaches emergence: macro patterns generated bottom-up by interacting agents, and agent-based models as the tool for studying it. The angle is a double warning: aggregate patterns may have no author, and a model that can generate a pattern does not prove that is how the real pattern arose.
days.model_or_equation: Schelling's rule: each agent on a grid is content if at least a set share (for example one-third) of its neighbours are like itself, and otherwise moves to a random empty cell. Repeating the rule produces near-complete clustering from mild preferences.

story.title: A traffic jam with no cause
story.hook: In a 2008 paper in the New Journal of Physics, a team of Japanese physicists led by Yuki Sugiyama reported a simple experiment. They put 22 cars on a circular track 230 metres around, with no junctions, no lane changes and no merging, and asked the drivers to cruise steadily at about 30 kilometres an hour. At first the cars flowed evenly. Within minutes small fluctuations grew: one car braked slightly, the one behind braked a little harder, and a stop-and-go wave formed and travelled backward around the circle against the direction of traffic.
story.puzzle: Nobody crashed, nobody merged and no driver wanted a jam. Where did it come from, and whose fault was it?
story.payoff: The jam was emergent: each driver followed a sensible local rule, keep a safe distance and react to the car ahead, with a slight reaction delay, and above a critical density those rules amplify small fluctuations into a moving jam. No individual caused it, so blaming a driver misreads it.
sources: Sugiyama et al., 'Traffic jams without bottlenecks: experimental evidence for the physical mechanism of the formation of a jam', New Journal of Physics 10, 033001 (2008)

days.application: Thomas Schelling's 'Dynamic Models of Segregation' (Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 1971; Micromotives and Macrobehavior, 1978): working with coins on a checkerboard, he showed that people who would be happy as a minority in a mixed neighbourhood, wanting only that a modest share of neighbours be like them, can still produce near-total segregation. The model shows mild preferences are sufficient to segregate, not that real American segregation came from them; historians document laws and policies such as redlining and racial covenants (Richard Rothstein, The Color of Law, 2017).

builds_on.why: Each driver's reaction delay is a delayed balancing loop at the scale of two cars; emergence is what many such small delayed loops do together.
Day 18 showed aggregate patterns can mislead about individual-level relationships; emergence is a second reason you cannot infer motives from aggregates.

across.link: Émile Durkheim's Suicide (1897) found national suicide rates stable year to year although each death was an individual act, his evidence for 'social facts' that exist at the level of the group.

days.apply_question: On 6 May 2010 the Dow Jones index fell nearly 1,000 points within minutes and then mostly recovered; the joint SEC-CFTC report traced it to one large automated sell order interacting with high-frequency traders. Using the idea of emergence, explain why 'who decided to crash the market?' may be the wrong question to ask.
days.evidence_note: Settled: phantom jams emerge without bottlenecks (Sugiyama et al.), and Schelling's model reliably generates segregation from mild preferences. Debated: how much residential preferences, as opposed to law, lending policy and income, explain real segregation; the model shows possibility, not historical cause.

resource.title: Parable of the Polygons
resource.creator: Vi Hart & Nicky Case, 2014
resource.why: A free interactive version of Schelling's model: you drag the agents yourself and watch mild preferences produce segregation, then try rules that reverse it.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the piece. Cite without a link; a later run may add the creator-hosted URL only if a search shows it.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.headline_hint: Donella Meadows Walked to a Flip Chart and Ranked Every Way to Change a System. The Numbers Came Last.
days.concept: Interventions in a system differ enormously in power: changing parameters such as taxes or quotas is usually weak, while changing feedback structure, information flows, rules, goals and the paradigm behind them is strong but harder and more resisted.
days.focus: Teaches Meadows's hierarchy of leverage points as a practical way to ask where a change will actually move a system. The angle includes its limits: the list is an experienced modeller's heuristic, not a tested law, and high-leverage changes can push a system the wrong way just as hard.
days.model_or_equation: Meadows's twelve leverage points, weakest to strongest: (12) constants and parameters; (11) buffer sizes; (10) stock-and-flow structure; (9) delays; (8) balancing loops; (7) reinforcing loops; (6) information flows; (5) rules; (4) power to self-organize; (3) goals; (2) paradigms; (1) the power to transcend paradigms.

story.title: A list written on a flip chart
story.hook: Donella Meadows, lead author of The Limits to Growth and a Dartmouth professor who wrote a weekly newspaper column, told in her 1999 essay 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System' how the list began. Sitting in a meeting about the new global trade regime of NAFTA, GATT and the World Trade Organization, she grew frustrated as the discussion fixed on details. She got up, went to the flip chart and wrote out a list of places to intervene in a system, from weakest to strongest. Her experience as a modeller, she wrote, was that people almost always push the levers in the wrong direction and put most of their effort into the weakest ones.
story.puzzle: Why would the measures people fight over hardest, the tax rates, quotas and budget numbers, so often be the ones that change a system least?
story.payoff: Parameters adjust flows inside an unchanged structure, so the system's loops absorb the change. Rules, information flows and goals rewire the loops themselves; that is why Meadows ranked them higher, and why they are fought over less often but resisted harder.
sources: Donella H. Meadows, 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System' (Sustainability Institute, 1999); an earlier version appeared in Whole Earth, 1997
Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems (2008), ch. 6

days.application: The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments (Title IV) set a national cap on power-plant sulfur dioxide, about half of 1980 emissions, and let utilities trade allowances: a change in the rules and in who had the information and incentive to find cuts, rather than a uniform technology mandate. Emissions fell ahead of schedule and compliance costs came in far below early projections (Schmalensee & Stavins, Journal of Economic Perspectives 27(1), 2013), helped also by cheap low-sulfur Powder River Basin coal after rail deregulation. Later court rulings and new rules effectively collapsed the allowance market after about 2010.

builds_on.why: Several of Meadows's strongest levers act on feedback loops themselves, adding, strengthening or removing the reinforcing and balancing loops of Day 26.
Goals are high on Meadows's list, and Goodhart's law shows why: change what a system is told to maximize and its behaviour changes, sometimes perversely.

across.link: Meadows ranked paradigms as the second-strongest leverage point, drawing on Thomas Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), whose account of paradigm shifts in science is taught in Philosophy I.

days.apply_question: Singapore began charging drivers to enter its central business district in 1975 and moved to electronic road pricing in 1998, with charges that vary by time and place. Where on Meadows's list does that intervention sit, and what would have counted as a weaker or a stronger lever for the same traffic problem?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the SO2 programme cut emissions at lower cost than projected. Debated: how much credit belongs to trading itself versus cheap low-sulfur coal; and Meadows's ranking, which is an expert heuristic that has not been tested systematically, so treat its order as a guide rather than a finding.

resource.title: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
resource.creator: Donella H. Meadows, Sustainability Institute, 1999
resource.why: The essay itself, in Meadows's own voice, including the flip-chart story and her warnings that leverage points are counterintuitive and the list is tentative.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the essay, which the Donella Meadows Project distributes free. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: How systems models fail: the Limits to Growth debate
days.headline_hint: Paul Ehrlich Mailed Julian Simon a Cheque for $576.07. It Settled the Bet, Not the Argument.
days.concept: A model is a structured set of assumptions, so its scenarios are conditional 'if-then' statements rather than forecasts, and a model that leaves out adaptation, prices or feedback can be confidently wrong, or right for the wrong reasons.
days.focus: Teaches how to judge a systems model: what is a scenario versus a forecast, how structure and omitted loops drive results, and why a single outcome cannot settle a model dispute. The Limits to Growth debate, the Simon-Ehrlich wager and the dispute over RCP8.5 give three angles; neither the 'doom was wrong' nor the 'Limits was right' victory lap survives the evidence.
key_concepts: all models are wrong, some are useful
days.model_or_equation: World3 (Meadows et al., 1972) linked five sectors, population, industrial capital, food, non-renewable resources and pollution, through reinforcing growth loops and delayed balancing loops; with fixed assumptions its 'standard run' overshoots and declines in the 21st century. The structure, not the computer, produces the result.

story.title: A cheque in the mail, October 1990
story.hook: In 1980 the economist Julian Simon challenged the biologist Paul Ehrlich, author of The Population Bomb, to bet on scarcity. Ehrlich and two colleagues chose $1,000 worth of five metals, chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten, and bet their inflation-adjusted prices would rise between 29 September 1980 and 29 September 1990. During that decade the world added more people than in any decade before. All five prices fell. In October 1990 Ehrlich mailed Simon a sheet of price calculations and a cheque for $576.07.
story.puzzle: Simon won the bet. Did that prove that warnings of resource limits, such as The Limits to Growth of 1972, were wrong?
story.payoff: No single outcome tests a model. Kiel, Matheson and Golembiewski (Ecological Economics, 2010) found Ehrlich would have won in roughly three of five ten-year windows over 1900-2008, and Graham Turner (2008) found data to 2000 tracking Limits' standard run fairly closely, though that run's decisive turns lay later. The bet showed price feedback, substitution and recession at work, which Ehrlich's view underweighted; it did not show limits never bind. Both sides' victory laps outrun the evidence.
sources: Paul Sabin, The Bet (Yale UP, 2013)
Kiel, Matheson & Golembiewski, 'Luck or skill? An examination of the Ehrlich-Simon bet', Ecological Economics 69(7), 2010
Graham Turner, 'A comparison of The Limits to Growth with 30 years of reality', Global Environmental Change 18, 2008

days.application: The dispute over the IPCC's highest-emissions pathway, RCP8.5: it was designed as a high-end scenario but often described as 'business as usual'. Zeke Hausfather and Glen Peters (Nature, 2020) argued that with cheaper renewables and slower coal growth it is now unlikely and misleading as a baseline; Christopher Schwalm and colleagues (PNAS, 2020) replied that it tracks cumulative CO2 emissions to date well. The argument is about which assumptions belong in a scenario, the central issue of this lesson.

builds_on.why: Pearl and Reed's 1920 logistic put a ceiling on US population that was an assumption, not a law; World3's limits and overshoot are the same lesson about structure deciding the curve.
One bet is one draw; Kiel et al. estimate the probability Ehrlich wins across many windows, the difference Day 11 drew between an outcome and an expected value.

across.link: Karl Popper's falsification criterion (The Logic of Scientific Discovery, 1934/1959): a scenario stated as 'if these assumptions hold' is hard to falsify by events, because a miss can always be blamed on the assumptions, a problem taught in Philosophy I.

days.apply_question: On 16 March 2020 Imperial College's Report 9 estimated about 510,000 deaths in Great Britain if COVID-19 were left completely unmitigated; actual UK deaths in the first year were far lower, after a lockdown began a week later. Was Report 9 a failed forecast? Explain using the difference between a scenario and a forecast.
days.evidence_note: Settled: Simon won the 1980-90 bet, and all five metals fell in real price. Debated: how well Limits' standard run has tracked data (Turner 2008 and later updates versus critics such as Nordhaus, who in 1973 attacked Forrester's World Dynamics as 'measurement without data'); and the plausibility of RCP8.5 (Hausfather and Peters versus Schwalm et al.). Value judgment: how much weight to give low-probability, high-cost scenarios in policy.

resource.title: The Bet: Paul Ehrlich, Julian Simon, and Our Gamble over Earth's Future
resource.creator: Paul Sabin, Yale University Press, 2013
resource.length: the chapters on the 1980 wager, about 40 pages
resource.why: A historian's even-handed account of the wager and how it hardened into a political divide, showing both men's blind spots rather than crowning either.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from knowledge of the book. Cite without a link; the routine should name the specific chapter if it can confirm it.

days.phase: Systems Thinking: Stocks, Loops and Their Limits
days.subject: Systems Thinking
days.topic: Innovation as a system, not a pipeline
days.headline_hint: Bayer Sold Aspirin for Seventy-Two Years Before Anyone Knew How It Worked.
days.concept: Innovation is not a pipeline running from science to invention to production to use; it runs through coupled feedback loops in which practice often leads science, users and markets reshape inventions, and demand is built as much as found.
days.focus: Teaches Kline and Rosenberg's chain-linked model against the 'linear model' of innovation, and uses it to challenge Logan's own need-to-feedback chain directly: the chain is a useful checklist of domains, not a sequence of causes. The angle is balanced: science-led inventions are real too.
key_concepts: feedback between research, design and market
days.model_or_equation: Kline and Rosenberg's chain-linked model (1986): a central chain (market need -> invent or design -> detailed design and test -> redesign and produce -> distribute and market) with feedback loops from every stage back to earlier ones and from the market to design, plus links to existing knowledge and to research, which is consulted when knowledge runs out rather than being the starting point.

story.title: A drug sold by the ton, explained in 1971
story.hook: For centuries people chewed willow bark for fever and pain; in 1763 the Reverend Edward Stone reported its effect on agues to the Royal Society. At Bayer's laboratory in Elberfeld, Germany, the chemist Felix Hoffmann recorded a pure, stable synthesis of acetylsalicylic acid in August 1897. Bayer registered the name Aspirin in 1899 and sold it worldwide, as powder and then tablets. In 1949 Hoffmann's former superior Arthur Eichengrün, a Jewish chemist written out of the story under the Nazis, claimed he had directed the work. For more than seventy years, nobody could say how aspirin worked. In 1971 the British pharmacologist John Vane showed in Nature that it blocks the body's production of prostaglandins, work that shared the 1982 Nobel Prize.
story.puzzle: If science comes first and products follow, how could one of the best-selling drugs in history be invented, mass-produced and sold for seven decades before science understood it?
story.payoff: Innovation does not have to wait for theory: practice, chemistry, manufacturing and market feedback ran ahead, and science arrived later to explain, then improve, what practice had found. Vane's explanation fed back in turn, toward low-dose aspirin for heart attacks and new anti-inflammatory drugs: the chain-linked model, loops running in both directions.
sources: Edward Stone, letter to the Royal Society, Philosophical Transactions 53 (1763)
Walter Sneader, 'The discovery of aspirin: a reappraisal', BMJ 321, 2000
John R. Vane, 'Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis as a mechanism of action for aspirin-like drugs', Nature New Biology 231, 1971

days.application: Vannevar Bush's July 1945 report to President Truman, 'Science, the Endless Frontier', called basic research 'the pacemaker of technological progress' and helped lead to the National Science Foundation (1950); the 'linear model' was later read into it, though Benoît Godin (Science, Technology & Human Values, 2006) argues Bush never spelled it out. Policy then tested it: the Defense Department's Project Hindsight (Sherwin & Isenson, Science, 1967) traced 20 weapon systems and found that under 1% of the key research 'events' were undirected basic science, while the NSF's reply, TRACES (1968), traced five civilian innovations further back and found a large role for earlier basic research. Both patterns are real; the transistor, a science-led invention taught in Computing, fits the linear story better than aspirin does.

builds_on.why: Car I set out Logan's chain and its first documented reversal, Britain's 1865 Locomotive Act regulating road vehicles before the car; today generalizes that reversal into a model of innovation as loops.
The chain-linked model is a set of feedback loops between design, market and research; Day 26's loop vocabulary is what replaces the pipeline.

across.link: German chemical firms such as Bayer and BASF built some of the first industrial research laboratories in the late nineteenth century, organizing invention itself; this 'invention of invention' is taught in History II.

days.apply_question: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman reported modified-nucleoside mRNA in 2005 after years of rejected grant applications, and the BioNTech-Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines were authorized in December 2020. Does that story fit the linear model or the chain-linked model better, and what part of it would each model miss?
days.evidence_note: Settled among historians of innovation: the strict linear model does not describe most innovation, and practice often precedes theory.
