days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Ford's Engineers Priced a Burn Death at $200,725 - the Government's Own Number. The Arithmetic Was Right. Was the Ethics?
days.concept: Consequentialism holds that the right act is the one that produces the best overall outcomes - in utilitarianism, the greatest total well-being (Bentham, Mill); its power is impartial aggregation, everyone's welfare counted and added, and its danger is what aggregation can justify.
days.focus: Bentham (1789), Mill (1861), Sidgwick and Singer; the Anglican William Paley's theological utilitarianism (1785) as a reminder that the theory has Christian as well as secular defenders; act vs rule versions; expected value under uncertainty (Day 11). Its strength: honest trade-offs under scarcity (cost-benefit analysis, QALYs, triage). Its objections: the separateness of persons (Rawls 1971), integrity (Williams 1973), demandingness, distribution, and the practical impossibility of foreseeing consequences (Day 29).
days.model_or_equation: Utilitarian choice: pick the act a that maximizes the sum over everyone i and every possible outcome s of p(s) x u_i(a, s) - each person's well-being, weighted by the outcome's probability. Health version: incremental cost-effectiveness ratio ICER = (C_new - C_old) / (QALY_new - QALY_old), compared with a threshold. Grush-Saunby check: 180 x $200,000 + 180 x $67,000 + 2,100 x $700 = $49.5 million of benefits, against 12.5 million vehicles x $11 = $137 million of costs.

story.title: The memo that priced a burn death at $200,725
story.hook: In 1973, responding to a proposed federal rule to limit fuel leakage when vehicles roll over, Ford engineers E. S. Grush and C. S. Saunby filed a cost-benefit analysis titled 'Fatalities Associated with Crash-Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires'. The fix would cost $11 a vehicle across 12.5 million cars and light trucks - $137 million. It would prevent an estimated 180 burn deaths, 180 serious burn injuries and 2,100 burned vehicles; valued at $200,000 per death (the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's own 1972 figure was $200,725), $67,000 per injury and $700 per vehicle, the benefits came to $49.5 million, so costs exceeded benefits almost three to one. In 1977 Mark Dowie's Mother Jones article 'Pinto Madness' presented the memo as Ford's calculation about the Pinto's rear-mounted fuel tank, and it became the most famous document in business ethics. As the law professor Gary Schwartz later showed ('The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case', 1991), it concerned rollovers across the whole industry, not Pinto rear impacts, and its value of a life came from the government.
story.puzzle: Every government that regulates safety puts a number on a life, and NHTSA supplied this one. So what, if anything, was wrong with the memo - the numbers, the method, or the very idea of adding up deaths and dollars?
story.payoff: Consequentialism says the method is right in principle: when resources are finite, refusing to compare is itself a choice with a body count. The memo's real vulnerabilities are the ones critics of aggregation name - the people who would burn are not the people saving $11, so a sum hides who pays; whether a firm may sell a product it expects to kill some customers is a question about rights and consent (Day 46), not arithmetic; and the inputs decide the answer. The outrage tracks a genuine objection, the separateness of persons, rather than a calculation error.
sources: E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, 'Fatalities Associated with Crash-Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires' (Ford Motor Company, 1973)
Mark Dowie, 'Pinto Madness', Mother Jones, September/October 1977
Gary T. Schwartz, 'The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case', Rutgers Law Review 43 (1991) 1013-1068

days.application: NICE, England's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, appraises new medicines by cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained - a year in full health counts as 1, a year in worse health as less - and has generally recommended treatments costing below a threshold long set at £20,000-30,000 per QALY (reported in late 2025 to be rising; the run should confirm the current figure). Consequentialist aggregation at work: money spent on a drug at £100,000 per QALY buys fewer healthy years than the same money spent elsewhere in the NHS. Its critics press the objections the lesson names: the 'rule of rescue' for identifiable dying patients, special end-of-life allowances, and the charge that QALYs count years lived with a disability as worth less.

builds_on.why: Expected value: consequentialism under uncertainty is expected-value maximization - Bernoulli's 1760 smallpox calculation and d'Alembert's objection were an early round of today's debate.
Unintended consequences: the theory's practical weak point is that outcomes are hard to foresee, as Merton showed with purposive action.

across.link: Executive Order 12291 (Ronald Reagan, February 1981) required cost-benefit analysis of major federal regulations, and US agencies now use a 'value of a statistical life' - the EPA's central figure is about $7.4 million in 2006 dollars, adjusted for inflation - the Grush-Saunby arithmetic turned into standing policy.

days.apply_question: Oregon's 1990 draft Medicaid priority list, ranked largely by cost-effectiveness, reportedly placed tooth capping above surgery for ectopic pregnancy and was withdrawn after an outcry invoking the 'rule of rescue'. Was the outcry evidence that the calculation was done badly, or that consequentialism itself leaves something out?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Grush-Saunby figures and their regulatory context (Schwartz 1991); that regulators routinely value statistical lives. Debated: how many deaths Pinto fires caused (Dowie's 1977 claim of 500-900 vs. Schwartz's figure of 27 from federal data) and whether the Pinto was unusually dangerous. Value judgment: whether aggregating welfare across persons is the right way to decide - utilitarians (Bentham, Mill, Singer; Paley in a theological form) against critics from the separateness of persons (Rawls 1971), integrity (Williams 1973), and Christian ethics that denies one may do evil that good may come (Romans 3:8; Veritatis Splendor, 1993).

resource.title: Utilitarianism (Crash Course Philosophy)
resource.creator: CrashCourse (host Hank Green; PBS Digital Studios), 2016
resource.why: A brisk visual introduction to Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism and the classic objections, useful for fixing the vocabulary before the harder cases.
resource.verified_how: An episode of the Crash Course Philosophy series (other episodes of the series were confirmed on youtube.com and thecrashcourse.com by web search this session); this episode's title and length are cited from knowledge and were not web-checked because the shared search budget ran out, so no link is given.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: Kant Said You May Not Lie Even to a Murderer at Your Door. He Meant It.
days.concept: Deontology holds that some acts are required or forbidden whatever the consequences; Kant's formula of humanity says to treat humanity, in yourself or anyone else, always as an end and never merely as a means - which is why consent, rights and promises can outweigh a better outcome.
days.focus: Kant's Groundwork (1785): the good will, hypothetical vs categorical imperatives, the formula of universal law (the lying-promise example) and the formula of humanity ('merely' as a means - we use the baker, with his consent). Rights as side constraints (Nozick 1974); W. D. Ross's prima facie duties (1930) as the pluralist alternative; the murderer at the door as the hard case, with Kant's own answer and Korsgaard's (1986) reading that deceiving someone who exploits your honesty may be permitted.
key_concepts: Formula of humanity (never merely as a means)
days.model_or_equation: Formula of universal law: 'act only in accordance with that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law.' Formula of humanity: 'So act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.' (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785, Academy edition 4:421 and 4:429, trans. Mary Gregor.)

story.title: The murderer at the door
story.hook: In 1797 Benjamin Constant, a Swiss-born French liberal, published an essay on political reactions attacking a principle he attributed to 'a German philosopher': that it would be a crime to lie even to a murderer who asks whether a friend he is pursuing has taken refuge in your house. Taken unconditionally, Constant argued, the duty to tell the truth would make society impossible; truth is owed only to those who have a right to it, and a murderer has none. Immanuel Kant, then 73, did not retreat. In 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' (1797) he answered that truthfulness in statements one cannot avoid is a duty to everyone, however great the harm; that a lie wrongs humanity generally by making all declarations untrustworthy; and that if you lie and your friend has meanwhile slipped out and meets the murderer, you are answerable for what follows - whereas if you tell the truth, what the murderer does is on him.
story.puzzle: Almost everyone thinks Kant gave the wrong answer, yet he was the most careful moral philosopher of his age. What principle could make lying to a murderer wrong - and is it worth keeping even if Kant misapplied it?
story.payoff: The principle is that persons may not be used merely as means, and that a maxim you could not will for everyone is impermissible: a lie works only by exploiting others' trust, using their reason without their consent. That principle is why medical research needs informed consent and why rights can block good outcomes. Whether it really forbids lying to a murderer is disputed even among Kantians - Christine Korsgaard argues that someone who exploits your honesty for murder falls outside the case the formula governs - and Kant's absolutism shows the cost of a theory with no way to weigh one duty against disaster, which Ross's prima facie duties try to supply.
sources: Immanuel Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' (1797), in Practical Philosophy, trans. Mary J. Gregor (Cambridge UP, 1996)
Benjamin Constant, 'Des reactions politiques' (1797)
Christine M. Korsgaard, 'The Right to Lie: Kant on Dealing with Evil', Philosophy & Public Affairs 15 (1986) 325-349

days.application: The Nuremberg Code (August 1947), part of the judgment in United States v. Karl Brandt et al., the 'Doctors' Trial' of 23 defendants, 20 of them physicians; 16 were convicted and 7 hanged. Defendants justified some experiments - freezing, high-altitude decompression - by the knowledge they would yield for saving airmen, a consequentialist defence. The Code's first principle, 'The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential', is the formula of humanity in institutional form: a person may not be used merely as a means even for good expected results, and consent is what turns being used into taking part.

builds_on.why: Deontology is defined against consequentialism: the critics of the Grush-Saunby memo appealed to rights and consent, which no sum of costs and benefits captures.
Randomized controlled trials: assigning people to treatment at random is permissible only with their consent - the 1954 Salk trial enrolled children whose parents had volunteered them.

across.link: Joshua Greene and colleagues (Science, 2001) used fMRI to show that 'personal' dilemmas, such as pushing a man off a footbridge to stop a runaway trolley, engage emotion-related brain regions more than impersonal ones, such as flipping a switch - evidence about where deontological intuitions come from; whether it bears on whether they are right is disputed (Selim Berker, 'The Normative Insignificance of Neuroscience', 2009).

days.apply_question: In February 2006 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court struck down a law allowing the armed forces to shoot down a hijacked airliner to stop a 9/11-style attack, holding that killing the innocent passengers would treat them as mere objects of state action. Would Kant's formula of humanity support that ruling even if shooting the plane down would save thousands of people on the ground?
days.evidence_note: Settled: what Kant and Constant wrote; the content and origin of the Nuremberg Code. Debated: whether Kant's ethics really forbids lying to the murderer (Korsgaard 1986 and others read it otherwise); how to rank duties that conflict (Ross 1930); what Greene's brain-imaging results imply for ethics (Greene vs. Berker). Value judgment: whether some acts are wrong whatever the consequences - deontologists, rights theorists and much Christian ethics (for example Catholic teaching on intrinsically evil acts, Veritatis Splendor, 1993) say yes; consequentialists say no.

resource.title: On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy (1797)
resource.creator: Immanuel Kant, in Practical Philosophy, trans. Mary J. Gregor (Cambridge UP, 1996)
resource.why: Kant's own reply to Constant - his theory's hardest case, argued in his words - so Logan can decide whether the principle or its application is what fails.
resource.verified_how: Primary text in the standard Cambridge translation, cited from knowledge; not web-checked this session because the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so no link is given.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: No Checklist Covered It. Sullenberger Had About Three and a Half Minutes - and Forty-Two Years of Practice.
days.concept: Virtue ethics puts character at the centre: virtues such as courage, honesty and justice are stable dispositions acquired by practice, and the right act is what a person of practical wisdom (phronesis) - who perceives what matters in this situation and acts well on it - would do.
days.focus: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: flourishing (eudaimonia), virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency, habituation ('we become just by doing just acts'), and phronesis as the virtue that perceives particulars no rule anticipates; the modern revival (Anscombe 1958; MacIntyre, After Virtue, 1981; Hursthouse 1999) and Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotle's virtues with faith, hope and charity. Objections: action-guidance, cultural variation in the list of virtues, and the situationist challenge from psychology (Harman 1999; Doris 2002).
days.model_or_equation: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean (Nicomachean Ethics II.6): virtue is a disposition to feel and act 'at the right times, about the right things, towards the right people, for the right end, and in the right way', lying between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency - courage between rashness and cowardice; truthfulness between boastfulness and false modesty. Rosalind Hursthouse's criterion (On Virtue Ethics, 1999): an action is right if and only if it is what a virtuous agent would characteristically do in the circumstances.

story.title: Three and a half minutes over the Hudson
story.hook: On the afternoon of 15 January 2009, about two minutes after US Airways Flight 1549 left LaGuardia for Charlotte, the Airbus A320 flew into a flock of Canada geese at roughly 2,800 feet and both engines lost thrust. Captain Chesley Sullenberger, 57, took the controls while First Officer Jeffrey Skiles worked the engine-failure checklist - written for a failure at cruising altitude, not over the Bronx. Air traffic control offered a runway back at LaGuardia, then Teterboro in New Jersey; Sullenberger judged he could reach neither and told the controller, 'We're gonna be in the Hudson.' He glided the airliner onto the river beside midtown Manhattan about three and a half minutes after the bird strike (208 seconds is the figure usually cited), and all 155 people aboard survived. The National Transportation Safety Board later ran simulations: pilots who turned back toward LaGuardia the instant the birds hit could sometimes make it, but with a realistic 35-second delay to recognize the emergency and decide, they did not.
story.puzzle: No rule told Sullenberger what to do - the checklist did not fit and the controllers were offering runways. Yet nearly everyone judges his choice right. What did he have that a rulebook or a calculation could not supply?
story.payoff: Practical wisdom: a trained perception of what this situation required, built over decades. Sullenberger later told CBS News that for 42 years he had been 'making small, regular deposits in this bank of experience, education and training', and that on 15 January the balance was sufficient for a very large withdrawal. Virtue ethics says moral excellence looks like that: not a formula applied, but a character formed by practice that sees what matters and acts in time. The case also shows the theory's limit - we judged the decision right partly by its outcome, and the NTSB had to reconstruct what a reasonable pilot could have seen.
sources: National Transportation Safety Board, Loss of Thrust in Both Engines After Encountering a Flock of Birds and Subsequent Ditching on the Hudson River, US Airways Flight 1549, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-10/03 (2010)
CBS News interview of Chesley Sullenberger by Katie Couric, February 2009

days.application: William LeMessurier and the Citicorp Center (601 Lexington Avenue, New York, completed 1977). In 1978, after a question from an engineering student, Diane Hartley of Princeton, he re-checked the tower's response to 'quartering' winds that strike two faces diagonally and learned that the contractor had substituted bolted joints for welded ones in the diagonal braces; under quartering winds some brace forces rose by about 40%, and he estimated that a storm able to topple the building could come about once every 16 years. He told the owners, the architects and the city, and the repair went ahead in secret: through the summer and autumn of 1978 welders worked at night to weld heavy steel plates over some 200 bolted joints, while emergency evacuation plans were drawn up as Hurricane Ella approached in September. The public learned only in 1995 (Joe Morgenstern, 'The Fifty-Nine-Story Crisis', The New Yorker, 29 May 1995). Virtue in action - the honesty and courage to report his own error at the risk of his career, the practical wisdom to manage the fix - and the candour question: was keeping the public uninformed prudence or a lapse?

builds_on.why: Rules and duties run out: no checklist on Flight 1549 and no maxim in LeMessurier's office specified the right act - the gap virtue ethics says practical wisdom fills.
Vectors: a quartering wind resolves into components on two faces at once, which is why the Citicorp tower's diagonal braces carried about 40% more force than a perpendicular-wind check suggested.

across.link: Evidence-based medicine was defined as 'integrating individual clinical expertise with the best available external clinical evidence from systematic research' (David Sackett and colleagues, BMJ, 1996) - medicine's explicit admission that guidelines need practical wisdom to apply them to the patient in front of you.

days.apply_question: On 30 December 2019 the Wuhan ophthalmologist Li Wenliang warned colleagues in a private chat group about a SARS-like illness; police made him sign a statement admitting to spreading 'rumours' on 3 January 2020, and he died of COVID-19 on 7 February. What would a virtue ethicist ask about his choice that neither a consequentialist calculation nor a list of duties would?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the NTSB's findings on Flight 1549; the Citicorp repair as documented by Morgenstern (1995) and later accounts. Debated: whether virtue ethics can guide action ('do what a virtuous person would do' presumes we know what that is), and the situationist challenge - Harman (1999) and Doris (2002) argue psychology shows behaviour depends more on situations than on stable traits; virtue ethicists reply that full virtue is rare, not absent. Value judgment: whether LeMessurier's silence toward the public was prudence or a failure of candour.

resource.title: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapters 1-6
resource.creator: Aristotle (translations by W. D. Ross, revised by J. O. Urmson, or by Terence Irwin; the Ross translation is free online)
resource.why: Aristotle's own account of how virtues are acquired by practice and why each is a mean 'relative to us' - the source that Aquinas, MacIntyre and every later virtue ethicist builds on.
resource.verified_how: Classic primary text, cited from knowledge; not web-checked this session because the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so no link is given.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Philosophy
days.headline_hint: From a Birmingham Jail Cell, a Baptist Preacher Quoted a 13th-Century Friar - and Said Some Laws Are Not Laws at All.
days.concept: Natural-law theory holds that morality is grounded in human nature and the basic goods that fulfil it - life, knowledge, friendship and others - knowable by reason to anyone, so a human law that violates them is defective as law; critics press Hume's gap and moral pluralism.
days.focus: Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II, qq. 90-97): law as an ordinance of reason for the common good; the first principle of practical reason and the natural inclinations (q. 94 a. 2); unjust law as 'not law but a perversion of law' (q. 95 a. 2). Then the 'new natural law' of Germain Grisez (1965) and John Finnis (Natural Law and Natural Rights, 1980): basic goods grasped as self-evidently good, not inferred from facts - a reply to Hume's gap that classical Thomists dispute. Critics: Hume, Darwin's removal of fixed natural purposes, and pluralism. Protestant reception ranges from Karl Barth's rejection to Reformed natural-law theory; Philosophy II takes up Protestant social ethics.
key_concepts: First principle of practical reason ('good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided')
Lex iniusta non est lex (an unjust law is no law)
days.model_or_equation: Aquinas's hierarchy of law (Summa Theologiae I-II, qq. 91-95): eternal law (God's reason ordering creation) -> natural law (the rational creature's share in it, known through inclinations to preserve life, raise offspring, know the truth and live in society) -> human law, which binds in conscience only insofar as it derives from natural law. Finnis's basic goods (1980): life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability (friendship), practical reasonableness and religion.

story.title: A friar quoted from a jail cell
story.hook: On Good Friday, 12 April 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. was arrested for leading a march in Birmingham, Alabama, in defiance of a state court injunction. The same day eight white Alabama clergymen published 'A Call for Unity', calling the demonstrations 'unwise and untimely' and urging that grievances be pressed in the courts. Writing first in the margins of a newspaper and on scraps of paper, King answered in what became the 'Letter from Birmingham Jail', dated 16 April 1963. To the charge that he urged people to break some laws while demanding obedience to the Supreme Court's 1954 desegregation ruling, he replied that there are two types of laws, just and unjust: 'I would agree with St. Augustine that "an unjust law is no law at all."' And: 'To put it in the terms of St. Thomas Aquinas: An unjust law is a human law that is not rooted in eternal law and natural law. Any law that uplifts human personality is just. Any law that degrades human personality is unjust.'
story.puzzle: A Baptist minister was quoting a medieval Catholic friar to Protestant, Catholic and Jewish clergy, and claiming that a law duly passed by Alabama's legislature was 'no law at all'. By what standard can a validly enacted law fail to be law - and why should people who did not share his faith accept it?
story.payoff: Natural-law theory's answer: law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, and human law binds because, and insofar as, it derives from a moral law knowable by reason; a law that degrades persons lacks law's authority even while it sits on the books. Because natural law is held to be knowable by reason and not only by revelation, King could appeal to it across confessional lines, alongside the Declaration of Independence's 'self-evident' truths. The critics' question also shows: who decides what 'degrades human personality'? King's answer included a discipline - breaking an unjust law 'openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty' - that separates civil disobedience from lawlessness.
sources: Martin Luther King Jr., 'Letter from Birmingham Jail', 16 April 1963 (Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University)
'A Call for Unity', statement by eight Alabama clergymen, 12 April 1963
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 94 a. 2 and q. 95 a. 2

days.application: Jacques Maritain and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. In 1947 UNESCO canvassed philosophers on the theoretical foundations of human rights; in his introduction to the resulting volume, Human Rights: Comments and Interpretations (1949), the Catholic natural-law philosopher Jacques Maritain recalled that at one meeting someone expressed astonishment that champions of violently opposed ideologies had agreed on a list of rights: 'Yes, they said, we agree about the rights but on condition that no one asks us why.' The UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration in Paris on 10 December 1948, 48 votes to none, with eight abstentions. Natural law explains how practical agreement on rights can coexist with deep disagreement about their foundations - and its critics' warning that a list without an agreed 'why' is fragile when interpretations clash.

builds_on.why: Hume's gap is the classic objection to natural law, and the new natural law's reply - that basic goods are grasped as good directly rather than inferred from facts about human nature - is aimed squarely at it.

Natural law is a form of moral realism: in Aquinas a rational creature's share in God's eternal law, in Finnis objective goods that reason can know before settling God's existence - with the Euthyphro and debunking pressures both applying.

across.link: The 'Radbruch formula' (1946), proposed by the German legal philosopher Gustav Radbruch after Nazism - a statute whose injustice is intolerable must yield to justice - was applied by Germany's Federal Court of Justice in 1992 to convict East German border guards for shooting people at the Berlin Wall despite East German law, and the European Court of Human Rights upheld related convictions in Streletz, Kessler and Krenz v. Germany (2001).

days.apply_question: By Aquinas's test, was the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 - which required citizens of free states to assist, when called upon, in returning people who had escaped slavery - binding in conscience on a citizen of Ohio, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: what Aquinas, King and Maritain wrote; the 1948 vote. Debated: whether natural law survives Hume's gap and the loss of fixed natural purposes after Darwin (Hume; H. L. A. Hart vs. Finnis 1980); whether the new natural law is faithful to Aquinas (Grisez and Finnis vs. classical Thomists such as Ralph McInerny and Russell Hittinger); how universal the basic goods are across cultures. Value judgment: specific contested applications such as sexual ethics and end-of-life questions, where natural-law theorists, Catholic teaching and many Protestant thinkers draw conclusions others reject; Protestant views of natural law range from Barth's rejection to Reformed defences (David VanDrunen, Divine Covenants and Moral Order, 2014).

resource.title: The Natural Law Tradition in Ethics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
resource.creator: Mark Murphy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
resource.length: about 20-25 minutes (the opening section on Aquinas's paradigmatic view)
resource.why: An authoritative, even-handed account of Aquinas's theory - the good, the basic goods, how the precepts are known - and of the main variations and objections, at the depth today's lesson can only sketch.
resource.verified_how: Long-standing SEP entry by Mark Murphy, cited from knowledge; not web-checked this session because the shared web-search budget was exhausted, so no link is given.

days.phase: Philosophy I: Knowledge, Evidence and Values
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 3: Leaded gasoline and the burden of proof
days.headline_hint: Five Men Died Making It. Its Inventor Washed His Hands in It for the Press. America Burned It for Sixty More Years.
days.concept: The case's one question: when a new chemical's harm is uncertain, who should carry the burden of proof - and what did sixty years of leaded gasoline cost because the answer, in 1925, was 'the critics'?
days.focus: Walk leaded gasoline through Logan's chain as a loop, not a pipeline: an engineering need (engine knock), an invention (tetraethyl lead, December 1921), a joint venture (1924), a workplace disaster, a 1925 decision that put the burden of proof on critics (the Kehoe paradigm), decades of lock-in, evidence from outsiders (Patterson 1965, Needleman 1979), then removal by a side door (catalytic converters, 1975) and court-backed precaution (Ethyl Corp. v. EPA, 1976). Deep on Philosophy I and the How We Know and Systems days; previews for chemistry, engineering, government and law.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1 octane lock-in (reinforcing, 1920s-1970s): cheap antiknock -> higher-compression engines -> demand for high-octane fuel -> more leaded fuel. B1 evidence-to-regulation (balancing, slowed by delay and by the burden of proof): lead added -> lead stock in air, soil and bodies grows over decades -> measurement (Patterson 1965; Needleman 1979) -> regulation -> less lead added. Side loop (a documented reversal): the 1970 Clean Air Act's limits on carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons -> catalytic converters from the 1975 model year -> lead poisons the catalyst -> unleaded fuel required -> leaded share falls. Second-order effects: octane had to come from elsewhere (aromatics, MTBE, ethanol), and MTBE in turn contaminated groundwater and was phased out in the 2000s; piston aircraft still burn leaded fuel (EPA endangerment finding, October 2023).

story.title: The 'loony gas' building at Bayway
story.hook: In late October 1924, in a new building at Standard Oil of New Jersey's Bayway works where tetraethyl lead was made, workers began to hallucinate, rave and convulse; other men had already nicknamed it the 'loony gas building'. Within days five were dead and more than thirty hospitalized (accounts give 35 to 44). On 30 October, at a press conference in New York, the additive's inventor, the General Motors chemist Thomas Midgley Jr., poured tetraethyl lead over his hands and breathed its vapour for about a minute to show it was safe in the dilutions used in fuel - though he had himself needed a long rest to recover from lead poisoning the year before. New York City, Philadelphia and New Jersey banned or suspended sales. In May 1925 the US Surgeon General convened a one-day conference and the Ethyl Gasoline Corporation suspended sales while a committee studied the question; in January 1926 the committee reported no good grounds for prohibiting the fuel, if properly regulated, while urging further study, and sales resumed.
story.puzzle: Five men had died making it and the inventor had been poisoned by it, yet a federal committee let it back on sale and Americans burned it for sixty more years. With harm to the public uncertain in 1925, who should have had to prove what?
story.payoff: In 1925 the burden was placed on critics to prove harm to the public - what historians call the Kehoe paradigm, after Robert Kehoe, the industry-funded toxicologist who argued for four decades that without evidence of harm at ordinary exposures the fuel should stay. That evidence took forty to fifty years because lead is a slowly accumulating stock and the tools to measure natural background lead did not exist until Clair Patterson built them. Choosing the burden was an inductive-risk value judgment (Day 42) presented as science (Day 43). And when the evidence finally won, a rule aimed at different pollutants removed lead faster than direct regulation had.
sources: US Public Health Service, Proceedings of a Conference to Determine Whether or Not There Is a Public Health Question in the Manufacture, Distribution, or Use of Tetraethyl Lead Gasoline, Public Health Bulletin No. 158 (1925)

William Kovarik, 'Ethyl-leaded gasoline: how a classic occupational disease became an international public health disaster', International Journal of Occupational and Environmental Health 11 (2005) 384-397
Jamie Lincoln Kitman, 'The Secret History of Lead', The Nation, 20 March 2000
Gerald Markowitz & David Rosner, Deceit and Denial: The Deadly Politics of Industrial Pollution (University of California Press, 2002)

days.application: The measured consequence, as a worked example: as US gasoline lead was phased down, mean blood lead in Americans fell about 78% between the national surveys of 1976-80 and 1988-91 (Pirkle et al., JAMA, 1994), and an earlier analysis of the 1976-80 survey had found blood lead tracking gasoline lead sales closely (Annest et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 1983). The regulatory record: EPA phase-down rules from 1973; Ethyl Corp. v. EPA (D.C. Circuit, 1976) upheld precautionary regulation without proof of actual harm; 0.1 grams per gallon from 1 January 1986; a ban for US road vehicles from 1 January 1996; and the last leaded petrol for cars sold anywhere, in Algeria, in July 2021 (UNEP).

builds_on.why: Inductive risk: deciding in 1925 that critics must prove harm was a choice about which error - banning a useful additive or poisoning a generation - was worse.
Is and ought: 'there is no proof of harm' was treated as entailing 'sales ought to continue', with the value premise left unstated.

Replication and publication bias: the lead-crime literature is the worked example - the 2022 meta-analysis by Higney, Hanley and Moro found publication bias and a much smaller effect than headline claims.
Stocks and flows: lead accumulates in soil, dust and bone, so the stock kept rising long after anyone measured the flow, and fell only slowly after it stopped.

across.link: Clair Patterson's measurement of the age of the Earth - about 4.55 billion years, from lead isotopes in meteorites (Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 1956) - forced him to build an ultra-clean laboratory to escape contamination, which revealed how much industrial lead was everywhere; his 1965 paper 'Contaminated and Natural Lead Environments of Man' opened the scientific case against leaded petrol.

days.apply_question: PFAS 'forever chemicals' were in wide use from the 1950s, and the EPA set the first enforceable US drinking-water limits for two of them, PFOA and PFOS, at 4 parts per trillion in April 2024. Using this case's reasoning about inductive risk, where should the burden of proof have sat when PFAS were introduced, given what could then be known?
days.evidence_note: Settled: lead is a neurotoxin with no known safe level for children (CDC; WHO); US blood lead fell about 78% between 1976-80 and 1988-91 as gasoline lead was phased down (Pirkle et al. 1994); the chronology of the 1924 deaths, the 1925 conference, the 1970 Clean Air Act, the phase-down rules, the 1996 US ban for road vehicles and the last sale in Algeria in 2021. Debated: how much leaded gasoline contributed to crime (Nevin 2000; Reyes 2007 vs. the 2022 meta-analysis by Higney, Hanley and Moro); UNEP's model-based estimate that the global phase-out prevents more than a million premature deaths a year; whether GM chose tetraethyl lead over ethanol partly because it was patentable (Kovarik; Kitman) or for technical reasons. Value judgment: who gained (GM, Standard Oil, DuPont and Ethyl; drivers who got cheaper octane and stronger engines), who paid (refinery workers, and children whose exposure was involuntary), who consented (the children did not). A consequentialist tallies health and cognitive losses against decades of cheap octane; a Kantian asks whether exposing non-consenting children to uncertain harm used them merely as means; a virtue ethicist examines Midgley's demonstration and Kehoe's career; natural-law and Christian ethics stress duties to the vulnerable and the common good. The counterfactual - an ethanol or refinery-octane path from 1925 - is unknowable.

chain.point: Engine knock - fuel auto-igniting ahead of the flame - capped compression ratios and so power and efficiency; General Motors' research chief Charles Kettering made a knock suppressant a priority. The Engineering block teaches compression and the engine.

After years of screening thousands of compounds (ethanol, which also suppresses knock, among the known options), Midgley's team found tetraethyl lead on 9 December 1921; ethylene dibromide was later added to carry lead deposits out of the engine. Why a trace of lead stops knock waits for the chemistry of reactions and combustion.

Tetraethyl lead is absorbed through skin and lungs (the Bayway deaths); burned in an engine, its lead leaves as fine particles that settle in roadside soil and household dust and never degrade. The chemistry block covers combustion products.

With knock suppressed, compression ratios climbed over the following decades, raising power and efficiency - the success that tied engine design to cheap octane. The Engineering block teaches the internal combustion engine.

chain.field: Financing (named at CFA level, not taught)
chain.point: General Motors and Standard Oil of New Jersey formed the Ethyl Gasoline Corporation as a 50-50 joint venture in August 1924, earning on a patented additive sold to refiners, with DuPont manufacturing it; Albemarle Paper later bought Ethyl in 1962 in a heavily debt-financed deal reported at about $200 million.

chain.link: Regulation: who bears the burden of proof
chain.point: The May 1925 conference and January 1926 report put the burden on critics, and the Kehoe paradigm held for four decades: an inductive-risk choice about which error was worse, presented as if 'no proof of harm' entailed 'continue'. In Ethyl Corp. v. EPA (D.C. Circuit, 1976, en banc) the court shifted the burden: the Clean Air Act's 'will endanger' standard is precautionary and does not require proof of actual harm.

The 1970 Clean Air Act and the new EPA; phase-down rules from 1973; 0.1 grams per gallon from 1986; leaded fuel banned for US road vehicles from 1 January 1996. How agencies write rules, how capture and courts shape them, and how tort law handles diffuse harms wait for Government and Law.

'Ethyl' gasoline spread through the 1920s and 1930s and became the standard way to make octane; refineries and engines co-evolved around it - increasing returns and lock-in - so unleaded fuel became widely available only when catalytic converters demanded it, from the 1975 model year.

Lead accumulates in soil, dust and bone - a stock fed by a flow, with decades of delay between emission, measurement and response; US blood lead fell about 78% from 1976-80 to 1988-91 as the flow was cut (Pirkle et al., JAMA, 1994).

The lead-crime hypothesis (Rick Nevin, 2000; Jessica Wolpaw Reyes, 2007, using states' different phase-down timing as a natural experiment) must contend with confounding by everything else that changed in the 1990s and with publication bias: Higney, Hanley and Moro's 2022 meta-analysis found a much smaller effect.
How lead damages the developing nervous system, and how its effect on measured intelligence is estimated, are taught in the Biology and Psychology blocks.

Four readings of harm to children who never consented: the consequentialist sum (Day 45), the Kantian ban on using people merely as means (Day 46), the virtue ethicist's look at Midgley and Kehoe (Day 47), and the natural-law duty to protect the vulnerable and the common good (Day 48).

A rule aimed at carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons removed lead - an unintended consequence running the right way - and the knowledge loop closed only when outsiders (Patterson's clean laboratory, 1965; Herbert Needleman's 1979 study of lead in children's teeth) produced the evidence the 1925 burden demanded. The loop is still open for piston aircraft.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: a body keeps its motion unless a net force acts, and F = ma says how much it changes. Story: on 10 Dec 1954 John Paul Stapp rode a rocket sled from 632 mph to rest in about 1.4 seconds - some 46 g - and walked away; he then campaigned for car seat belts. App: why a freight train at 55 mph can need a mile or more to stop (Operation Lifesaver) - and what that means at a level crossing.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Momentum and impulse: why crumple zones work
days.focus: Concept: impulse (force times time) equals change in momentum, so lengthening a stop lowers the force; momentum is conserved in collisions. Story: IIHS's 50th-anniversary test (2009) crashed a 1959 Chevrolet Bel Air into a 2009 Malibu at 40 mph; the Bel Air's cabin collapsed. App: in a crash between vehicles of unequal mass, conservation of momentum gives the lighter one's occupants the larger change in velocity (D14).

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: energy changes form but is never created or destroyed; work is force times distance and kinetic energy grows as speed squared. Story: James Joule's paddle-wheel experiments (1845-47) measured the mechanical equivalent of heat; later tradition says he took a thermometer to a waterfall on his honeymoon (told as legend). App: regenerative braking - an EV turns kinetic energy back into battery charge, and why it cannot recover all of it.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: power is the rate of energy use; kilowatts and kilowatt-hours are different questions. Story: James Watt defined the horsepower (33,000 foot-pounds per minute) in the early 1780s to sell engines to brewers and mill owners. App: why a 350 kW fast charger and a 7 kW home charger fill the same battery at such different speeds - and why a human body runs at about 100 W.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Heat engines and the Carnot limit
days.focus: Concept: no engine can turn all its heat into work; the ceiling is 1 - Tcold/Thot (the second law). Story: Sadi Carnot's 1824 Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, written to explain why British steam engines worked. App: only about 12-30% of a petrol car's fuel energy reaches the wheels (fueleconomy.gov), while a combined-cycle gas plant passes 60% - the car chain's physical-constraint link.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Entropy and why useful energy runs out
days.focus: Concept: spontaneous processes move toward more probable arrangements; what we 'use up' is not energy but low-entropy, useful energy (exergy). Story: Ludwig Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna carries S = k log W. App: Earth runs on low-entropy sunlight and radiates high-entropy heat - Schrödinger's 1944 point in What Is Life? about how organisms survive.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: fluid pressure rises with depth (P = rho g h), buoyancy equals the weight of fluid displaced, and stability depends on where weight sits relative to buoyancy. Story: the warship Vasa capsized about 1,300 m into her maiden voyage (10 Aug 1628); a pre-launch test of 30 men running across the deck had already shown she was unstable. App: Hoover Dam is about 660 ft thick at its base and 45 ft at its crest because water pressure grows with depth.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: drag grows with the square of speed (and drag power with the cube); lift comes from turning airflow. Story: the Wright brothers' 1901 wind tunnel showed the accepted Smeaton coefficient was wrong and that published lift tables did not fit their wings; with their own data they flew on 17 Dec 1903. App: why highway fuel economy falls steeply above about 50 mph (D8) and why EV makers chase drag coefficients.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: a wave carries energy, not matter; its speed is set by the medium (shallow-water waves travel at the square root of g times depth). Story: the 26 Dec 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami crossed deep ocean at jet speed, barely a metre high, then rose at the shore; ten-year-old Tilly Smith recognized the receding sea from a geography lesson and cleared a Phuket beach. App: active noise cancellation in car cabins and headphones - destructive interference.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: voltage pushes charge, current is its flow, resistance opposes it (Ohm's law), and power is current times voltage. Story: Alessandro Volta's letter of 20 Mar 1800 to Joseph Banks announced the pile - the first steady current - ending his dispute with Galvani over 'animal electricity'. App: why a car's starter motor needs thick cables from a 12-volt battery, and why power lines use very high voltage (I-squared-R losses).

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: a changing magnetic field drives a current (Faraday's law), so a motor and a generator are the same machine run in opposite directions. Story: Michael Faraday's iron-ring experiment of 29 Aug 1831. App: the electric car's motor and the wind turbine's generator - Tesla, Inc. took its name from Nikola Tesla, whose 1888 induction motor its early cars descended from.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, X-rays and gamma rays are one phenomenon at different frequencies, and energy per photon rises with frequency. Story: James Clerk Maxwell calculated in the 1860s that electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light; Heinrich Hertz made them in 1887. App: car radar at 76-81 GHz and lidar near 905 or 1550 nm - and why non-ionizing radio cannot break DNA as UV can.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: moving clocks run slow (special relativity) and clocks higher in a gravity field run fast (general relativity). Story: in October 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew four cesium clocks around the world; eastward they lost about 59 ns and westward gained about 273 ns, as predicted. App: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day; uncorrected, positions would drift by kilometres within a day.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: atoms have a tiny nucleus and electrons restricted to discrete energy levels, so matter absorbs and emits light only at particular energies. Story: Geiger and Marsden's 1909 gold-foil experiment - Rutherford said it was as if a 15-inch shell had bounced back off tissue paper - and Bohr's 1913 atom. App: LEDs, whose colour is set by an energy gap - the blue LED won the 2014 Nobel and made white LED lighting possible.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: mass is energy (E = mc^2), and nuclear binding energy means splitting heavy nuclei or fusing light ones releases millions of times more energy per atom than chemistry. Story: at Christmas 1938 in Kungälv, Sweden, Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, sitting on a log in the snow, worked out that a split uranium nucleus releases about 200 MeV. App: a uranium fuel pellet of a few grams holds roughly the energy of a tonne of coal (industry comparison).

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Physics
days.focus: Concept: unstable nuclei decay and emit ionizing radiation; harm depends on dose (sieverts), and the shape of the risk curve at low doses (linear no-threshold) is debated. Story: the 'Radium Girls' who painted watch dials at US Radium in Orange, New Jersey; Grace Fryer's suit (1927) helped establish occupational-disease law. App: radon in homes - the EPA's action level and its standing as a leading cause of lung cancer - compared with a CT scan's dose.

days.phase: Physics: Forces, Energy and Fields
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 4: The electric grid - why the world runs on AC
days.focus: Story: on 4 Sep 1882 Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station in Manhattan begins lighting a few hundred lamps for a handful of customers. Question: how did a physical constraint pick the winner between Edison's DC and Westinghouse's AC, and turn electricity into a regulated monopoly? Deep: I-squared-R losses and why high voltage needs transformers, which need changing fields (D59, D60, D53); Niagara's AC power reaching Buffalo in 1896; energy per second as load (D52). Preview: generation fuels (Energy, Chemistry & Materials), reliability (Engineering), Samuel Insull's regulated-monopoly bargain and state utility commissions from 1907 (Government), the 1930s utility-holding collapse named at CFA level. Loop: industry asked for regulation; electrification's productivity payoff lagged decades because factories had to be redesigned (Paul David, 'The Dynamo and the Computer', 1990); rooftop solar now reverses the one-way flow.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: The periodic table: why elements behave as they do
days.headline_hint: Mendeleev Told the Man Who Found Gallium He Had Weighed It Wrong. He Had Never Seen It. He Was Right.
days.concept: An element's chemistry is set by its outer (valence) electrons, so properties repeat in a periodic pattern that can predict elements nobody has yet found.
days.focus: Teaches the periodic table as a map of electron structure: rows are filling shells, columns share valence electrons, so behaviour repeats (the periodic law). The quantum atom (D63) supplies the shells; this lesson turns them into chemistry, and shows the table's power as a predictive model, not a filing system.

story.title: A letter from St Petersburg about a metal its writer had never held
story.hook: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev published a table that ordered the elements by atomic weight and grouped them by behaviour, and he left gaps, predicting the properties of missing elements, among them 'eka-aluminium' with a density of about 6 g/cm3. In August 1875 the French chemist Paul-Emile Lecoq de Boisbaudran spotted a new violet spectral line in zinc ore from the Pyrenees and soon isolated the metal, gallium. He reported its density as about 4.7. Mendeleev wrote that the figure must be wrong and should be nearer 5.9. Lecoq purified his sample, remeasured, and got about 5.9.
story.puzzle: How could a man in St Petersburg who had never seen the metal correct the measurement of the chemist holding it?
story.payoff: Gallium sits under aluminium because it has the same three valence electrons; the table encodes electron structure, so an element's neighbours fix its chemistry and roughly its physical properties. Mendeleev's gaps were predictions from that pattern, and Lecoq's first sample was impure.
sources: Mendeleev, Zeitschrift fur Chemie 1869 and his 1871 predictions of eka-aluminium
Lecoq de Boisbaudran, Comptes rendus 1875 (discovery of gallium)
Eric Scerri, The Periodic Table: Its Story and Its Significance (Oxford UP, 2007)

days.application: Why lithium dominates rechargeable batteries: the lightest metal (about 0.53 g/cm3), it gives up its single valence electron very readily, which gives lithium cells a high voltage (lithium's standard electrode potential is about -3.04 V, the most negative of the common metals) and high energy per kilogram.

builds_on.why: The quantum atom's discrete energy levels are the shells whose outer electrons set each column's chemistry.
Mendeleev's gaps were risky, falsifiable predictions, Popper's criterion in action; gallium, scandium and germanium confirmed them.

across.link: Philosophers of science use Mendeleev as the test case for whether a successful novel prediction counts for more than fitting known facts (prediction versus accommodation; Peter Lipton, 'Testing Hypotheses: Prediction and Prejudice', Science 2005).

days.apply_question: Sodium sits directly below lithium in the table, and sodium-ion batteries are now being sold in China; using what the table says about the two elements, what would you expect a sodium-ion cell to gain and to give up compared with a lithium-ion cell?

resource.creator: Hank Green, Crash Course (2013)
resource.why: Tells Mendeleev's story and walks through how the table's layout reflects recurring properties, a quick visual companion to the lesson.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Two Physicists Peeled Pencil Lead With Scotch Tape and Got the Strongest Material Ever Measured. Same Carbon as Diamond.
days.concept: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds, and how they are arranged in space, explain why materials are hard or soft, brittle or ductile, conducting or insulating.
days.focus: Teaches the three bond types as different ways atoms share or trade valence electrons (D67), then shows that the arrangement of bonds matters as much as their type: carbon as diamond, graphite and graphene is the proof. Ends with why metals bend and ceramics shatter.

story.title: Friday-night experiments in Manchester
story.hook: At the University of Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, both trained in Russia, ran 'Friday night experiments' on ideas too odd for grant proposals. Around 2004 they used ordinary adhesive tape to peel flakes off graphite, the stuff of pencil lead, again and again until some flakes were a single layer of carbon atoms. Their October 2004 paper in Science reported the sheet, graphene, which theory had long suggested could not exist stably on its own; a 2008 Columbia study measured it as the strongest material ever tested. They shared the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
story.puzzle: Pencil lead smears onto paper and diamond cuts glass, yet both are pure carbon, and one atom-thin layer of the soft one is stronger than steel. How can the same atoms be soft, hard and super-strong?
story.payoff: Within a graphite layer every carbon is covalently bonded to three neighbours, extremely strong; between layers only weak van der Waals forces hold, so layers slide (soft pencil). Diamond bonds every atom covalently in 3D (hard). Graphene is one layer, all strong bonds and no weak ones. Properties follow the bond type and its geometry.
sources: Novoselov, Geim et al., 'Electric Field Effect in Atomically Thin Carbon Films', Science 306 (22 Oct 2004)
Nobel Prize in Physics 2010 press release
Lee, Wei, Kysar & Hone, Science 321 (2008), strength of monolayer graphene

days.application: Why a steel bumper dents and a windscreen shatters: metallic bonds are non-directional, so planes of atoms can slip by moving dislocations without the material separating (ductility); in glass the directional covalent and ionic bonds cannot re-form after slipping, so a crack runs (brittleness), which is why laminated windscreens hold the pieces in plastic.

builds_on.why: Bond type follows from valence electrons: metals give them up easily, non-metals share or grab them.
The sea of free electrons in a metallic bond is what carries current, explaining why metals conduct and covalent solids like diamond do not.

across.link: Material choice in the car body is a bond-level trade-off: steel's ductility absorbs crash energy by deforming, which is why crumple zones are built from metal rather than ceramics.

days.apply_question: Ceramic brake discs and ceramic knives are harder than steel but are made thicker or used more gently; using what bonding says about how each material fails, why would an engineer still choose steel for a car's crash structure?

resource.creator: Mark Miodownik (Penguin / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2013)
resource.why: A materials scientist tells the carbon story from pencil to diamond to graphene, showing bond structure turning into everyday properties.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Beirut's Warehouse Held 2,750 Tonnes of a Farm Fertilizer for Six Years. Then It Exploded.
days.concept: Reactions release or absorb energy by breaking and making bonds; an activation barrier lets stored chemical energy sit safely until something lifts it over, and a catalyst lowers that barrier without being used up.
days.focus: Teaches reaction energy (exothermic versus endothermic, from bond energies, D52) separately from reaction rate (the activation barrier), and shows a catalyst changes the route, not the destination. Heat speeds reactions roughly exponentially, which is why a fire can trigger a runaway.
days.model_or_equation: Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(-Ea/RT): the rate constant k rises exponentially as temperature T rises or as the activation energy Ea falls (A a frequency factor, R the gas constant).

story.title: Hangar 12, Port of Beirut
story.hook: About 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate, unloaded from the stricken ship Rhosus in 2014, sat in Hangar 12 at Beirut's port for six years, despite officials' warnings. On 4 August 2020 a fire broke out in the warehouse, and shortly after 6 pm the store detonated, one of the largest non-nuclear explosions recorded, killing more than 200 people (counts are about 218-220), injuring thousands and leaving much of the city damaged.
story.puzzle: Ammonium nitrate is a common fertilizer that farmers spread by hand, and this pile lay inert for six years. Why was it harmless for so long, and why did a fire turn it into a bomb?
story.payoff: Decomposing ammonium nitrate releases energy, but an activation barrier keeps it stable at room temperature. Fire supplied heat; because rates rise exponentially with temperature, decomposition sped up, released more heat, and ran away into detonation. The energy was always there; the barrier was holding it.
sources: Lebanese government and port records as reported by Reuters and BBC, August 2020
Human Rights Watch, 'They Killed Us from the Inside' (August 2021)
Rigby et al., 'Preliminary yield estimation of the 2020 Beirut explosion', Shock Waves (2020)

days.application: The car's catalytic converter (fitted to most new US cars from the 1975 model year): platinum, palladium and rhodium on a ceramic honeycomb let carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides react to CO2, water and nitrogen at exhaust temperatures, where they would otherwise pass through unchanged. It is the regulation link of the car chain, and it needed unleaded fuel because lead poisons the catalyst (D49).

builds_on.why: Reaction energy is conservation of energy at the level of bonds: the energy released is the difference between bonds broken and bonds made.
Catalytic converters, required to meet the Clean Air Act's limits, were poisoned by lead, the regulation that pushed leaded gasoline out.

across.link: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation barriers so that reactions such as the breakdown of food run fast at body temperature, the mechanism behind metabolism as slow combustion.

days.apply_question: Lithium-ion battery fires in electric cars are hard to put out and can reignite hours later; using activation energy and the exponential effect of temperature on rate, explain why a battery that was stable for years can run away once one cell overheats.

resource.creator: Hank Green, Crash Course (2013)
resource.why: Explains reaction rates, activation energy and catalysts visually, the mechanism behind both the Beirut runaway and the catalytic converter.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); title recalled from the Crash Course Chemistry series. Routine should cite without a link; confirm title and length at the next build check.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: The Hindenburg Carried the Best Fuel per Kilogram Ever Burned. Nearly 90 Years Later, No Airliner Flies on It.
days.concept: Burning a fuel with oxygen releases bond energy, and energy per kilogram and per litre decide what a fuel can move.
days.focus: Teaches combustion as oxidation of carbon and hydrogen into CO2 and water, then the two energy densities (specific energy per kg, energy density per litre) and why liquid hydrocarbons win on both. Includes engine knock and octane briefly, the chemistry previewed in the leaded-gasoline case (D49).
days.model_or_equation: CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O + energy; a rough table: hydrogen about 120 MJ/kg but about 0.01 MJ/L as gas and about 8.5 MJ/L as liquid; gasoline and jet fuel about 43-46 MJ/kg and 32-35 MJ/L; lithium-ion cells about 0.5-1 MJ/kg.

story.title: Thirty-odd seconds at Lakehurst
story.hook: On the evening of 6 May 1937 the German airship Hindenburg, 245 metres long and lifted by about 200,000 cubic metres of hydrogen, was landing at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey, after crossing from Frankfurt. Fire broke out near the tail and the ship was consumed in roughly half a minute, in front of newsreel cameras. Thirty-six people died: 13 passengers, 22 crew and one ground crewman; 62 of the 97 on board survived. The disaster ended the passenger airship.
story.puzzle: Hydrogen holds nearly three times as much energy per kilogram as gasoline, so it should be the ideal fuel for flying. Why, nearly 90 years later, does every airliner still burn kerosene?
story.payoff: Hydrogen wins per kilogram but loses badly per litre: even liquefied at -253 C it holds about a quarter of kerosene's energy per litre, and needs heavy insulated tanks. Aircraft are limited by both weight and volume, so kerosene's combination wins. The Hindenburg's huge gas volume held surprisingly little energy for its size.
sources: US Commerce Department, Report of the Hindenburg accident investigation (1937)
Navy Lakehurst Historical Society casualty list
US DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center, fuel properties comparison

days.application: Why batteries cannot yet carry a 737 across the Atlantic: jet fuel stores about 43 MJ/kg against roughly 0.9 MJ/kg (about 250 Wh/kg) for good lithium-ion cells, a gap of about fifty times; even crediting electric motors' roughly three-times better efficiency, a transatlantic battery pack would weigh far more than the aircraft can lift, which is why electric aviation targets short hops.

builds_on.why: Day 1 compared gasoline's ~12 kWh/kg with a battery pack's ~0.2 kWh/kg; this lesson explains where those numbers come from.
Fuel energy only becomes motion through a heat engine whose Carnot limit wastes most of it, which narrows the battery's gap.

across.link: Lavoisier and Laplace's 1782-83 ice calorimeter showed a guinea pig's body heat matched the burning of the carbon it exhaled: respiration is combustion slowed down, and fat (about 37 MJ/kg) is the body's high-density fuel.

days.apply_question: Container ships are now being ordered to run on methanol or ammonia instead of heavy fuel oil; using specific energy and energy per litre, what would you expect those ships to give up, and why might a ship tolerate it when an airliner cannot?

resource.title: How the World Really Works, chapter 1 'Understanding Energy: Fuels and Electricity'
resource.creator: Vaclav Smil (Viking, 2022)
resource.length: about 40 minutes (read the sections on energy densities and fuels)
resource.why: Smil sets fuels side by side by energy density and explains why liquid hydrocarbons are so hard to replace in flight and shipping.
