days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Drake Drilled for Lamp Oil and Threw Away the Gasoline. One Barrel Now Makes 20 Gallons of It.
days.concept: Coal, oil and gas are buried photosynthesis cooked into hydrocarbons over millions of years, and refining separates and reshapes crude by boiling point into the products an economy wants.
days.focus: Teaches where fossil fuels come from (plankton and plants, burial, heat and pressure) and how a refinery turns crude into products: fractional distillation by boiling point, then cracking and reforming to shift the mix toward what sells. Explains why a fossil fuel is stored solar energy at enormous density.

story.title: The drive pipe at Oil Creek
story.hook: In 1859 Edwin Drake, hired by the Seneca Oil Company and styled 'Colonel' to impress the locals, was drilling beside Oil Creek near Titusville, Pennsylvania, with the salt-well driller William 'Uncle Billy' Smith. His key trick was driving an iron pipe down through the gravel so the hole would not cave in. On 27 August 1859, at 69.5 feet, the bit dropped into a crevice; the next day Smith found oil standing in the pipe. The product everyone wanted was kerosene for lamps; the light, volatile fraction we call gasoline was a near-worthless byproduct, often dumped.
story.puzzle: How can one black liquid yield lamp oil, gasoline, jet fuel and asphalt, and how did gasoline go from waste to the main product of the same barrel?
story.payoff: Crude is a mixture of hydrocarbons of many chain lengths; distillation splits them by boiling point (short chains boil low: gasoline; longer ones: kerosene, diesel, then residue). Refiners later learned to crack long molecules into short ones, so they can tilt the barrel toward whatever the market wants, and the car made gasoline the prize.
sources: Drake Well Museum (Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission)
Daniel Yergin, The Prize (1991), ch. 1
American Chemical Society National Historic Chemical Landmark, 'Development of the Pennsylvania Oil Industry'

days.application: What a 42-gallon barrel becomes: US refineries output roughly 45 gallons (processing gain) of which about 19-20 gallons are motor gasoline, about 11-12 diesel and heating oil, about 4 jet fuel, the rest petrochemical feedstocks, asphalt and other products (EIA 'Oil and petroleum products explained'). This is the physical-constraint and production link of the car chain: the fuel is one cut of a joint-product process.

builds_on.why: Fossil fuels are low-entropy stores of ancient sunlight; burning them releases energy that photosynthesis concentrated over millions of years.
Deepwater Horizon's flow integral was this same crude; the integral turned a rate in barrels per day into a total.

across.link: Because refining and crude are geographically concentrated, oil is a chokepoint: the October 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled prices within months and prompted the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

days.apply_question: Europe's refineries are geared to produce more diesel than gasoline while the US makes more gasoline; using what you know about distillation and cracking, why can't a refinery simply switch its whole output from one to the other when demand changes?

resource.title: The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money and Power, chapter 1 'Oil on the Brain: The Beginning'
resource.creator: Daniel Yergin (Simon & Schuster, 1991)
resource.why: The Pulitzer-winning history opens with Drake and the kerosene trade, showing how an illuminant business became the oil industry.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); chapter title cited from prior knowledge. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: Resources versus reserves: why peak predictions fail
days.headline_hint: Hubbert Said US Oil Would Peak Around 1970. It Did. Then It Broke the Record.
days.concept: Reserves are the part of a resource that is economic to extract with today's technology and prices, so reserves move when prices and technology move; the resource is what is physically there.
days.focus: Teaches the resource-reserve distinction (a definition, not a discovery) and the Hubbert curve as the derivative of a logistic (D7, D4): right when its ceiling holds, wrong when technology and price move the ceiling. Hedges both the peak-oil and the 'never runs out' views.
days.model_or_equation: Hubbert curve: if cumulative production Q(t) follows a logistic toward a ceiling URR, annual production dQ/dt = kQ(1 - Q/URR) is bell-shaped and peaks when half the URR is gone. The peak date depends entirely on the assumed URR.

story.title: A Shell geologist in San Antonio, March 1956
story.hook: In March 1956, at an American Petroleum Institute meeting in San Antonio, Texas, Shell geophysicist M. King Hubbert presented 'Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels'. Fitting bell-shaped curves to US discovery and production, he predicted that lower-48 crude output would peak between about 1965 and 1970 and then decline. US production peaked in 1970 at about 9.6 million barrels a day and fell for nearly four decades, making Hubbert famous. Then horizontal drilling and fracking in shale lifted output, and in 2018 annual US crude production passed the 1970 record.
story.puzzle: Was Hubbert right or wrong? His curve called the peak, and yet the US now pumps more oil than at that peak.
story.payoff: Hubbert's curve treated the recoverable total as fixed; it was a model of reserves, and reserves are an economic and technological category. When prices rose and fracking made shale rock economic, part of the resource became reserve and the ceiling moved. His mathematics was sound; his assumed URR was a snapshot.
sources: M. King Hubbert, 'Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels', Shell Development Co. Publication 95 (1956)
US EIA, annual US field production of crude oil series (1970 and 2018)
Deffeyes, Hubbert's Peak (2001)

days.application: Lithium and cobalt: USGS world lithium reserves have roughly doubled in a decade (on the order of 14 million tonnes in the mid-2010s to roughly 28-30 million tonnes in recent Mineral Commodity Summaries) as prices rose and exploration expanded, while identified resources are several times larger. 'Running out' claims depend on ore grade, price, extraction technology and recycling, not just tonnes in the ground; cobalt adds concentration risk (most is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo).

builds_on.why: The Hubbert curve is the rate of a logistic: production rises and falls as cumulative output approaches an assumed ceiling.
Like Limits to Growth and the Simon-Ehrlich wager, peak forecasts fail when models omit price and adaptation.

across.link: Reserve estimates are political assets: OPEC members' reported reserves jumped in the late 1980s when quotas were partly tied to reserves, an example of Goodhart's law in official statistics (D23).

days.apply_question: Helium is extracted from a few natural-gas fields and periodically declared 'running out'; using the distinction between resources and reserves, what would you need to know before deciding whether a helium shortage is geological or economic?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the definitions and that reserves rise with price and technology. Debated: how much oil and critical minerals will ultimately be recoverable, and whether peak oil demand (from EVs) will arrive before any supply peak. Value judgment: whether to keep extracting what is economic, which turns on climate (D85).

resource.title: Nuclear Energy and the Fossil Fuels (the sections on US crude oil)
resource.creator: M. King Hubbert (Shell Development Company, Publication No. 95, 1956)
resource.length: about 20 minutes for the oil sections
resource.why: Hubbert's own paper shows the logistic reasoning, the assumed ultimate totals and the dated forecast, so Logan can see exactly which assumption failed.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); paper cited from prior knowledge (widely reproduced). Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: A 57-Year-Old at Oxford Swapped One Powder for Another and Doubled a Battery's Voltage. Your Phone Runs on It.
days.concept: A battery is a controlled redox reaction that forces electrons to travel through an outside circuit, and the chemistry of its electrodes sets its voltage and its energy per kilogram.
days.focus: Teaches oxidation and reduction as electron transfer, how separating the two halves makes electrons do work in a circuit (D59), why voltage comes from the difference in the electrodes' appetite for electrons, and how lithium-ion 'rocking chair' cells shuttle lithium ions between graphite and a metal oxide.
days.model_or_equation: Energy stored = voltage x charge: E (Wh) = V x Q (Ah). Doubling cell voltage at the same charge capacity doubles the energy.

story.title: The cathode that changed the voltage
story.hook: In the 1970s Stanley Whittingham at Exxon built a rechargeable lithium battery with a titanium disulfide cathode; it worked at a bit over 2 volts. At Oxford, John Goodenough, then 57, reasoned that a metal oxide would hold lithium at a much higher potential; in 1980 his group (with Koichi Mizushima and others) reported lithium cobalt oxide, giving about 4 volts. In 1985 Akira Yoshino in Japan paired it with a carbon anode, and Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion cells in 1991. In 2019 the three shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Goodenough, at 97, was the oldest laureate ever.
story.puzzle: Both batteries shuttled the same lithium ions. Why did swapping the cathode powder nearly double the voltage, and with it the energy the battery could hold?
story.payoff: Voltage is the difference in how strongly the two electrodes bind electrons (and lithium). An oxide cathode holds lithium at a much lower energy than a sulfide, so each electron falls through a bigger potential drop, about 4 V instead of 2; energy is voltage times charge, so the same shuttle carries roughly twice the energy.
sources: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019, press release and popular background (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences)
Mizushima, Jones, Wiseman & Goodenough, Materials Research Bulletin 15 (1980)

days.application: The car's battery pack: BloombergNEF's annual survey put average lithium-ion pack prices above $1,000/kWh around 2010 and about $115/kWh in 2024, a fall that plots as a straight line on a log scale (D2) and that Engineering will explain as a learning curve (Day 97). Chemistry choices matter too: cobalt-free lithium iron phosphate cells trade some energy density (lower voltage, about 3.2 V) for cost and safety, which is why many cheaper EVs use them.

builds_on.why: Volta's pile was the first redox battery; voltage, current and charge are the circuit quantities a battery supplies.
Pack prices falling by a steady percentage a year are a straight line on a log plot.

across.link: Battery supply chains are a chokepoint: China refines most of the world's lithium and graphite and makes most cells, which is why the US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) tied EV tax credits to where battery materials come from.

days.apply_question: Grid storage projects increasingly choose lithium iron phosphate cells over the nickel-rich cells used in long-range cars; using what sets a cell's voltage and energy per kilogram, why might a battery that is worse for a car be better for a power station?

resource.title: Popular science background, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019: 'They developed the world's most powerful battery'
resource.creator: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (nobelprize.org, 2019)
resource.why: The Nobel committee's illustrated account walks through Whittingham's, Goodenough's and Yoshino's steps and why each raised voltage or safety.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); title cited from prior knowledge of the 2019 popular information page on nobelprize.org. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: Steel: iron with just enough carbon
days.headline_hint: Bessemer Blew Cold Air Into Molten Iron. It Got Hotter.
days.concept: Steel is iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon; making it means first stripping oxygen from iron ore (reduction) and then burning excess carbon and impurities out of the iron (oxidation).
days.focus: Teaches the two-step chemistry of iron and steel: blast-furnace reduction with carbon monoxide, which leaves pig iron with about 4% carbon (brittle), then oxidation to bring carbon down to about 0.1-1% (strong and ductile). Shows why carbon content controls properties and why steel's CO2 is chemical, not just fuel.
key_concepts: iron ore, pig iron and steel
days.model_or_equation: Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2 (blast furnace); with hydrogen instead: Fe2O3 + 3 H2 -> 2 Fe + 3 H2O.

story.title: Malleable iron 'without fuel', Cheltenham, August 1856
story.hook: In August 1856 Henry Bessemer, an inventor with no metallurgical training, read a paper to the British Association meeting at Cheltenham titled 'The Manufacture of Malleable Iron and Steel without Fuel'. His claim: blow cold air through a vessel of molten pig iron and, instead of freezing, the metal grows hotter, in a roaring shower of sparks, and in minutes becomes malleable. Ironmasters rushed to license it; many got brittle, useless metal, and Bessemer had to buy back licences before the process (with Robert Mushet's manganese additive and later Thomas and Gilchrist's 1878 fix for phosphorus) made cheap steel the material of railways and skyscrapers.
story.puzzle: Why does blowing cold air into molten iron heat it up rather than cool it, and why does that turn brittle iron into tough steel?
story.payoff: Pig iron from the blast furnace carries about 4% carbon plus silicon. Oxygen in the blast reacts with them, exothermically, so the impurities are the fuel. Burning carbon down to under 1% turns brittle cast iron into strong, ductile steel. The licensees' failures came from phosphorus in their ores, which the air blast could not remove.
sources: Bessemer's British Association paper, reported in The Times, 14 August 1856
Henry Bessemer, An Autobiography (1905)
Thomas J. Misa, A Nation of Steel (Johns Hopkins, 1995)

days.application: Steel's climate problem is chemistry: carbon is the reducing agent, so CO2 comes out of the ore itself. Iron and steel produce roughly 7-9% of global CO2 emissions (worldsteel and IEA estimates). In 2021 Sweden's HYBRIT venture (SSAB, LKAB, Vattenfall) delivered the first steel made with hydrogen-reduced iron to Volvo, whose by-product is water; it costs more, and scaling depends on cheap clean electricity for the hydrogen. This sits at the materials and consequences links of the car chain.

builds_on.why: Steelmaking runs on exothermic oxidation; the energy released by burning carbon and silicon keeps the Bessemer converter molten.
Small amounts of carbon pin the metallic lattice's dislocations, trading ductility for strength.

across.link: Cheap Bessemer steel built the American transcontinental rail network and Andrew Carnegie's Edgar Thomson Works (1875), part of the second industrial revolution's surge in materials output.

days.apply_question: Electric arc furnaces make new steel by melting scrap with electricity rather than reducing ore; using the chemistry of reduction, explain why recycled steel has a far smaller carbon footprint than ore-based steel, and what limits how much of the world's steel can be made this way.

resource.title: Stuff Matters, chapter 1 'Indomitable' (steel)
resource.creator: Mark Miodownik (Penguin / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2013)
resource.why: A materials scientist explains why carbon in iron's crystal lattice makes steel strong, from razor blades to the Bessemer converter.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); chapter title cited from prior knowledge. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Rome's Pantheon Has No Steel and Has Stood 1,900 Years. Modern Concrete Bridges Crumble in 50.
days.concept: Cement is made by baking limestone, which releases CO2, and hardens by reacting with water (hydration); the resulting concrete is very strong in compression and weak in tension, which is why it is reinforced with steel.
days.focus: Teaches clinker chemistry (calcination: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2), hydration as a chemical reaction, not drying, and the compression-tension asymmetry. Explains why reinforcing steel both makes modern concrete possible and limits its life (corrosion), and why cement's CO2 is hard to remove.
days.model_or_equation: CaCO3 + heat -> CaO + CO2: about 0.5 tonne of CO2 per tonne of clinker comes from the limestone itself, before any fuel is burned.

story.title: The dome Hadrian finished
story.hook: The Pantheon in Rome, rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian and finished around 125-128 AD, is roofed by a dome about 43.3 metres across, with a 9-metre open oculus at its crown. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, and it has stood for about 1,900 years with no steel inside. Its builders made the concrete lighter toward the top, grading the aggregate from heavy stone at the base to pumice near the oculus. In January 2023 an MIT-led team (Admir Masic and colleagues) reported in Science Advances that lime lumps in Roman concrete, once dismissed as poor mixing, can dissolve and re-seal cracks.
story.puzzle: Modern reinforced-concrete bridges and car parks can need major repair within 50-100 years. How has a steel-free Roman dome outlasted them by nearly two millennia?
story.payoff: A dome, properly shaped, carries its weight almost entirely in compression, where concrete is strong, so it needs no rebar, and with no steel there is nothing to rust and burst the concrete from inside. Modern concrete must carry tension in beams and slabs, so it relies on steel that corrodes when water and salts get in. Roman chemistry (and possibly self-healing lime) helps, but structure and the absence of steel explain most of it.
sources: Seymour, Masic et al., 'Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete', Science Advances 9 (6 Jan 2023)
William L. MacDonald, The Pantheon: Design, Meaning, and Progeny (1976)

days.application: Cement's climate weight: cement production accounts for roughly 7-8% of global CO2 (Chatham House, 'Making Concrete Change', 2018), more than half of it from calcination rather than fuel. Vaclav Smil's comparison (Making the Modern World, 2014): China used more cement in 2011-2013 (about 6.6 billion tonnes) than the United States in the whole twentieth century (about 4.5 billion tonnes), a measure of how fast urbanization consumes materials.

builds_on.why: The square-cube law: a dome's weight grows faster than its supporting area, which is why the Romans lightened the upper concrete with pumice.
Compression and the weight of material above are the same pressure reasoning as Hoover Dam's thick base.

across.link: Cement consumption tracks urbanization: China's 2011-13 surge was the physical side of hundreds of millions of people moving to cities, the concentration of people that urban sociology studies.

days.apply_question: Some engineers propose building bridges with stainless-steel or fibre-reinforced polymer bars instead of ordinary rebar despite higher cost; using what you know about compression, tension and corrosion, what would you need to know to judge whether the extra cost is worth it?
days.evidence_note: Settled: calcination chemistry and the compression-tension asymmetry. Debated: how much the lime-clast 'self-healing' mechanism contributes to Roman concrete's durability in real structures, versus structural form and the absence of rebar.

resource.title: How the World Really Works, chapter 3 'Understanding Our Material World: The Four Pillars of Modern Civilization'
resource.creator: Vaclav Smil (Viking, 2022)
resource.length: about 40 minutes (the cement and steel sections take about 15)
resource.why: Smil sets cement beside steel, plastics and ammonia, with the tonnages and energy costs that make them hard to replace.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); chapter title cited from prior knowledge. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Stephanie Kwolek's Solution Looked Like Something to Throw Away. It Spun a Fibre Five Times Stronger Than Steel.
days.concept: Polymers are long chains of repeating units, and the length of the chains and how they line up and grip each other set a plastic's properties, including the durability that makes plastics both useful and a lasting problem.
days.focus: Teaches polymerization, chain length, crystallinity and alignment, and the difference between thermoplastics (melt and reshape) and thermosets. Uses nylon (Carothers, DuPont, 1935) as background and Kevlar as the story; ends with why chains that resist breaking persist in the environment, and why recycling shortens them.

story.title: The cloudy solution at DuPont's Experimental Station
story.hook: In 1965 Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist at DuPont's laboratory near Wilmington, Delaware, was searching for a light, strong fibre for tyres. One polymer solution came out thin and cloudy, unlike the clear, syrupy solutions that normally spun well, and a technician, Charles Smullen, at first refused to run it through the spinneret, fearing it would clog. Kwolek persisted. The fibre that came out was extraordinarily stiff and strong; it became Kevlar, launched in 1971 and about five times stronger than steel on an equal-weight basis. It now stops bullets and reinforces tyres and cables.
story.puzzle: Why would a watery, cloudy liquid that looked like a failure make a fibre stronger than steel?
story.payoff: Kevlar's chains are rigid rods. In solution they spontaneously line up like logs in a river (a liquid crystal), which made it cloudy and runny; spinning locks that alignment into the fibre, and hydrogen bonds tie neighbouring chains together. Strength comes from long chains pointing the same way and gripping each other.
sources: Science History Institute, biography of Stephanie Kwolek
American Chemical Society National Historic Chemical Landmark, 'Kevlar' (2014)
Kwolek, US Patent 3,671,542 (1972)

days.application: Why recycling plastic is hard: Geyer, Jambeck and Law (Science Advances, 2017) estimated that of all plastic made to 2015 only about 9% had been recycled, about 12% incinerated and about 79% landfilled or left in the environment. Mechanical recycling melts and reshapes the plastic, and each cycle breaks chains (chain scission) and mixes in other polymers and additives, so the recycled material is weaker and usually 'downcycled'. The same long, stable chains that make plastic durable make it persist for decades or more.

builds_on.why: Polymers combine strong covalent bonds along each chain with weaker hydrogen or van der Waals bonds between chains, the same split that made graphite soft.
Most plastics are made from refinery and gas-processing feedstocks such as ethane and naphtha.

across.link: Proteins and DNA are natural polymers: spider silk, like Kevlar, gets its strength from aligned chains held by hydrogen bonds, which is why materials scientists study it.

days.apply_question: Polyethylene terephthalate drink bottles are among the few plastics recycled at scale, often back into bottles; using chain length and contamination, why does a clear PET bottle recycle better than a multi-layer crisp packet?
days.evidence_note: Settled: polymer structure-property relationships. Debated: the size of plastic leakage into oceans and the health effects of microplastics, where measurement is still immature.

resource.creator: Hank Green, Crash Course (2013)
resource.why: Shows how monomers join into chains and how chain structure gives plastics their properties.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); title recalled from the Crash Course Chemistry series (believed episode 45). Cite without a link; confirm title and length at the next build check.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: A Cracked Rod of Silicon Made Half a Volt Under a Desk Lamp. Bell Labs Had Found the P-N Junction.
days.concept: Adding tiny amounts of impurities (doping) to silicon makes p-type and n-type material; where they meet, a junction lets current flow one way and turns absorbed light into a voltage.
days.focus: Teaches the band gap (from the quantum atom, D63), doping with boron and phosphorus, how a p-n junction forms a built-in electric field, and how that field separates electrons and holes freed by light, which is the solar cell. The transistor (D106) is left to Computing.

story.title: The rod with the crack, Holmdel, February 1940
story.hook: Russell Ohl, a Bell Labs researcher at Holmdel, New Jersey, was purifying silicon to make better radio detectors. In February 1940 he tested a rod that had cracked as it cooled and found that when light from a lamp fell on it, it produced about half a volt, with no battery anywhere in the circuit. He demonstrated it to colleagues including Walter Brattain, who later co-invented the transistor. Ohl worked out that impurities had separated on either side of the crack as the melt froze, making two kinds of silicon that met at a sharp boundary.
story.puzzle: How can a lump of nearly pure silicon generate electricity from a desk lamp?
story.payoff: One side of the crack held excess phosphorus-like impurities (spare electrons: n-type), the other boron-like ones (missing electrons, holes: p-type). Where they meet, a built-in electric field forms; light frees electrons, and the field pushes them one way and holes the other, so a voltage appears. Ohl had made the first p-n junction, the heart of every solar cell, diode and transistor.
sources: Russell Ohl, US Patent 2,402,662 'Light-Sensitive Electric Device' (filed 1941)
Michael Riordan & Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire (1997), ch. on the p-n junction
Computer History Museum, 'Silicon Engine' timeline, 1940

days.application: Swanson's law: crystalline-silicon module prices fell from roughly $76 per watt in 1977 (in today's dollars) to well under $0.50, and by the mid-2020s to roughly $0.10-0.15 per watt for Chinese modules, about a 20% drop for each doubling of cumulative shipments. The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2020 said that for projects with cheap finance and good sun, solar PV now offers 'the cheapest source of electricity in history'. Engineering explains the fall as a learning curve (Day 97).

builds_on.why: The band gap is the quantum atom's discrete energy levels spread into bands in a crystal; a photon must carry at least the gap energy to free an electron.
Photon energy rises with frequency, which is why only light above silicon's band gap (about 1.1 eV, near-infrared) makes current.

across.link: The same p-n junctions, arranged as transistors, became Bardeen and Brattain's 1947 point-contact transistor and today's chips, so the solar cell and the microprocessor are siblings.

days.apply_question: Solar panels on Mars rovers and satellites use expensive multi-junction cells instead of cheap silicon; using band gaps and how p-n junctions turn photons into voltage, why might stacking junctions with different gaps capture more of sunlight's energy?

resource.title: Crystal Fire: The Invention of the Transistor and the Birth of the Information Age (the chapter on Ohl's p-n junction)
resource.creator: Michael Riordan and Lillian Hoddeson (W. W. Norton, 1997)
resource.why: Two historians of physics tell the Bell Labs silicon story, including Ohl's cracked rod, with the physics of doping explained clearly.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); book cited from prior knowledge, chapter number not confirmed. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: A Lake in Cameroon Exhaled One Night and 1,700 People Died in Their Sleep.
days.concept: Reversible reactions and dissolving gases settle at an equilibrium, and a change in pressure, temperature or concentration shifts that equilibrium in the direction that opposes the change (Le Chatelier's principle).
days.focus: Teaches dynamic equilibrium (forward and reverse running at equal rates), the equilibrium constant as a description of where the balance sits, and Le Chatelier's principle as a predictor. Uses gas solubility under pressure as the clearest case and sets up the ammonia equilibrium for Haber-Bosch (D86).
days.model_or_equation: Le Chatelier applied to N2 + 3 H2 <=> 2 NH3 (exothermic): four gas molecules become two, so high pressure pushes toward ammonia; heat favours the reverse, so low temperature raises yield but slows the rate.

story.title: The night Lake Nyos turned over
story.hook: On the night of 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos, a deep crater lake in north-west Cameroon, suddenly released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide, estimates run to over a million tonnes. Heavier than air, the gas poured down the valleys at speed and suffocated about 1,700 people (often given as 1,746) and some 3,500 livestock in villages up to about 25 km away, most of them in their sleep. Survivors woke to silence. The lake's water, normally blue, turned red with iron stirred up from its depths.
story.puzzle: A lake is not a volcano. How could still water hold that much gas, and what let it all out at once?
story.payoff: Carbon dioxide seeping from volcanic sources dissolved into the lake's deep water, where high pressure held far more gas in solution than the surface could. When something (perhaps a landslide) lifted deep water upward, pressure fell, the equilibrium shifted toward gas, bubbles formed, the rising bubbly water lifted more water, and the release ran away like a shaken bottle being opened. Since 2001 pipes have been degassing the lake in a controlled way.
sources: Kling et al., 'The 1986 Lake Nyos Gas Disaster in Cameroon, West Africa', Science 236 (1987)
Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, Oku Volcanic Field / Lake Nyos report
USGS and Lake Nyos degassing project reports (2001 onward)

days.application: Ocean acidification runs the same chemistry in reverse: the oceans absorb roughly a quarter of human CO2 emissions; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which shifts the carbonate equilibria, releasing hydrogen ions and consuming carbonate ions that shell-builders need. Average surface-ocean pH has fallen by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times, roughly a 30% rise in hydrogen-ion concentration, because pH is a logarithmic scale (D2).

builds_on.why: Pressure rising with depth is what lets deep lake water hold so much dissolved CO2.
Nyos was a threshold system: once lifting water began degassing, a reinforcing loop flipped the lake from stable to erupting.

across.link: Divers' decompression sickness is the same pressure-solubility equilibrium in blood: nitrogen dissolved at depth comes out as bubbles if the diver rises too fast.

days.apply_question: Coca-Cola keeps its fizz in a sealed bottle and goes flat in an open glass, faster when warm; using Le Chatelier's principle for both pressure and temperature, explain both effects and say which way the dissolving reaction's heat must run for warmth to drive gas out.
days.evidence_note: Settled: equilibrium chemistry and the measured fall in ocean pH. Debated: the trigger of the Nyos release (landslide, rain-cooled surface water or a gradual tipping point) and how strongly acidification will harm particular species.

resource.title: Equilibrium: Crash Course Chemistry #28
resource.creator: Hank Green, Crash Course (2013)
resource.why: A clear visual introduction to dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle, with the ammonia reaction as an example.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: French Uranium From Gabon Was Missing Some Atoms. Nature Had Run a Nuclear Reactor There Two Billion Years Ago.
days.concept: A reactor holds a neutron chain reaction exactly at balance, each fission causing on average one more (k = 1), using a moderator to slow neutrons, control rods to absorb them, and negative feedback and delayed neutrons to keep the balance stable and controllable.
days.focus: Teaches the multiplication factor k, why slowed (thermal) neutrons split uranium-235 more readily, enrichment, and the feedbacks that make a reactor self-limiting or unstable. Builds on fission energy (D64) and radiation (D65); risk perception and nuclear politics belong to Psychology and the nuclear case (D277).
key_concepts: chain reaction and multiplication factor k
days.model_or_equation: Neutron population after n generations: N = N0 x k^n. With k = 1.001 and a generation of about a millisecond the population would race upward, but the roughly 0.65% of neutrons from U-235 that arrive seconds late (delayed neutrons) stretch the effective generation time so operators and feedbacks can keep up.

story.title: The missing uranium-235 of Oklo
story.hook: In June 1972 an analyst at the French enrichment plant at Pierrelatte noticed that uranium from the Oklo mine in Gabon carried slightly too little uranium-235: about 0.717% instead of the 0.720% found in uranium everywhere else on Earth, the Moon and meteorites. A tiny gap, but in a business that tracks fissile material for bomb-proliferation reasons, a gap means a question. By September 1972 France's Atomic Energy Commission announced the answer: about two billion years ago, parts of the Oklo ore body had run as natural nuclear reactors, on and off, for hundreds of thousands of years.
story.puzzle: How could a reactor start, run and switch itself off without engineers, control rods or a containment building, and why didn't it explode?
story.payoff: Two billion years ago natural uranium held about 3% U-235, like modern reactor fuel. Groundwater seeping into the ore slowed neutrons (a moderator) so the chain reaction reached k = 1. As it heated up, the water boiled away, moderation dropped, k fell below 1 and the reaction stopped; when the rock cooled, water returned and it restarted. Meshik's 2005 analysis suggests cycles of about 30 minutes on and 2.5 hours off: negative feedback holding k near 1.
sources: Meshik, Hohenberg & Pravdivtseva, Physical Review Letters 93 (2004), and Meshik, 'The Workings of an Ancient Nuclear Reactor', Scientific American (Nov 2005)
Bodu et al., Comptes rendus (1972); IAEA 1975 symposium 'The Oklo Phenomenon'
Contrast: Chicago Pile-1, the first human-made reactor, critical on 2 Dec 1942

days.application: France's Messmer plan (announced March 1974 after the oil shock) built a fleet of standardized pressurized-water reactors, essentially the Oklo recipe engineered: enriched uranium, water as moderator and coolant, and a design in which losing the water stops the reaction. Nuclear now supplies roughly two-thirds or more of France's electricity (about 65-70% in most recent years), one of the lowest-carbon grids in Europe. Its cost history is Day 97's subject.

builds_on.why: Each fission releases about 200 MeV from mass turned into energy, and the extra neutrons make a chain reaction possible.
Oklo and modern water-moderated reactors are stabilized by a balancing feedback loop: more heat, less moderation, fewer fissions.

across.link: Chernobyl's RBMK reactor (26 April 1986) had a positive void coefficient: losing cooling water raised reactivity, a reinforcing loop where Oklo and Western water-moderated designs have a balancing one.

days.apply_question: Naval submarines run for decades on highly enriched uranium while power reactors use fuel of about 3-5% U-235; using the multiplication factor and the role of the moderator, why does richer fuel let a reactor be much smaller, and what does that imply for proliferation risk?
days.evidence_note: Settled: reactor physics and Oklo's interpretation. Debated (handled in Day 277): nuclear power's cost and the right level of regulation; its safety record per terawatt-hour is well measured, its place in policy is a value judgment.

resource.title: The Workings of an Ancient Nuclear Reactor
resource.creator: Alex P. Meshik, Scientific American (November 2005)
resource.why: The physicist who decoded Oklo's on-off cycle explains how groundwater moderated and regulated a natural reactor, the clearest illustration of criticality control.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); article cited from prior knowledge; may be paywalled. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Germany Had Twice Its Peak Demand in Wind and Solar Panels. One November Evening They Ran at a Few Percent.
days.concept: Capacity factor (average output divided by rated output) and the timing of output decide what a gigawatt of solar or wind is worth compared with a gigawatt of steady plant.
days.focus: Teaches nameplate capacity versus energy delivered, typical capacity factors (solar roughly 10-25% depending on latitude, onshore wind 25-35%, offshore 40-50%, nuclear about 90%), and correlation in time: when many wind farms are calm together, capacity does not add. Separates cheap energy from firm capacity.
days.model_or_equation: Annual energy = capacity x 8,760 hours x capacity factor. 1 GW of German solar at about 10% gives about 0.9 TWh a year; 1 GW of nuclear at about 90% gives about 7.9 TWh.

story.title: The dark doldrums of 6 November 2024
story.hook: By late 2024 Germany had installed roughly 170 GW of wind turbines and solar panels, about twice its peak electricity demand. On 6 November 2024 a high-pressure system parked over central Europe: grey skies, almost no wind, the long November night falling by late afternoon. Wind and solar output dropped to a few gigawatts, coal and gas plants and imports filled the gap, and the day-ahead price for the early-evening hour spiked to roughly 800 euros per megawatt-hour, many times normal. Germans have a word for it: Dunkelflaute, 'dark doldrums'.
story.puzzle: How can a country own more than twice its peak demand in renewable capacity and still be short of power?
story.payoff: Nameplate capacity is the maximum, not the average or the guaranteed. German solar's capacity factor is around 10%, and in a November evening it is zero; wind's output is correlated across the country, so on a calm day every turbine idles together. What a gigawatt is worth depends on when it produces, which is why systems with much wind and solar still need storage, imports or dispatchable plants.
sources: Fraunhofer ISE, Energy-Charts, net generation and day-ahead prices for 6 Nov 2024
Bundesnetzagentur / SMARD data on installed capacity (end-2024)
Reuters and Clean Energy Wire coverage of the November and December 2024 Dunkelflaute price spikes

days.application: California's 'duck curve': in 2013 the grid operator CAISO published a chart forecasting that midday solar would hollow out net load (demand minus wind and solar) while leaving a steep evening ramp; the midday belly arrived years earlier than projected. Each added gigawatt of solar is worth less when it all produces at noon (value deflation), so the system adds storage: California's batteries grew past roughly 10 GW by 2024, shifting midday solar into the evening.

builds_on.why: Capacity is power (GW); what the grid needs over a year is energy (TWh); capacity factor converts one to the other.
Correlation matters: wind farms' outputs are positively correlated by shared weather, so they do not average out as independent sources would.

across.link: Portfolio diversification uses the same mathematics: combining wind in distant weather systems with solar reduces variance only to the degree their outputs are uncorrelated, exactly as with assets (D11, D18).

days.apply_question: An offshore wind farm of 1 GW at a 45% capacity factor and a solar farm of 2 GW at 20% produce similar annual energy; using capacity factor and timing, what more would you need to know to say which is worth more to a northern European grid in winter?
days.evidence_note: Settled: capacity factors and the arithmetic. Debated: the full system cost of high wind-and-solar shares (storage, backup, transmission), where studies differ widely by assumptions. Value judgment: how much reliability to buy, and at whose cost.

resource.title: Sustainable Energy - Without the Hot Air, chapter 26 'Fluctuations and storage'
resource.creator: David J. C. MacKay (UIT Cambridge, 2009; free online)
resource.why: MacKay, a Cambridge physicist, works through how much wind fluctuates and what storage it would take to cover lulls, with transparent arithmetic.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); book and chapter cited from prior knowledge (the book is free on the author's site). Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.topic: The grid as a balancing act
days.headline_hint: Texas Came Four and a Half Minutes From a Blackout That Could Have Lasted Months.
days.concept: On an AC grid, supply must match demand every second; frequency (60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in Europe and Australia) is the signal of imbalance, and spinning inertia and reserves buy the seconds needed to fix it.
days.focus: Teaches why frequency falls when generation is short (generators slow down), inertia as stored rotational energy, the sequence of primary, secondary and tertiary reserves, and under-frequency load shedding as the last defence. Shows why inverter-based wind and solar need grid-forming controls or synthetic inertia.
days.model_or_equation: Swing equation, simplified: the rate of frequency fall is proportional to the power shortfall divided by the system's inertia; less inertia means a faster fall for the same lost plant.

story.title: Early morning, 15 February 2021, ERCOT control room
story.hook: As Winter Storm Uri froze Texas, gas wells, pipelines and power plants failed in the cold. Shortly before 2 am on 15 February 2021, generation in the ERCOT grid, which serves most of Texas and is barely connected to its neighbours, fell far below demand. Frequency dropped below 59.4 Hz and stayed there for over four minutes; had it lasted about four and a half more minutes, plants would have tripped automatically and the grid could have collapsed entirely, needing a 'black start' that could have taken weeks or months. Operators ordered rolling blackouts that left about 4.5 million homes and businesses without power for days; Texas officially counted 246 deaths, and independent estimates run higher.
story.puzzle: Why does a power shortfall show up as a falling frequency, and why does a few minutes below 59.4 Hz risk a months-long blackout?
story.payoff: Generators spin in lockstep with the grid; when demand exceeds supply, the extra energy comes out of their rotation and they slow, so frequency falls. Protection relays disconnect plants below safe frequencies to save them from damage, which deepens the shortfall: a reinforcing collapse. Shedding load restored the balance; the cascade it prevented would have required restarting the grid from nothing.
sources: FERC-NERC Staff Report, 'The February 2021 Cold Weather Outages in Texas and the South Central United States' (Nov 2021)
ERCOT presentation to its board, 24 Feb 2021 (the 4 minutes 37 seconds figure)
Texas Department of State Health Services, Winter Storm Uri mortality report (2021-22)

days.application: South Australia, 28 September 2016: storms with tornadoes toppled transmission towers; wind farms' fault ride-through protection settings, set to disconnect after repeated voltage dips, cut about 456 MW of output within seconds; the interconnector to Victoria overloaded and tripped, and the whole state went dark. AEMO's final report (March 2017) blamed the settings, not wind's variability; the response included new ride-through standards, a 100 MW Tesla battery at Hornsdale (December 2017) that sells fast frequency response, and synchronous condensers to restore inertia.

builds_on.why: The AC grid case explained why the world runs on synchronous alternating current; frequency is that synchrony's heartbeat.
The 2003 Northeast blackout showed failures cascading through a network; protection that saves one plant can push the next over the edge.

across.link: Texas's grid is deliberately isolated from interstate lines largely to stay outside federal (FERC) wholesale-market regulation, a jurisdictional choice that limited emergency imports during Uri.

days.apply_question: Ireland's grid operator now lets wind and solar supply up to about three-quarters of demand at any moment but sets a minimum number of conventional generators online; using inertia and frequency, explain why a grid might cap the instantaneous share of inverter-based power even when the wind is free.
days.evidence_note: Debated: the Texas death toll (official 246; independent estimates several hundred higher) and how far ERCOT's energy-only market design, versus weatherization failures, explains Uri. Settled: the physics of frequency and inertia.

resource.title: What Really Happened During the Texas Power Grid Outage?
resource.creator: Grady Hillhouse, Practical Engineering (2021)
resource.why: A civil engineer explains frequency, reserves and load shedding through the Uri timeline, the mechanism behind the near-collapse.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); title recalled from the Practical Engineering channel, not confirmed. Cite without a link and confirm before use, or fall back to the FERC-NERC report summary.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: 173,500 Mirrors, 3,500 Acres of Mojave, and an Average Output a Single Gas Turbine Could Match.
days.concept: Power density, the watts produced per square metre of land, differs by orders of magnitude between fossil extraction, solar, wind and biofuels, and so decides how much land an energy system needs.
days.focus: Teaches Smil's power density (Power Density, MIT Press 2015): fossil fuel extraction and thermal plants run at hundreds to thousands of W/m2, solar PV at roughly 5-20 W/m2 of land, wind at about 0.5-3 W/m2 of wind-farm area, biofuels well under 1 W/m2. Distinguishes land occupied from land excluded, and average from peak.
days.model_or_equation: Power density = average power / land area. Ivanpah: roughly 650-800 GWh a year is about 75-90 MW average, over about 14 km2 (3,500 acres): roughly 5-6 W/m2. Corn ethanol: about 0.2-0.3 W/m2.

story.title: Ivanpah opens in the Mojave, February 2014
story.hook: In February 2014 the Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System opened near the California-Nevada border: about 173,500 computer-steered heliostats, each carrying two mirrors, aimed sunlight at boilers on three towers some 140 metres tall. It cost about $2.2 billion, backed by a $1.6 billion federal loan guarantee, and was rated at 392 MW on roughly 3,500 acres of desert. In its first years it produced well below its projected output, and in 2025 its utility buyer agreed to end contracts early, with units slated to close as cheaper photovoltaics won.
story.puzzle: A plant rated at 392 MW and covering five and a half square miles delivers, on average, about what one mid-sized gas turbine on a few acres does. Why do the two differ so much in land?
story.payoff: Sunlight at the ground averages only about 200 W/m2 in a desert, and after conversion losses, spacing between mirrors and night, a solar plant delivers single-digit watts per square metre. A gas plant concentrates energy that geology collected over millions of years and pipelines bring in, so its land density is hundreds of times higher. Neither is good or bad in itself: power density tells you the land bill.
sources: US DOE Loan Programs Office, Ivanpah project page
US EIA electricity data browser, Ivanpah annual generation
Vaclav Smil, Power Density (MIT Press, 2015)

days.application: US corn ethanol: in recent years roughly 35-40% of the US corn crop has gone to ethanol (EIA, USDA), yet ethanol supplies only about a tenth of US gasoline by volume and less by energy (ethanol carries about two-thirds of gasoline's energy per litre). At well under 1 W/m2, biofuels are the least land-efficient energy source, which is why their climate and food-price effects are argued over.

builds_on.why: Power is energy per second; power density divides that rate by area, the unit that decides land needs.
Average output (capacity factor) not nameplate is what goes into power density.

across.link: Photosynthesis converts only about 1% or less of sunlight into stored crop energy, which is why biofuels' power density is so low and why land for fuel competes with food.

days.apply_question: The UK's Drax power station burns millions of tonnes of imported wood pellets a year to generate a few percent of Britain's electricity; using power density, how would you estimate the forest area that must keep growing to supply it, and what would that comparison leave out?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the power-density figures to within a factor of about two. Debated: how to count land (panels alone or whole site, shared farmland under turbines) and whether biofuels cut emissions once land-use change is included.

resource.title: Sustainable Energy - Without the Hot Air, chapter 18 'Can we live on renewables?'
resource.creator: David J. C. MacKay (UIT Cambridge, 2009; free online)
resource.why: MacKay totals the power per square metre of each renewable against Britain's land area, the clearest worked example of power density deciding what is possible.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); chapter title cited from prior knowledge. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: Watt Made Steam Engines Use Far Less Coal. Britain Burned Far More. Jevons Called It No Accident.
days.concept: Making energy use more efficient lowers the effective price of the service it provides, which can raise use and eat part of the saving (the rebound effect); whether it eats all of it (Jevons's paradox, backfire) is an empirical question, usually answered 'part'.
days.focus: Teaches direct, indirect and economy-wide rebound, why efficiency still usually saves energy, and the cases where backfire is plausible (a new general-purpose technology). Assumes Logan's CFA-level price elasticity and names it in a clause.
days.model_or_equation: Rebound = (expected savings - actual savings) / expected savings. 0% means efficiency saves fully; 100% means no saving; over 100% is backfire.

story.title: A 29-year-old's warning about coal, 1865
story.hook: In 1865 William Stanley Jevons, a 29-year-old lecturer in Manchester, published The Coal Question, asking whether Britain's prosperity could last as its cheap coal was used up. He met the comforting reply that better engines would stretch supplies with a striking claim: 'It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.' James Watt's engines, far more efficient than Newcomen's, had not saved coal; Britain's consumption had soared. Prime Minister Gladstone cited the book, and it made Jevons's name.
story.puzzle: If each engine burns less coal per unit of work, how can better engines make a country burn more coal?
story.payoff: Efficiency made steam power cheaper per unit of work, which opened uses that had never paid before: mines, mills, railways, ships. Total coal use rose because demand for steam power was very responsive to its cost and steam was a general-purpose technology. Jevons was right about his case; whether efficiency backfires in general depends on how much cheaper service raises demand.
sources: W. S. Jevons, The Coal Question (1865), ch. VII 'Of the Economy of Fuel'
Sorrell, 'Jevons' Paradox revisited', Energy Policy 37 (2009)

days.application: Fuel-efficient cars are driven more: Small and Van Dender (The Energy Journal, 2007), using US state data for 1966-2001, estimated a direct rebound of about 4.5% in the short run and about 22% in the long run, falling as incomes rise; later studies range from near zero to about 30%. So a car that is 20% more efficient saves perhaps 15-19% of fuel, not 20%, and not zero. This is the consequences-and-feedback link of the car chain.

builds_on.why: Rebound is a classic unintended consequence: the fix (efficiency) changes behaviour and partly undoes itself.
Watt's separate condenser raised steam engines' efficiency toward the Carnot limit, the gain whose effect Jevons studied.

across.link: Computing is the strongest modern candidate for backfire: energy per computation fell by many orders of magnitude (Koomey's law), and total data-centre electricity rose, with US data centres at about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 (LBNL 2024).

days.apply_question: LED bulbs use roughly a sixth of the electricity of incandescent bulbs for the same light, and outdoor lighting has spread with them; using the rebound effect, what would you need to measure to decide whether LEDs have reduced lighting's total electricity use?
days.evidence_note: Debated: the size of economy-wide rebound; most estimates find partial rebound for household energy services, while some economists argue backfire is common for general-purpose technologies (Saunders) and others that it is rare (Gillingham, Rapson & Wagner, 2016). Value judgment: whether more cheap energy services are themselves a benefit, as they are to the person who drives further.

resource.title: The Coal Question (1865), chapter VII 'Of the Economy of Fuel'
resource.creator: William Stanley Jevons (Macmillan, 1865; public domain)
resource.why: The original argument in Jevons's own words, with his evidence from steam engines and iron smelting, so Logan can judge the paradox at its source.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); chapter cited from prior knowledge; the book is public domain. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: A Swedish Statistician Called the Washing Machine the Greatest Invention of the Industrial Revolution. He Had Watched His Mother Load the First One.
days.concept: Energy use per person rises steeply with living standards at first and then with diminishing returns, and energy transitions are slow because the system that supplies it is vast and long-lived.
days.focus: Teaches the energy ladder (from muscle and biomass to electricity and liquid fuels), the concave relation between energy per head and human development measures, and Smil's point that transitions take decades because of the size and lifetimes of the infrastructure. Keeps the empirical curve apart from the moral question of how much is enough.

story.title: Laundry day in Sweden, as Hans Rosling told it
story.hook: In a December 2010 TEDWomen talk, the Swedish public-health professor Hans Rosling described the day in the early 1950s, when he was about four, that his family's first washing machine arrived. His mother had saved for years; his grandmother, who had hand-washed laundry all her life, heating water over a wood fire, sat watching the machine work for the whole programme, 'mesmerized'. His mother used the hours it freed to take him to the library. Rosling called the washing machine the greatest invention of the industrial revolution, and noted that most of the world's people still washed clothes by hand.
story.puzzle: Why would a statistician rank a laundry machine above the steam engine or the computer, and what does it say about how energy turns into human welfare?
story.payoff: The first units of modern energy, electricity and hot water replacing hours of human muscle, buy enormous gains: time, health, education, especially for women. Later units add comfort with diminishing returns. That concave curve means a kilowatt-hour does far more good at the bottom of the ladder than at the top, which is why access matters so much.
sources: Hans Rosling, 'The magic washing machine', TEDWomen, December 2010
Our World in Data, 'Energy' and 'Access to energy' pages (Ritchie, Rosado & Roser)
Vaclav Smil, Energy and Civilization: A History (MIT Press, 2017)

days.application: The world's energy ladder today: the IEA estimates roughly 700-750 million people still lack electricity, most in sub-Saharan Africa, and over two billion cook with polluting fuels; meanwhile primary energy per person in the richest countries is on the order of 100 times that of the poorest (Our World in Data). Smil's warning: fossil fuels still supply about 80% of global primary energy, and earlier transitions (wood to coal, coal to oil) took many decades.

builds_on.why: A human body at work delivers about 100 W; Buckminster Fuller's 'energy slaves' and Rosling's washing machine are that comparison turned into welfare.
A concave curve is a power law with an exponent below one; on log-log axes development indices flatten as energy per head rises.

across.link: Household electrification shifted women's work: Dinkelman's natural-experiment study of rural electrification in South Africa (American Economic Review, 2011) found female employment rose by about 9-10 percentage points.

days.apply_question: Some climate campaigners argue rich countries should cut energy use per head while poor countries raise theirs; using the concave energy-development curve, what would you need to know to judge where a cut costs the least welfare, and what would you need to value to decide whether it should be made?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the strong, concave correlation between energy use and development indices. Debated: causation (energy enables development, development raises energy use, or both) and how low rich-country use could go without welfare loss ('decent living energy' estimates). Value judgment: what level of energy use is 'enough', and who should cut.

resource.title: The magic washing machine
resource.creator: Hans Rosling, TED (TEDWomen 2010)
resource.why: Rosling's own telling of the story, with his famous chart dividing the world's people by energy use, a fast, vivid view of the energy ladder.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted); talk cited from prior knowledge (on ted.com). Cite without a link.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Energy, Chemistry & Materials
days.headline_hint: In 1856 Eunice Foote Put Carbon Dioxide in the Sun and Wrote That It Could Change the Climate. A Man Read Her Paper Aloud.
days.concept: Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases let sunlight in but absorb and re-emit the infrared Earth radiates; adding CO2 raises the forcing roughly with the logarithm of its concentration, and warming per doubling (climate sensitivity) is likely about 2.5-4 C.
days.focus: Teaches why molecules with three or more atoms absorb infrared (their vibrations), the energy balance, why the effect is logarithmic and why the emission height matters, and the distinction between radiative forcing (physics, well measured) and sensitivity (includes feedbacks, still a range). The one home for the greenhouse effect in the path.
days.model_or_equation: Delta F = 5.35 x ln(C/C0) W/m2 (Myhre et al., 1998): doubling CO2 gives about 3.7 W/m2. Warming = sensitivity x (forcing / forcing per doubling); IPCC AR6: likely 2.5-4 C per doubling, best estimate 3 C.

story.title: Two cylinders in the sun, Albany, August 1856
story.hook: At the American Association for the Advancement of Science meeting in Albany, New York, in August 1856, a paper by Eunice Newton Foote, 'Circumstances affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays', was read, by the Smithsonian's Joseph Henry, not by Foote. She had filled glass cylinders with different gases, set them in sunlight and recorded the temperatures; the one with 'carbonic acid gas' heated most and cooled slowest. She wrote that an atmosphere of that gas 'would give to our earth a high temperature'. Three years later in London, John Tyndall measured precisely how CO2 and water vapour absorb infrared, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling CO2 would warm Earth by several degrees.
story.puzzle: CO2 is transparent to sunlight and makes up only about 0.04% of the air. How can so little of an invisible gas warm a planet?
story.payoff: Sunlight passes through, but Earth radiates heat as infrared, and CO2 molecules vibrate at infrared frequencies, so they absorb and re-emit that heat, some of it back down. More CO2 makes the air opaque higher up, where it is colder, so the planet sheds heat less efficiently until it warms. A trace gas matters because it acts on the one band of radiation that controls the energy balance. (Foote's sunlit setup mixed several effects; Tyndall's infrared measurements isolated the mechanism.)
sources: Foote, American Journal of Science and Arts, 2nd series, 22 (Nov 1856)
Tyndall, Bakerian Lecture, Philosophical Transactions (1861); Proceedings of the Royal Institution (1859)
Arrhenius, Philosophical Magazine 41 (1896)
IPCC AR6 Working Group I, Summary for Policymakers (2021)

days.application: The Keeling curve and the carbon budget: Mauna Loa CO2 rose from about 315 ppm in 1958 to about 425 ppm by 2025 (D4). Because warming tracks cumulative emissions roughly linearly, scientists convert targets into a remaining budget: IPCC AR6 gave about 500 billion tonnes of CO2 from 2020 for a 50% chance of 1.5 C, and later updates (Forster et al., Indicators of Global Climate Change) put the remainder at roughly 130 billion tonnes from the start of 2025, a few years of current emissions. Transport, including cars, emits roughly a fifth of energy CO2: the consequences link of the car chain.

builds_on.why: The greenhouse effect is about the electromagnetic spectrum: visible sunlight in, infrared out, and molecules absorbing at particular frequencies.
Forcing grows with the logarithm of concentration, so each doubling adds the same push.
CO2 is a stock filled by emissions and drained slowly by oceans and land; stabilizing emissions does not stabilize the stock.

across.link: The Paris Agreement (2015) turned the carbon budget into nationally determined pledges reviewed every five years, a design chosen because, unlike the Montreal Protocol's few CFC producers, CO2 has billions of emitters.

days.apply_question: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 but breaks down in about a decade, while CO2 persists for centuries; using forcing and stocks and flows, why might cutting methane slow warming quickly but not substitute for cutting CO2?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the greenhouse mechanism, the measured rise in CO2 and that human emissions caused it, and that warming is under way (IPCC: 'unequivocal'). Debated: the exact climate sensitivity within the 2.5-4 C range, regional impacts and their costs, and tipping points. Value judgment: how fast to cut, at what cost, and who pays, which is policy, not physics.

resource.title: The Discovery of Global Warming, essay 'The Carbon Dioxide Greenhouse Effect'
resource.creator: Spencer R. Weart (American Institute of Physics, online edition; book Harvard UP, 2003/2008)
resource.why: A physicist-historian traces how Tyndall, Arrhenius and later scientists established the CO2 effect, including the early objections and how they were answered.

days.phase: Energy, Chemistry & Materials: What the World Is Made Of and Runs On
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 5: Haber-Bosch - bread from air
days.headline_hint: A Tabletop Machine in Karlsruhe Dripped Ammonia in 1909. Today Half of Humanity Eats Because of It, and It Also Made the Shells of the Western Front.
days.concept: How one reaction, fixing the air's nitrogen into ammonia, came to feed about half of humanity, and what that system has cost.
days.focus: Walks synthetic nitrogen through the chain as a loop: Crookes's 1898 warning (need), Haber's equilibrium and catalyst (invention), the pressure-temperature compromise (constraint), Bosch's scale-up (engineering), war (production), the fertilizer S-curve (adoption), population and pollution (consequences), and Haber himself (moral reading). Deep on equilibrium, catalysis, fossil feedstock, stocks and flows and ethics; previews engineering, biology and the war.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops: (1) Reinforcing: more fixed nitrogen -> more food -> more people -> more demand for fixed nitrogen. (2) Reinforcing (war): blockade of Chilean nitrate -> need for synthetic nitrate for explosives -> state-backed scale-up at Leuna (1917). (3) Balancing, delayed: excess nitrogen -> runoff -> dead zones and N2O -> nutrient rules and precision farming. (4) Energy coupling: ammonia depends on natural gas, so gas price shocks (2021-22) feed straight into fertilizer and food prices.

story.title: The drip in Karlsruhe, 2 July 1909
story.hook: On 2 July 1909, in Fritz Haber's laboratory at the Technical University of Karlsruhe, a tabletop apparatus built with his English assistant Robert Le Rossignol held nitrogen and hydrogen at about 200 atmospheres over an osmium catalyst. Before BASF's chemist Alwin Mittasch, it ran for hours, producing a steady drip of liquid ammonia, nitrogen pulled from the air. BASF's Carl Bosch then spent four years turning a lab bench into a factory: new steels for pressures that burst ordinary vessels, a cheap iron catalyst found by Mittasch after thousands of trials. In September 1913 the Oppau plant began producing ammonia at industrial scale.
story.puzzle: How did one reaction come to feed about half of humanity, and what has it cost?
story.payoff: Equilibrium said high pressure and moderate heat; catalysis made it fast enough; Bosch's engineering made it possible at scale; war paid for the scale-up; fossil gas made it cheap; fertilizer multiplied harvests. The same nitrogen now overloads rivers and seas, and the same chemistry made explosives. Every link is a reason it fed billions and a reason it costs something.
sources: Vaclav Smil, Enriching the Earth (MIT Press, 2001)
Thomas Hager, The Alchemy of Air (Harmony, 2008)
Erisman, Sutton, Galloway, Klimont & Winiwarter, 'How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world', Nature Geoscience 1 (2008)
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1918 (Haber) and 1931 (Bosch, with Bergius)

days.application: The Gulf of Mexico 'dead zone': nitrogen and phosphorus washed down the Mississippi from Midwestern farms feed algal blooms whose decay strips oxygen from bottom water each summer, over an area that has averaged roughly 14,000-15,000 km2 in recent decades (NOAA), against a federal-state task force goal of 5,000 km2 that has never been met.

builds_on.why: Le Chatelier sets the compromise: high pressure favours ammonia (four gas molecules become two), low temperature favours yield but slows the rate.
The iron catalyst lowers the activation barrier for breaking nitrogen's triple bond, making the reaction fast at 400-500 C.
Natural gas (or coal earlier) supplies the hydrogen and the energy, so fertilizer is fossil energy turned into food.
Reactive nitrogen is a stock with leaky flows: what crops do not take up leaches into water or escapes as N2O.

across.link: Germany's synthetic nitrate let it keep making explosives after the British blockade cut off Chilean saltpetre; without Haber-Bosch, many historians argue, Germany's war effort could not have lasted past about 1915-16.

days.apply_question: Green ammonia made with hydrogen from wind- or solar-powered electrolysis is being proposed both as fertilizer and as a ship fuel; using the loops in this case, what would you need to know to judge whether it could change the system's climate cost without changing its food benefit?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the chemistry, the global scale (synthetic fertilizer supplies roughly half the nitrogen in human food) and the nitrogen-pollution mechanisms. Debated: the exact share of humanity fed (Erisman et al. 48% for 2008; Smil about 40% for 2000) and the counterfactual, since without Haber-Bosch other routes (more legumes, more land) would have been pursued. Value judgment: weighing billions fed against war use, pollution and fossil dependence; consequentialist and virtue readings of Haber himself differ sharply. Who gained (eaters, farmers, BASF), who paid (soldiers at Ypres, coastal fisheries, future climate), and who consented: none of the downstream payers.

chain.point: Crookes's September 1898 British Association address in Bristol warned that wheat demand would outrun supply unless chemists could fix atmospheric nitrogen; Chilean saltpetre, the main nitrate source, was finite and controlled by a few exporters. Need here really did come before invention.
Haber and Le Rossignol's 2 July 1909 demonstration: N2 + 3 H2 <=> 2 NH3 at about 200 atm and around 500 C with an osmium catalyst, recycling unreacted gas because each pass converts only a fraction.

Nitrogen's triple bond is among the strongest in chemistry; equilibrium yield per pass is modest at workable temperatures; hydrogen at high pressure and temperature attacks steel. Pressure and heat are energy costs: modern plants use roughly 28-30 GJ per tonne of ammonia at best.
Hydrogen first came from coal-derived water gas, now mostly from steam reforming of natural gas; ammonia uses roughly 1-2% of world energy and emits on the order of 1% of global CO2.

Bosch's scale-up: double-walled reactors with a soft-iron liner against hydrogen embrittlement, high-pressure compressors and Mittasch's promoted iron catalyst found in thousands of trials. Engineering (the next block, Days 87-103) teaches the structures, fatigue and safety factors behind it.

BASF funded Oppau itself (1913); the far larger Leuna works (1917) were built under the Reich's wartime nitrate programme with state money, a war-financed scale-up. History II's World War I lesson (Day 230) teaches industrial war; the financing mechanism is named here, not taught.
Synthetic fertilizer use was small before 1950 and then followed an S-curve to roughly 110-120 million tonnes of nitrogen a year by the 2020s, with China the largest user.

Erisman et al. (2008) estimated that about 48% of the world's people were fed by Haber-Bosch nitrogen; it is the reinforcing loop of food and population. The crop side, semi-dwarf varieties bred to use fertilizer, is Biology's Green Revolution lesson (Day 146).

Humans now fix more reactive nitrogen than all natural land processes; runoff creates coastal dead zones (thresholds in oxygen), and N2O is a greenhouse gas about 270 times as potent as CO2 over a century. A fix for hunger feeding a new problem.

Nutrient rules such as the EU Nitrates Directive (1991) and the Dutch nitrogen crisis after a 2019 court ruling show regulation arriving decades after the harm; Government (Days 236-249) teaches how regulation works.

The same Haber directed chlorine gas at Ypres on 22 April 1915 (History, Day 230); his wife Clara Immerwahr, a chemist, killed herself days later. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize, and in 1933, as a Jew, was driven from Germany. A consequentialist tallies billions fed against war deaths; virtue ethics asks what his choices show about character and whether great benefit excuses them.

resource.creator: Thomas Hager (Harmony Books, 2008)
resource.length: book; the chapters on the 1909 demonstration and Oppau take about 45 minutes
resource.why: A narrative history of the whole system, Crookes's warning, Haber's lab, Bosch's factories and the wars, that lets Logan trace the loops in one story.
