days.model_or_equation: The Loops. R1, network effects: more users make the network more useful, which brings more users (Day 26). R2, permissionless innovation: open layers invite new applications (e-mail, the web, video), which bring more users and more investment in capacity. B1, congestion: more traffic causes delay and packet loss, TCP backs off, and operators add capacity. R3, concentration: preferential attachment makes the big hubs, networks and platforms bigger (Day 13), the internet's open design feeding its own centralization. R4, an attack-and-defence arms race: more value online draws more attacks, which spur encryption and security (Days 112, 114). Documented reversal: invention before need. E-mail (1971) was not in the plan.

story.title: 'LO' - and then the crash
story.hook: On the evening of 29 October 1969, in Boelter Hall at UCLA, the student programmer Charley Kline sat at a terminal connected to an Interface Message Processor, a ruggedized Honeywell minicomputer programmed by Bolt Beranek and Newman, which was linked by a leased 50-kilobit-per-second line to a second IMP at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, more than 300 miles to the north. Under Leonard Kleinrock's supervision, Kline began typing LOGIN while Bill Duvall at SRI confirmed each letter by telephone. The 'L' arrived, then the 'O'; at the 'G' the SRI system crashed. Later that night they got through, and the handwritten IMP log records 'talked to SRI host to host'. By December 1969 the ARPANET had four nodes.
story.puzzle: How did a four-node network built to share scarce research computers become infrastructure for about 5.5 billion people? And why, having been paid for by governments, is it governed by no single government?
story.payoff: Packet switching and end-to-end design (Day 111) let anyone add networks and applications without asking permission. Uses nobody planned, first e-mail and then the web, drove adoption up an S-curve (Day 7). Network effects reinforced growth while preferential attachment concentrated traffic into a few hubs and platforms (Day 13). Governance followed the architecture: open technical standards through the IETF's 'rough consensus and running code', and names and numbers through ICANN (1998), whose US government oversight ended in 2016, with states now pushing back.
sources: Leonard Kleinrock, accounts of 29 Oct 1969 (UCLA Samueli School of Engineering; Kleinrock Internet Heritage Site), including the IMP log entry
Katie Hafner & Matthew Lyon, Where Wizards Stay Up Late: The Origins of the Internet (Simon & Schuster, 1996)
Barry M. Leiner et al., 'A Brief History of the Internet' (Internet Society)
ITU, Measuring Digital Development: Facts and Figures 2024

days.application: The internet itself, traced through Logan's chain as a loop: from four ARPANET nodes at the end of 1969 to about 5.5 billion users (68% of humanity) in the ITU's 2024 count, with about 2.6 billion people still offline.

builds_on.why: Packet switching, layering and the end-to-end principle are the internet's architecture, the reason anyone could build on it without permission.
Networks: hubs and preferential attachment explain both the internet's robustness to random failure and its concentration into a few dominant nodes and platforms.
Logistic S-curves: internet adoption is a textbook diffusion S-curve, whose ceiling (the 2.6 billion offline) is the policy question.
Bits and channel capacity: the climb from 50-kilobit lines to fibre carrying many terabits per second is the physical constraint that every application rode.

across.link: Romualdo Pastor-Satorras and Alessandro Vespignani ('Epidemic Spreading in Scale-Free Networks', Physical Review Letters, 2001) showed, using data on computer viruses, that on networks with the internet's hub-dominated structure an infection can persist even when it spreads weakly: the epidemic threshold effectively vanishes. It is the same mathematics epidemiologists use for disease spreading through human contact networks, and it explains why internet worms linger and why protecting hubs matters most.

days.apply_question: Kenya's M-Pesa mobile-money service (launched 2007) was first piloted as a way to repay microloans. Using the chain as a loop, trace how M-Pesa, like the ARPANET with e-mail, found its main need only after it was invented.
days.evidence_note: Evidence check (mandatory). Settled: the 1969 timeline, the architecture, and the ITU's 2024 counts (about 5.5 billion online, about 2.6 billion offline, concentrated in low-income countries). Accounts differ on the exact hour of the first message: Kleinrock usually puts the 'LO' at about 10:30 p.m., while the IMP log's 22:30 entry records the successful host-to-host connection, so say 'that evening'. Debated, naming the sides: (1) how much credit public funding deserves (Mariana Mazzucato, The Entrepreneurial State, 2013, against critics such as Deirdre McCloskey and Alberto Mingardi, The Myth of the Entrepreneurial State, 2020); (2) the internet's net effects on well-being and democracy, including teen mental health (Haidt and Twenge against Odgers, Orben and Przybylski; taught in Psychology); (3) the often-cited 1973 finding that e-mail was about three-quarters of ARPANET traffic, which should be given as 'often cited'. Value judgment: who gained (users, platform owners, the economies that adopted early), who paid (taxpayers who funded the early research; victims of fraud, surveillance and harassment), and who consented (users to data collection under terms few read). A Rawlsian reading asks whether the digital divide leaves the worst-off behind; Catholic social teaching's universal destination of goods asks a similar question in different terms. Keep the counterfactual of a world without the internet marked as unknowable.

chain.point: In 1966 Bob Taylor, head of ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office, had three terminals in his Pentagon office for three incompatible research computers. The need was to share scarce, expensive machines; by Taylor's account ARPA director Charles Herzfeld gave him about $1 million in a meeting of some twenty minutes.

Packet switching (Baran 1964, Davies 1965), BBN's IMPs (1969), TCP/IP (Cerf and Kahn, 1974; adopted network-wide on 1 January 1983), then Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web (proposed at CERN in March 1989, public in 1991, released by CERN into the public domain on 30 April 1993).

Bandwidth is bounded by channel capacity (Day 104): from 50 kbit/s lines in 1969 to fibres carrying many terabits per second, carried on infrared light (Day 61). Latency is bounded by light in glass, about 200,000 km/s, so a New York to London round trip through fibre can never beat about 55 ms. Energy and heat appear in data centres (Day 113).

Layering and the end-to-end principle keep the core simple. The resulting hub-dominated structure is robust to random failures but fragile to attacks on hubs (Albert, Jeong & Barabasi, Nature, 2000). Submarine cables carry the great majority of intercontinental traffic, redundant paths matter (Days 13, 93), and Tonga's single cable showed the cost of having none.

chain.field: Financing (named at CFA level; no block teaches it)
chain.point: Public money built the core: ARPA funded the ARPANET, and the NSF funded NSFNET (1985-95) as the backbone. Congress allowed commercial traffic in 1992, the NSFNET backbone was retired on 30 April 1995, and private carriers took over; today hyperscalers' capital spending funds the cables and data centres. Name the mechanism; do not teach finance.

Light-touch rules shaped what grew: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) shields platforms from liability for most user posts, a choice the Law block takes up with intermediary liability and the Collingridge dilemma.

A diffusion S-curve (Day 7): tens of millions of users in the mid-1990s, about a billion in the mid-2000s, about 5.5 billion (68%) in 2024 (ITU). The remaining 2.6 billion are concentrated in low-income countries, where only about a quarter of people are online.

Openness invited attack: from the Morris worm (1988) to state operations like Sandworm's (Day 114), with encryption (Day 112) spreading in response so that most web traffic now runs over HTTPS. The physical footprint grows with use (Day 113).

Effects on teenage mental health are contested (Haidt and Twenge against Odgers, Orben and Przybylski), as is how far false news outruns true news (Vosoughi, Roy & Aral, 2018). These are taught in Psychology's social-media case and Sociology's media-effects lesson.

Governance follows the architecture: the IETF sets open standards, and ICANN (1998) manages names and numbers, with US government oversight of IANA ending on 1 October 2016. States push back with national firewalls and Russia's 2019 'sovereign internet' law, the 'splinternet' that the International Relations block takes up with chokepoints and international institutions.

Ray Tomlinson's network e-mail (1971) was not in the ARPANET's plan, yet by an often-cited 1973 estimate it made up about three-quarters of the traffic. The users found the need after the invention, the reverse of the chain's textbook order, and openness then drove growth that ended in concentration into a few platforms.

resource.title: A Brief History of the Internet
resource.creator: Barry M. Leiner, Vinton G. Cerf, David D. Clark, Robert E. Kahn, Leonard Kleinrock, Daniel C. Lynch, Jon Postel, Lawrence G. Roberts, Stephen Wolff (Internet Society)
resource.why: The internet's history told by the people who built it: the ARPANET's origins and the correction of the nuclear-war myth, TCP/IP, NSFNET's role, and the open, community-based way the internet came to be governed. It adds the builders' own view of today's 'who governs it?' question.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search in either pass (the session's shared search budget was exhausted, and direct page fetches failed in this environment); cited from prior knowledge of the Internet Society's published history and its nine authors. Confirm its page on internetsociety.org before linking; no URL given.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: one inverse-square law explains the falling apple, the Moon's orbit and the tides. Story: in summer 1774 Nevil Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal, camped on the Scottish mountain Schiehallion to measure how far its mass pulled a plumb line from the vertical; Charles Hutton's analysis (1778) put Earth's mean density at about 4.5 times water (the modern value is 5.5) - the first weighing of the planet - and Hutton is often credited with inventing contour lines to compute the mountain's volume (earlier isobath maps existed). App: the GRACE satellites weigh groundwater from orbit and showed northern India's aquifers draining (Rodell et al., Nature 2009).

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: an orbit is free fall with enough sideways speed - about 7.8 km/s near Earth; higher orbits are slower, and Kepler's laws follow. Story: Sputnik 1 (4 Oct 1957), 83.6 kg, circling every 96 minutes and beeping to the world. App: why astronauts float on the ISS where gravity is still about 90% of surface strength, and why geostationary satellites sit 35,786 km up (Arthur C. Clarke, 1945).

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: The solar system: a disk, its leftovers and impacts
days.focus: Concept: the planets formed from a flattened disk of gas and dust around the young Sun - which is why they orbit in one plane, rocky worlds inside and giants outside - and the disk's leftovers, asteroids and comets, still strike planets at rates that fall steeply with size (D118, D12). Story: from 16 to 22 Jul 1994 more than 20 fragments of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 hit Jupiter; the largest, fragment G, released energy estimated at about 6 million megatons of TNT and left a dark scar about the size of Earth. App: Luis and Walter Alvarez's 1980 iridium-layer argument (Science) that an impact ended the dinosaurs - resisted for a decade until the Chicxulub crater was identified (Hildebrand et al., Geology 1991) - and why NASA now surveys near-Earth asteroids.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: a rocket's change in speed is exhaust speed times the logarithm of its mass ratio (D2, D51), so most of a rocket is propellant and staging helps. Story: Robert Goddard's first liquid-fuel rocket flew 2.5 seconds at Auburn, Massachusetts (16 Mar 1926); the New York Times had mocked him in 1920 and printed a correction on 17 Jul 1969. App: Saturn V - about 2,900 tonnes on the pad to send roughly 45 tonnes toward the Moon.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Reusability and the cost of reaching orbit
days.focus: Concept: launch cost per kilogram is the master variable of spaceflight, and reusing hardware attacks it. Story: on 21 Dec 2015 a Falcon 9 first stage landed upright at Cape Canaveral for the first time. App: NASA's estimates of cost per kg to low orbit falling from tens of thousands of dollars (Shuttle) to a few thousand (Falcon 9), and the satellite constellations that made possible.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: Apollo was a prestige project in a superpower contest - a mission-driven state programme - and its wider payoffs are often exaggerated (spin-off myths), though careful estimates find real if modest gains for space-related manufacturing (Kantor & Whalley, 'Moonshot', AER 2025). Story: Kennedy's address to Congress on 25 May 1961 committing to a Moon landing 'before this decade is out'. App: Apollo's roughly $25.8 billion and peak of over 4% of the federal budget, compared with Artemis and the Space Launch System's overruns (NASA Inspector General).

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: orbit choice follows the job - geostationary for broadcast, low orbit for imaging and low latency, sun-synchronous for Earth observation. Story: Telstar 1 relayed the first live transatlantic television on 23 Jul 1962. App: weather satellites and hurricane-track forecasts, whose errors the National Hurricane Center has cut sharply since 1990 - measured progress.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Space debris and the orbital commons
days.focus: Concept: collisions create fragments that cause more collisions - the Kessler syndrome, a reinforcing loop in a commons (D26, D30). Story: on 10 Feb 2009 Iridium 33 and the dead Kosmos 2251 collided over Siberia; China's 2007 anti-satellite test had already made thousands of tracked fragments. App: Russia's 15 Nov 2021 anti-satellite test sent the ISS crew to shelter.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: solar storms and coronal mass ejections disturb Earth's magnetic field and induce currents in long conductors - a rare, fat-tailed hazard to grids and satellites (D12). Story: the Carrington Event (1 Sep 1859) sparked telegraph lines; on 13 Mar 1989 a storm blacked out Quebec. App: in February 2022 a modest geomagnetic storm destroyed about 40 newly launched Starlink satellites.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: a star balances gravity against the pressure of fusion in its core; its mass sets its life. Story: Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis showed stars are mostly hydrogen; Henry Norris Russell called it impossible, then confirmed it in 1929. App: fusion on Earth - the National Ignition Facility got 3.15 MJ out from 2.05 MJ of laser energy (5 Dec 2022), still far from a power plant.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.focus: Concept: elements beyond hydrogen and helium were forged in stars, supernovae and neutron-star mergers (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler & Hoyle 1957). Story: Fred Hoyle's 1953 prediction of a carbon resonance near 7.65 MeV, confirmed in Fowler's lab - later retold as an 'anthropic' prediction and cited in fine-tuning arguments, a retelling the historian Helge Kragh (2010) argues Hoyle did not make at the time. App: the neutron-star merger GW170817 (17 Aug 2017), whose kilonova showed mergers forge heavy elements such as gold - how much of the universe's gold they make is debated.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Measuring the cosmos: the distance ladder
days.focus: Concept: astronomers chain methods - parallax, then standard candles - to measure distances no one can travel. Story: Henrietta Leavitt's 1912 period-luminosity law for Cepheid stars; Edwin Hubble's October 1923 plate of Andromeda, where he wrote 'VAR!', showed it lay beyond the Milky Way, settling the 1920 Shapley-Curtis debate. App: the 'Hubble tension' - about 67 versus 73 km/s/Mpc - a live disagreement.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: The expanding universe and the Big Bang
days.focus: Concept: redshifts, the cosmic microwave background and the light-element abundances together establish a hot, expanding early universe. Story: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson's 1964-65 antenna hiss at Holmdel, New Jersey, which they first blamed on pigeon droppings (Nobel 1978); Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest, had proposed the expanding universe in 1927. App: dark matter and dark energy - roughly 95% of the universe's content still unexplained.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Space & Astronomy
days.topic: Other worlds and the search for life
days.focus: Concept: planets are found by the wobble and the shadow they cause; the Drake equation (1961) structures our ignorance about life elsewhere rather than resolving it. Story: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced 51 Pegasi b in October 1995 - a giant planet in a four-day orbit that theory said could not exist (Nobel 2019). App: the 2025 claim of a possible biosignature gas on K2-18b and why other astronomers doubt it.

days.phase: Space & Astronomy: Orbits, Stars and Space as Infrastructure
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 8: GPS - the invisible utility
days.focus: Story: on 1 Sep 1983 Soviet fighters shoot down Korean Air Lines 007 after it strays into Soviet airspace, killing 269; on 16 Sep the Reagan White House says GPS will be open to civilians. Question: how did a military clock in the sky become global infrastructure - and what happens if it fails? Deep: orbits (D118); relativity's 38 microseconds a day (D62); radio signals (D61); solving four unknowns (x, y, z and clock error) with vectors (D9); space weather and jamming (D125). Preview: US Air Force funding as a free public good (named at CFA level); Selective Availability switched off on 1-2 May 2000 (Government); spectrum fights such as LightSquared (Law); Galileo, BeiDou and GLONASS as sovereignty (International Relations). Loop: a disaster opened the system; dependence grew faster than backups; jamming and spoofing near conflict zones now feed back into calls for alternatives (an RTI study for NIST estimated about $1.4 trillion in US benefits since the 1980s).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: the cell is the unit of life - a membrane, a metabolism and a genome - and every cell comes from a cell (Virchow 1855). Story: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's October 1676 letter to the Royal Society describing 'animalcules' in water; sceptical Fellows had Robert Hooke confirm it. App: cancer as cells escaping the controls on division.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: cells capture food energy by controlled oxidation and store it as ATP (D70, D52); a resting human runs at about 100 W. Story: Lavoisier and Laplace's ice calorimeter (1782-83) showed a guinea pig's heat matched the burning of the carbon it breathed out. App: the calorie on a food label and why marathoners 'hit the wall' when glycogen runs out.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction produces adaptation; the evidence from fossils, genomes and observed change is overwhelming (settled science). Story: after the 1977 drought on Daphne Major, Peter and Rosemary Grant measured average beak depth in medium ground finches rising about 4% in one generation (Boag & Grant, Science 1981). App: Omicron and later COVID variants - selection observed in real time.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: DNA stores information as a base sequence copied by complementary pairing; genes are read into proteins (the central dogma). Story: Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 (May 1952) was shown to James Watson in January 1953 without her knowledge; the double helix appeared in Nature on 25 Apr 1953. App: DNA fingerprinting - Alec Jeffreys's method convicted Colin Pitchfork in 1988 after first clearing an innocent suspect.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: inheritance runs through discrete genes; most traits are polygenic, and heritability is a population statistic, not a fixed destiny. Story: Gregor Mendel's 1866 pea paper was ignored until 1900; R.A. Fisher later argued (1936) that his data were 'too good to be true' - still debated. App: Huntington's disease, a single dominant gene, mapped with Nancy Wexler's work among Venezuelan families from 1979.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: CRISPR-Cas9 cuts DNA at a programmed sequence (Doudna & Charpentier 2012; Nobel 2020); editing body cells and editing heritable embryos are ethically different acts. Story: in November 2018 He Jiankui announced twin girls edited as embryos; a Chinese court jailed him for three years in December 2019. App: Casgevy, the first approved CRISPR therapy, for sickle-cell disease (FDA, 8 Dec 2023).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Ecology: food webs and trophic cascades
days.focus: Concept: populations grow toward carrying capacity (D7) and interact through food webs; removing a top predator can cascade down (keystone species, Paine 1966). Story: grey wolves returned to Yellowstone in January 1995; claims that they rewired the whole ecosystem are now debated in size. App: why ecosystem interventions surprise their designers (D29).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: extinction risk rises with habitat loss and small numbers (Allee effects); how to measure biodiversity decline is itself contested. Story: Martha, the last passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 Sep 1914 - from billions to none in a century. App: the Living Planet Index's reported 73% average decline (WWF 2024) and the critique that a few collapsing populations drive it (Leung et al., Nature 2020).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: specific microbes cause specific diseases (Pasteur; Koch's postulates), replacing miasma; it turned hygiene into science. Story: Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths in Vienna's doctor-run maternity clinic in 1847 by making doctors wash in chlorinated lime; he was rejected and died in an asylum in 1865. App: checklists against hospital infection - Peter Pronovost's Michigan ICU programme cut catheter bloodstream infections by about two-thirds (NEJM 2006).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: adaptive immunity remembers; vaccination trains it without the disease, and herd immunity needs coverage above 1 - 1/R0, where R0 is the number of people one case infects in a susceptible population (D11: Bernoulli's inoculation sum). Story: Boston, 1721 - Cotton Mather learned of inoculation from Onesimus, an enslaved West African man; Zabdiel Boylston's inoculated patients died at about 2% against about 14% from natural smallpox, and a bomb was thrown into Mather's house. App: smallpox eradication (last natural case, Merca, Somalia, Oct 1977; declared 1980) and measles, whose R0 of 12-18 needs about 95% coverage.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: whether an outbreak becomes a pandemic depends on R0 (D141), generation time, severity and how much spread happens before symptoms (Fraser et al., PNAS 2004). Story: West Africa's Ebola epidemic began with a toddler in Meliandou, Guinea, in December 2013 and grew to about 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths. App: why SARS (2003) was contained and COVID-19 was not - presymptomatic transmission.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: when you cannot randomize, cohort and case-control studies plus Bradford Hill's 1965 viewpoints (strength, consistency, dose-response, temporality...) build causal cases (D18). Story: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's 30 Sep 1950 BMJ case-control study of smoking and lung cancer, followed by the British Doctors Study. App: how the CDC reasoned that Zika virus causes microcephaly (Rasmussen et al., NEJM 2016).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: population-scale public-health engineering - filtration, chlorination, sewers - cut waterborne disease faster than any medicine of its time. Story: in September 1908 John Leal began continuous chlorination of Jersey City's water at Boonton Reservoir, defending it in court. App: how much of the US urban mortality decline clean water explains - about half (Cutler & Miller, Demography 2005) or much less (Anderson, Charles & Rees, AEJ: Applied 2022).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: life expectancy is a period statistic (a definition, not a lifespan), and its doubling came mostly from collapsing child mortality - whose causes (nutrition, sanitation, medicine, income) are debated (D144, D140, D141). Story: Thomas McKeown's 1976 argument that most of the fall in tuberculosis deaths came before any effective drug, so nutrition, not medicine, did it - answered by Preston (1975) and Szreter (1988). App: global under-five mortality from roughly 4 in 10 children around 1800 to under 4 in 100 today.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: yields multiplied through dwarf varieties bred to use fertilizer (D86) and irrigation; the costs (groundwater, inequality, diversity) are debated. Story: Norman Borlaug shipped semi-dwarf wheat seed to India and Pakistan in 1965-66 despite riots and a war delaying the shipment (Nobel Peace 1970). App: Punjab's falling water table - the bill for the gains.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Why nutrition science is so hard
days.focus: Concept: diet studies face confounding, measurement error and funding bias, so single findings are weak evidence (D18, D22). Story: the Sugar Research Foundation paid Harvard scientists for a 1967 NEJM review that played down sugar and blamed fat (Kearns, Schmidt & Glantz, JAMA Internal Medicine 2016). App: 'Is everything we eat associated with cancer?' - Schoenfeld & Ioannidis (2013) found studies linking 40 of 50 common cookbook ingredients to cancer risk, often in both directions.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.topic: Chronic disease and the epidemiological transition
days.focus: Concept: as infections fall, chronic diseases dominate (Omran 1971), and 'risk factors' become the unit of prevention. Story: the Framingham Heart Study began in 1948 with 5,209 adults and gave medicine the phrase 'risk factor' (1961). App: GLP-1 drugs - about 15% weight loss in the STEP-1 trial (2021) and 20% fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths in SELECT (2023).

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: research on people requires respect for persons (consent), beneficence and justice - the Belmont Report's principles (1979). Story: the Tuskegee study (1932-72) followed 399 Black men with syphilis without treatment, even after penicillin; Jean Heller's AP story in July 1972 led to its end that year. App: Henrietta Lacks's cells, taken without consent in 1951, and her family's 2023 settlement with Thermo Fisher.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: neurons signal electrically along axons and chemically at synapses (D59); brain regions specialize but behaviour comes from networks, and connections change with use (plasticity). Story: Phineas Gage survived a tamping iron through his frontal lobe (13 Sep 1848) and was reported to be 'no longer Gage' - accounts grew in the retelling. App: brain-computer interfaces - Neuralink's first implant (January 2024) let a paralysed man move a cursor.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Biology, Medicine & Health
days.focus: Concept: dopamine neurons signal reward prediction error - better or worse than expected - which drives learning and, when hijacked, addiction (Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997). Story: James Olds and Peter Milner's 1954 rats pressed a lever again and again to stimulate their own brains. App: the opioid epidemic - about 108,000 US drug overdose deaths in 2022, roughly three-quarters involving opioids (CDC) - and the debate over calling addiction a brain disease.

days.phase: Biology, Medicine & Health: Life, Disease and the Mortality Revolution
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 9: Antibiotics - from mould to resistance
days.focus: Story: in September 1928 Alexander Fleming returns to St Mary's and finds mould killing staphylococci on a dish (the open-window detail is legend); in February 1941 the Oxford team of Florey and Chain treat a policeman, Albert Alexander, who improves and then dies when the drug runs out. Question: how did a mould become a mass-produced miracle - and why is it failing? Deep: germ theory (D140); evolution of resistance by selection (D134); epidemiology and trials (D143, D20); the mortality revolution (D145); production - US wartime deep-tank fermentation and Peoria's 1943 cantaloupe strain, scaled like any mass-production process (D96, D97); resistance as a commons with a reinforcing loop (D30, D26). Preview: patents and the empty pipeline named at CFA level; farm-antibiotic rules and drug approval (Government). Loop: success bred overuse; drug-resistant infections were linked to about 1.14 million deaths in 2021 (GRAM, Lancet 2024), and the market for new antibiotics broke, prompting England's subscription contracts from 2022.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: Millions Saw White and Gold, Millions Saw Blue and Black - From the Same Pixels. Nobody's Eyes Were Broken.
days.concept: Perception is the brain's best guess about the world, built by combining sparse, ambiguous sensory input with prior expectations - Helmholtz's 'unconscious inference', which modern researchers describe in Bayesian terms.
days.focus: Teach perception as an inverse problem: the light reaching the eye could have come from many different worlds, so the brain infers the most probable one using priors (for colour, a prior about the lighting). The dress shows two priors disagreeing; inattentional blindness shows expectation and attention deciding what reaches awareness at all. This is Day 15's Bayes running inside the head.
key_concepts: prior and likelihood in perception (Bayesian and predictive accounts)
days.model_or_equation: Perception as Bayesian inference: P(scene | image) is proportional to P(image | scene) x P(scene). For colour, the light reaching the eye is roughly the illuminant's spectrum multiplied by the surface's reflectance, so one image fits many (illuminant, surface) pairs; the prior over illuminants picks the answer you consciously see.

story.title: One photo of a dress, two internets
story.hook: In February 2015 Cecilia Bleasdale photographed a dress at the Cheshire Oaks outlet near Chester, England, and sent the picture to her daughter Grace, who was about to marry on the Scottish island of Colonsay. Grace and her fiance could not agree what colour it was. On 26 February (some accounts say the 25th) the couple's friend Caitlin McNeill posted it on Tumblr; BuzzFeed picked it up, and at the peak Tumblr counted about 840,000 views a minute. The dress was royal blue and black. When Rosa Lafer-Sousa, Katherine Hermann and Bevil Conway surveyed about 1,400 people (Current Biology, 2015), 57% saw blue and black, 30% white and gold, and 11% blue and brown.
story.puzzle: The same pixels reached every eye, and both camps had normal colour vision and complete confidence. How can one photograph be two different colours?
story.payoff: The photo is ambiguous about the light falling on the dress, and every colour you see has had an assumed illuminant 'subtracted' (colour constancy). People who unconsciously assumed bluish daylight or shade discounted the blue and saw white and gold; those who assumed warm artificial light saw blue and black. Same input, same likelihood, different priors - and Witzel, Racey and O'Regan (2017) could steer what people saw by changing their assumption about the lighting first.
sources: Lafer-Sousa, Hermann & Conway, 'Striking individual differences in color perception uncovered by "the dress" photograph', Current Biology 25 (2015)
Witzel, Racey & O'Regan, 'The most reasonable explanation of "the dress": Implicit assumptions about illumination', Journal of Vision 17 (2017)
Wellesley College news release on the Conway study, June 2015
Wikipedia, 'The dress' (dates; Tumblr and BuzzFeed sequence; 840,000 views per minute per Tumblr)

days.application: 'Looked but failed to see' crashes. In the UK's in-depth study of more than 1,000 motorcycle crashes (Clarke, Ward, Bartle & Truman, Department for Transport Road Safety Research Report 54, 2004), right-of-way violations at junctions were a leading crash type, in many of which a car driver reported looking but not seeing the rider. Inattentional blindness - about half of Simons and Chabris's 1999 observers, counting basketball passes, missed a person in a gorilla suit - explains how a driver can look straight at a motorcycle and not perceive it: the brain is predicting cars, not small, rare vehicles. (Car chain: consequences - and the engineering response of conspicuity, such as headlights on by day.)

builds_on.why: Bayes' theorem: perception weighs the likelihood of the image under each possible scene by a prior, exactly the posterior-from-prior-and-likelihood logic of Day 15.
Light and the spectrum: the light entering the eye is the illuminant's spectrum times the surface's reflectance, which is why colour is ambiguous and must be inferred.

across.link: Digital cameras face the dress problem every time they set automatic white balance: the 'grey-world' algorithm (Buchsbaum, 1980) assumes a scene averages to grey and divides out the estimated illuminant - an engineered prior that fails on scenes that are not grey on average (a beach, a forest), much as human colour constancy split on the dress.

days.apply_question: In a 2013 study by Trafton Drew, Melissa Vo and Jeremy Wolfe, 20 of 24 radiologists searching lung CT scans for nodules failed to notice a gorilla image about 48 times the size of a typical nodule, though eye-tracking showed many looked right at it. Using perception as inference, why did the radiologists' expertise - the very thing that makes them good at finding nodules - fail to protect them here?
days.evidence_note: Settled: perception depends on context and expectation; colour constancy and inattentional blindness are robust, widely replicated findings. Debated: whether the brain literally performs Bayesian inference, or 'predictive processing' as a general theory of mind (Friston, Clark, Seth), versus Bayes as a useful description of some tasks; and why individuals differ on the dress (the lighting-assumption account has the best support; a link to chronotype, early birds versus night owls, is weaker).

resource.title: Your brain hallucinates your conscious reality
resource.creator: Anil Seth (TED2017)
resource.why: A neuroscientist's account of perception as 'controlled hallucination' - prediction checked against the senses - the strongest version of today's idea, which Logan can weigh against the debate in the Evidence note.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session: talk page indexed at ted.com under this slug (TED2017, Anil Seth); not fetched. Length is from memory and was not confirmed by the search.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: She Studied His Face So She Could Never Forget It. She Picked the Wrong Man - and Grew More Certain.
days.concept: Remembering is reconstruction, not playback: each recall rebuilds an event from stored fragments plus present knowledge, so later information - a question's wording, a photograph, a word of feedback - can be absorbed into the memory itself (the misinformation effect).
days.focus: Teach memory as encoding, storage and reconstructive retrieval; show how post-event information and confirming feedback reshape both content and confidence, and what that means for evidence. Include the modern correction (Wixted & Wells 2017): confidence at a first, fair, uncontaminated identification is informative; confidence expressed later is not.
days.model_or_equation: Recollection = stored fragments + general knowledge + cues present at retrieval (questions, photos, feedback). The rebuilt version can be stored again, so each retelling can change what is retrieved next time - a loop, not a recording.

story.title: The face she memorized on purpose
story.hook: In July 1984, in Burlington, North Carolina, a man broke into the apartment of Jennifer Thompson, a 22-year-old college student, and raped her. During the attack she deliberately studied his face so that she could identify him. She picked Ronald Cotton from a photo lineup and then from a live lineup; in January 1985 a jury convicted him, and he was sentenced to life plus 50 years. When the North Carolina Supreme Court ordered a new trial, the defence had Bobby Poole - another inmate, who had reportedly claimed the crime - brought into the courtroom. Thompson looked at him and, by her own account, said she had never seen him in her life. Cotton was convicted again in November 1987. In 1995 DNA testing excluded Cotton and matched Poole; Cotton walked free on 30 June 1995 after more than ten years in prison.
story.puzzle: Thompson was careful, intelligent and honest, and she had tried hard to remember. How could her memory be so wrong - and grow more certain with every telling?
story.payoff: Her memory was rebuilt each time she retrieved it. Cotton's face - from the photo array, the live lineup, the courtroom - was folded into the reconstruction until it replaced the attacker's, and confirming feedback raised her confidence. By her own later account her first identification was hesitant; the certainty came afterwards. By 1987 she was faithfully recalling a memory that had been rewritten.
sources: Innocence Project case profile, 'Ronald Cotton'
National Registry of Exonerations, Ronald Cotton
Thompson-Cannino, Cotton & Torneo, Picking Cotton (St. Martin's Press, 2009)
PBS Frontline, 'What Jennifer Saw' (1997)

days.application: Loftus and Palmer's 1974 experiments (Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior): students watched films of car crashes. Asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed into' each other, they estimated about 40.8 mph; with 'hit', about 34 mph. A week later 16 of 50 in the 'smashed' group remembered broken glass - there was none - against 7 of 50 for 'hit' and 6 of 50 with no speed question. The same science drove the National Academy of Sciences report Identifying the Culprit (2014): double-blind lineups, standard instructions, and recording a witness's confidence at the first identification, before memory is contaminated.

builds_on.why: Recall uses the same constructive machinery as perception: a best guess filled in from expectation, so later information can be built into the 'memory' as priors are built into a percept.
Testimony, priors and extraordinary claims: how much weight a witness's word deserves depends on how the testimony was produced, which reconstructive memory now explains.

across.link: In State v. Henderson (2011) the New Jersey Supreme Court, after a court-appointed special master reviewed the memory research, required new jury instructions explaining how factors such as suggestive procedures and confirming feedback affect eyewitness identifications - the psychology written into the rules of evidence.

days.apply_question: Many US police departments let officers watch their body-camera footage before writing a use-of-force report. Using reconstructive memory, should an officer's own account be taken before or after viewing the footage, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: memory is reconstructive and suggestible; misleading post-event information can alter what people report (hundreds of studies). Debated: how often this distorts real testimony; the 1990s 'recovered memory' disputes; and the confidence-accuracy question, where Wixted and Wells (2017) argue that high confidence at an initial, fair, double-blind identification is quite diagnostic even though later confidence is not. Eyewitness misidentification played a role in roughly 70% of the Innocence Project's DNA exonerations - a figure about known failures, not the overall error rate.

resource.title: How reliable is your memory?
resource.creator: Elizabeth Loftus (TEDGlobal 2013)
resource.why: The researcher behind the misinformation effect explains, through real wrongful-conviction cases and her own experiments, how false memories are made - the lesson's mechanism told by the person who found it.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session: talk page indexed on ted.com at this slug (TEDGlobal 2013, posted June 2013); duration 17:36 from Amara's subtitle listing; not fetched.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: B.F. Skinner Taught Pigeons to Steer a Bomb. The Hard Part Wasn't the Pigeons.
days.concept: Behaviour is shaped by its consequences - actions followed by reinforcement become more frequent, actions followed by punishment less - and rewards delivered unpredictably (variable schedules) build the most persistent habits (Skinner's operant conditioning).
days.focus: Teach operant conditioning: positive and negative reinforcement versus punishment, shaping by successive approximation, and schedules of reinforcement, with the variable-ratio schedule's resistance to extinction. Then its limits - Chomsky's 1959 critique - and the gap between changing behaviour and winning consent. Day 151 gave the neural signal; this is the behavioural law it serves.
key_concepts: positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement and punishment
schedules of reinforcement (fixed or variable, ratio or interval)
days.model_or_equation: Consequences, two by two: add something pleasant (positive reinforcement) or remove something aversive (negative reinforcement) and the behaviour rises; add something aversive (positive punishment) or remove something pleasant (negative punishment) and it falls. Schedules: fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, variable-interval. Variable-ratio produces high, steady responding that is slowest to extinguish when rewards stop.

story.title: A bird in the nose cone
story.hook: In 1943, on the top floor of a General Mills flour mill in Minneapolis, the psychologist B. F. Skinner was training pigeons to steer a bomb. Under a small wartime contract from the National Defense Research Committee (about $25,000 by most accounts; one account says $30,000), his team built a nose cone for the Pelican glide bomb with three pigeons inside, each facing a screen showing the target; a pigeon's pecks at an off-centre image moved the steering. While waiting for approval to go on, Skinner and his students Keller Breland and Norman Guttman tried to teach a pigeon to 'bowl' a small wooden ball down a miniature alley - and found they could do it quickly by reinforcing, by hand, each closer approximation. The pigeons tracked targets well in demonstrations, yet the project was cancelled on 8 October 1944; the Navy revived it as Project Orcon in 1948 and dropped it in 1953 once electronic guidance proved reliable.
story.puzzle: A pigeon has no language and no idea what a ship is. How do you get one to perform a skill no pigeon has ever performed - and keep pecking accurately, with no grain, inside a falling bomb?
story.payoff: Shaping: reinforce each small step toward the target behaviour, immediately, until the whole skill appears. Persistence: train on intermittent, unpredictable reinforcement, which makes behaviour slow to extinguish - exactly what a bird in a dive with no reward needs. And the cancellation is part of the lesson: as Skinner later wrote, the method worked; persuading the committee to take a pigeon seriously did not.
sources: B. F. Skinner, 'Pigeons in a Pelican', American Psychologist 15 (1960)
Gail B. Peterson, 'A day of great illumination: B. F. Skinner's discovery of shaping', Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior 82 (2004)
Wikipedia, 'Project Pigeon' (cancellation date 8 Oct 1944; Project Orcon 1948-53)

days.application: The 1974 seat-belt interlock. Federal rules for 1974-model cars required a system that kept the engine from starting until front-seat occupants buckled. By one study belt use rose from about 7% in 1973 cars to about 48% - and the public revolted. The House voted 339 to 49 to end the requirement; the Motor Vehicle and Schoolbus Safety Amendments of 1974 (October 1974) barred interlocks and limited the warning buzzer to eight seconds, and NHTSA dropped the requirement on 29 October 1974. Compare Ford's BeltMinder (from the 2000 model year): an intermittent chime the driver can end by buckling - negative reinforcement - which raised observed driver belt use from 71% to 76% at 12 Oklahoma dealerships (Williams, Wells & Farmer, Injury Prevention, 2002). (Car chain: regulation and adoption.)

builds_on.why: Dopamine's reward-prediction-error signal is the neural mechanism of reinforcement; today's lesson is the behavioural law that signal produces.
Feedback control: the pigeon was the error-sensing element in a closed guidance loop, pecking harder the further the target drifted off-centre.

across.link: Natasha Dow Schull's ethnography Addiction by Design (Princeton University Press, 2012) documents how Las Vegas slot machines are engineered around the variable-ratio schedule - frequent small wins, near misses, uninterrupted play - operant conditioning built into a product and a business.

days.apply_question: In April 2018 Belgium's gaming regulator found that paid 'loot boxes' - video-game purchases with randomized contents - in several games amounted to illegal gambling. Using schedules of reinforcement, why would a loot box keep a player paying more persistently than a shop that sells the same items at a fixed price?
days.evidence_note: Settled: reinforcement, shaping, schedule effects and extinction are among psychology's most replicated findings across species and underpin applied behaviour analysis. Debated: how much human behaviour they explain (Chomsky's 1959 review of Skinner's Verbal Behavior argued language cannot be learned this way), and whether 'variable reward' design in apps and games produces addiction or ordinary habit. The interlock adds a value question: a rule can change behaviour and still lose legitimacy.

resource.title: Pigeons in a Pelican
resource.creator: B. F. Skinner (American Psychologist 15(1), 1960)
resource.why: Skinner's own account of Project Pigeon - the shaping, the demonstrations and why the committee said no - gives the story the lesson can only summarize, in the voice of the man who developed the method.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (the session's search budget ran out); a standard citation, cited in this form throughout the history-of-psychology literature. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: A Wheel Everyone Knew Was Random Moved Their Answers by Twenty Points.
days.concept: Heuristics are fast mental shortcuts - availability, representativeness, anchoring - that usually serve well but err systematically in predictable situations (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974); whether those errors show irrationality or shortcuts used outside the environment they fit is debated (Gigerenzer's ecological rationality).
days.focus: Teach the heuristics-and-biases programme through anchoring, availability and representativeness (with base-rate neglect from Day 15), and teach Gigerenzer's counter-case - simple rules beating complex models when the world is uncertain - so Logan learns the debate, not a list of 'biases'.

story.title: A wheel rigged to mean nothing
story.hook: In the early 1970s two Israeli psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, rigged a wheel of fortune marked 0 to 100 so that it stopped only at 10 or 65. In an experiment Kahneman later recalled running at the University of Oregon, students watched it spin and wrote down the number. Then they were asked whether the percentage of African nations among the members of the United Nations was higher or lower than that number - and for their best estimate. Those who had seen 10 gave a median estimate of about 25%; those who had seen 65, about 45%. The result appeared in 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases', Science, 27 September 1974.
story.puzzle: Everyone could see the number was random and had nothing to do with Africa or the UN. Why did it move their answers by twenty points?
story.payoff: Facing a hard question, the mind starts from whatever number is at hand and adjusts - too little - while the anchor makes anchor-consistent facts easier to bring to mind. Anchoring is usually harmless because most numbers we start from carry information; the wheel exposed the shortcut by supplying one that carried none.
sources: Tversky & Kahneman, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases', Science 185 (1974)
Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), ch. 11 'Anchors'
Klein et al., 'Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project', Social Psychology 45 (2014)

days.application: After 11 September 2001 many Americans avoided flying and drove instead. Gerd Gigerenzer (Risk Analysis, 2006) estimated that about 1,500 more people died on US roads in the following year than the trend predicted - fear driven by vivid, available images of the attacks, applied to a choice where the statistics pointed the other way. The estimate is contested: Sivak and Flannagan (2004) argued much of the post-attack increase was on local roads rather than long trips, and a 2019 critique noted the analysis reported no significance tests. (Car chain: consequences - a shift of travel from air to road.)

builds_on.why: Base rates: the representativeness heuristic produces base-rate neglect, and Day 15's natural-frequency format is Gigerenzer's evidence that the format of a problem changes how well people reason.
Perception as inference: Kahneman modelled cognitive biases on visual illusions - fast, automatic best guesses that persist even when you know they are wrong.

across.link: DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (Review of Financial Studies, 2009) found that none of 14 portfolio-optimization models consistently beat naive 1/N diversification out of sample across seven datasets, because estimation error swamped the optimizers' gains - Gigerenzer's favourite example of a simple heuristic winning in an uncertain environment.

days.apply_question: In Northcraft and Neale's 1987 study, real-estate agents who toured the same Tucson house but were handed different listing prices gave appraisals that moved with the listing price, though most said they had ignored it. What would have to be true of a housing market for leaning on the listing price to be a sensible shortcut rather than a bias?
days.evidence_note: Settled: anchoring is one of the most reliable effects in psychology (it replicated strongly in Many Labs 1, 2014), and availability and representativeness errors are well documented. Debated: what the errors mean - Kahneman and Tversky versus Gigerenzer (their 1996 exchange in Psychological Review) over whether 'biases' reflect flawed reasoning or tasks stripped of their natural format; the size of the post-9/11 road toll; and some priming findings in the early chapters of Thinking, Fast and Slow that failed to replicate, as Kahneman acknowledged.

resource.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow - chapter 11, 'Anchors' (chapter 12, 'The Science of Availability', optional)
resource.creator: Daniel Kahneman (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011)
resource.length: about 12 pages; roughly 20 minutes (ch. 12 adds about 15)
resource.why: Kahneman's own account of the wheel and the many anchoring results since, with the two mechanisms (insufficient adjustment and priming) he distinguishes - the source of today's story, by its author.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); chapter numbers and titles from established knowledge of the book. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: Same 600 Lives, Same Odds. Change 'Saved' to 'Die' and 72% Becomes 22%.
days.concept: Prospect theory: people judge outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point, feel losses about twice as strongly as equal gains, are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking for losses, and overweight small probabilities - so describing the same outcomes differently (framing) can reverse choices.
days.focus: Teach Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979; cumulative version 1992) as the descriptive alternative to expected utility: the S-shaped value function, loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity and probability weighting, with framing and defaults as the visible consequences. Logan knows the finance applications from the CFA; this lesson is the psychology underneath and the current state of its evidence.
key_concepts: diminishing sensitivity and the S-shaped value function
probability weighting and the fourfold pattern
days.model_or_equation: Value function (Tversky & Kahneman 1992): v(x) = x^alpha for gains (x >= 0) and v(x) = -lambda(-x)^beta for losses, with median estimates alpha = beta = 0.88 and lambda = 2.25. A 2024 meta-analysis of 607 estimates puts the mean lambda near 1.96 (95% interval about 1.82-2.10). Outcomes are weighted by w(p), which overweights small probabilities and underweights moderate and large ones.

story.title: Six hundred lives, two descriptions
story.hook: In a paper published in Science on 30 January 1981, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman reported what students at Stanford and the University of British Columbia did with an imaginary epidemic: 'Imagine that the U.S. is preparing for the outbreak of an unusual Asian disease, which is expected to kill 600 people.' One group of 152 students chose between Program A - 200 people will be saved - and Program B - a one-third chance that all 600 are saved and a two-thirds chance that no one is. 72% chose A. A second group chose between Program C - 400 people will die - and Program D - a one-third chance that nobody dies and a two-thirds chance that 600 die. Only 22% chose C; 78% gambled.
story.puzzle: A and C are the same programme; so are B and D. Nothing about the outcomes or the odds changed - only the words. Why did the majority flip?
story.payoff: 'Saved' sets the reference point at 600 dead, so outcomes look like gains, where people are risk-averse and take the sure 200. 'Die' sets it at nobody dead, so the same outcomes look like losses, where people are risk-seeking and gamble to avoid a sure loss. The S-shaped value function, bending opposite ways on either side of the reference point, predicts the reversal.
sources: Tversky & Kahneman, 'The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice', Science 211 (1981)
Kahneman & Tversky, 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk', Econometrica 47 (1979)
Brown, Imai, Vieider & Camerer, 'Meta-analysis of empirical estimates of loss aversion', Journal of Economic Literature 62 (2024)

days.application: Organ-donation defaults. Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein (Science, 2003) compared European countries: where citizens had to opt in to be donors, effective consent ran from about 4% (Denmark) to about 28% (the Netherlands); where they had to opt out, from about 86% (Sweden) to above 99% (Austria, France, Hungary and others) - Germany about 12%, neighbouring Austria about 99.98%. The default sets the reference point, so leaving it feels like giving something up. Two cautions keep the example honest: Johnson and Goldstein named effort and the implied recommendation as rival explanations, and registration is not donation - actual donor rates differ far less, with Abadie and Gay (2006) estimating presumed consent raises them by roughly a quarter once other factors are controlled.

builds_on.why: Expected value and Bernoulli's utility are the normative benchmark; prospect theory describes how real choices depart from it (reference points, loss aversion, probability weighting).
Same research programme: framing works like anchoring, with the description supplying the reference point the mind then adjusts from.

across.link: McNeil, Pauker, Sox and Tversky (New England Journal of Medicine, 1982) found that describing lung-cancer surgery's outcomes as survival rates rather than mortality rates made patients, students and physicians markedly more willing to choose surgery over radiation - framing at work in clinical consent, with the same numbers.

days.apply_question: A car dealer offers you a $1,500 extended warranty on a new car, though the repairs it would cover during the warranty period would on average cost far less. Using prospect theory, why do so many buyers say yes?
days.evidence_note: Settled: framing effects and reference dependence are robust (gain-loss framing replicated in Many Labs 1, 2014), and most estimates find losses loom larger than gains, with a meta-analytic mean near 2 (Brown, Imai, Vieider & Camerer, 2024). Debated: how general loss aversion is - Gal and Rucker (2018) argue it is overstated and context-dependent, especially for small stakes - and how much defaults change actual organ donation as opposed to registration. Value judgment: whether governments should set defaults to steer choices ('libertarian paternalism', Thaler and Sunstein) is a question about liberty and welfare, not psychology.

resource.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow - chapter 25, 'Bernoulli's Errors', and chapter 26, 'Prospect Theory'
resource.creator: Daniel Kahneman (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2011)
resource.length: two short chapters, about 25 pages; roughly 35-40 minutes (ch. 26 alone about 20)
resource.why: Kahneman tells how he and Tversky saw what Bernoulli's utility theory missed - the reference point - and draws the value function, linking straight back to Day 11's expected value.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); chapter numbers and titles from established knowledge of the book. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: Experts Ranked Nuclear Power 20th of 30 Hazards. The League of Women Voters Ranked It First. Neither Group Was Confused.
days.concept: Lay people judge risk not only by expected deaths but by qualities such as dread, catastrophic potential, involuntariness and unfamiliarity (Slovic's psychometric paradigm), so experts and publics often rank the same hazards differently - and whose ranking should govern policy is a value question as well as an empirical one.
days.focus: Teach the psychometric paradigm - the 'dread risk' and 'unknown risk' factors and the affect heuristic - and show that the expert-public gap is partly a disagreement about what 'risk' means, not only public error. Then separate the evidence (deaths per unit of energy) from the value question (should policy weigh dread, consent and catastrophe?).
key_concepts: risk as expected harm versus risk as perceived
days.model_or_equation: Technical risk = expected annual deaths (probability x consequence, Day 11). Lay 'riskiness' also tracks two factors: dread (uncontrollable, catastrophic, involuntary, fatal, inequitably shared) and unknown (unobservable, new, delayed harm). Slovic's 'cognitive map' plots hazards on these two axes; nuclear power sits at the far corner of both.

story.title: Thirty hazards, four rankings
story.hook: In the late 1970s Paul Slovic, Baruch Fischhoff and Sarah Lichtenstein of Decision Research in Eugene, Oregon, asked four groups to rank 30 activities and technologies - from handguns, smoking and motorcycles to X-rays, vaccinations and home appliances - by their risk of death to Americans. The groups were members of the League of Women Voters, college students, members of a business and professional 'Active Club', and 15 professional risk assessors. The experts put motor vehicles first and nuclear power twentieth. The League of Women Voters and the students put nuclear power first; the Active Club, eighth. Slovic summarized the programme in Science in April 1987 ('Perception of Risk').
story.puzzle: When the researchers asked lay respondents to estimate how many people each hazard actually killed in an average year, their figures for nuclear power were among the lowest. They did not think it killed many people - yet they ranked it the most dangerous. Were they confused?
story.payoff: No: they were answering a different question. For lay respondents 'risk' included catastrophic potential, dread and unfamiliarity - asked about a disastrous year rather than an average one, their nuclear estimates soared. The experts were measuring expected deaths. Each ranking is coherent on its own terms; which should guide policy is a choice about values.
sources: Slovic, 'Perception of Risk', Science 236 (1987)
Slovic, Fischhoff & Lichtenstein, 'Rating the Risks', Environment 21(3) (1979)
Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein, Read & Combs, 'How safe is safe enough?', Policy Sciences 9 (1978)

days.application: Deaths per terawatt-hour of electricity. Markandya and Wilkinson (Lancet, 2007) estimated about 25 deaths per TWh for coal (accidents plus air pollution), about 18 for oil, about 3 for gas and well under 0.1 for nuclear; Our World in Data's compilation, which counts Chernobyl and Fukushima, puts nuclear near 0.03, comparable to wind and solar. On expected deaths nuclear is among the safest sources; on dread, the most feared - and public fear has shaped which plants get built. (Grid chain: regulation and adoption.)

builds_on.why: Fat tails: catastrophic potential matters when harms are fat-tailed, so the public's weight on the rare disaster is not simply an error about averages.
Radiation dose and the linear no-threshold model: why estimates of nuclear deaths (Chernobyl's especially) vary so widely, which feeds the 'unknown' factor.

across.link: Executive Order 12866 (1993) requires US agencies to weigh the costs and benefits of major regulations, reviewed by the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs - the institutional home of the expert ranking. Cass Sunstein, who later ran that office, argued in Laws of Fear (2005) that policy should correct for public misperception; Slovic answered that lay concerns about dread and fairness are legitimate values.

days.apply_question: Should regulators require self-driving cars to be much safer than human drivers before allowing them on public roads, or merely as safe? Answer by separating what you would need to know from what you would need to value, using Slovic's dread and unknown factors.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the psychometric pattern - dread and unknown factors predicting lay risk judgments - has been reproduced in many countries; per unit of energy, coal and oil kill far more people than nuclear, wind or solar. Debated: how many deaths Chernobyl will eventually cause (estimates built on the linear no-threshold model, Day 65, range from about 4,000 to tens of thousands); and whether risk perception is better explained by cultural worldviews (Douglas and Wildavsky; Kahan's cultural cognition) than by hazard features. Value judgment: whether policy should follow expected-death rankings (Sunstein) or also weigh dread, consent and catastrophe (Slovic).

resource.title: Perception of Risk
resource.creator: Paul Slovic (Science 236, 1987)
resource.why: The paper that names the dread and unknown factors, with the 30-hazard ranking table and the two-axis 'cognitive map' of hazards that the lesson can only describe in words.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); a standard citation (Science 236:280-285, 1987). Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: Management's Most Famous Pyramid Was Never Drawn by the Man It's Named After - and the Ladder Doesn't Hold.
days.concept: Human needs are many and broadly universal but are not satisfied in a strict ladder: Maslow's ordering is weakly supported, while needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness (self-determination theory) predict well-being across cultures - so 'need' is rarely a single first cause of behaviour.
days.focus: Teach what Maslow actually claimed (1943), what the evidence shows (Wahba & Bridwell 1976; Tay & Diener 2011), and self-determination theory's three needs with the intrinsic/extrinsic distinction. Then challenge the first link of Logan's own chain: 'human needs' are plural, partly created by the technologies that meet them, and not a fixed starting point.
days.model_or_equation: Not a ladder but overlapping, partial satisfactions. Maslow's own illustration (1943): the average person might be perhaps 85% satisfied in physiological needs, 70% in safety, 50% in love, 40% in esteem and 10% in self-actualization - all at once. Self-determination theory's alternative: three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) whose satisfaction predicts well-being and self-motivated behaviour.

story.title: The pyramid nobody drew
story.hook: In July 1943 Abraham Maslow, a 35-year-old psychologist at Brooklyn College, published 'A Theory of Human Motivation' in Psychological Review. It set out five kinds of need - physiological, safety, love, esteem and self-actualization - in an order of 'prepotency'. It contains no pyramid. Maslow cautioned that the order was not rigid and illustrated it with rough percentages of each need being met at the same time in an average person. The pyramid came later, from management writers: Bridgman, Cummings and Ballard (2019) trace the first to a 1960 Business Horizons article by the consultant Charles McDermid. It has since become a fixture of management and introductory textbooks.
story.puzzle: If Maslow never drew the pyramid and said the ladder was not rigid, where did the ladder come from - and is it true that people pursue belonging or meaning only after their bodily needs are met?
story.payoff: The pyramid was a teaching device built by management writers. Tested directly, the strict ladder fails: Tay and Diener's (2011) Gallup World Poll study of about 60,000 people in 123 countries found the needs broadly universal, but people reported meeting social and respect needs - and drawing well-being from them - even when basic needs were unmet. Needs run in parallel, as Maslow's own percentages implied.
sources: Maslow, 'A Theory of Human Motivation', Psychological Review 50 (1943)
Bridgman, Cummings & Ballard, 'Who Built Maslow's Pyramid?', Academy of Management Learning & Education 18 (2019)
Tay & Diener, 'Needs and Subjective Well-Being Around the World', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 101 (2011)
Wahba & Bridwell, 'Maslow reconsidered: A review of research on the need hierarchy theory', Organizational Behavior and Human Performance 15 (1976)

days.application: The 'human needs' link of the car chain. In Middletown (1929), Robert and Helen Lynd's study of Muncie, Indiana, they reported working-class families who owned a car but had no bathtub, and quoted a wife: 'We'd rather do without clothes than give up the car.' A car met several needs at once - access to work and shops, autonomy, belonging, status - and Maslow's ladder would not have predicted the car before the plumbing. (Car chain: need - which turns out to be plural, and partly created by the car itself.)

builds_on.why: Innovation as a system: demand is built, not found - so a 'need' at the head of the chain is partly a product of the inventions that later meet it.
Dopamine signals 'wanting' and drives pursuit; motivation research asks which goals that machinery is pointed at, and why.

across.link: Marie Jahoda, Paul Lazarsfeld and Hans Zeisel's study of Marienthal, an Austrian village whose mill closed around 1930 (Die Arbeitslosen von Marienthal, 1933), found that the unemployed lost time structure, social contact, purpose and status, not only income - evidence, later formalized in Jahoda's 'latent deprivation' model, that work meets several needs at once.

days.apply_question: Using self-determination theory, would you expect drivers on an app platform such as Uber - free to choose their hours, but paid and dispatched by an algorithm - to fare better or worse in well-being than salaried drivers on fixed shifts, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: a strict, step-by-step hierarchy of needs is poorly supported (Wahba & Bridwell 1976; Tay & Diener 2011). Debated: whether self-determination theory's three needs are universal or partly a Western ideal of autonomy (most cross-cultural studies support universality; Iyengar and Lepper 1999 found some children more motivated by choices made for them by trusted others); and how far rewards undermine intrinsic motivation (Deci, Koestner & Ryan's 1999 meta-analysis versus Cameron and Pierce). Value judgment: which needs a society ought to secure first is a moral question no needs survey can settle.

resource.title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
resource.creator: Richard M. Ryan and Edward L. Deci (American Psychologist 55(1), 2000)
resource.why: The founders' own short statement of self-determination theory - the three needs, intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation and the evidence behind them - the positive theory the lesson puts where the pyramid was.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); a standard, heavily cited article. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: The Lines Weren't Close. Three in Four People Still Named the Wrong One at Least Once.
days.concept: People adjust their judgments and behaviour toward a group's - because others' choices carry information (informational influence) and because standing apart carries a social cost (normative influence) - and 'social proof' harnesses both.
days.focus: Teach conformity's two routes (Deutsch & Gerard 1955), what Asch actually found (most answers stayed independent; one ally or a private answer collapsed conformity), cross-cultural variation (Bond & Smith 1996), and social-norms interventions at scale - with the cautions about textbook exaggeration and site-selection bias.
days.model_or_equation: Two routes to conformity (Deutsch & Gerard, 1955): informational influence - others' answers treated as evidence, producing private acceptance - and normative influence - others treated as judges, producing public compliance. The diagnostic test: make responses private. Normative conformity drops; informational conformity does not.

story.title: A minority of one
story.hook: At Swarthmore College around 1951 Solomon Asch, a Polish-born psychologist, seated a student at a table with seven to nine others and asked each in turn which of three lines matched a standard line. The answer was plain: judging alone, people erred less than 1% of the time. But everyone else at the table was a confederate, and on 12 of 18 trials they all gave the same wrong answer aloud before the real subject's turn. In his fullest report (1956, 123 subjects) about 37% of answers on those trials went along with the majority; roughly three-quarters of subjects conformed at least once, and about a quarter never did.
story.puzzle: The lines were not close, and no one was threatened or paid. Why would three out of four people say what they could see was false, at least once?
story.payoff: Some subjects began to doubt their own eyes (informational influence: 'they must see something I don't'); more knew the majority was wrong but would not stand alone (normative influence). Asch's variations separated the two: when one other person gave the right answer, conformity fell sharply, and when subjects could answer in writing, it dropped too - the signature of normative pressure.
sources: Asch, 'Effects of group pressure upon the modification and distortion of judgments', in Guetzkow (ed.), Groups, Leadership and Men (1951)
Asch, 'Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority', Psychological Monographs 70(9) (1956)
Asch, 'Opinions and Social Pressure', Scientific American 193(5) (1955)

days.application: Opower's Home Energy Reports. From 2008 the company mailed households letters comparing their electricity use with their neighbours'. Across randomized trials covering about 600,000 households, Hunt Allcott (Journal of Public Economics, 2011) found the letters cut use by about 2% on average - an effect he compared to a short-run price rise of roughly 11-20%. An earlier San Marcos, California study (Schultz et al., Psychological Science, 2007) showed the trap: households already below average drifted up toward the norm, unless the letter added a smiley face approving their thrift. (Grid chain: consequences and demand - social proof as a load-management tool.)

builds_on.why: The relatedness need: the wish to belong is the motive behind normative influence.
Randomized trials: Opower's letters were randomly assigned, which is why the 2% is a causal effect and not a selection artefact.

across.link: Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch's theory of informational cascades (Journal of Political Economy, 1992) shows that people who rationally update on others' choices (Day 15) can all herd onto the wrong option and stop revealing their private information - informational conformity as rational, yet fragile.

days.apply_question: In Muchnik, Aral and Taylor's 2013 experiment on a news-comment site, a single random 'up-vote' made a comment's later ratings markedly higher - about a quarter higher on average by the end. What does that imply about how much weight you should give a product's early star ratings, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: social influence on judgment is robust across many studies and cultures (Bond and Smith's 1996 meta-analysis of 133 Asch-type studies in 17 countries found it larger in more collectivist societies and declining in the US since the 1950s), and randomized social-comparison letters reliably cut energy use. Debated: the textbook framing of Asch - about two-thirds of answers were independent (Friend, Rafferty & Bramel 1990); later Opower sites showed smaller effects than early ones (Allcott 2015, site-selection bias); and the hotel towel-card result (Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius 2008, reuse about 35% to 44%) has had mixed replications.

resource.title: Opinions and Social Pressure
resource.creator: Solomon E. Asch (Scientific American 193(5), November 1955)
resource.why: Asch's own account for general readers, with photographs of a subject under pressure and the variations - a single ally, the size of the majority - that show what drives conformity.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); a standard citation. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.topic: Obedience and the power of situations
days.headline_hint: Sixty-Five Percent Went to 450 Volts. Then Someone Listened to the Tapes.
days.concept: Situations can push ordinary people toward harming others - authority, gradual escalation and a purpose they share matter a great deal - but how far the famous experiments show blind obedience is now debated after archival re-analysis.
days.focus: Teach Milgram's obedience studies through their variations (obedience swung from about 10% to over 90% with the situation), the archival critique (Perry 2012), the 'engaged followership' reinterpretation (Haslam & Reicher), Burger's 2009 partial replication, and the Stanford Prison Experiment's collapse as evidence (Le Texier 2019): the power of situations is real; the cartoon of automatic obedience is not.
