days.model_or_equation: Obedience by situation (Milgram, Obedience to Authority, 1974; full obedience to 450 V): learner in another room, heard through the wall, about 65%; learner in the same room, 40%; teacher must press the learner's hand onto a shock plate, 30%; experimenter gives orders by telephone, about 20%; two fellow 'teachers' refuse, 10%; subject only reads the words while a peer presses the switch, about 92%. The same people, different situations.

story.title: The tapes in the Yale archive
story.hook: In August 1961, months after Adolf Eichmann's trial opened in Jerusalem, Stanley Milgram began experiments at Yale University in New Haven. Men answering a newspaper ad, paid $4.50, were told the study concerned punishment and learning. As 'teacher', each was to give a 'learner' - an actor strapped into a chair in the next room - a shock 15 volts stronger for every mistake, up to 450 volts, marked 'XXX'. The learner protested, screamed, then fell silent. When a teacher hesitated, the experimenter used scripted prods, ending with 'You have no other choice, you must go on.' In the first published study (1963), 26 of 40 men - 65% - went to 450 volts. Half a century later the Australian psychologist Gina Perry spent years with Milgram's recordings and papers at Yale and reported, in Behind the Shock Machine (2012), that the experimenter often improvised beyond the script and that many participants doubted the shocks were real.
story.puzzle: Do two-thirds of ordinary people really obey an order to torture a stranger - or did the experiment show something else?
story.payoff: Both less and more than the headline. Across Milgram's own variations obedience swung from about 10% to over 90% with the situation, so it was never a fixed trait of human nature. And it did not track bare orders: in Burger's replication, participants who heard the one true command - 'you have no other choice' - refused to go on (Burger, Girgis & Manning 2011). People continued when they identified with the experimenter's scientific purpose and were drawn on in small steps; doubts about whether the shocks were real complicate the rest.
sources: Milgram, 'Behavioral Study of Obedience', Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 67 (1963)
Milgram, Obedience to Authority (1974)
Perry, Behind the Shock Machine (2012)
Burger, Girgis & Manning, 'In their own words: Explaining obedience to authority through an examination of participants' comments', Social Psychological and Personality Science 2 (2011)

days.application: Jerry Burger's partial replication (American Psychologist, 2009). Burger, of Santa Clara University, reran Milgram's basic procedure with ethical safeguards: screening out vulnerable volunteers and stopping at 150 volts - the point where Milgram's learner first demanded to be released, and after which most of Milgram's participants who continued went all the way. Seventy percent of Burger's participants were willing to continue past 150 volts, against about 82.5% at the same point in the comparable Milgram condition; the difference was not statistically significant. Nearly fifty years on, the situation still had much of its pull.

builds_on.why: Conformity: in Milgram's variant where two fellow 'teachers' refused, obedience fell to about 10% - peers' behaviour, Asch's single dissenter, matters as much as authority.
Replication: archival re-analysis and partial replications are how the field is re-grading its most famous findings.

across.link: At Tenerife on 27 March 1977 a KLM captain began his take-off without clearance; his flight engineer's doubt about another aircraft on the runway was brushed aside, and the collision killed 583 people. Aviation's answer was crew resource management - from a 1979 NASA workshop and United Airlines' first programme in 1981 - which trains junior crew to challenge a captain: an institution designed against the authority gradient.

days.apply_question: In Charles Hofling's 1966 hospital study, 21 of 22 nurses began to give a patient twice the stated maximum dose of an unfamiliar drug ('Astroten') on a telephone order from a doctor they did not know; when Rank and Jacobson (1977) repeated the idea with a familiar drug (Valium) and nurses free to consult colleagues, 16 of 18 refused. Using today's lesson, which features of the two situations best explain the difference?
days.evidence_note: Settled: in structured settings many people comply with authority's requests to do things they would not otherwise do, and Burger's partial replication found rates similar to Milgram's at 150 volts. Debated: what Milgram's studies show - blind obedience in an 'agentic state', or willing commitment to a cause people identify with (Haslam and Reicher) - and how far Perry's archival findings weaken them. The Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) is now widely regarded as weak evidence: Le Texier (American Psychologist, 2019) documented that guards were coached, though Zimbardo disputed this. Value judgment: whether deception research of this kind was ever ethical.

resource.title: Contesting the 'nature' of conformity: What Milgram and Zimbardo's studies really show
resource.creator: S. Alexander Haslam and Stephen D. Reicher (PLoS Biology 10(11), 2012)
resource.length: a short open-access essay; roughly 20 minutes
resource.why: The leading reinterpretation of both famous studies - that people harm others not because they blindly obey but because they come to identify with a cause - which gives Logan the strongest alternative to the textbook reading.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); citation from established knowledge of the literature. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: The Dog Was Already Dead and No One Was Harmed. In Recife, Most People Still Said Eating It Was Wrong.
days.concept: Most moral judgments arise from fast, automatic intuitions, with reasoning usually coming afterwards to justify and persuade (Haidt's social-intuitionist model, 2001); which intuitions people weigh varies with culture and politics, though moral foundations theory's particular list is contested.
days.focus: Teach the social-intuitionist model against the rationalist picture (Kohlberg), with moral dumbfounding and its critics, and moral foundations theory as one contested map of the intuitions. Keep Day 43's is-ought line bright: a theory of how judgments are caused does not tell you which judgments are true.
key_concepts: post-hoc reasoning ('the rider and the elephant')
moral foundations theory (care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity, liberty)
days.model_or_equation: The social-intuitionist model (Haidt 2001): eliciting situation -> intuition -> judgment -> reasoning (mostly post hoc) -> persuasion of others, whose intuitions then shift. Rarer links: reasoning that overrides an intuition, and private reflection that changes one.

story.title: Is it wrong to eat your dog?
story.hook: In the early 1990s a young American psychologist, Jonathan Haidt, with Silvia Koller and Maria Dias, interviewed about 360 people in Recife and Porto Alegre in Brazil and in Philadelphia - adults and children from richer and poorer neighbourhoods. He read them short stories built to offend but harm no one: a family whose dog has been killed by a car cooks and eats it; a woman cuts up an old national flag to clean her bathroom; a man buys a dead chicken, has sex with it, then cooks and eats it. No one sees; no one is hurt. Asked whether the act was wrong - and whether it would be wrong in a country where it was customary - most working-class adults in Recife said yes, everywhere; most University of Pennsylvania students called it disgusting but nobody's business. Many who condemned the acts conceded that no one was harmed (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1993).
story.puzzle: If an act harms no one, why do people insist it is wrong - and why can they not say why?
story.payoff: The judgment came first, from an intuition - disgust, disrespect - and reasons were sought afterwards; when every reason was removed, the judgment stayed. In Haidt's later image, the reasoning rider mostly serves the intuitive elephant. Culture and class shaped which intuitions counted as moral: purity and respect for many in Recife, harm alone for the Penn students.
sources: Haidt, Koller & Dias, 'Affect, culture, and morality, or is it wrong to eat your dog?', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 65 (1993)
Haidt, 'The emotional dog and its rational tail: A social intuitionist approach to moral judgment', Psychological Review 108 (2001)
Haidt, The Righteous Mind (2012), chapters 1-2

days.application: Graham, Haidt and Nosek (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2009) found in large US samples that self-described liberals weighted care and fairness far above loyalty, authority and sanctity, while conservatives weighted all five more evenly - so each side's best arguments land on intuitions the other weighs less. Feinberg and Willer showed the practical consequence: arguments framed in the arguer's own moral language persuade opponents poorly, while reframing - environmental protection in terms of purity, or a liberal policy in terms of patriotism - moved them more (Psychological Science 2013; Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 2015).

builds_on.why: Is and ought: describing how intuitions cause moral judgments is an 'is'; whether those judgments are correct is an 'ought' that the psychology cannot settle.
Metaethics: evolutionary and psychological debunking arguments (Street) ask whether intuitions explained this way can still track moral truth.

across.link: Emile Durkheim's The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912) argued that the sacred binds groups together; Haidt explicitly builds his 'binding' foundations - loyalty, authority, sanctity - on Durkheim's account (The Righteous Mind, ch. 11), a direct intellectual path from sociology to moral psychology.

days.apply_question: Italy banned the production and sale of cultivated (lab-grown) meat in November 2023, and Florida did the same in May 2024. Using the social-intuitionist model, why would new safety data alone be unlikely to change the minds of the bans' supporters?
days.evidence_note: Settled: intuition and emotion strongly shape moral judgment, and people often cannot fully state their reasons. Debated: how real 'dumbfounding' is (Royzman, Kim & Leeman 2015 argue many participants still believed harm was possible; later studies find it, but less often); whether moral foundations theory's list and questionnaire are right (Gray's 'dyadic morality' says perceived harm underlies all moral judgment; a 2023 cross-cultural revision split fairness into equality and proportionality); and how often reasoning changes minds. Value judgment: whether intuitions are evidence of moral truth (intuitionists and the natural-law tradition) or biases to be debunked (Greene, Singer) - a metaethical question (Day 44), not a psychological one.

resource.title: The Righteous Mind - chapter 2, 'The Intuitive Dog and Its Rational Tail'
resource.creator: Jonathan Haidt (Pantheon, 2012)
resource.why: Haidt's own accessible statement of the social-intuitionist model, with the dumbfounding interviews and the evidence he marshals - the theory at full strength, to set against the critics named in the lesson.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); chapter number and title from established knowledge of the book. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.topic: Motivated reasoning: seeing what your side needs
days.headline_hint: Princeton and Dartmouth Watched the Same Film of the Same Game. They Counted Different Fouls.
days.concept: Motivated reasoning: people weigh evidence through what they want to be true - demanding more of unwelcome evidence than welcome - most strongly when a belief marks membership of a group (identity-protective cognition), and education or numeracy does not reliably protect against it.
days.focus: Teach motivated reasoning (Kunda 1990) and Kahan's identity-protective cognition, distinguish it carefully from honest Bayesian disagreement (Day 15), and present the 'motivated numeracy' result with its partial replications. Then turn it on the reader: an author writing from any worldview, religious or secular, is the person most exposed.
key_concepts: the Bayesian alternative: different priors and different trust
days.model_or_equation: Bayes in odds form (Day 15): posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio. Honest disagreement can come from different priors or different trust in sources (different likelihood ratios for the same report). Motivated reasoning is when the likelihood ratio you assign depends on whether you like the conclusion - discounting unwelcome evidence and taking welcome evidence at face value.

story.title: They saw a game
story.hook: On 23 November 1951 Princeton played Dartmouth at Palmer Stadium in the last game of the season. It was rough from the start: Princeton's star tailback Dick Kazmaier, that season's Heisman Trophy winner, left in the second quarter with a broken nose; in the third, a Dartmouth player's leg was broken. Princeton won, and the campus newspapers traded accusations. Two psychologists, Albert Hastorf of Dartmouth and Hadley Cantril of Princeton, showed students from both schools the same film of the game and asked them to note every infraction. Princeton students recorded Dartmouth committing about twice as many as Princeton; Dartmouth students saw the two teams as roughly even ('They Saw a Game: A Case Study', 1954).
story.puzzle: They watched the same film, frame for frame. How can honest students count different fouls?
story.payoff: Each side's wish - that its team was the wronged party - set how hard it scrutinized each play: ambiguous contact by the other side looked like a foul, by its own side like football. Hastorf and Cantril concluded there was no single 'game' that everyone saw; each group constructed its own. The motive did not change the pixels; it changed the evidential weight given to them.
sources: Hastorf & Cantril, 'They Saw a Game: A Case Study', Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 49 (1954)
Kunda, 'The case for motivated reasoning', Psychological Bulletin 108 (1990)

days.application: Dan Kahan, Ellen Peters, Erica Dawson and Paul Slovic ('Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government', Behavioural Public Policy, 2017) gave about 1,100 US adults a two-by-two table of results and asked what it showed. When the table was about a skin cream, the most numerate people got it right most often. When identical numbers concerned a ban on carrying concealed handguns, numerate people got it right mainly when the correct answer suited their politics - and the partisan gap was widest among the most numerate. Later replications, including one by Connor and colleagues (Behavioural Public Policy, 2024), reproduced the pattern only in part, so the claim that numeracy amplifies the bias is debated.

builds_on.why: Bayes' theorem: the key test is whether a disagreement comes from different priors and trust (rational) or from likelihood ratios bent toward the wanted conclusion (motivated).
Intuitions first: reasoning recruited afterwards as a lawyer for an intuition is the moral-psychology form of motivated reasoning.

across.link: Richards Heuer's Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence, 1999) introduced the 'Analysis of Competing Hypotheses' - list every hypothesis, score each piece of evidence against all of them, and look for evidence that disconfirms - a procedure built into US intelligence training to counter exactly this bias.

days.apply_question: In the University of Michigan's consumer surveys, Republicans' and Democrats' ratings of the economy swap places within weeks of a presidential election, though the economy itself has barely changed. What single observation would tell you whether this is motivated reasoning rather than rational updating on news about future policy?
days.evidence_note: Settled: people scrutinize unwelcome evidence harder than welcome evidence, and partisan bias appears about equally on the left and the right (Ditto and colleagues' 2019 meta-analysis of 51 studies). Debated: whether numeracy and education amplify it (Kahan versus partial replications), and how much 'motivated reasoning' is really Bayesian updating with different priors and different trust in sources (Druckman and McGrath, Nature Climate Change, 2019). Value judgment: none needed for the science - but for an author writing from a worldview, Christian or secular, the working rule is the same scrutiny for welcome and unwelcome findings.

resource.title: Why you think you're right - even if you're wrong
resource.creator: Julia Galef (TEDxPSU, 2016)
resource.why: Galef's contrast between the 'soldier mindset' that defends a belief and the 'scout mindset' that maps the terrain turns today's research into a habit Logan can practise while writing.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); talk known to be published by TED from TEDxPSU; length from memory. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: A Foster Home at 18 Months Did Far More Than the Same Kind of Home at 30. Why Would the Calendar Matter?
days.concept: Early experience shapes development most powerfully during sensitive periods - windows when the developing brain expects certain input, such as responsive care - so the timing of an intervention can matter as much as the intervention itself, though recovery after the window is usually partial rather than impossible.
days.focus: Teach sensitive (not strictly 'critical') periods and attachment through the strongest evidence, the randomized Bucharest Early Intervention Project, with Harlow's monkeys and Bowlby's attachment theory as background; then the limits - ordinary variation in parenting may matter far less than deprivation does - and the ethics of randomizing vulnerable children.

story.title: Randomizing a childhood
story.hook: Under Nicolae Ceausescu, Romania's Decree 770 (1966) banned most abortion and contraception, and tens of thousands of children ended up in state institutions; when the regime fell in December 1989 the world saw the orphanages - rows of cots, a few caregivers for dozens of infants. In 2000-2001 Charles Nelson, Nathan Fox and Charles Zeanah, with Romanian colleagues, began the Bucharest Early Intervention Project: 136 institutionalized children aged roughly 6 to 31 months were randomly assigned either to high-quality foster care, which the project created because Bucharest had almost none, or to care as usual. At 54 months the foster-care group's average IQ was about 81 and the institutional group's about 73; never-institutionalized Bucharest children averaged about 109 (Science, 2007).
story.puzzle: Foster care helped - but children placed before about age two gained much more than those placed later, though they went to the same kind of families. Why would the calendar matter?
story.payoff: Because the developing brain 'expects' responsive care during a sensitive period: input arriving inside the window builds circuits that later input can only partly build. Random assignment rules out the usual confound - that healthier children get fostered first - so the timing effect is causal. Recovery after the window was partial, not absent.
sources: Nelson, Zeanah, Fox, Marshall, Smyke & Guthrie, 'Cognitive recovery in socially deprived young children: The Bucharest Early Intervention Project', Science 318 (2007)
Nelson, Fox & Zeanah, Romania's Abandoned Children (Harvard University Press, 2014)
Harlow, 'The Nature of Love', American Psychologist 13 (1958)

days.application: The Nurse-Family Partnership. David Olds's programme began as a randomized trial in Elmira, New York, in 1977: nurses visited about 400 low-income first-time mothers from pregnancy to the child's second birthday. Fifteen years later the visited families had substantially fewer verified reports of child abuse and neglect (Olds et al., JAMA, 1997), and later US trials in Memphis and Denver found further benefits. But the UK's Building Blocks trial (Lancet, 2016) and a large South Carolina trial (JAMA, 2022) found little effect on their main outcomes - a reminder that an early-window programme's effect depends on what comparison families already receive.

builds_on.why: Plasticity: connections change with use, and sensitive periods are windows of heightened plasticity when particular input is expected.
Randomized trials: the BEIP's random assignment is what lets it separate the effect of timing from the selection of healthier children into foster care.

across.link: The US Family First Prevention Services Act (2018) limits federal foster-care funding for group homes ('congregate care') beyond two weeks except in qualified treatment programmes, steering money toward family placements - a policy shift that reflects the evidence that young children do better in families than in institutions.

days.apply_question: US regulators lowered the approved age for cochlear implants to 9 months in 2020. Using sensitive periods, why should the age at which a congenitally deaf child receives an implant matter so much for learning spoken language?
days.evidence_note: Settled: severe early deprivation harms cognitive and social development, and earlier placement into family care produces larger recovery (the BEIP; the English and Romanian Adoptees study, Lancet 2017). Debated: how much ordinary differences in parenting matter, as opposed to deprivation (twin and adoption studies find little lasting 'shared environment' effect on many adult traits); and how well home-visiting results transfer across places. Value judgment: whether it was ethical to randomize institutionalized children - the investigators argued no foster system existed and the government kept every option open; the question was debated in Science (Millum & Emanuel 2007) and elsewhere.

resource.title: Cognitive recovery in socially deprived young children: The Bucharest Early Intervention Project
resource.creator: Charles A. Nelson and colleagues (Science 318, 2007)
resource.why: The trial's headline paper: the design, the IQ results by group and the age-at-placement analysis that is the evidence for a sensitive period - the primary source behind the lesson's numbers.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); citation from established knowledge of the literature. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: IQ Is Substantially Heritable. Dutch Conscripts Still Gained Twenty Points in Thirty Years.
days.concept: Heritability is the share of variation in a trait, within a particular population and its environments, that is associated with genetic differences; adult IQ is substantially heritable, yet heritability says nothing about whether the trait can change - environments can move a whole population's average, as the Flynn effect shows.
days.focus: Teach what IQ tests measure and predict, what heritability is (a population ratio, not a fixed share of one person), why it rises with age, and why high heritability is compatible with large environmental gains (Flynn) and harms (lead). Handle group differences with Lewontin's point: heritability within groups does not explain gaps between them.
days.model_or_equation: h^2 = V_G / V_P = V_G / (V_G + V_E), where V_P is the variance of the trait in the population, V_G the part associated with genetic differences and V_E the part associated with environmental differences (ignoring interaction and covariance). If environments become more equal, V_E shrinks and h^2 rises - while the population's average can still move.

story.title: Twenty points in thirty years
story.hook: In the early 1980s James Flynn, a political philosopher at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, noticed something buried in IQ tests' norm tables: each time a test was re-standardized, people scored higher on the old norms. In 1984 he showed that Americans had gained about 14 points between 1932 and 1978. In 1987 he gathered data from 14 nations ('Massive IQ gains in 14 nations', Psychological Bulletin). The most striking came from the Netherlands, where nearly all 18-year-old men sat a Raven's-type reasoning test at military induction: scores rose about 20 points between 1952 and 1982.
story.puzzle: Twin and adoption studies say adult IQ is substantially heritable - roughly half or more of its variation. Genes do not change in thirty years. How can a highly heritable trait rise by more than a standard deviation in one generation?
story.payoff: Heritability describes why people differ within a population at one time, under that population's environments; it says nothing about what moves the average. Better nutrition and health, more and different schooling, and habits of abstract thinking (Flynn's own explanation) lifted everyone. Height shows the same thing: highly heritable, yet far taller than a century ago.
sources: Flynn, 'The mean IQ of Americans: Massive gains 1932 to 1978', Psychological Bulletin 95 (1984)
Flynn, 'Massive IQ gains in 14 nations: What IQ tests really measure', Psychological Bulletin 101 (1987)
Pietschnig & Voracek, 'One century of global IQ gains', Perspectives on Psychological Science 10 (2015)

days.application: Lead and IQ. McFarland, Hauer and Reuben (PNAS, 2022) estimated that more than 170 million Americans alive in 2015 - over half the population - had blood-lead levels above 5 micrograms per decilitre in early childhood, largely from leaded gasoline, and that the exposure cost the US population about 824 million IQ points: a few points per person on average, more for those born in the peak years of the late 1960s and 1970s. An environmental change shifted the national distribution down regardless of heritability; removing the lead let it recover. (Car chain: consequences - a cost of the fuel, Day 49.)

builds_on.why: Heredity and genetics taught heritability as a population statistic, not destiny; today applies it to the most contested trait it is used for.
Leaded gasoline: the lead that case followed into children's blood is today's example of environment moving a heritable trait's average.

across.link: Norway's 1960s school reform extended compulsory schooling from seven to nine years, rolled out municipality by municipality; Brinch and Galloway (PNAS, 2012) used it as a natural experiment and found each extra year of schooling raised IQ, measured at military conscription, by about 3.7 points - education policy moving a 'heritable' trait.

days.apply_question: Height is roughly 80% heritable in well-fed populations, yet Dutch men grew around 20 cm taller over about a century and a half. If every Dutch child received equally good nutrition and health care, would the heritability of height rise or fall, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: IQ scores predict school and job outcomes; adult IQ is substantially heritable in the mostly Western populations studied (estimates often 50-80%); scores rose across the 20th century (Pietschnig and Voracek's 2015 meta-analysis: about 3 points a decade). Debated: what caused the Flynn effect and why it has stalled or reversed in some countries (Norwegian data point to environmental causes within families, Bratsberg and Rogeberg, PNAS 2018); whether heritability is lower in poor US families (Turkheimer 2003, not found in several other countries); and what polygenic scores, which capture about a tenth of the variation in educational attainment, will add. Value judgment: how a society should use intelligence measures; the eugenics era (Day 43, Buck v. Bell) shows the cost of confusing a statistic with a verdict on persons.

resource.title: Why our IQ levels are higher than our grandparents'
resource.creator: James Flynn (TED2013)
resource.why: Flynn himself explains the gains he discovered - that modern life trained minds to think abstractly and hypothetically - the leading environmental account, from its author.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); talk known to be published by TED; length from memory. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.topic: Mental illness: diagnosis and treatment evidence
days.headline_hint: Eight Sane People Got Themselves Committed - or Did They? The Study That Shook Psychiatry, and What Survived It.
days.concept: Psychiatric diagnoses are categories defined by agreed criteria, chosen for reliability and usefulness rather than discovered like a virus, and the main treatments - medication and psychotherapy - have real but modest average effects; both claims hold at once.
days.focus: Teach what a diagnosis is (DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria, reliability measured by kappa, categories versus dimensions), how Rosenhan's famous study shaped DSM-III and what Cahalan later found, and how to read the treatment evidence (Cipriani's network meta-analysis, publication bias, the serotonin-hypothesis dispute). This sets up the measurement question in Day 169.
days.model_or_equation: Cohen's kappa measures how far two clinicians agree beyond chance: kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e), where p_o is the proportion of cases on which they agree and p_e the agreement expected by chance from how often each uses each diagnosis. Kappa = 1 is perfect agreement; 0 is no better than chance.

story.title: Eight sane people in insane places
story.hook: On 19 January 1973 Science published 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' by David Rosenhan, a Stanford psychologist. Eight sane people, he reported, himself among them, had gained admission to 12 psychiatric hospitals in five states by saying they heard voices saying 'empty', 'hollow' and 'thud'. Once inside they behaved normally, yet all but one were diagnosed with schizophrenia, stayed an average of 19 days (7 to 52) and were discharged 'in remission'; fellow patients, he wrote, sometimes spotted them as fakes. When one hospital was told to expect impostors, its staff flagged 41 of 193 new patients as suspects - though none had been sent. The paper helped push American psychiatry toward the explicit criteria of DSM-III (1980). In 2019 the journalist Susannah Cahalan, in The Great Pretender, reported that Rosenhan's own records contradicted his account of his symptoms, that she could trace only one other pseudopatient, and that one participant with a positive experience had been left out.
story.puzzle: If psychiatrists could not tell the sane from the insane, are psychiatric diagnoses meaningless? And if the study itself was unreliable, what do we actually know?
story.payoff: A diagnosis is a criteria-defined category whose first test is reliability - do trained clinicians agree? - which DSM-III's checklists improved, though agreement still varies by disorder. Even taken at face value, Rosenhan could not show diagnoses are meaningless: lying about a symptom fools any diagnostic system, as the psychiatrist Seymour Kety replied in 1974 (a man who drank blood and vomited it would be diagnosed with a bleeding ulcer). The right questions are how reliable each category is, what it predicts, and whether treatment helps those who meet it.
sources: Rosenhan, 'On Being Sane in Insane Places', Science 179 (1973)
Cahalan, The Great Pretender (Grand Central, 2019)
Spitzer, 'On pseudoscience in science, logic in remission, and psychiatric diagnosis', Journal of Abnormal Psychology 84 (1975)

days.application: Andrea Cipriani and colleagues (Lancet, 2018) combined 522 double-blind trials involving 116,477 adults with major depression in a network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants. Every drug beat placebo over about eight weeks, with odds ratios for response from about 1.4 to 2.1 - real, modest average effects, similar in size to psychotherapy's. The same literature shows why 'modest' needs care: Turner and colleagues (NEJM, 2008), comparing FDA files with journals, found publication bias had inflated antidepressants' apparent effect by about a third.

builds_on.why: Randomized trials: placebo-controlled, double-blind trials are what separate a drug's effect from the large placebo response and natural recovery in depression.
Replication and publication bias: Turner's comparison of FDA files with published papers is a textbook case of a literature overstating an effect.

across.link: The M'Naghten rules (House of Lords, 1843) define legal insanity as not knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong - a category drawn for the purpose of assigning responsibility, which does not coincide with any psychiatric diagnosis: the same person can meet DSM criteria for schizophrenia and still be legally sane.

days.apply_question: In US states with a 1 September school-entry cutoff, children born in August - the youngest in their class - were diagnosed with ADHD about a third more often than children born in September (Layton and colleagues, NEJM 2018). Does that show ADHD is not a real condition, or something else about how the category is applied - and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: diagnoses are defined by criteria; reliability varies widely by disorder (DSM-5 field trials found good agreement for some, such as PTSD, and poor agreement for others, such as major depression); antidepressants outperform placebo on average in acute trials. Debated: whether the average drug-placebo difference is clinically meaningful (Kirsch against Cipriani and most psychiatric bodies); whether depression involves low serotonin (an umbrella review, Moncrieff et al. 2022, found no consistent evidence - which does not by itself show the drugs fail); categorical versus dimensional systems (HiTOP); and the extent of Rosenhan's misreporting (Cahalan's evidence is strong; he died in 2012). Value judgment: where to draw the line between distress and disorder - the medicalization critique.

resource.title: On Being Sane in Insane Places
resource.creator: David L. Rosenhan (Science 179, 1973)
resource.why: Reading the original shows how a vivid, well-written study persuaded a profession; read it with the lesson's evidence of misreporting in mind and mark where its claims run past its data - practice for judging any famous study.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); a standard citation (Science 179:250-258). Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.headline_hint: The Estimate Said 'High Confidence.' It Was Wrong. That Alone Doesn't Prove the Forecasters Were Bad.
days.concept: A forecaster is well calibrated when the events they call 70% likely happen about 70% of the time; calibration can be judged only across many forecasts stated as numbers and scored with tools such as the Brier score - and forecasters who draw on many perspectives (Tetlock's 'foxes') are better calibrated than those with one big idea.
days.focus: Teach calibration and discrimination, the Brier score, why one outcome cannot grade a probability, why vague words cannot be graded at all (Sherman Kent's 1951 'serious possibility', which colleagues read as anything from 20% to 80%), and what Tetlock's two research programmes found: experts barely beat simple rules (Expert Political Judgment, 2005, about 28,000 forecasts by 284 experts), while trained, teamed, numerate forecasters did much better (the Good Judgment Project).
key_concepts: base rates and the outside view
days.model_or_equation: Brier score: BS = (1/N) x sum of (f_t - o_t)^2, where f_t is the forecast probability for event t and o_t is 1 if it happened and 0 if not; 0 is perfect, and always saying 50% scores 0.25. Worked example: ten forecasts of 70%, seven events happen: BS = (7 x 0.3^2 + 3 x 0.7^2) / 10 = (0.63 + 1.47) / 10 = 0.21. Perfectly calibrated - and still far from perfect, because 70% is not very discriminating.

story.title: 'High confidence'
story.hook: On 1 October 2002 the US intelligence community delivered a National Intelligence Estimate, 'Iraq's Continuing Programs for Weapons of Mass Destruction'. Among the judgments its key findings listed with 'high confidence' was that Iraq was continuing its weapons of mass destruction programmes; it judged that Baghdad had chemical and biological weapons. Within two weeks Congress voted to authorize force. After the 2003 invasion the Iraq Survey Group found no stockpiles, and on 31 March 2005 a presidential commission (Robb-Silberman) concluded the community had been 'dead wrong in almost all of its pre-war judgments' about Iraq's weapons. The intelligence community's research agency, IARPA, created in 2006, went on in 2011 to fund a forecasting tournament to learn whether prediction itself could be measured and improved.
story.puzzle: The estimate was confident, and it was wrong. Does that prove the analysts were bad forecasters - and since 'high confidence' was not a number, how could anyone have checked?
story.payoff: One outcome cannot grade a probability: a forecaster who says 80% should be wrong one time in five. Skill shows up only across many numerical forecasts - calibration - and a phrase like 'high confidence' cannot be scored at all. Tetlock and Gardner argue the Iraq error was as much one of overconfidence as of direction: a calibrated estimate might still have leaned toward weapons, but nowhere near certainty.
sources: National Intelligence Estimate, 'Iraq's Continuing Programs for Weapons of Mass Destruction' (October 2002), declassified key judgments
Commission on the Intelligence Capabilities of the United States Regarding Weapons of Mass Destruction (Robb-Silberman), Report to the President, 31 March 2005
Tetlock & Gardner, Superforecasting (2015)
Sherman Kent, 'Words of Estimative Probability', Studies in Intelligence (1964)

days.application: The Good Judgment Project. From 2011 to 2015 IARPA's Aggregative Contingent Estimation tournament asked thousands of forecasters about hundreds of real geopolitical questions, scored with Brier scores. The team led by Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers won: training in probabilistic reasoning, teaming, tracking the top 2% ('superforecasters') and statistically aggregating forecasts beat the other research teams and the tournament's control group by wide margins (Mellers et al., Psychological Science, 2014). The best forecasters stayed near the top year after year - skill, not luck. Press reports said they also outperformed intelligence analysts with classified information; that comparison has not been published in full.

builds_on.why: Probability: a forecast is a probability, and calibration asks whether stated probabilities match long-run frequencies.
Bayes and base rates: superforecasters start from the base rate (the 'outside view') and update in small steps as evidence arrives.

across.link: The Brier score was invented for weather forecasting (Glenn Brier, Monthly Weather Review, 1950), and US National Weather Service precipitation forecasts became famously well calibrated (Murphy and Winkler, 1977) because forecasters get fast, unambiguous feedback every day - the condition most expert judgment lacks.

days.apply_question: Nate Silver reported (The Signal and the Noise, 2012) that some commercial weather forecasters deliberately say '20% chance of rain' when their models say about 5%, because viewers resent unexpected rain more than unexpected sun. How would that habit show up on a calibration plot of the station's forecasts?
days.evidence_note: Settled: calibration and Brier scores are standard, well-understood measures; forecasting tournaments show stable individual differences, and simple training improves accuracy. Debated: how large the forecasters' edge over intelligence analysts was (reported by journalists, not fully published); whether skill on questions that resolve within a year transfers to rare, long-range, high-impact events (Taleb's fat-tail critique, Day 12); and how to apportion the 2002 failure among overconfidence, flawed sources and outside pressure, which the official inquiries weighed in different ways.

resource.title: Superforecasting - chapter 3, 'Keeping Score'
resource.creator: Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner (Crown, 2015)
resource.why: Tetlock explains, with Kent's 'serious possibility' and his own 20-year expert study, why forecasts must be numerical and scored, and how calibration and Brier scores work - the lesson's tools in the words of the researcher who built the field.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); chapter number and title from established knowledge of the book. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Psychology
days.topic: Well-being and how to measure it
days.headline_hint: Two Studies Asked Whether Money Buys Happiness Past $75,000 and Disagreed - So the Rivals Wrote a Third Paper Together.
days.concept: Well-being has distinct measurable forms - how you evaluate your life as a whole, how you feel moment to moment, and whether life feels meaningful - and they can move differently: life evaluation keeps rising with income, while whether day-to-day emotion does depends on the measure and on who you are.
days.focus: Teach the measures (the Cantril ladder, experience sampling, the day reconstruction method, eudaimonic scales), the log-income relationship, and the $75,000 dispute resolved by adversarial collaboration - itself a model for Logan's book. Then apply the same measurement discipline to a claim that flatters his worldview: religious attendance and flourishing.
days.model_or_equation: Well-being = a + b x ln(income): on a log scale each doubling of income adds the same increment, so going from $50,000 to $100,000 adds as much as going from $100,000 to $200,000 - which is why a curve that looks flat on a dollar axis can still be rising.

story.title: A conflict resolved
story.hook: In 2010 Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton analysed more than 450,000 responses to a daily Gallup survey of Americans (PNAS). Life evaluation rose steadily with income, but emotional well-being - measured by yes-or-no questions about yesterday's feelings - stopped improving at about $75,000 a year, and the figure became famous. In 2021 Matthew Killingsworth, using 1.7 million real-time reports from about 33,000 working Americans who rated their feelings on a smartphone app, found that happiness kept rising with income well past $75,000 (PNAS). Instead of trading rebuttals, the two sides agreed an adversarial collaboration with the psychologist Barbara Mellers as arbiter, setting out in advance how they would test their disagreement. Their joint paper, 'Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved', appeared in PNAS in March 2023.
story.puzzle: Two careful studies of large American samples gave opposite answers to the same question. How can money both stop and not stop buying better days?
story.payoff: They measured different things in different people. Reanalysis showed the plateau is real for the unhappiest people - roughly the bottom fifth, whose happiness stops rising around $100,000 - while for everyone else it keeps climbing with log income, fastest among the happiest. Kahneman and Deaton's yes-or-no questions had a ceiling: they could register less unhappiness but not more happiness. The measure decided the answer.
sources: Kahneman & Deaton, 'High income improves evaluation of life but not emotional well-being', PNAS 107 (2010)
Killingsworth, 'Experienced well-being rises with income, even above $75,000 per year', PNAS 118 (2021)
Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers, 'Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved', PNAS 120 (2023)

days.application: Religious attendance and flourishing. Ying Chen and Tyler VanderWeele (American Journal of Epidemiology, 2018) followed about 5,000 young people from the Growing Up Today Study, the children of participants in the Nurses' Health Study II. Those who attended religious services at least weekly in adolescence were, as young adults, roughly 18% more likely to report high happiness, about 29% more likely to volunteer and about a third less likely to use illicit drugs, after adjusting for many earlier characteristics. The design is observational: families who attend may differ in ways not measured (conscientiousness, family stability, health), so the associations are suggestive, not proof of cause - the same standard a finding hostile to religion would face.

builds_on.why: Confounding: whether religious attendance causes flourishing, or the kind of family that attends causes both, is a confounding question.
Goodhart's law: once a government targets a well-being number, the number can be gamed or drift from the thing it measures.

across.link: Since April 2011 the UK's Office for National Statistics has asked four well-being questions in its large household surveys - life satisfaction, whether life is worthwhile, happiness yesterday and anxiety yesterday - one evaluative, one eudaimonic and two experiential: the lesson's distinction built into official statistics.

days.apply_question: Kahneman and colleagues' 2004 day-reconstruction study of 909 working women in Texas found the morning commute the least pleasant part of the day. Why might a family's life evaluation rise after moving to a bigger house farther out, even as their experienced well-being falls?
days.evidence_note: Settled: life evaluation rises roughly with the logarithm of income, within and across countries; different well-being measures diverge. Debated: whether rising national incomes raise average happiness over decades (Easterlin's paradox versus Stevenson and Wolfers); whether 0-10 scale answers are comparable across cultures; and how much of religion's association with flourishing is causal (Chen and VanderWeele; the 22-country Global Flourishing Study, 2025). Value judgment: what well-being is - pleasure, life satisfaction, or flourishing as Aristotle, Aquinas and many religious traditions describe it - and which of these a government should try to maximize.

resource.title: The riddle of experience vs. memory
resource.creator: Daniel Kahneman (TED2010)
resource.why: Kahneman distinguishes the 'experiencing self' from the 'remembering self' and shows why they give different answers about a happy life - the distinction between experienced well-being and life evaluation, in the words of the scientist at the centre of today's story.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); talk known to be published by TED; length from memory. Cite without a link.

days.phase: Psychology: How Minds Work, as the Evidence Shows
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 10: Social media and teenage mental health
days.headline_hint: Facebook's Own Slide Said 'We Make Body Image Issues Worse for One in Three Teen Girls.' Proving What Caused the Teen Mental-Health Crisis Is Far Harder.
days.concept: Case question: did smartphones and social media cause the rise in teenage depression and anxiety after about 2012 - and what should be done when a harm is plausible, the evidence contested and the technology already everywhere?
days.focus: Walk social media through Logan's chain as a loop - need, invention, physical constraints, engineering, financing, regulation, adoption, consequences, feedback - deep where Psychology and the How We Know lessons apply (belonging, variable rewards, measurement, risk perception, causal inference), previewing ranking algorithms (AI) and the law. The case's distinctive reversal: consequences, and then policy, arrived before the evidence could settle.
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. Reinforcing: engagement -> advertising revenue -> better ranking and new features -> more engagement. Reinforcing: the network effect - the more peers on a platform, the costlier it is for any one teen to leave (a collective trap that individual choice cannot escape). Reinforcing (contested): posting -> comparison -> anxiety -> more checking. Balancing: parental controls, school phone bans, age laws and user fatigue. Delay: features shipped 2006-2012; rigorous causal evidence arrived about a decade later. Unintended consequences: age-verification rules raise privacy costs for everyone and may push teens toward less-moderated services.

story.title: The slide from inside
story.hook: On 14 September 2021 the Wall Street Journal published 'Facebook Knows Instagram Is Toxic for Teen Girls, Company Documents Show'. The documents had been copied by Frances Haugen, a Facebook product manager. One internal slide from 2019 read: 'We make body image issues worse for one in three teen girls' - a finding about girls who already reported body-image problems. Another said teens blamed Instagram for increases in the rate of anxiety and depression. Facebook replied that the same research found many teens felt better after using Instagram, and that the surveys were small and could not show cause. On 5 October 2021 Haugen testified before a US Senate subcommittee.
story.puzzle: The company's own research seemed to say it. Did it? What would it take to know whether social media caused the rise in teenage depression - and what should be done before anyone knows?
story.payoff: The slide reported what some teens believed about their own feelings - a survey of perceived effects, not a causal estimate. The causal evidence is mixed: experiments and natural experiments in adults and college students find real but modest harms; correlational studies of teens find small average associations, larger for girls and heavy users; the teen-specific causal case remains debated. Policy has moved ahead on precaution - and that, too, is part of the system.
sources: Wells, Horwitz & Seetharaman, 'Facebook Knows Instagram Is Toxic for Teen Girls, Company Documents Show', Wall Street Journal, 14 September 2021
US Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection hearing with Frances Haugen, 5 October 2021
Haidt, The Anxious Generation (Penguin Press, 2024)
Odgers, 'The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?', Nature (2024)

days.application: Australia's Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 requires major platforms to keep under-16s from holding accounts from 10 December 2025 - the first national ban, and a live test: if teen mental-health measures in Australia diverge from comparable countries' in the following years, it will become a natural experiment (Day 21) that both sides of the debate have said they are watching.

builds_on.why: Conformity and social proof: likes and follower counts make others' approval visible and countable, the normative pressure Asch measured, at scale.
Variable-ratio reinforcement: a feed that pays out unpredictably is the schedule most resistant to extinction.
Diagnosis and measurement: whether rising rates reflect more illness or changed screening, labelling and reporting is the first question to ask of the trend.
Natural experiments: Facebook's staggered college rollout is the strongest causal design in the debate, and Australia's ban may become another.

across.link: In 1954 the psychiatrist Fredric Wertham's Seduction of the Innocent and US Senate hearings blamed comic books for juvenile delinquency, and the industry adopted the Comics Code that October; decades later Carol Tilley (Information & Culture, 2012) showed Wertham had manipulated and misrepresented his clinical evidence - a past panic to weigh against today's, remembering that some alarms (tobacco) proved right.

days.apply_question: Television reached US cities at different times in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and Gentzkow and Shapiro (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2008) used that staggered arrival to study children's later test scores: they found no harm, and small gains for some groups. Why might that finding fail to transfer to Instagram and teenage depression?
days.evidence_note: Settled: US measures of teenage depression, anxiety and self-harm rose sharply after about 2012, most for girls; average correlations between total screen time and adolescent well-being are small (Orben & Przybylski 2019). Debated: whether social media caused much of the rise - Jonathan Haidt and Jean Twenge point to the timing across many countries, larger associations for girls and heavy social-media users, and experimental and natural-experiment evidence; Candice Odgers, Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski answer that effects are small, possibly reversed (distressed teens use more), confounded, and partly a change in how distress is measured and labelled (Day 166). Value judgment: who should decide - parents, platforms or the state - weighing teens' liberty and the support some find online against precaution for children who cannot meaningfully consent to engagement-maximizing design; utilitarian, rights-based and Christian accounts of moral formation weigh these differently, and the counterfactual of a 2010s without smartphones cannot be known.

chain.point: Adolescents judge their standing by comparing themselves with peers (Festinger's social comparison theory, 1954); platforms made belonging and status visible and countable - likes, followers, streaks. By 2022 about 46% of US teens said they were online 'almost constantly' (Pew Research Center).

The features came first: Facebook's News Feed (September 2006), the Like button (February 2009), the iPhone 4's front-facing camera (June 2010) and Instagram (October 2010) each shipped and spread years before any study of teen mental health could test them; Instagram replaced its chronological feed with a ranked one in 2016.

A camera-and-feed in every pocket, on all day, needed lithium-ion cells dense enough for a day's use (Day 73), cheap silicon (Day 77) and 4G mobile broadband, which US carriers began rolling out around 2010 - hardware that made the feed constant rather than a desk-bound activity.

A feed pays out unpredictably - a new like or post on some refreshes, nothing on others - a variable-ratio schedule, the pattern most resistant to extinction (Day 155), acting on dopamine's reward-prediction-error signal (Day 151); whether the result is 'addiction' or strong habit is debated.

What each teen sees is chosen by recommender systems trained to predict engagement; how such systems learn is taught in the AI block (Days 170-184). Here, only that the ranking is learned from behaviour, not written by hand.

chain.field: Finance (named at CFA level, not taught)
chain.point: The business is advertising: Meta reported about $135 billion of revenue in 2023, roughly 98% of it from ads, so revenue scales with attention and engagement became the target metric - Goodhart's law (Day 23) applied to a proxy that is not the user's well-being.

COPPA (1998) made 13 the age below which US sites need parental consent to collect children's data, which became platforms' de facto minimum age; Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) shields platforms from liability for users' posts; Australia barred under-16 accounts from 10 December 2025. Taught in Government (Days 236-249) and Law (Days 250-263).

US teens' smartphone access rose from roughly a third (2012) to about 95% (2018) in Pew's surveys - a logistic S-curve (Day 7) compressed into six years, sped by network effects as each platform grew more valuable, and harder to leave, as peers joined. How adoption spreads through peers is Sociology's diffusion lesson (Day 213).

On the CDC's Youth Risk Behavior Survey, high-school girls reporting persistent sadness or hopelessness rose from 36% (2011) to 57% (2021), and past-year major depressive episodes among 12-17-year-olds roughly doubled between 2011 and 2019 (NSDUH). Day 166's question applies - more illness, or changed screening, labelling and willingness to report? - though emergency visits for self-harm among young girls, which depend less on labels, also rose.

Orben and Przybylski (Nature Human Behaviour, 2019) ran a specification curve on data from 355,358 adolescents: technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being. Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer and Gentzkow (American Economic Review, 2020) paid adults to deactivate Facebook for four weeks: reported well-being rose modestly. Braghieri, Levy and Makarin (AER, 2022) used Facebook's staggered 2004-06 rollout across US colleges as a natural experiment: students' mental health worsened. None is a randomized trial on young teenagers.

Dread, novelty and harm to children amplify perceived risk (Day 158), and every new medium has met a panic - novels, radio, comics, video games (Orben, 'The Sisyphean Cycle of Technology Panics', Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2020) - yet a panic can also be right. After Haidt's The Anxious Generation (March 2024), schools and legislatures restricted phones, Instagram introduced restricted 'Teen Accounts' (September 2024) and Australia legislated its ban: policy moving before the evidence settled, and feeding back into the platforms' design.

resource.title: The great rewiring: is social media really behind an epidemic of teenage mental illness?
resource.creator: Candice L. Odgers (Nature, book review of Haidt's The Anxious Generation, March 2024)
resource.why: The sharpest short statement of the sceptics' case, by a developmental psychologist, against Haidt's book - read it as one side, named as such, since the lesson itself sets out Haidt and Twenge's argument.
resource.verified_how: Not web-checked this session (search budget exhausted); review known from the literature on this debate (Nature, 29 March 2024). Cite without a link.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Two roads to AI: rules versus learning
days.focus: Concept: AI can be hand-coded rules (symbolic AI, expert systems) or functions learned from data; learning plus computation won (Sutton's 'Bitter Lesson', 2019). Story: the August 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth summer workshop claimed 'every aspect of learning... can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it'. App: spam filtering moved from handwritten rules to learned word statistics (Paul Graham, 'A Plan for Spam', 2002) (D15).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Learning from data: fitting, overfitting, shift
days.focus: Concept: a model learns a function from examples; it can memorize noise (overfitting) and fail when the world changes (distribution shift), so it must be tested on data it never saw. Story: Google Flu Trends (Nature 2009) later predicted more than double the CDC's flu levels for 2012-13 (Lazer et al., Science 2014). App: Epic's widely used sepsis model performed far worse in an independent hospital evaluation than claimed (Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine 2021).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: an artificial neuron takes a weighted sum (a dot product of vectors, D9) and applies a nonlinearity; a layer is a matrix multiplication, and stacked layers learn features. Story: the New York Times of 8 Jul 1958 reported Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron as the 'embryo' of a computer that would walk, talk and see; Minsky and Papert's 1969 critique helped bring an 'AI winter'. App: Yann LeCun's convolutional networks reading handwritten cheque amounts in US banks in the 1990s (D150).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: training lowers a loss by stepping downhill along its gradient (D4, D8); backpropagation is the chain rule's bookkeeping for millions of weights. Story: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' (Nature, October 1986). App: training GPT-3 took about 3 x 10^23 operations (Brown et al. 2020) - orders of magnitude (D1).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: depth, large labelled datasets and GPUs together made learned features beat hand-built ones. Story: AlexNet won ImageNet 2012 with a 15.3% top-5 error against 26.2% for the runner-up, trained on two gaming graphics cards. App: IDx-DR, the first FDA-authorized autonomous AI diagnostic (April 2018), screening for diabetic eye disease.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: embeddings place words, images or products as vectors so that similar things are close (cosine similarity, D9); they also absorb society's biases. Story: word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013) - 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' lands near 'queen'; Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found 'man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker' - a result later shown to depend partly on how analogy queries were constrained (Nissim, van Noord & van der Goot, Computational Linguistics 2020). App: recommendation and search systems built on nearest-neighbour lookups.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: an agent learns from reward by trial and error, using temporal-difference errors like dopamine's (D151, D155), often combined with search. Story: AlphaGo against Lee Sedol in Seoul, March 2016 - Move 37 in game two, a play its own policy network judged about 1 in 10,000 for a human. App: DeepMind reported cutting the energy used to cool Google data centres by up to 40% (2016) (D113).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: attention lets every token weigh every other token through dot products, in parallel, which made training on huge text corpora practical (D175). Story: 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., June 2017) by eight Google researchers, all of whom later left Google. App: AlphaFold 2's protein-structure predictions (CASP14, 2020), which won the 2024 Chemistry Nobel - attention outside language.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: a language model's loss falls as a smooth power law in compute, data and parameters (D3), so capability can be bought - within limits of data and energy. Story: DeepMind's Chinchilla (2022) - a 70-billion-parameter model trained on more data beat the 280-billion-parameter Gopher. App: frontier training runs of 10^25-10^26 operations and the power plants now being contracted for them (D113).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: getting a system to do what we intend, not what we literally rewarded, is hard - optimizers exploit flaws in their objectives (D23); RLHF trains models on human preferences (Christiano et al. 2017). Story: OpenAI's CoastRunners boat (December 2016) circled forever hitting the same targets for points instead of finishing the race. App: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update on 29 Apr 2025 after it became sycophantic.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Hallucination and how to evaluate AI
days.focus: Concept: language models produce plausible text, not retrieved facts, so they confabulate; evaluation needs uncontaminated benchmarks and calibration checks (D167). Story: in Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y., 22 Jun 2023) two lawyers were fined $5,000 for filing ChatGPT-invented cases. App: retrieval with citations - and why a benchmark score can rise without the ability rising (D23).

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.topic: Self-driving cars and the long tail
days.focus: Concept: rare situations are endless (a fat tail, D12), so the last 1% of driving takes most of the effort; perception fuses radar, lidar and cameras (D61). Story: DARPA's Grand Challenge (13 Mar 2004) - no robot finished; the best went 7.4 miles of about 142. App: the Uber test-car crash that killed Elaine Herzberg in Tempe (18 Mar 2018), and Waymo's growth to roughly 250,000 paid driverless rides a week in 2025.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: automation acts on tasks, not jobs - substituting some, complementing others - so who gains depends on the task mix (Autor, Levy & Murnane 2003). Story: a generative-AI assistant raised call-centre agents' productivity about 14%, and about 34% for novices (Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond, 5,179 agents). App: Geoffrey Hinton's 2016 advice to stop training radiologists - radiologist numbers kept rising.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: AI
days.focus: Concept: AI risks fall into misuse, accidents and misalignment, and structural effects; governance tools include risk tiers, compute thresholds and evaluations - experts disagree sharply on magnitudes. Story: the 22 Mar 2023 open letter calling for a six-month pause and the 30 May 2023 one-sentence statement on extinction risk, against prominent sceptics. App: the EU AI Act (in force 1 Aug 2024) and its 10^25-operation threshold, with the Vatican's 'Antiqua et nova' (Jan 2025) as one moral voice among others.

days.phase: AI: Machines That Learn
days.subject: Systems Case
days.focus: Story: on 30 Nov 2022 OpenAI releases ChatGPT as a 'research preview'; within about two months it has an estimated 100 million users. Question: how did next-token prediction become a general-purpose technology in two years - and who bears its costs? Deep: transformers, scaling and alignment (D177, D178, D179); compute and energy (D173, D113); hallucination (D180); labour effects (D182); adoption as an S-curve - about 40% of US adults had used generative AI by late 2024 (Bick, Blandin & Deming) (D7). Preview: chips and export controls (International Relations); hyperscaler spending named at CFA level; copyright suits such as New York Times v. OpenAI (Dec 2023) and EU obligations (Law, Government). Loop: capability arrived before uses were defined; demand for power is reviving nuclear deals; cheaper open-weight models (DeepSeek, Jan 2025) feed back into the race.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: How historians know: source criticism and the Whig warning
days.headline_hint: A Deed Dated to the 310s Gave the Pope the Western Empire. In 1440 a Grammarian Proved It Fake From Its Latin.
days.concept: Historians test a source by its provenance (who made it, when and why), by its anachronisms (anything later than its claimed date) and by independent corroboration, and they guard against 'Whig history', which reads the past as a march toward the present (Butterfield, 1931).
days.focus: Teach source criticism as the historian's method of weighing evidence. It is D41's question (how much should testimony move belief?) made practical: provenance, anachronism, corroboration by independent sources, and the argument from silence and its limits. The angle: Valla had an obvious political motive, yet his verdict stands because it rests on evidence anyone can check. Motive tells you where to look, not what is true. Then Butterfield's warning, shown through the flat-earth myth: it was not a medieval belief but a 19th-century story that flattered its tellers' own age. Close by stating the block's rule: one standard of evidence for claims that flatter and claims that indict.
days.model_or_equation: Corroboration as Bayes (D15): posterior odds = prior odds × LR(source A) × LR(source B), where LR is how much likelier the source's content is if the claim is true than if it is false. Multiply only for independent sources: two chroniclers copying one rumour count once.

story.title: A grammarian against the Pope's title deed
story.hook: In 1440 Lorenzo Valla, a Roman-born humanist, was serving King Alfonso of Aragon, Sicily and Naples, who was then in conflict with the papacy over Naples. That year Valla wrote a declamation against the 'Donation of Constantine'. The document said that Emperor Constantine, cured of leprosy by Pope Sylvester I, had handed the pope Rome and authority over the western empire, and popes had cited it for centuries. Valla attacked it through its Latin. He found words and usages that no fourth-century imperial chancery would have used (he singled out terms such as 'satrap'). It referred to Constantinople as if the city already existed under that name. And every contemporary source was silent about so vast a gift. Nicholas of Cusa had raised doubts around 1433. Valla's text circulated in manuscript and was printed only in 1517, by Ulrich von Hutten.
story.puzzle: Valla's patron was in conflict with the pope, so Valla had every reason to want the document to be fake. Why do historians accept his verdict anyway? And how can anyone prove a document false without a witness to its forging?
story.payoff: Motive is a reason to check, not a reason to dismiss. Valla's case rests on evidence anyone can re-examine: anachronism (language and institutions later than the claimed date in the 310s) and failed corroboration (no independent source mentions the gift). Later scholarship confirmed the forgery and placed it in the eighth century, probably the 750s-760s.
sources: Lorenzo Valla, De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione (1440), trans. Christopher B. Coleman (Yale, 1922)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Donation of Constantine'
Christian History magazine, issue 72, 'Church History's Biggest Hoax'
historyofinformation.com entry on Valla (source of the 'satrap' detail)

days.application: The flat-earth myth. Washington Irving's A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (1828) dramatized a council at Salamanca where clergy supposedly opposed Columbus because they thought the earth was flat. Jeffrey Burton Russell's Inventing the Flat Earth (1991) showed that medieval scholars taught a spherical earth: Bede did, and so did Sacrobosco's De sphaera (c. 1230), a standard university text. Russell traced the myth from Irving and Letronne to the 'warfare' histories of Draper and White. The real dispute with Columbus was over the earth's size, and on that his critics were right.

builds_on.why: Hume's question of how much testimony should move belief, given its reliability and the claim's prior plausibility, is what source criticism puts into practice, with the same standard for claims we like and claims we dislike.
Motivated reasoning explains why Whig stories like the flat-earth myth spread: they flattered their tellers' side, so nobody checked them.

across.link: US Federal Rule of Evidence 901(b)(8) authenticates an 'ancient document' with the historian's tests: its condition creates no suspicion, it was found where it would likely be if authentic, and it is at least 20 years old. In 2017 the related hearsay exception, Rule 803(16), was narrowed to documents prepared before 1 January 1998, out of concern that a flood of old electronic records would otherwise qualify.

days.apply_question: In April 1983 the German magazine Stern published extracts from dozens of volumes of 'Hitler diaries', which the historian Hugh Trevor-Roper had at first judged genuine. In early May the West German Federal Archives declared them forgeries after tests found post-war materials in the paper and bindings. Why could an eminent historian's endorsement not settle whether the diaries were genuine, when a laboratory test of the paper could?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Donation is a forgery, probably composed in the 750s-760s; educated medieval Europeans knew the earth was a sphere; Irving's Salamanca scene is fiction. Debated: who forged the Donation and exactly when; how far historians should pass moral judgement on the past (Butterfield argued against it in 1931, and many historians disagree). Value judgment: none central, since the lesson is about method.

resource.title: The Whig Interpretation of History, chapters 1-2 ('Introduction' and 'The Underlying Assumption')
resource.creator: Herbert Butterfield (G. Bell & Sons, 1931)
resource.length: about 30 minutes (two short chapters of a short book)
resource.why: The original statement of the Whig warning, by the Cambridge historian who named it. It explains why reading the past for its resemblance to the present distorts it, and why the historian must try to enter minds unlike our own.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session confirmed the chapter titles against the full-text edition hosted by Eliohs (Electronic Library of Historiography, University of Florence) and a thesis abstract. URL left empty because Eliohs is not the publisher's host. Reading time is an estimate.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: The agricultural revolution and its costs
days.headline_hint: Foragers Raised Pillars Weighing Up to Ten Tons Before Anyone Farmed. Many of the Farmers Who Followed Were Shorter and Sicker.
days.concept: Farming multiplied food per hectare, and so the number of people a landscape could hold. On much skeletal evidence it also worsened many individuals' health, and later it made grain-taxing states possible. That is a trade-off between totals and individual welfare, not simple progress.
days.focus: Teach the difference between aggregate and individual outcomes. Domestication began in southwest Asia about 11,500-10,000 years ago and arose independently in several regions: China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and Africa. The evidence of cost: shorter stature, enamel defects and more infectious disease in many early farming populations (Cohen & Armelagos 1984; Mummert et al. 2011), and wear on women's skeletons from grinding grain (Theya Molleson's study of Abu Hureyra, 1994). The osteological paradox (Wood et al. 1992) is the caution here: skeletons are a biased sample. Why people farmed anyway: no one chose the whole package. Intensification was gradual, each step fed more people, and a larger population could not go back (a ratchet). Scott (2017) argues grain suited taxation because it is visible, storable and ripens all at once; Graeber & Wengrow (2021) stress that societies took many paths. The full Malthusian logic waits for D217.
days.model_or_equation: Food per person = (food per hectare × hectares farmed) ÷ population. Farming raised food per hectare many times over. When population grows to match, food per person falls back toward subsistence while total numbers stay higher. That is the split between totals and individuals this lesson is about; the full Malthusian model is D217.

story.title: Monuments before farms at Göbekli Tepe
story.hook: On a limestone ridge near Şanlıurfa in southeastern Turkey, earlier surveyors had dismissed a site as a medieval cemetery. In 1995 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began excavating it. Beneath lay rings of carved, T-shaped limestone pillars decorated with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures. The tallest stand about 5 metres and weigh an estimated 7 to 10 tons, and they were raised from about 9500 BC (UNESCO gives 9600-8200 BC). The builders had no pottery and no metal. As far as the plant remains show, they had no domesticated crops either: they harvested wild wheat and barley and hunted gazelle. Schmidt summed it up as 'first the temple, then the city'. Since his death in 2014, excavators have argued that people also lived there. Within a few thousand years, people across the region were farming.
story.puzzle: People who could organize monuments and feasts on wild food turned to farming over the generations. In many places their farming descendants were shorter and sicker than the foragers had been. Why would anyone make that trade?
story.payoff: No one made it as a single choice. Intensive harvesting of wild cereals, perhaps to feed gatherings like those at Göbekli Tepe, slid step by step into cultivation. Each step produced more food per hectare and supported more people, and once populations were dense, foraging could no longer feed them. The gains showed up in totals; the costs fell on individuals.
sources: Andrew Curry, 'Göbekli Tepe: The World's First Temple?', Smithsonian Magazine (2008)
UNESCO World Heritage listing, Göbekli Tepe (2018)
Oliver Dietrich and colleagues' papers on feasting at Göbekli Tepe
Mummert, Esche, Robinson & Armelagos, 'Stature and robusticity during the agricultural transition', Economics & Human Biology 9(3): 284-301 (2011)

days.application: Marshall Sahlins's 'original affluent society' (1966; reprinted in Stone Age Economics, 1972) used Richard Lee's data on the !Kung (Ju/'hoansi) of the Kalahari to argue that foragers worked only a few hours a day for food. Critics answer that this count left out food processing, tool-making and housework; Lee's fuller figures run to roughly 40-45 hours a week. They add that foragers often faced hunger and high child mortality (David Kaplan, 'The Darker Side of the Original Affluent Society', Journal of Anthropological Research, 2000). The real questions are what counts as 'work' and whose welfare is being measured.

builds_on.why: Farming raised the ceiling of a logistic curve, the carrying capacity, and population grew to fill it. That is why food per person did not stay high.
Skeletons are a selected sample, not a random one. The osteological paradox is D16's warning that how a sample was drawn matters more than its size.

across.link: Farming changed human genes. Evershed et al. (Nature, 2022) found that Europeans drank milk for thousands of years before the lactase-persistence variant became common, and linked its spread to episodes of famine and disease. This is gene-culture coevolution driven by a farming practice.

days.apply_question: Average heights of American-born men fell for cohorts born from about the 1830s even as income per head rose (John Komlos's 'antebellum puzzle'). What would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to decide whether that period was progress?
days.evidence_note: Settled: domestication began about 11,500-10,000 years ago in southwest Asia and arose independently elsewhere; farming supported far denser populations. Debated: how general and how large the health decline was (Cohen & Armelagos 1984 and Mummert et al. 2011, against the osteological paradox and regional exceptions); whether farming led to hierarchy and states (Scott 2017) or allowed many paths (Graeber & Wengrow 2021); Sahlins's claim about forager leisure (Kaplan 2000). Value judgment: whether more people living shorter, sicker lives counts as progress depends on whether totals, averages or the worst-off matter most.

resource.title: The Agricultural Revolution: Crash Course World History #1
resource.creator: John Green, Crash Course (2012)
resource.why: A fast, funny tour of why foragers became farmers that takes the 'worst mistake in human history' question seriously. A good second pass on the trade-off, from a popular rather than specialist perspective.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session: URL indexed on thecrashcourse.com, Crash Course's own site; title and series number corroborated by World History Encyclopedia and Lumen Learning listings; length about 11 minutes per one listing. Not fetched.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: The First Name in History May Belong to an Accountant Counting Barley
days.concept: Writing began largely as accounting, a technology for storing information outside human memory. Its records let early states ration, tax and coordinate at scales that memory could not manage. But the Inca show that writing in the usual sense was a powerful aid to states, not a precondition for them.
