days.focus: Teach writing as an information technology (D104): it stores, copies and audits information across time and between people. Mesopotamia's sequence ran from numerical tablets to proto-cuneiform at Uruk around 3300-3000 BC. Those tablets were overwhelmingly administrative (rations, livestock, land, labour), plus lexical lists for training scribes. Writing that records full spoken language, and literature, came centuries later. Denise Schmandt-Besserat's thesis that clay tokens led to writing is influential but debated. Writing was also invented independently in Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. The state angle: what can be recorded can be taxed and rationed. Two pointed versions of that claim are Lévi-Strauss's provocation in Tristes Tropiques (1955) that writing's first function was to make subjugation easier, and James C. Scott's 'legibility'. Then the Inca counter-case.

story.title: A receipt for barley, signed 'Kushim'
story.hook: Uruk, in what is now southern Iraq, around 3400-3000 BC: one of the largest cities of its time, run from temple households. On a palm-sized clay tablet, a scribe pressed signs for barley, a quantity read as about 29,000 measures (published readings differ: 29,086 or 28,086), a span of 37 months, and two signs read KU and ŠIM. Many scholars take 'Kushim' as the name of the official responsible, which would make it the earliest name of a person we can read. Others think it may be a title or an office. The same signs appear on other tablets, sometimes beside SANGA, a temple administrator's title.
story.puzzle: The first name we may be able to read belongs not to a king, a god or a poet but to a barley account. What does that tell us about why writing was invented?
story.payoff: Writing's first job was administration. Temples and palaces that handed out rations and collected goods needed records that outlasted memory and could be checked. The name is there because accountability needed a responsible person. Literature and history came later, borrowing a tool built for bookkeeping.
sources: Hans Nissen, Peter Damerow & Robert Englund, Archaic Bookkeeping (University of Chicago Press, 1993)
Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) materials on proto-cuneiform
Yuval Noah Harari, Sapiens (2014), which popularized the Kushim reading
Guinness World Records news item on 'Sanga Kushim' (2026)

days.application: The Inca counter-case. Tawantinsuyu stretched some 4,000 km along the Andes and ruled perhaps 10 million people (estimates vary widely), all without writing in the usual sense. Specialists called khipukamayuq kept censuses, tribute and labour accounts on khipu, knotted cords whose knots encode numbers in base ten, as L. Leland Locke showed in 1912. Whether khipu also recorded language is debated. Gary Urton argued for a binary coding system; Sabine Hyland (Current Anthropology, 2017) reported two 18th-century narrative khipus from Collata, Peru, with possibly phonetic elements.

builds_on.why: Shannon treated information as a reduction of uncertainty that can be stored and transmitted, and a ration tablet does exactly that: it carries a count across time and between people without loss.
Source criticism of an archive: clay survives where papyrus and cords rot, so what we can read is a biased sample of what was recorded, and whether a sign is a name or a title needs corroboration.

across.link: James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State (1998) argues that states make populations 'legible' so they can tax and conscript them. His example is the Spanish Philippines, where an 1849 decree under Governor Narciso Clavería assigned families surnames from an official catalogue. That is Uruk's logic: a name on a record makes a person accountable to the state.

days.apply_question: India's Aadhaar programme has issued biometric identity numbers to over 1.3 billion residents, and the government routes welfare payments through it. Using the contrast between Uruk's tablets and Inca khipu, is a register like Aadhaar a precondition for a state to deliver welfare at that scale, or an aid to it?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the earliest Mesopotamian tablets are overwhelmingly administrative, and writing was invented independently more than once. Debated: whether 'Kushim' is a personal name or a title; Schmandt-Besserat's sequence from tokens to writing; whether khipu recorded language (Urton; Hyland 2017); whether writing was necessary for states. Value judgment: Lévi-Strauss's and Scott's view that writing served domination mixes evidence with judgment, since record-keeping also enabled famine relief, contracts and law.

resource.title: A History of the World in 100 Objects, episode 15: 'Early Writing Tablet'
resource.creator: Neil MacGregor, BBC Radio 4 with the British Museum (2010)
resource.why: Built around a Mesopotamian tablet of about 3100-3000 BC recording workers' beer rations. The philosopher John Searle discusses what writing does for the mind, and former Cabinet Secretary Gus O'Donnell treats the tablet as early bureaucracy: exactly this lesson's link between writing and the state.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session found episode listings on Global Player and WNYC that credit BBC Radio 4 and describe the tablet and the Searle and O'Donnell contributions. The BBC programme page was not reachable by search, so there is no URL. The length is the series' standard 15 minutes, not confirmed for this episode.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: Ancient growth and its ceiling: Rome
days.headline_hint: Greenland's Ice Kept the Books on Rome's Economy, and Recorded the Plague That Broke It
days.concept: Ancient economies could grow for centuries through peace, trade and specialization ('Smithian' growth). Without a steady flow of new technology, though, that growth stayed modest per person, could be reversed by shocks, and was capped by land and population.
days.focus: Teach Smithian growth (gains from a wider market and the division of labour) against innovation-led growth, using Rome. Under the Pax Romana, a Mediterranean-wide market, sea transport, coinage and Roman law let regions specialize: olive oil from Baetica, grain from Egypt. Historians read the growth from proxies such as Greenland lead (McConnell et al. 2018), shipwreck counts, animal bones and Monte Testaccio's jars, and they argue over how big it was: Finley's 'primitivists' (The Ancient Economy, 1973) against Temin (The Roman Market Economy, 2013) and others. The ceiling: an organic economy running on muscle, wood and water, where population growth absorbs the gains (the full Malthusian model is D217). Then the shock: the Antonine plague from 165. The Malthusian trap itself is named only in a clause here.

story.title: A Roman account book frozen in Greenland
story.hook: In May 2018 a team led by Joseph McConnell of the Desert Research Institute in Reno published more than 21,000 measurements of lead in a Greenland ice core, layer by layer from 1100 BC to AD 800 (PNAS 115: 5726-5731). Roman silver came from smelting lead ore, much of it in Spain, and the smoke drifted thousands of kilometres north and settled in the snow. The lead curve rose with Roman expansion and swung with the wars of the late Republic. It stayed at its highest through the first two centuries AD, the Pax Romana. Then it plunged around the Antonine plague, which struck from AD 165, and stayed low for more than 500 years.
story.puzzle: Rome's economy grew for two centuries, strongly enough to be read in Arctic ice. Why could one epidemic undo it? And why did that growth never become the self-sustaining kind that began around 1800?
story.payoff: Rome's growth was Smithian. It came from peace, markets and specialization, all conditions a shock can destroy, rather than from an accumulating stock of new techniques that would survive the shock. Mining and minting tracked the market economy, and when people and trade collapsed, the lead fell with them.
sources: McConnell et al., 'Lead pollution recorded in Greenland ice indicates European emissions tracked plagues, wars, and imperial expansion during antiquity', PNAS 115(22): 5726-5731 (2018)
Oxford Roman Economy Project note on the paper

days.application: Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill about 35 metres high (some measurements give more), built from the broken pieces of an estimated 53 million amphorae. Most are Dressel 20 olive-oil jars shipped from Baetica in southern Spain between the reign of Augustus and the mid-third century. Many are stamped and painted with the names of shippers and of officials of the annona, the state food supply. The hill is a physical record of specialization: one province grew oil for a city of perhaps a million people, more than a thousand kilometres away by sea.

builds_on.why: Growth rates compound and read best on a log scale. Roman growth per person was small each year, which is why it took centuries to show and one shock could erase it.
Growth that slows near a ceiling traces an S. Rome's organic economy had a ceiling set by land and muscle power, not by ambition.

across.link: E. A. Wrigley's 'organic economy' (Continuity, Chance and Change, 1988): before coal, every economy's energy came from photosynthesis, as food, fodder and wood from a fixed area of land. That capped growth however good the markets were, and Rome is a textbook organic economy.

days.apply_question: On Robert Hartwell's estimate (which is disputed), Song China was producing on the order of 125,000 tonnes of iron a year by 1078, more than Europe would for centuries, yet China did not industrialize then. What evidence would tell you whether Song growth was Smithian, like Rome's, or the beginning of innovation-led growth?
days.evidence_note: Settled: lead emissions in the Greenland record rose and fell as described; the Roman Mediterranean was more commercial and specialized than earlier economies. Debated: how much income per person grew (Finley's primitivists against Temin and other 'market' historians); whether the Antonine plague caused the collapse in the lead record or merely coincided with changes in mining, and how many it killed (Duncan-Jones against Bruun; Elliott 2024); why Rome did not industrialize (Devereaux 2022 against Jason Crawford). Value judgment: none central.

resource.title: Collections: Why No Roman Industrial Revolution?
resource.creator: Bret Devereaux, A Collection of Unmitigated Pedantry (acoup.blog), 26 August 2022
resource.length: a long essay, likely 40 minutes or more (not timed); read it in two sittings
resource.why: A military and economic historian at North Carolina State University argues that Rome lacked the specific preconditions for an industrial breakout. It is the clearest free account of why Smithian growth had a ceiling. Jason Crawford's reply on Roots of Progress contests it, a reminder that the question is still open.
resource.verified_how: Web search this session: URL indexed on acoup.blog, the author's own blog, with the title and date; Roots of Progress coverage corroborates the title and author. The page fetch failed, so the length is an estimate.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: In 112 a Governor Said Christians Were Emptying the Temples. On Stark's Arithmetic They Were Barely One Roman in Five Thousand.
days.concept: Steady compound growth, at Rodney Stark's estimate of about 40% a decade, can explain how a movement of perhaps a thousand people around AD 40 became a majority of the Roman Empire by about 350 without mass conversions. Why it grew that fast is debated: networks, care in epidemics, fertility, conviction and, after 312, imperial favour.
days.focus: Teach the arithmetic first: 40% a decade is about 3.4% a year, doubling roughly every 20 years. Then the calibration: Stark fits his curve to scattered estimates, giving about 6 million (roughly 10%) by 300 and over 30 million (more than half) by 350. The order of magnitude is broadly shared by Keith Hopkins (1998) and Bart Ehrman (2018). Then the mechanisms proposed in Stark's The Rise of Christianity (1996): conversion along social networks; Christian nursing in the epidemics of the 160s and 250s (Dionysius of Alexandria's letter); higher fertility and more women converts. After Constantine (312-313) and the Edict of Thessalonica (380) came privilege and pressure, which Ramsay MacMullen emphasizes. Apply D185's source criticism to Pliny's 'deserted temples'.
days.model_or_equation: N(t) = 1,000 × 1.4^((t − 40)/10). At t = 300: 1,000 × 1.4^26 ≈ 6.3 million. At t = 350: 1,000 × 1.4^31 ≈ 33.9 million, out of perhaps 60 million people (Stark's figures). 40% a decade = 1.4^(1/10) − 1 ≈ 3.4% a year; doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ 3.4 ≈ 20.6 years.

story.title: A governor asks the emperor what to do about the Christians
story.hook: Around AD 112, Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus on the Black Sea coast of what is now Turkey, wrote to the emperor Trajan (Letters 10.96). Accusations were multiplying, some of them anonymous. He had asked the accused three times whether they were Christians, executed those who persisted and sent Roman citizens to Rome for trial. To learn the truth he had tortured two enslaved women 'who were called deaconesses' (ministrae). He found 'nothing but a depraved, excessive superstition': they met before dawn on a fixed day, sang a hymn 'to Christ as to a god', and bound themselves by oath not to steal or commit adultery. The 'contagion', he wrote, had spread through cities, villages and farms, and temples that had been 'almost deserted' were now filling again. Trajan replied (10.97): do not hunt them; punish those accused and convicted; pardon those who sacrifice; accept no anonymous accusations.
story.puzzle: Pliny describes a contagion emptying temples barely eighty years after the crucifixion, yet on any reconstruction Christians were then a tiny fraction of the empire. How can both be true? And how did that fraction become a majority within two and a half centuries?
story.payoff: Compound growth. At about 40% a decade, Christians would have numbered roughly 11,000 around 112, fewer than one Roman in five thousand. But they were concentrated in places like Bithynia, where they could be locally conspicuous, and Pliny, reporting a revival under his own rule, had reason to stress the danger. The same steady rate, compounded for another two centuries, reaches a tenth of the empire by 300 and a majority by 350, with no miracle of mass conversion.
sources: Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96, and Trajan's reply, 10.97 (c. 112)
Rodney Stark, The Rise of Christianity (Princeton, 1996), chapter 1
Keith Hopkins, 'Christian Number and Its Implications', Journal of Early Christian Studies 6 (1998)
Bart Ehrman, The Triumph of Christianity (2018)

days.application: Christianity's centre of gravity has moved south. Philip Jenkins's The Next Christendom (2002) and Pew's Global Christianity report (2011) estimate that about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe in 1910 and about a quarter in 2010. Over the same century, sub-Saharan Africa went from under a tenth Christian to roughly three-fifths. It is the same arithmetic of different growth rates compounding, now driven by conversion and by much higher fertility in the South.

builds_on.why: Stark's model is pure constant-percentage growth: tiny for generations, then explosive, and a straight line on a log scale.
Stark's main mechanism is network spread: faith passing along existing ties of family and friendship, the structure that decides how anything spreads.

across.link: John Lofland and Rodney Stark's 'Becoming a World-Saver' (American Sociological Review, 1965) followed early converts to a small millenarian movement in the San Francisco Bay Area, the American beginnings of the Unification Church. They found that converts joined through friendships with members, not by accepting the doctrine first. Stark later applied that observation to early Christianity.

days.apply_question: In 1984 Rodney Stark projected that the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, then growing about 30-50% a decade, could reach 64 to 265 million members by 2080. The church reported about 11 million members in 2000 and about 17 million in 2023. What does that slowdown suggest about trusting a constant 40%-a-decade rate to reconstruct early Christianity's growth?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Pliny's letter is authentic and shows organized Christian communities in Bithynia by about 112; Christians were a small minority before about 250; Christianity became the empire's official religion in 380. Debated: every number (there was no census, and Stark's curve is a model fitted to scattered estimates, though Hopkins and Ehrman reach similar magnitudes); the causes, with Stark's networks, epidemics and fertility set against MacMullen's stress on miracles, patronage and later coercion. Value judgment: whether fast growth says anything about a faith's truth is a philosophical question, not a historical one; the same arithmetic fits other fast-growing movements.

resource.title: Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96, and Trajan's reply, 10.97
resource.creator: Pliny the Younger (c. AD 112); any standard translation, e.g. Betty Radice (Penguin Classics) or the Loeb Classical Library
resource.why: The whole exchange in their own words: the earliest pagan account of Christian worship, and the template for Roman policy for a century. Reading it lets you practise D185's source criticism yourself: what Pliny knew, what he wanted Trajan to think, and what he could not see.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). A standard, widely translated classical text, cited from the planner's knowledge.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: Christianity and human dignity in late antiquity
days.headline_hint: In 379 a Bishop Called Slavery an Insult to God's Image. Christian Rome Kept Its Slaves for Centuries.
days.concept: Christian ideas — that every person is made in God's image, and that the poor are a public responsibility — changed some norms and institutions of late antiquity quickly: hospitals, organized poor relief, laws against infanticide. Others, above all slavery, they hardly changed at all. Judging how much they changed requires one standard of evidence for the flattering and the unflattering evidence alike.
days.focus: Present the thesis at its strongest: Tom Holland's Dominion (2019) and Larry Siedentop's Inventing the Individual (2014) argue that Western moral instincts about the weak, and about the equal worth of persons, are Christian in origin. The evidence for it: Basil's hospital; the emperor Julian's complaint, in a letter of 362, that the 'Galileans' fed pagan poor as well as their own; Valentinian I's law of 374 making infanticide a capital crime; Peter Brown's bishops as 'lovers of the poor'. The evidence that limits it: Gregory's lone voice on slavery; Augustine's City of God 19.15, which treats slavery as a penalty for sin; Christian emperors who enforced slave law (Kyle Harper, Slavery in the Late Roman World, 2011); Stoic precedents such as Seneca; and Samuel Moyn's Christian Human Rights (2015) on how recent the language of rights is. The lesson's real point: ideas change practice when institutions and interests carry them.
key_concepts: love of the poor as a public virtue

story.title: A Lenten sermon that put a price on the image of God
story.hook: During Lent, probably in 379, Gregory, bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia (central Turkey), preached the fourth of his homilies on Ecclesiastes. When he reached the verse 'I got me slaves and slave-girls' (2:7), he turned on his congregation: 'You condemn man to slavery, whose nature is free.' God had made humanity ruler of the earth, so who could buy a human being? 'For how many obols did you reckon the likeness of God?' His elder sister Macrina, whose life he later wrote, had already persuaded their mother to live on equal terms with the household's slave women. Historians of ancient slavery such as Peter Garnsey call the sermon perhaps the only surviving ancient argument against slavery as an institution. Yet within a generation Augustine treated slavery as a punishment for sin to be borne, Christian emperors went on enforcing slave law, and slavery lasted in the Christian Mediterranean for centuries.
story.puzzle: If Christian ideas implied what Gregory preached, why did Christian societies keep slavery so long? And does his sermon show that Christianity changed moral norms, or that it did not?
story.payoff: Ideas change practice when an institution and a constituency carry them. Gregory's argument had neither: slaveholding bishops, landowners and the law stood against it, so it stayed a lone voice. Care of the poor had both: bishops who built hospitals and relief and won authority by doing so, so it spread fast. Both facts must be counted. Citing Gregory without Augustine, or Augustine without Gregory, breaks the one standard of evidence.
sources: Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes, Homily IV (trans. Stuart G. Hall and Rachel Moriarty, in S. G. Hall, ed., Gregory of Nyssa: Homilies on Ecclesiastes, de Gruyter, 1993)
Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Macrina
Peter Garnsey, Ideas of Slavery from Aristotle to Augustine (Cambridge, 1996)
Augustine, City of God 19.15

days.application: Basil of Caesarea's foundation outside Caesarea, begun around 369-372 after a famine, which Gregory of Nazianzus called a 'new city'. It offered lodging for travellers and the poor, care for the sick and a section for people with leprosy, staffed and funded through the church. Timothy Miller's The Birth of the Hospital in the Byzantine Empire (1985) treats foundations like this as the origin of the hospital. The careful claim is narrower than 'the first hospital', because Roman military and household infirmaries already existed. What was new was free care for strangers and the poor as a religious duty.

builds_on.why: This lesson applies D185's method to Christianity itself: one standard for claims that flatter and claims that indict, and no reading of the past as a march to the present.
By the 370s Christianity's growth had made bishops powerful local patrons, and that is what let ideas about the poor become institutions.

across.link: Seneca's Letter 47 (first century AD) — 'They are slaves. No, they are human beings' — urged humane treatment of slaves without condemning slavery itself. It is a Stoic precedent that tests how distinctive the Christian claims were.

days.apply_question: The Indian emperor Ashoka's second rock edict, from the third century BC, says he provided medical treatment for people and for animals throughout his realm. Judged by the same standard of evidence as Basil's hospital, what would Ashoka's edict need to show to count against the claim that organized care for the sick was a distinctively Christian innovation?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Gregory's sermon, Basil's foundation, Julian's letter of 362, Valentinian's law of 374 and the persistence of slavery under Christian emperors are all documented. Debated: how far Christianity caused later Western moral norms. Holland (2019) and Siedentop (2014) say strongly yes; critics stress Stoic and other precedents, slow and uneven change, and the late origin of human-rights language (Moyn 2015). Harper (2011; From Shame to Sin, 2013) shows both slavery's continuity and real change in sexual morality. Value judgment: that slavery is a grave wrong (near-universal today, but still a moral claim); whether these changes count as moral progress is the question of D288.

resource.title: Poverty and Leadership in the Later Roman Empire, chapter 1, ''Lovers of the Poor': The Creation of a Public Virtue'
resource.creator: Peter Brown (University Press of New England, 2002)
resource.length: one chapter of a short book of lectures; roughly an hour
resource.why: The leading historian of late antiquity shows how bishops turned care of the poor into a public virtue and a source of their own power. Neither apologetic nor debunking, it supplies the institutional mechanism the lesson argues for.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Book and chapter title cited from the planner's knowledge; confirm the chapter title on the contents page.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: Carrying knowledge: the Islamic translation movement
days.headline_hint: A Cairo Scholar Rewrote Greek Optics Around 1020. Kepler's Optics of 1604 Still Started From Him.
days.concept: Knowledge survives only when institutions carry it: patrons who pay translators, cheap writing materials, libraries and teachers. Abbasid Baghdad translated Greek science into Arabic in the 8th-10th centuries. Scholars writing in Arabic corrected and extended it. Then 12th-century Toledo translated it into Latin.
days.focus: Teach transmission as an institutional process. Dimitri Gutas (Greek Thought, Arabic Culture, 1998) argues that the Baghdad movement was driven by demand from the Abbasid elite: astrology, medicine, engineering, administration, theological debate and a Persian imperial ideology. He also argues that the 'House of Wisdom' was more a library than a translation academy. Many translators were Syriac-speaking Christians, such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq (d. 873). Paper, adopted from the eighth century, cut the cost of books. This was extension, not mere preservation: al-Khwarizmi's algebra, Ibn al-Haytham's optics, Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine. Then the flow reversed after Castile took Toledo in 1085. Two myths to retire: Islamic scholars as 'mere transmitters', and a simple 'decline' after 1100.

story.title: A scholar in Cairo, a dark room and a small hole
story.hook: In Cairo, between about 1011 and 1021, al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra around 965 and known in Latin as Alhazen, wrote the seven books of his Kitab al-Manazir, the Book of Optics. Later biographers tell that he had promised the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim to regulate the Nile, failed, and feigned madness under house arrest until the caliph died in 1021; historians treat that story as tradition, not fact. The book itself is documented. Working from Ptolemy's Optics and the Greek geometers in Arabic translation, he rejected the idea that the eye sends out rays and argued that light travels from objects into the eye. He tested claims with controlled arrangements of dark rooms, small apertures, tubes and screens, a procedure he called i'tibar. Around 1200 the book was translated into Latin as De aspectibus. The Silesian scholar Witelo built his Perspectiva on it in the 1270s, and in 1604 Johannes Kepler titled his own optics a supplement to Witelo: Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena.
story.puzzle: Ptolemy wrote in Greek at Alexandria in the second century; Kepler read Latin in Prague in 1604. How did one line of reasoning survive fourteen centuries, two changes of language and the fall of the empires that produced it?
story.payoff: It survived because institutions carried it at every step. In Baghdad, Abbasid patrons paid for translation; paper made copies cheap; Cairo had libraries and teachers; then came Latin translators in Toledo and Sicily, and university curricula. Knowledge does not survive by itself. It is carried, at a cost, by people whose patrons want it, and it is extended by those who read it.
sources: A. I. Sabra (trans.), The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, Books I-III (Warburg Institute, 1989)
Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (Routledge, 1998)
David C. Lindberg, Theories of Vision from al-Kindi to Kepler (Chicago, 1976)

days.application: Gerard of Cremona (c. 1114-1187) went to Toledo to find Ptolemy's Almagest, learned Arabic and translated it, finishing around 1175. A list compiled by his students credits him with some 87 translations, including works of Euclid, Galen and al-Khwarizmi and Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, which European medical faculties taught for centuries. One man's output shows the mechanism at work: a city where Arabic, Hebrew and Latin scholars met, patrons in the cathedral, and demand from the new universities.

builds_on.why: Ibn al-Haytham argued that recognizing what we see requires inference and judgement, not just light striking the eye: an early statement of D153's claim that perception is inference.
As at Uruk, the state paid for the texts it needed. Gutas's argument is that Abbasid administrators, physicians and astrologers created the demand for translation.

across.link: The word 'algorithm' comes from 'Algoritmi', the Latin rendering of al-Khwarizmi's name in the 12th-century translation of his work on Hindu-Arabic numerals (Algoritmi de numero Indorum). 'Algebra' comes from al-jabr in the title of his Baghdad treatise of about 820. Vocabulary carried by the translation movement still names the procedures every computer runs.

days.apply_question: In 1771 the Japanese physician Sugita Genpaku watched a dissection in Edo with a Dutch anatomy book in hand. His team's translation, Kaitai Shinsho, appeared in 1774, although they had started with almost no Dutch. Which of the conditions that carried Greek science through Baghdad and Toledo did 'Dutch learning' in Japan have or lack?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Greek works were translated into Arabic in Abbasid Baghdad (about 750-1000) and Arabic works into Latin in 12th-century Spain and Italy; Ibn al-Haytham's optics shaped Latin optics through Witelo to Kepler. Debated: what the House of Wisdom was (Gutas: mainly a library); why the movement happened (Gutas's social-demand thesis against accounts that stress intellectual curiosity, e.g. Saliba 2007); whether Ibn al-Haytham's i'tibar counts as 'the scientific method' (a popular claim about which historians are more careful); whether and when science declined in the Islamic world. Value judgment: none central. Beware both the 'mere transmitters' story and the 'golden age of everything' story.

resource.title: The House of Wisdom: How Arabic Science Saved Ancient Knowledge and Gave Us the Renaissance (UK title: Pathfinders), the chapters on the Baghdad translation movement and on Ibn al-Haytham
resource.creator: Jim Al-Khalili (Penguin, 2011)
resource.why: A physicist who reads Arabic tells the story of the translators and of Ibn al-Haytham's experiments, crediting extension as well as preservation. It is livelier than the scholarship, though more celebratory; read it against Gutas's point that demand, not curiosity alone, drove the movement.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Book cited from the planner's knowledge; chapter numbers are not given because they could not be confirmed, so use the contents page.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: The medieval Church as an institution-builder
days.headline_hint: The Most Powerful Ruler in Europe Waited Three Days in the Snow at a Countess's Castle. The Pope Had No Army.
days.concept: The Investiture Controversy (1075-1122) left Latin Europe with two powers, church and crown, neither able to absorb the other. Their contest bred lasting institutions: separate spiritual and secular jurisdictions, a systematic canon law, and self-governing corporations such as universities. How much Western law and rights owe to this is debated (Berman 1983; Tierney 1997).
days.focus: Teach the dispute over who appoints bishops and who judges whom: Gregory VII's Dictatus papae (1075); Henry's synod of Worms (1076); the excommunication; Canossa (1077); Henry's capture of Rome (1084); and the Concordat of Worms (1122), which divided spiritual from temporal investiture. Then teach what it left behind: Gratian's Decretum (about 1140) and canon law as an academic discipline, the papal courts, and the legal idea of a corporation. Harold Berman's Law and Revolution (1983) calls this a 'Papal Revolution' that created the Western legal tradition. Brian Tierney (The Idea of Natural Rights, 1997) traces the language of rights to 12th-century canon lawyers. Contrast Byzantium's ideal of harmony between emperor and patriarch. The angle: a stalemate between two legitimate powers forced both to argue in law.

story.title: Three days at the gate of Canossa
story.hook: January 1077. Henry IV, king of the Germans and emperor-elect, 26 years old, had crossed the Alps in midwinter with his wife Bertha and their small son. A year earlier his bishops had told Pope Gregory VII to 'descend' from the papal throne. Gregory had answered by excommunicating Henry and releasing his subjects from their oaths, and the German princes had given Henry until February 1077 to be absolved or be replaced. Gregory, travelling north, took refuge at Canossa, the Apennine fortress of Countess Matilda of Tuscany, his strongest ally. By Gregory's own letter, and in the more dramatic version of the hostile chronicler Lampert of Hersfeld, Henry stood at the gate for three days, barefoot in penitent's wool in the snow. Matilda and Abbot Hugh of Cluny, Henry's godfather, mediated. On 28 January Gregory lifted the excommunication.
story.puzzle: Why would the most powerful ruler in Europe humble himself before a pope with no army? And why do legal historians trace Western legal institutions back to this quarrel?
story.payoff: The pope's power was legitimacy. Excommunication freed Henry's vassals from their oaths, and the princes threatened to elect another king. Henry's penance was also a strategic move, since a priest could hardly refuse absolution to a penitent. Neither side could destroy the other: Henry took Rome in 1084, and Gregory died in exile. So both turned to lawyers, texts and principles to argue their claims. The settlement of 1122, and the canon law that grew out of the fight, left two jurisdictions where there had been one.
sources: Gregory VII's letter to the German princes on Canossa (January 1077), in Brian Tierney, The Crisis of Church and State 1050-1300 (1964)
Lampert of Hersfeld, Annals
Harold Berman, Law and Revolution (Harvard, 1983)
Johannes Fried, Canossa: Entlarvung einer Legende (2012)

days.application: The university as a self-governing corporation. Bologna grew out of law teaching in the late 11th century (the traditional date is 1088), and Emperor Frederick I's Authentica Habita (about 1155-58) protected travelling scholars. At Paris, Pope Gregory IX's bull Parens scientiarum (1231) confirmed the masters' right to make statutes and to suspend lectures if wronged. Cambridge began around 1209, when scholars left Oxford. As corporations (legal persons that could own property, sue and govern themselves), universities could play pope against king and town, and could move when threatened.

builds_on.why: Canossa was a strategic game. Henry's public penance changed the pope's options, because refusing absolution to a penitent would cost Gregory legitimacy: a move chosen with the other player's response in mind.
Path dependence: a stalemate that produced two jurisdictions and a body of law in the 12th century locked in a pattern that later institutions grew around.

across.link: Gratian's Decretum (about 1140), the 'Concordance of Discordant Canons', arranged several thousand church texts into a reasoned system and became the foundation of the canon law taught at Bologna. Together with the revived study of Roman law, it marks the start of law as an academic discipline.

days.apply_question: In 2017 Hungary passed a higher-education law that pushed the Central European University, founded in Budapest in 1991, to move most of its teaching to Vienna by 2019. Medieval universities survived conflicts with kings and towns through rival powers to appeal to, chartered rights and the ability to migrate. Which of those protections did CEU have or lack?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the events of 1075-1122 and the Concordat of Worms; the systematizing of canon law from the 12th century. Debated: the details and meaning of Canossa (Lampert dramatized it, and Fried 2012 argues it was a negotiated peace rather than a humiliation); Berman's 'Papal Revolution' thesis and Tierney's account of natural rights originating with the canon lawyers, both influential and both contested on continuity and causation. Value judgment: whether separating spiritual and secular power served religion, liberty or both. Catholic, Protestant and secular traditions answer differently (D248).

resource.title: The Crisis of Church and State, 1050-1300: the documents on Gregory VII and Henry IV
resource.creator: Brian Tierney (Prentice-Hall, 1964; later reprinted)
resource.length: about 20-30 pages of short documents with commentary
resource.why: The quarrel in its participants' own words: Gregory's claims, Henry's letter telling him to descend, the excommunication, and Gregory's account of Canossa. The introductions are by the historian whose later work argued that the canon lawyers shaped the idea of rights.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). A standard sourcebook cited from the planner's knowledge; check that the documents of 1076-77 are in your edition.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: Medieval technology and the Dark Ages myth
days.headline_hint: William the Conqueror's 1086 Survey Lists 5,624 Water Mills. So Much for the Dark Ages.
days.concept: Medieval Europe was inventive. It spread water and wind power, the heavy plough and three-field rotation, and it invented eyeglasses and the mechanical clock. The 'Dark Ages' label is therefore largely a Renaissance and Enlightenment myth, though why innovation happened, and how much it raised living standards, are debated.
days.focus: Teach the difference between invention and diffusion. The watermill was Roman, but medieval Europe spread it into every valley and adapted it to fulling cloth, sawing, forging and brewing. The post windmill appears in England in the 1180s, eyeglasses around 1286, and the weight-driven clock with a verge escapement by about 1300. 'Dark Ages' began as Petrarch's humanist metaphor for an age without good Latin and grew into an Enlightenment, anti-clerical story; historians now use it, if at all, only for the West's thin written record of about 500-800. The explanations: Lynn White's Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962) offered the stirrup thesis, largely rejected after the 'Great Stirrup Controversy', and the claim that a Christian valuation of labour and the monasteries favoured machines (still debated). Rival explanations stress labour costs, markets and lords' mill monopolies. Growth per person stayed slow (Broadberry et al. 2015).
days.model_or_equation: Water power: P = η ρ g Q h (efficiency × water density × gravity × flow in m³/s × head in m). For an illustrative undershot mill with Q = 0.5 m³/s, h = 2 m and η ≈ 0.3: P ≈ 0.3 × 1,000 × 9.8 × 0.5 × 2 ≈ 2.9 kW, about 4 horsepower. That is the steady output of some 30-40 labourers working at about 75 W each. Now multiply by thousands of mills.

story.title: The king's commissioners count the mills
story.hook: At Christmas 1085, at Gloucester, William the Conqueror ordered a survey of England: who held each estate, what it contained and what it was worth. Within about a year his commissioners had worked through the country county by county. The result was later called Domesday Book because, like the Last Judgement, its verdict could not be appealed. It listed ploughs, villagers, woodland, pigs and mills, each a source of revenue. Counting its entries in 1939, the historian Margaret Hodgen found 5,624 water mills in some 3,000 places. By one common estimate that is roughly one mill for every 50 households in the counties surveyed, and the survey left out London, Winchester and the far north.
story.puzzle: The centuries that popular history calls the Dark Ages produced a dense network of mechanical power that no Roman survey records. Where did it come from, and why does the myth persist?
story.payoff: The watermill was a Roman invention. Medieval Europe's achievement was diffusion and adaptation, driven by lords who profited from mill fees, by monasteries, by plentiful rivers and by the cost of labour. The 'Dark Ages' label came from writers who judged an age by its Latin style and by its distance from their own: Whig history (D185).
sources: Domesday Book (1086)
Margaret T. Hodgen, 'Domesday Water Mills', Antiquity 13 (1939)
Jean Gimpel, The Medieval Machine (1976)

days.application: Eyeglasses. On 23 February 1306 the Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa told a congregation in Florence that the art of making spectacles had been discovered 'not yet twenty years' earlier. That dates the invention to about 1286, probably among the glassworkers of Pisa or Venice. Convex lenses correct presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focus that begins in one's forties. The historian David Landes argued that spectacles roughly doubled the working life of skilled craftsmen and scribes, a plausible claim that is hard to measure.

builds_on.why: Innovation as a system: the medieval story is diffusion, adaptation and incremental improvement of an old invention, not a lone breakthrough.
Power is energy per second. A single mill delivering a few kilowatts replaced dozens of people grinding by hand, which is why mills were taxable assets.

across.link: The verge escapement released a clock's falling weight in regular ticks. Christiaan Huygens's pendulum clock of 1656 replaced its crude oscillator with a pendulum and, by the usual estimate, cut errors from perhaps a quarter of an hour a day to seconds. The medieval clock was the base on which precision timekeeping was built.

days.apply_question: Many popular histories say science in the Islamic world 'declined' after the 12th century, often blaming the theologian al-Ghazali. Yet the Damascus astronomer Ibn al-Shatir (died 1375) built planetary models mathematically equivalent to some of Copernicus's. Using today's lesson, what kind of evidence, like Domesday's mill count, would you need to test the decline story?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the technologies and their approximate dates (eyeglasses about 1286; mechanical clocks by about 1300; Domesday's count of about 5,600 mills); 'Dark Ages' as a disparaging label coined in Petrarch's humanist circle and spread by later writers. Debated: why medieval Europe innovated (White's stirrup thesis is largely rejected, while the roles of monasteries, religious attitudes to labour, labour costs and markets are argued); how much living standards rose (Broadberry et al. 2015 find slow growth per person). Value judgment: none central.

resource.title: Medieval Technology and Social Change, chapter III, 'The Medieval Exploration of Mechanical Power and Devices'
resource.creator: Lynn White Jr. (Oxford, 1962)
resource.length: one long chapter (roughly an hour); read the parts on water mills, windmills and the clock
resource.why: The classic that launched the field: White's sweeping, footnote-dense case that medieval Europe was the first civilization to build on non-human power. Read it as the thesis this lesson tests, knowing that his stirrup chapter was largely rejected.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Book and chapter title cited from the planner's knowledge; confirm on the contents page.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Black Death and its consequences
days.headline_hint: 'I Buried My Five Children With My Own Hands.' The Plague That Killed Them Raised the Wages of Those Who Lived.
days.concept: A demographic shock shifts bargaining power between groups, but institutions decide the outcome. After the Black Death (1347-51), the scarcity of labour raised wages and helped end serfdom in Western Europe, while in much of Eastern Europe lords later tightened it. The mechanisms are debated.
days.focus: Teach the shock first. Ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis as the cause (Bos et al. 2011), and its origin has been traced to Central Asia around 1338-39 (Spyrou et al. 2022). It reached Sicily in October 1347 and killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe (Benedictow argues 60%). Then the mechanism: fewer workers with the same land and capital raised the value of labour. English real wages rose for a century; lords tried to freeze them with the Statute of Labourers and failed; serfdom faded. In much of Central and Eastern Europe a 'second serfdom' hardened from about 1500, and in Mamluk Egypt the same plague brought lasting decline (Borsch 2005). The explanations: Postan's demography, Brenner's class power (Past & Present, 1976), Domar's model of land and labour, critical junctures. Keep the focus on institutions; the wage arithmetic is CFA-level and needs only a clause.
days.model_or_equation: Evsey Domar's hypothesis (1970): of three things — free land, free peasants and non-working landowners — any two can coexist, never all three. When labour becomes scarce, lords can keep their income only by coercion, and whether they can coerce depends on state power, on towns and on peasants' ability to leave.

story.title: Siena, 1348: a chronicler buries his children
story.hook: In 1348 Siena was building a nave so vast that its existing cathedral would have become a mere transept. The plague reached the city that spring. The chronicler Agnolo di Tura, called 'the Fat', wrote that father abandoned child, wife husband and brother brother; that no one could be found to bury the dead for money or for friendship; that great pits were dug and filled. 'And I, Agnolo di Tura, called the Fat, buried my five children with my own hands.' So many died, he wrote, that all believed it was the end of the world. Siena lost perhaps half its people or more. The new cathedral was never finished, and its unfinished wall still stands beside the Duomo.
story.puzzle: Within a generation, many survivors in Western Europe ate better and earned more than their grandparents had. How could a catastrophe that killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe leave its survivors richer? And why didn't it do so everywhere?
story.payoff: Labour became scarce relative to land, so workers' bargaining power rose: they could demand higher wages or leave for a lord who paid more. Where lords and states could not hold them, as in much of Western Europe, wages rose and serfdom eroded. Where they could, as later in much of the East, and in Mamluk Egypt, the same shock brought tighter control or decline. The plague changed the bargaining position; institutions decided the result.
sources: Agnolo di Tura, Cronaca senese, trans. in William Bowsky (ed.), The Black Death: A Turning Point in History? (1971)
Bos et al., Nature 478 (2011)
Spyrou et al., Nature 606 (2022)

days.application: England's Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Statute of Labourers (1351) ordered workers to accept pre-plague wages and forbade them to leave their lords. Justices enforced the rules for decades, and evasion was widespread. Poll taxes in 1377-81 helped trigger the Peasants' Revolt of June 1381, when rebels took London. The preacher John Ball asked 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?', and Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield on 15 June. The revolt failed, but serfdom in England withered over the next century anyway.

builds_on.why: How plague spread and killed — transmission, severity, susceptibility — is D142's mechanics. This lesson starts where the epidemic ends.
Path dependence: the same shock produced opposite outcomes because Western and Eastern Europe started from different institutions.

across.link: Klunk et al. (Nature, 2022) sequenced DNA from people who died before, during and after the Black Death in London and Denmark. They found variants near the immune gene ERAP2 that the plague strongly favoured: natural selection on humans within a few years, with possible effects on autoimmune disease today.

days.apply_question: After epidemics emptied much of the Caribbean and central Mexico in the 1500s, labour there was scarcer than in post-plague England. Yet the result was forced labour and the import of enslaved Africans rather than rising wages. Using Domar's hypothesis, what made the difference?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Yersinia pestis caused the Black Death; mortality was enormous (estimates of about 30-50%, some higher); English real wages rose after about 1350. Debated: the death toll; why serfdom ended in the West and hardened in the East (demographic, class-power and political explanations from Postan, Brenner and Domar); whether the plague set Western Europe on its later divergent path (Voigtländer & Voth 2013 against their critics). Value judgment: whether survivors' gains in any sense offset the catastrophe, a question best kept apart from the economics.

resource.title: The Great Leveler, chapter 10, 'The Black Death'
resource.creator: Walter Scheidel (Princeton University Press, 2017)
resource.why: A Stanford historian sets the Black Death beside other pandemics and shows how its effect on wages and inequality depended on whether elites could coerce labour. That is exactly the shock-plus-institutions argument, with the wage evidence across Europe and the Middle East.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Chapter number and title cited from the planner's knowledge; confirm on the contents page.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: Smallpox Killed the New Aztec Emperor Within Months. The Same Exchange Later Fed the Old World With Potatoes.
days.concept: After 1492, two hemispheres that had long been separate exchanged crops, animals and microbes: Alfred Crosby's 'Columbian exchange' (1972). Disease ran overwhelmingly one way and killed much of the Americas' population, while food flowing the other way fed population growth across the Old World.
days.focus: Teach why the disease flow was so lopsided. Old World crowd diseases evolved in dense populations living with herd animals, and most adults there had been exposed as children. The Americas had few domesticated animals and no such exposure, so whole populations were susceptible at once (D141). David Jones's 'Virgin Soils Revisited' (2003) adds that war, enslavement, famine and displacement multiplied the deaths: biology and violence together. Scale: the Americas' population fell by perhaps 80-90% within a century, from a pre-1492 figure estimated anywhere from under 10 million to over 100 million. Food went both ways: maize, potatoes, cassava, tomatoes and chillies to the Old World; wheat, sugar cane, horses, cattle and pigs to the New. One consequence: the shortage of labour in the Americas fed the Atlantic slave trade (D196).

story.title: The great rash in Tenochtitlan
story.hook: In April 1520 an expedition under Pánfilo de Narváez landed on Mexico's Gulf coast. Tradition holds that one of its men, an enslaved African named in the sources as Francisco de Eguía, carried smallpox. At the end of June the people of Tenochtitlan, the island capital of perhaps 200,000 (estimates vary), drove Hernán Cortés and his army out of the city. That autumn the disease reached them. The Nahua account compiled decades later for Bernardino de Sahagún's Florentine Codex describes sores that covered people so they could not walk or turn over, and many who died of hunger because no one was left to care for them. The new ruler, Cuitláhuac, who had led the resistance, died of smallpox in late 1520 after about eighty days in power. When Cortés returned with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other allies, the city fell on 13 August 1521.
story.puzzle: Why did deadly diseases cross the Atlantic almost entirely in one direction? And how could a microbe help decide a war between empires?
story.payoff: Old World populations had lived for millennia with crowd diseases born among herd animals and in dense cities, and most adults had survived exposure as children. The Americas had few domesticated animals and no such exposure, so everyone was susceptible at once, adults included, and war and hunger compounded the deaths. Smallpox killed defenders and leaders while sparing most of the invaders, who had already been exposed.
sources: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book XII (trans. Anderson & Dibble)
Alfred W. Crosby, The Columbian Exchange (1972)
David S. Jones, 'Virgin Soils Revisited', William and Mary Quarterly 60 (2003)

days.application: The potato. Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2011) compared Old World regions whose soils and climate suited potatoes with regions that did not, before and after the crop arrived. They estimated that the potato explains about a quarter of the growth in Old World population and urbanization between 1700 and 1900. It is a natural-experiment design, with the usual caveat that suitability for potatoes might track other changes.

builds_on.why: Adaptive immunity and herd immunity explain the asymmetry: Old World adults were largely immune from childhood exposure, while in the Americas the whole population was susceptible.
Nunn and Qian's potato estimate is a difference-in-differences design, comparing suitable and unsuitable regions before and after adoption.

across.link: Lewis and Maslin (Nature, 2015) and Koch et al. (Quaternary Science Reviews, 2019) argue that farmland abandoned after the Americas' depopulation grew back as forest and drew atmospheric CO2 down by several parts per million, a dip visible in Antarctic ice around 1610. They propose it as a start date for the Anthropocene, which is still debated.

days.apply_question: Ireland's population grew to about 8 million by 1841 on a diet that leaned heavily on the potato. From 1845, potato blight, caused by a pathogen of American origin, brought a famine that killed about a million people and drove about a million more to emigrate. How does the Columbian exchange explain both Ireland's growth and its catastrophe?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Old World diseases, smallpox above all, caused catastrophic mortality in the Americas; crops and animals moved both ways and reshaped diets. Debated: the pre-1492 population of the Americas; the relative weight of biology versus violence, enslavement and famine (Jones 2003); Nunn and Qian's quarter estimate; the 1610 CO2 dip as an Anthropocene marker. Value judgment: epidemiology does not settle how to judge the conquest. Disease does not absolve the conquerors, and conquest does not explain away the disease.

resource.title: The Columbian Exchange: Crash Course World History #23
resource.creator: John Green, Crash Course (2012)
resource.why: A brisk survey of what crossed the Atlantic in each direction — microbes, crops, animals — and why it reshaped both hemispheres. A good overview to set beside the lesson's mechanism.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Episode number and title cited from the planner's knowledge; search Crash Course's own site or channel for the title before linking.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: The Most-Read Witness of the Middle Passage May Have Been Born in South Carolina. Thirty-Six Thousand Voyages Tell the Story Anyway.
days.concept: The Atlantic slave trade was an industry of enormous scale and calculated brutality. About 12.5 million people were embarked from Africa between 1501 and 1866, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing (SlaveVoyages). It fed a plantation system whose death rates, above all on sugar plantations, demanded a constant supply of new captives.
days.focus: Teach the scale and the mechanics. The trade began with the Portuguese, licensed by the papal bulls Dum Diversas (1452) and Romanus Pontifex (1455), which authorized the perpetual enslavement of 'Saracens and pagans'. Sugar moved from the Atlantic islands to Brazil and the Caribbean. African states and merchants sold captives to European buyers; the 'triangular trade' is a simplification. About one in seven died on the crossing, a rate that fell over time. Plantation demography is a matter of stocks and flows (D25): in the sugar colonies deaths exceeded births, while mainland North America saw natural increase. The evidence comes from some 36,000 voyage records, which can test any single testimony. Christian complicity here, and Christian abolitionism later (D227), are both part of the record.
days.model_or_equation: Stock and flow: change in the enslaved population = arrivals + births − deaths − manumissions. Jamaica received roughly a million Africans yet held about 311,000 enslaved people at emancipation in 1834. Mainland North America received under 400,000 directly from Africa yet held about 3.95 million enslaved people in 1860. The same trade gave births minus deaths opposite signs.

story.title: A best-seller from London, and a baptismal register
story.hook: In March 1789 a two-volume book appeared in London, sold by subscription: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African, Written by Himself. Equiano wrote that he was born in Essaka in Igbo country, kidnapped at about eleven, and carried across the Atlantic in a ship whose stench and crowding made him wish for death. Later, enslaved to a Quaker merchant on Montserrat, he bought his freedom in 1766 for £40. The book went through nine editions in his lifetime and armed the campaign against the trade. Then, from 1999, the scholar Vincent Carretta published two documents: Equiano's 1759 baptismal record at St Margaret's, Westminster, and a 1773 Royal Navy muster list. Both give his birthplace as South Carolina.
story.puzzle: If the most widely read eyewitness of the Middle Passage may never have made the crossing, how can historians know what it was like, or how many people it carried?
story.payoff: No single witness carries the weight. The trade is known from tens of thousands of voyage records — ships' papers, customs and insurance records — compiled in the SlaveVoyages database. They agree with what Equiano describes, whether he saw it himself or drew on others' accounts; Paul Lovejoy defends his African birth, and the question remains open. Applying source criticism to a beloved source does not weaken the history. Corroboration from independent records makes it stronger.
sources: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative (London, 1789)
Vincent Carretta, Equiano, the African: Biography of a Self-Made Man (2005)
Paul Lovejoy, 'Autobiography and Memory', Slavery & Abolition 27 (2006)
SlaveVoyages Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database

days.application: Nathan Nunn (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2008) found that the African countries from which more people were taken in the slave trades are poorer today, using distance to the slave markets as an instrument. Nunn and Wantchekon (American Economic Review, 2011) linked the trade to lower trust today. These 'persistence' findings are influential and also contested: Morgan Kelly (2019) showed that many regressions of this kind can be produced by spatial patterns in the data, so the size of the long-run effect remains uncertain.

builds_on.why: Provenance and corroboration: Equiano's account is tested against independent records, and the trade's scale rests on many sources rather than one.
Stocks and flows: an enslaved population changes only through arrivals, births, deaths and manumissions, which is why the sugar colonies needed endless imports.

across.link: In Gregson v Gilbert (1783), the Zong case, the crew of a Liverpool slave ship had thrown more than 130 captives overboard, and the owners claimed for them under their insurance policy as lost cargo. The court treated it as an insurance dispute, and the abolitionist Granville Sharp's attempt to bring murder charges failed. Here was law that priced people as goods.

days.apply_question: Brazil received about 4.8 million enslaved Africans, more than any other country, yet its 1872 census counted about 1.5 million enslaved people. The United States received under 400,000 and held about 3.95 million in 1860. Reasoning with stocks and flows, what explains the reversal?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the trade's scale (within the database's ranges), its mortality and the papal bulls' licensing language; and, as a near-universal value judgment, that chattel slavery was a grave wrong. Debated: Equiano's birthplace (Carretta 2005 against Lovejoy 2006); the long-run effects on Africa (Nunn 2008 and Nunn & Wantchekon 2011 against doubts about persistence regressions, Kelly 2019); how much the trade enriched Europe (D226). Value judgment: who bears responsibility today, and what repair would be owed, are contested moral questions.

resource.title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, chapter 2
resource.creator: Olaudah Equiano (London, 1789); public domain, many editions
resource.why: The kidnapping and the Middle Passage in Equiano's own words, the passage that moved British readers in 1789. Read it with today's question in mind: what in it do the voyage records corroborate, and what rests on his testimony alone?
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). A standard public-domain text cited from the planner's knowledge.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: Luther May Never Have Nailed His Theses to a Door. They Split Western Christianity Anyway.
days.concept: The Reformation's core claims — scripture alone as the highest authority, salvation by faith, the priesthood of all believers — moved authority away from the Roman hierarchy toward texts, readers and territorial rulers, with long consequences for literacy, war and the state.
days.focus: Teach the redistribution of authority. Luther's attack on indulgences (1517) had become, by 1520, a challenge to papal authority itself. Charles V's Diet of Worms (1521) condemned him, but Elector Frederick the Wise protected him. Princes and city councils gained control of their churches, confiscated monastic property and a clergy under their own rule; the Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each prince choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory. Readers gained Luther's German New Testament (1522) and full Bible (1534), catechisms and schools. Economists have since tested the consequences: Becker & Woessmann (2009) on literacy; Cantoni (2015), who finds no effect on city growth; and Cantoni, Dittmar & Yuchtman (QJE 2018) on the shift of resources from church to secular uses. Printing's role is D200's question.
days.model_or_equation: Becker & Woessmann's causal chain: distance from Wittenberg → share Protestant (1871) → literacy → income and tax revenue. Distance acts as an instrument: it changed the chance of a county becoming Protestant but, they argue, affected prosperity only through Protestantism. The design fails if distance from Wittenberg also tracked something else that mattered, such as trade routes.

story.title: A letter to an archbishop, and a door that may never have been nailed
story.hook: On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor of theology at the young University of Wittenberg in Saxony, wrote to Archbishop Albert of Mainz, enclosing 95 Latin theses against the preaching of indulgences. Indulgences were grants remitting the punishment due for sin. Johann Tetzel was preaching one nearby to fund St Peter's in Rome, and a share of the proceeds was to repay Albert's own debts. The famous scene of Luther hammering the theses to the door of the Castle Church comes from Philip Melanchthon, who wrote it after Luther's death in 1546 and had arrived in Wittenberg only in 1518. In 1961 the Catholic historian Erwin Iserloh argued that the posting never happened. In 2006 a note by Luther's secretary Georg Rörer was found saying the theses had been posted on the doors of Wittenberg's churches, and the dispute reopened. By the end of 1517, printers in Leipzig, Nuremberg and Basel had published the theses.
story.puzzle: These were academic propositions in Latin, by a friar at a minor university, about one fundraising campaign. How did they split Western Christianity within a decade?
story.payoff: They reassigned authority. If scripture alone is the highest authority and every believer may read it, the hierarchy's monopoly on interpretation weakens. Princes who protected reformers gained control of churches and their property, and printers gained a best-selling author. Whether a nail was ever struck matters less than who gained power from the ideas.
sources: Erwin Iserloh, Luthers Thesenanschlag: Tatsache oder Legende? (1962)
Reports of the Georg Rörer note found in 2006
Andrew Pettegree, Brand Luther (2015)
Lyndal Roper, Martin Luther: Renegade and Prophet (2016)

days.application: Was Max Weber wrong? Sascha Becker and Ludger Woessmann (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2009) used Prussia's 1871 census to show that Protestant counties were richer mainly because they were more literate, since Luther wanted everyone to read the Bible. They used distance to Wittenberg to argue that the link was causal. Davide Cantoni (Journal of the European Economic Association, 2015) found no Protestant effect on the growth of 272 German cities between 1300 and 1900. Two careful studies with different measures reached different answers.

builds_on.why: The Reformation was the next round of the contest D192 began: now princes, not just emperors, challenged Rome's jurisdiction, and they won control of the churches in their lands.
Distance to Wittenberg works like a natural experiment: geography, not a region's other qualities, assigned the 'treatment' of becoming Protestant.

across.link: Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904-05) argued that Calvinist ideas of calling and worldly discipline helped create modern capitalism. It is a founding text of sociology and the hypothesis Becker and Woessmann set out to test.

days.apply_question: Robert Woodberry (American Political Science Review, 2012) found that countries with more historical Protestant missionary activity are more democratic today. Nikolova and Polansky (British Journal of Political Science, 2021) reported that the link largely disappears under other reasonable specifications. What would you need to see before believing that missions caused democracy, rather than both simply following where colonial powers and settlers went?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Luther's letter of 31 October 1517; the confessional split; the Peace of Augsburg (1555). Debated: whether the theses were posted (Iserloh against the Rörer note); whether Protestantism raised prosperity (Becker & Woessmann 2009 against Cantoni 2015); how much printing caused the movement (D200). Value judgment: whether the Reformation was a recovery of the gospel and of conscience, a tragedy of division, or both. Protestant, Catholic and secular historians differ: Brad Gregory's The Unintended Reformation (2012) blames it for modern fragmentation, while many Protestant historians see liberation.

resource.title: Luther and the Protestant Reformation: Crash Course World History #218
resource.creator: John Green, Crash Course (2015)
resource.why: A fast, even-handed narrative of Luther's challenge and its spread that also asks why the reformers' ideas found powerful backers. A good companion to the lesson's focus on who gained authority.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Episode number and title cited from the planner's knowledge; search Crash Course's own site or channel before linking.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: Wars of religion, toleration and the sovereign state
days.headline_hint: Three Men Fell From a Prague Castle Window in 1618 and Lived. Thirty Years of War Followed.
days.concept: The wars of religion ended not with one faith's victory but in settlements, at Augsburg in 1555 and Westphalia in 1648. These strengthened rulers' control of their territories and, slowly and often reluctantly, made room for religious coexistence. The popular claim that 1648 founded the modern system of sovereign states is partly myth (Osiander 2001).
days.focus: Teach the Thirty Years' War (1618-48) as a stalemate. A Bohemian revolt widened into a European war in which Catholic France fought the Catholic Habsburgs for reasons of state. Perhaps 4.5 to 8 million people died, and some German regions lost a third or more of their people. The Peace of Westphalia, signed at Münster and Osnabrück in October 1648, recognized Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism, fixed 1624 as the 'normative year' for church property, confirmed the princes' rights within the Empire and recognized Dutch independence. It did not invent sovereignty or non-intervention (Osiander; Krasner). Toleration came first as a truce between exhausted powers and only later as a principle: Castellio after Servetus was burned (1553), then Roger Williams, Locke and Bayle.

story.title: Out of the chancellery window
story.hook: On 23 May 1618, in Prague Castle, Protestant nobles of Bohemia were furious that the Catholic Habsburg government was breaking the religious guarantees of the 1609 Letter of Majesty. In the Bohemian Chancellery they cornered two of the emperor's regents, Vilém Slavata and Jaroslav Bořita of Martinic, together with their secretary Philip Fabricius, and threw all three out of a high window, a fall of roughly 15 to 20 metres (accounts differ). All three survived. Catholic writers said angels or the Virgin Mary had caught them; Protestant pamphlets said they had landed in a heap of refuse in the moat. Fabricius was later ennobled as 'von Hohenfall', 'of the high fall'. The revolt became a war that drew in Denmark, Sweden, France and Spain and lasted thirty years.
story.puzzle: A war fought largely over religion ended in 1648 with three confessions recognized and no side victorious. Why did it end that way? And did it really give birth to the modern sovereign state, as textbooks long said?
story.payoff: No side could win, and thirty years of war had exhausted them all, so the bargain left was a negotiated settlement that let rulers decide religion in their territories, within limits. It stabilized the territorial princes inside the Holy Roman Empire, but sovereignty and toleration grew slowly over the next two centuries. The 'Westphalian system' is largely a label that 19th- and 20th-century writers read back into 1648.
sources: Peter H. Wilson, Europe's Tragedy: A History of the Thirty Years War (2009)
Andreas Osiander, 'Sovereignty, International Relations, and the Westphalian Myth', International Organization 55(2) (2001)
Contemporary Catholic and Protestant accounts of the defenestration

days.application: Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1635 for arguing that magistrates had no power over conscience. In 1636 he founded Providence on land obtained from the Narragansett sachems, and Rhode Island's royal charter of 1663 promised a 'lively experiment' with 'full liberty in religious concernments'. John Locke's A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689) argued that belief cannot be compelled, so force is useless as well as wrong. Yet Locke excluded atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless, and Catholics, whom he saw as owing allegiance to a foreign prince. Toleration grew by stages, and each stage had limits.

builds_on.why: The Reformation created the rival confessions, and Augsburg's rule that the ruler picks the religion set up the conflict that exploded in 1618.
Game theory: a costly war between sides that cannot win ends when a bargain beats continued fighting for all of them. Westphalia was a negotiated equilibrium, not a victory.

across.link: Stephen Krasner's Sovereignty: Organized Hypocrisy (1999) argues that powerful states have violated the 'Westphalian' norm of non-intervention whenever they found it useful. It is the international-relations side of Osiander's historical point that 1648 did not create the system named after it.

days.apply_question: Henry IV's Edict of Nantes (1598) gave French Protestants freedom of worship in defined places and fortified towns of their own. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, after which perhaps 150,000-200,000 Huguenots fled. Using the difference between toleration as a truce and toleration as a principle, why did the edict fail within a century?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the defenestration and its survivors; the war's devastation; the 1648 treaties' recognition of Calvinism and confirmation of the princes' rights. Debated: the death toll (roughly 4.5-8 million); how far Westphalia created state sovereignty (Osiander 2001 and Krasner 1999 against the conventional IR story); how much toleration came from principle rather than exhaustion. Value judgment: whether toleration rests best on religious grounds (Williams's liberty of conscience, Locke) or on secular ones (Bayle, Mill), which is still argued.

resource.title: Sovereignty, International Relations, and the Westphalian Myth
resource.creator: Andreas Osiander, International Organization 55(2): 251-287 (2001)
resource.length: about 37 pages; the introduction and conclusion take about 20 minutes
resource.why: The standard scholarly demolition of the idea that 1648 founded the sovereign-state system. It sets what the treaties actually said against what later international-relations textbooks claimed: a model of checking a myth by reading the primary text.
resource.verified_how: Not checked by web search this session (the shared search budget ran out). Citation from the planner's knowledge. Usually paywalled (JSTOR or Cambridge Core), so a library copy may be needed.

days.phase: History I: From the First Farms to the Scientific Revolution
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Scientific Revolution and the Christianity-and-science question
days.headline_hint: Galileo Knelt in Rome and Recanted in 1633. Historians Now Call the 'War Between Science and Religion' Mostly Myth. Mostly.
days.concept: Historians of science have largely replaced the 'conflict thesis' of Draper (1874) and White (1896) with a 'complexity thesis' (Brooke 1991; Numbers, ed., 2009; Harrison 2015): relations between Christianity and science varied by time, place, institution and question. The opposite claim, that Christianity uniquely gave birth to modern science (Stark 2003; Hannam 2009), has its critics too, and some scientists still defend a conflict view (Coyne 2015).
days.focus: Teach the Galileo affair in context, then the historiography. The sequence: Copernicus (1543); Galileo's telescope discoveries (1610); the 1616 decree against Copernicanism; the Dialogue (1632); the trial (1633). The evidence was not yet decisive. No stellar parallax had been detected (Bessel first measured it in 1838; D128 teaches parallax), and Tycho's hybrid system, with the earth at the centre, fitted the observations. The deciding issues were who had authority to interpret scripture after the Council of Trent, Pope Urban VIII's sense of betrayal, and Galileo's combative tactics; Kuhn's paradigm change (D40) was also a fight about authority. Then the historians. Draper and White wrote amid the 1870s battles over papal infallibility and Darwin. Brooke, Numbers and Harrison replaced their account, and Heilbron (1999) documented how heavily the Church funded astronomy. Stark and Hannam push on to a pro-Christian thesis that critics such as Noah Efron reject. Coyne's argument is philosophical, not historical.

story.title: A kneeling astronomer at Santa Maria sopra Minerva
story.hook: On 22 June 1633, in the Dominican convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, Galileo Galilei, 69 years old, knelt before the cardinals of the Holy Office. He read a formula abjuring the opinion that the sun stands still at the centre of the world and that the earth moves. He was sentenced to imprisonment at the Inquisition's pleasure, commuted to house arrest at his villa at Arcetri near Florence, and his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632) was banned. The story that he muttered 'Eppur si muove' ('and yet it moves') first appears in print in 1757. Twenty-two years before the trial, in 1611, the Jesuit astronomers of the Collegio Romano had confirmed his telescope discoveries and honoured him at a gathering in Rome.
story.puzzle: If science and religion were at war, why were the Church's own astronomers among the first to confirm Galileo's discoveries? And why did the Church condemn him anyway?
story.payoff: Because the affair was not a timeless war between faith and reason. It turned on who had authority to interpret scripture after the Council of Trent, on a pope who felt mocked in the Dialogue, on Galileo's tactics, and on evidence that was not yet decisive. The complexity thesis explains both facts. It does not excuse the verdict, which was the coercion of a scholar.
sources: Maurice A. Finocchiaro (ed.), The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989)
Ronald L. Numbers (ed.), Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion (Harvard, 2009)
J. L. Heilbron, The Sun in the Church (1999)

days.application: The Merton thesis. In 'Science, Technology and Society in Seventeenth-Century England' (Osiris, 1938), the sociologist Robert K. Merton argued that Puritan values — glorifying God through useful work and the study of creation — helped drive English science, and he noted how many Puritans were among the early members of the Royal Society. Critics reply that many founders were Anglicans and royalists and that 'Puritan' is hard to define. The thesis is still argued: a careful pro-religion hypothesis that remains unsettled.

builds_on.why: The conflict thesis is Whig history, reading the past as a march toward the present's victors, and its stock stories, the flat earth among them, are the myths D185 taught you to test.
Kuhn's account of paradigm change — rival frameworks, unresolved anomalies, a fight over authority as well as evidence — fits the Copernican dispute better than a story of reason against faith.

across.link: James Bradley's discovery of the aberration of starlight (1729) and Friedrich Bessel's measurement of the parallax of the star 61 Cygni (1838), about a third of an arcsecond, supplied the direct evidence of the earth's motion that Galileo did not have in 1633.

days.apply_question: In the 1920s and 1930s the Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître proposed that the universe is expanding from a 'primeval atom'. In 1951 Pope Pius XII praised the idea as consonant with creation, and Lemaître is reported to have urged that it not be used that way. Which facts of Lemaître's story would a conflict historian, a complexity historian and a Stark-style historian each be tempted to leave out?
days.evidence_note: Settled among historians of science: the Draper-White conflict thesis fails as a general history; Galileo was tried and abjured in 1633; 'eppur si muove' is legend.
