Meanwhile Gallup's series on trust in mass media fell from about 72% in 1976 to about 31% in 2024.

builds_on.why: Motivated reasoning: people accept and share claims that fit their side, which shapes which falsehoods travel.
The social-media case: moral panics about new media are part of that system - Orben's 'Sisyphean cycle' fits the 1938 radio panic too.
How historians know: Pooley and Socolow's debunking is source criticism of newspaper accounts against ratings data.

across.link: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) shields US platforms from liability for users' posts, which shapes how much they invest in moderating or demoting false news - a legal rule that sets the incentives behind the cascades Vosoughi and colleagues measured (taught in the Law block, Day 262).

days.apply_question: During a hurricane, a dramatic false rumour about a dam failure spreads faster on social media than the authorities' accurate update; using agenda-setting and the novelty finding, what would you change about how the authority words and times its messages to compete, and why would simply posting a correction be weak?
days.evidence_note: Settled: agenda-setting effects and the faster spread of false news on Twitter in 2006-17 are well replicated. Debated: how large misinformation's effects on beliefs and votes actually are (exposure concentrated in small groups; Guess, Nyhan & Reifler), and whether the 1938 panic was wholly myth or a smaller real fright (Schwartz 2015 found many frightened letters).

resource.title: The Myth of the War of the Worlds Panic
resource.creator: Jefferson Pooley and Michael J. Socolow (Slate, 28 October 2013)
resource.why: The short historians' account of where the panic story came from and the ratings evidence against it - a model of checking a famous media claim at its source.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from established knowledge of the article. The routine should confirm before citing.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Sociology
days.headline_hint: New York Had 2,245 Murders in 1990. Two Decades Later, Under 400. Everyone Claimed the Credit.
days.concept: Large crime trends have many candidate causes - policing, incarceration, drug markets, demography, lead, the economy - and because they move together, separating their contributions is hard, so the strongest evidence comes from designs that isolate one cause at a time.
days.focus: Teaches why aggregate trends cannot be attributed by eye, using New York's decline and the national crime drop of the 1990s, then shows the narrower but firmer evidence from randomized hot-spots policing. Angle: a famous success story with too many fathers.

story.title: The rotting apple, 1990
story.hook: In 1990 New York City recorded 2,245 murders, its all-time high; Time magazine's cover that September called it 'The Rotting Apple'. In 1994 Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and Police Commissioner William Bratton adopted 'broken windows' policing - cracking down on fare-beating and squeegee men, on the theory of James Q. Wilson and George Kelling (The Atlantic, March 1982) that visible disorder invites serious crime - and introduced CompStat. Murders fell to 335 in 2013 and below 300 in some later years. Broken windows got the credit and was exported worldwide.
story.puzzle: Crime also fell steeply in the 1990s in San Diego, which did not adopt broken windows, and across the country and in Canada - so how much of New York's fall did its policing cause?
story.payoff: Many causes moved at once - more police, more prisoners, the waning crack market, an ageing population, perhaps declining childhood lead exposure - so a single city's trend cannot reveal which mattered. Levitt (2004) credited police numbers, incarceration, crack's decline and (controversially) legalized abortion, and doubted policing strategy; Zimring (2012) argued New York's extra decline beyond the national trend did owe much to policing. Randomized trials answer narrower questions more firmly.
sources: NYPD historical murder counts (2,245 in 1990; 335 in 2013)
Wilson & Kelling, 'Broken Windows', The Atlantic, March 1982
Levitt, 'Understanding Why Crime Fell in the 1990s', Journal of Economic Perspectives 18(1), 2004
Zimring, The City That Became Safe (2012)

days.application: Hot-spots policing: since the Minneapolis Hot Spots Experiment (Sherman & Weisburd 1995), randomized trials have concentrated patrols on the small number of street segments that produce much of a city's crime. Braga and colleagues' systematic reviews (Campbell Collaboration 2019) find modest, real reductions, with crime more often diffusing benefits to nearby areas than displacing to them - a causal result about one tactic, not an explanation of the whole trend.

builds_on.why: Confounding: in aggregate data every candidate cause moved with the crime rate at once.
Replication and publication bias: the lead-crime literature's shrinking effect sizes show how a vivid single-cause story can overstate.
Leaded gasoline: the lead hypothesis links that case's harm to crime trends a generation later.
Regression to the mean: crackdowns launched after a crime spike can claim credit for a fall that would have come anyway.

across.link: Criminology's finding that the certainty of punishment deters more than its severity (Nagin, 2013) bears directly on how criminal law allocates enforcement - the Law block's Day 257 takes up punishment's justifications.

days.apply_question: US murders rose about 30% in 2020 and then fell sharply in 2023-24; using today's lesson, list how you would go about deciding whether a new city policy adopted in 2022 caused its local decline, and why comparing the city only with its own past would mislead you?
days.evidence_note: Settled: US crime fell steeply in the 1990s; hot-spots policing produces modest reductions in randomized trials. Debated: the contributions of incarceration, police numbers, broken-windows tactics, abortion legalization (Donohue & Levitt versus Foote & Goetz), lead and drug markets; the costs of aggressive stop-and-frisk policing. Value judgment: how to weigh crime reduction against the burdens of policing and prison on communities.

resource.title: Understanding Why Crime Fell in the 1990s: Four Factors that Explain the Decline and Six that Do Not
resource.creator: Steven D. Levitt (Journal of Economic Perspectives 18(1), 2004)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the factor-by-factor sections
resource.why: A clear, argued attribution exercise - one economist's verdict, contested on abortion and policing - that shows how researchers try to apportion a trend among causes.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified this session (shared search budget exhausted); cited from established bibliographic knowledge. The routine should confirm before citing.

days.phase: Sociology: How Societies Hold Together and Change
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 13: Car III - the car remakes society
days.headline_hint: In 1923, 42,000 Cincinnatians Signed a Petition to Limit Every Car to 25 mph. The Auto Industry Made Sure It Lost.
days.concept: The car won not only as a machine but as a social system: status and needs, diffusion, new street norms and laws, suburbs and lost social ties, and induced demand formed reinforcing loops that keep remaking cities around it.
days.focus: Car III goes deep on the social links of Logan's chain - needs and status, adoption, norms and street law, cities and sprawl, social capital and induced demand - and previews law, government and financing. Angle: the street was redefined before the car could own it, and the loops it set up still reinforce car dependence, though the Netherlands shows they can be turned.
days.model_or_equation: Loops: R1 cars -> suburbs -> longer trips -> more cars; R2 new lanes -> faster travel -> more driving -> congestion -> calls for lanes (induced demand); B1 road deaths -> protest and regulation -> safer streets; R3 sprawl -> lost walking and transit -> weaker local ties -> more driving.

story.title: Cincinnati votes on the speed governor, November 1923
story.hook: In 1923 about 42,000 Cincinnati residents, alarmed at children and pedestrians killed in the streets, signed a petition for a city ordinance requiring cars to carry governors that would mechanically limit them to 25 mph. Local auto clubs and dealers, with national industry support, campaigned hard against it, and in November 1923 voters defeated it heavily. The historian Peter Norton (Fighting Traffic, 2008) treats the vote as a turning point: in the same years motor interests promoted the word 'jaywalker' and model ordinances, beginning with Los Angeles in 1925, that redefined the street as a place for cars.
story.puzzle: In 1923 most city people still saw streets as public spaces where cars were the intruders; within a generation, a pedestrian in the road was the one at fault - how did the car rewrite the street, the city and social life, and why do its loops keep reinforcing it?
story.payoff: The car's victory required changing norms and laws before it could change cities; once suburbs, highways and habits were built around it, reinforcing loops made each car more necessary. The loops are strong, not fixed - Dutch protests in the 1970s turned some of them.
sources: Norton, Fighting Traffic: The Dawn of the Motor Age in the American City (MIT Press, 2008)
Duranton & Turner, 'The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion', American Economic Review 101(6), 2011
Putnam, Bowling Alone (2000)
GHSA, Pedestrian Traffic Fatalities by State, 2022 data

days.application: The car, end to end on its social links: the need it served, the norms and street law that let it in, the adoption curve, the suburbs and lost local ties it produced, and the induced demand that keeps roads full - with the Netherlands as the documented reversal.

builds_on.why: Diffusion of innovations: the car's adoption S-curve and the role of credit, roads and status in speeding it.
Norms: 'jaywalking' and the later turn against drunk driving are norm changes that set who belongs on the street.
Cities and density: the expressway fights and sprawl are the car's urban consequence.
Feedback loops: induced demand and car dependence are reinforcing loops.

across.link: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 committed the federal government to pay about 90% of a 41,000-mile Interstate system - a public financing decision that built the road side of the car's reinforcing loop and that the Government block's regulation lessons can analyse.

days.apply_question: Paris has removed traffic lanes along the Seine and on the Rue de Rivoli since the 2010s and 2020s; using induced demand and the car-dependence loop, what would you predict for total driving in the city, and what evidence would show whether the traffic vanished or merely moved?
days.evidence_note: Settled: driving rises roughly one-for-one with new urban interstate lane-kilometres (Duranton & Turner 2011); US pedestrian deaths reached about 7,500 in 2022, the most since 1981 (GHSA). Debated: how much the auto industry's campaigns versus genuine consumer preference made streets car-centred (Norton's account versus demand-led histories); Putnam's estimate that each ten minutes of commuting cuts civic involvement about 10% is correlational. Value judgment: who gained (mobility, freedom, suburban space), who paid (pedestrians, children, the carless, neighbourhoods razed for highways) and who consented (Cincinnati's 1923 voters did; the residents of many highway routes did not) - consequentialist, rights-based and Catholic social teaching's common-good frameworks weigh these differently, and the counterfactual of a less car-centred century is unknowable.

chain.point: One car served autonomy, access and status at once (self-determination theory), so 'need' was never a single first cause; early cars were status goods before they were necessities.
Ford's moving line cut Model T chassis assembly from about 12.5 to about 1.5 hours (1913-14), making the price fall that let the social loops start.

chain.field: Finance (named at CFA level; no block teaches it)
chain.point: Instalment credit through GMAC (1919) and its rivals let households buy cars from income; by the late 1920s most new cars were bought on credit - named, not taught.

Motor interests promoted 'jaywalking' and model traffic ordinances (Los Angeles 1925) that moved pedestrians off the roadway; later MADD and designated drivers turned drunk driving from joke to shame.
US registrations rose from about 8,000 in 1900 to about 23 million in 1929 along an S-curve, sped by price, credit, roads and imitation.
Cars plus mortgages and highways made low-density suburbs such as Levittown (1947) possible; urban expressways cut through dense neighbourhoods, and Jacobs's fight showed the alternative.
Putnam estimates each ten extra minutes of daily commuting cuts involvement in community affairs by about 10% - a correlation that fits the loss of walkable local ties.
Vehicle-kilometres travelled rise about one-for-one with new interstate lane-kilometres in US metro areas (Duranton & Turner 2011), so widening rarely cures congestion.
US pedestrian deaths reached about 7,500 in 2022; the Haddon matrix and Sweden's Vision Zero show the energy-transfer view of preventing them.
The 1956 Interstate act and federal safety regulation will be taught in the Government block; here only named.
Who is liable when a car kills - product liability from MacPherson v. Buick (1916) to today - belongs to the Law block.

The Dutch 'Stop de Kindermoord' ('stop the child murder') campaign, launched 1972-73 after more than 3,000 road deaths a year including hundreds of children, pushed the Netherlands toward traffic-calmed streets and cycling - proof the loop can turn.

resource.title: Fighting Traffic: The Dawn of the Motor Age in the American City
resource.creator: Peter D. Norton (MIT Press, 2008)
resource.why: The history of how the street was redefined for cars - the Cincinnati referendum, safety campaigns and the invention of 'jaywalking' - and the source for this case's central reversal.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified this session (shared search budget exhausted); a well-known 2008 MIT Press history, cited from established knowledge (also named in this project's audits). The routine should confirm before citing.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: Malthus Proved Living Standards Couldn't Rise for Long. He Published in 1798, Just as They Began To.
days.concept: Before about 1800, gains in technology and land were absorbed by population growth rather than raising income per person, so living standards hovered near subsistence: the Malthusian trap.
days.focus: Teaches the Malthusian model as a balancing loop between income per head and population: technology shows up as more people rather than richer people, and shocks such as plague raise wages only until numbers recover. It then poses the block's central question (how some economies escaped after about 1800) and sets Gregory Clark's strong 'no progress before 1800' version against evidence of earlier gains in north-west Europe.
key_concepts: population density versus income per head
balancing feedback between income and population
days.model_or_equation: Output Y = A·T^α·N^(1−α), with land T fixed, so income per head y = A·(T/N)^α. Population rises when y > y* (subsistence) and falls when y < y*, so in equilibrium y = y* and N* = T·(A/y*)^(1/α). A rise in technology A therefore raises the population N*, not income per head. Symbols: Y output, A technology, T land, N population, α land's share of output (0 < α < 1), y* subsistence income.

story.title: An anonymous essay from a Surrey curate, 1798
story.hook: In 1798 the London publisher Joseph Johnson brought out an anonymous Essay on the Principle of Population. Its author was Thomas Robert Malthus, a 32-year-old Anglican curate in Surrey, and he wrote it to answer William Godwin and the Marquis de Condorcet, who believed society could be perfected. His argument fitted in two lines: population, if unchecked, grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8...), while food grows at best arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4...), so misery, vice or restraint must always hold numbers down. As evidence he cited the northern American states, where he said population doubled about every twenty-five years. Britain took its first national census three years later, in 1801, amid the debate Malthus had sharpened.
story.puzzle: If Malthus's model fitted thousands of years of history, why did English living standards begin a sustained rise within a few decades of his book, at the very time the population was growing faster than ever?
story.payoff: Malthus had the pre-1800 mechanism right: a balancing loop in which higher income raised population until income fell back. He could not see that from around 1800 British productivity would grow faster than population could absorb it, or that fertility itself would later fall and cut the loop's link from income to births. His theory was a good model of the world before him and a poor forecast of the world after.
sources: T. R. Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (London: J. Johnson, 1798)
Gregory Clark, A Farewell to Alms (Princeton UP, 2007), ch. 2
E. A. Wrigley & R. S. Schofield, The Population History of England, 1541-1871 (1981)

days.application: English real wages, 1300-1850 (Clark, Journal of Political Economy 2005; Allen, Explorations in Economic History 2001). Builders' and labourers' real wages roughly doubled after the Black Death and drifted back as population recovered toward 1600. They then stayed near that level for two centuries and rose for good only after about 1800-1830, so one series shows the Malthusian loop and then the escape.

builds_on.why: The logistic model's ceiling is Malthus's subsistence limit, and as Pearl and Reed found, that ceiling is an assumption that technology can move.
The Black Death ran the Malthusian model in reverse: halving the population raised wages until numbers recovered.

across.link: Charles Darwin read Malthus's Essay in autumn 1838 (his notebook dates it 28 September; his Autobiography says October). He saw at once that overproduction against limited resources would preserve favourable variations, which became the core of natural selection (Day 134): Malthus's arithmetic, applied to every species.

days.apply_question: Tokugawa Japan's population grew to about 30 million by the 1720s, then stayed nearly flat until the 1850s while farming and commerce kept improving. If fewer births rather than more deaths held that plateau, what does the Malthusian model predict happened to income per head over that century?
days.evidence_note: Settled: before about 1800, sustained growth in income per head was rare and population absorbed most technical gains. Ashraf & Galor (AER 2011) find that, across countries in 1-1500 CE, more advanced technology raised population density but not income per head. Debated: how flat living standards really were. Clark's strong 'no progress before 1800' view is challenged by evidence of a pre-industrial rise in north-west Europe (Allen 2001; Broadberry et al., British Economic Growth 1270-1870, 2015). There is also the optimist-pessimist dispute over when English real wages turned up, around 1800 or only in the 1830s-40s (Feinstein, JEH 1998). Value judgment: Malthus's own policy conclusions, such as his opposition to the Poor Laws, are moral-political claims, not implications of the model.

resource.title: A Farewell to Alms: A Brief Economic History of the World, chapter 2, 'The Logic of the Malthusian Economy'
resource.creator: Gregory Clark (Princeton University Press, 2007)
resource.length: about 20 pages (30-40 minutes); the first half carries the model
resource.why: The clearest modern statement of the Malthusian model, with the English wage and birth data behind it. Clark holds the strong view that nothing fundamental changed before 1800, which Allen and Broadberry dispute, so read it as one side.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified. The session's shared web-search budget was exhausted before this block's research began, and reference sites were blocked. Book and chapter are cited from knowledge; confirm the chapter title before publishing.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: An Economist Burned Sesame Oil in a Roman Lamp to Test Two Centuries of Statistics. The Statistics Failed.
days.concept: Real income per person in today's rich countries is very roughly ten to thirty times its 1800 level. That multiplier is a reconstruction built from historical output estimates, price indexes and purchasing-power conversions, which are conventions with wide error bars, and it is weakest where new goods appear.
days.focus: Shows how the Great Enrichment is measured: national accounts projected backwards (Angus Maddison's life work, continued by the Maddison Project), deflated by price indexes and converted by purchasing-power parity. It explains why new and vastly improved goods make the true gain uncertain and probably understated. Logan already knows CPI biases from the CFA; the lesson teaches him to read '20-fold' as an estimate with a method, not a fact of nature.
key_concepts: price indexes and the new-goods problem
days.model_or_equation: Real income = nominal income ÷ price index. If the measured index rises b percentage points a year faster than true prices, real growth over T years is understated by a factor of (1 + b)^T. For b = 1% and T = 200 years, (1.01)^200 ≈ 7.3. Symbols: b is the annual index bias and T the number of years. Small biases compound like any growth rate (Day 2).

story.title: Sesame oil, a Roman lamp and a light meter
story.hook: In the early 1990s the Yale economist William Nordhaus, later a Nobel laureate (2018) for climate economics, ran an experiment unusual for an economist. He burned sesame oil in a Roman-era lamp, measured its light and fuel use, and did the same for candles, kerosene lamps and electric bulbs. He turned each result into a true price of light: the hours of work needed to buy a fixed amount of illumination. His paper, published in 1997 in the NBER volume The Economics of New Goods, carried a pointed title: 'Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not.' Measured in labour time, light had become cheaper by a factor orders of magnitude larger than the official price indexes implied.
story.puzzle: If the standard statistics missed most of the fall in the price of something as basic as light, how large is the real rise in living standards since 1800, and how can anyone put a single number on it?
story.payoff: The Great Enrichment's multiplier divides incomes by price indexes that track a fixed basket of goods over time. Those indexes handle new or transformed goods (electric light, antibiotics, telephones) poorly, so long-run real growth is probably understated. The honest answer is a range resting on stated conventions, and Nordhaus's lamp shows where the error bars are widest.
sources: William D. Nordhaus, 'Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not', in T. F. Bresnahan & R. J. Gordon (eds.), The Economics of New Goods (University of Chicago Press for NBER, 1997)
Angus Maddison, The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective (OECD Development Centre, 2001)
Maddison Project Database (Groningen Growth and Development Centre)

days.application: Bourguignon & Morrisson's reconstruction of the world income distribution since 1820 (American Economic Review, 2002). They combined Maddison's country GDP estimates with assumed income distributions inside each country and estimated that roughly 84% of humanity lived below a dollar-a-day line in 1820, against about 24% in 1992. The lesson shows how that headline shifts with each input assumption; where to set the line itself is Day 234's subject.

builds_on.why: Exponential growth: a one-point annual error in a price index compounds over two centuries into a roughly sevenfold error in the level.
Source criticism: early output figures are reconstructed from scattered wage, price and tax records, and each needs the provenance questions historians ask of any source.

across.link: Nordhaus's light series is a story of energy conversion. Luminous efficacy rose from a fraction of a lumen per watt for a candle to roughly 10-15 for an incandescent bulb and over 100 for a modern LED, the physical change the price indexes failed to register (Day 84 on energy and living standards).

days.apply_question: A 2007 smartphone replaced a camera, a map, a music player and a phone in one device. Given how real income is measured, would you expect official statistics to have overstated or understated the gain in living standards it brought, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: real income per head in rich countries has risen by an order of magnitude or more since 1800, and the share of humanity in extreme poverty has fallen steeply (Maddison Project; Bourguignon & Morrisson 2002). Debated: the exact multiplier, which depends on price indexes, PPP benchmarks and quality adjustment and probably understates gains from new goods (Nordhaus 1997); the reliability of pre-1820 estimates; and whether GDP-based figures capture welfare at all (Day 234). Value judgment: calling the change 'enrichment' or 'progress' weighs things the numbers leave out, such as leisure, community and ecology.

resource.title: Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not
resource.creator: William D. Nordhaus, in T. F. Bresnahan & R. J. Gordon (eds.), The Economics of New Goods (University of Chicago Press for NBER, 1997)
resource.length: about 40 pages; the introduction and conclusion take 15-20 minutes
resource.why: The original study behind today's story, in Nordhaus's own words: how he measured the true price of light, and why he concluded that conventional price indexes miss most of the gains from new goods.
resource.verified_how: Not web-verified. The shared web-search budget was exhausted before this block's research began. Cited from knowledge of the NBER volume; confirm availability and access before citing.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: The First Steam Engine Wasted More Than 99% of Its Coal. At a Coal Mine, That Didn't Matter.
days.concept: Robert Allen's induced-innovation thesis: Britain industrialized first because its unusually high wages and cheap coal made labour-saving, energy-using machines profitable there before anywhere else.
days.focus: Relative prices steer invention: where labour is dear and energy cheap, it pays to develop machines that swap one for the other, and later engineering improvements make them profitable elsewhere. The lesson walks through Allen's argument and evidence (wage and price series, profitability calculations), then its critics: Humphries & Schneider's 2019 spinning-wage data, Kelly, Mokyr & Ó Gráda's skills-and-nutrition alternative, and Mokyr's point that prices explain the direction of invention, not the supply of ideas.
days.model_or_equation: Adopt a machine when the wages it saves exceed its costs: (wage × labour hours saved) > (machine cost × (interest + depreciation)) + (fuel price × fuel used). The same machine clears this bar where wages are high and coal is cheap, and fails it where wages are low or coal is dear. Improvements that cut fuel use or machine cost later move the bar for everyone.

story.title: An engine near Dudley Castle, 1712
story.hook: In 1712, at a coal works near Dudley Castle in Staffordshire, Thomas Newcomen, an ironmonger from Dartmouth in Devon, and his partner John Calley set up an engine to pump water out of a mine. Steam filled a large cylinder and a jet of cold water condensed it. The weight of the atmosphere then pushed the piston down, rocking a great beam that worked the pumps. By modern measures the machine was astonishingly wasteful: it turned well under one per cent of its coal's energy into work, with estimates around half a per cent. Yet engines of this kind spread across Britain's coalfields over the following decades, and they were still being built when James Watt patented his separate condenser in 1769.
story.puzzle: Why would anyone build a machine that threw away more than 99% of its fuel, and why did it take hold in Britain when France, the Low Countries and China also had mines, skilled craftsmen and knowledge of air pressure?
story.payoff: At the pithead coal was nearly free (the engines could burn small coal that was hard to sell), while the alternative was dear: horses and men hauling water in a high-wage economy. Induced innovation explains the choice. The engine paid only where energy was cheap and labour expensive, which was Britain's peculiar price combination, and it did not pay elsewhere until decades of British improvement had cut its coal use.
sources: L. T. C. Rolt & J. S. Allen, The Steam Engine of Thomas Newcomen (1977)
Robert C. Allen, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (Cambridge UP, 2009)
Black Country Living Museum, Dudley: working replica of the 1712 Newcomen engine

days.application: Allen's 'The Industrial Revolution in Miniature' (Journal of Economic History, 2009) calculated that James Hargreaves's spinning jenny (about 1764) earned a high return in England but little or none in France and India, where spinners' wages were lower. Humphries & Schneider (Economic History Review, 2019) replied that English hand-spinners were mostly poorly paid women and children, which undercuts the high-wage premise in this, Allen's showcase case.

builds_on.why: Heat engines and the Carnot limit: Newcomen's sub-1% engine sat far below the thermodynamic ceiling, so fuel price, not physics, decided where it could run.
Energy and human development: each tonne of coal did work that people and horses would otherwise have done, the substitution Allen's wage-to-energy price ratio measures.

across.link: Cornwall's copper and tin mines had no local coal and shipped it from Wales, so Cornish engineers pushed steam-engine efficiency hardest. From 1811 Lean's Engine Reporter published each engine's monthly 'duty' (work per bushel of coal), and average duty rose several-fold over the following decades (Nuvolari & Verspagen, Transactions of the Newcomen Society, 2007). This is induced innovation running the other way: where energy was dear, the effort went into saving it.

days.apply_question: China became the world's largest buyer of industrial robots in 2013 (International Federation of Robotics), while it was still building large numbers of coal-fired power plants. Which change in Chinese relative prices would Allen's induced-innovation thesis tell you to check first?
days.evidence_note: Settled: London's (and Amsterdam's) wages were among the highest in 18th-century Europe, and coal near British industrial centres was very cheap. Debated: wage comparisons with Asia, and whether these prices caused the key inventions. Allen (2009) says yes; Humphries & Schneider (2019) dispute the spinning-wage data; Kelly, Mokyr & Ó Gráda ('Precocious Albion', Annual Review of Economics 2014) credit British workers' skills and nutrition; and Mokyr argues that prices steer the direction of invention but not the supply of new ideas (Day 220). Value judgment: none is central here.

resource.title: Coal, Steam, and the Industrial Revolution: Crash Course World History #32
resource.creator: John Green, Crash Course (2012)
resource.why: A brisk, entertaining survey of the 'why Britain?' question. It weighs several explanations and gives high wages and cheap coal a central place, close to Allen's argument; use it for the big picture, not for the wage data.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: Joseph Priestley Invented Soda Water and Gave the Recipe Away. A Jeweller in Geneva Built Schweppes on It.
days.concept: Joel Mokyr's Industrial Enlightenment: a culture that prized useful knowledge, published it openly and connected scientists with craftsmen and entrepreneurs lowered the cost of finding and using knowledge, so inventions kept building on one another instead of fizzling out.
days.focus: Explains why British invention after 1750 compounded instead of stalling like earlier bursts. The tools are Mokyr's distinction between propositional knowledge (what is known about nature) and prescriptive knowledge (techniques), linked by low access costs, and the institutions that carried them: societies, journals, public lectures, encyclopedias and a pan-European 'Republic of Letters'. Mokyr shared the 2025 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this work; the lesson also covers how the thesis is tested and where it must coexist with Allen's prices (Day 219).
key_concepts: Republic of Letters and the market for ideas
days.model_or_equation: Mokyr's feedback model, as a described loop: propositional knowledge Ω (what is known about nature) and prescriptive knowledge λ (techniques) feed each other. When access costs are low, each new technique raises questions that science can study, and each scientific answer suggests new techniques: a reinforcing loop. When access costs are high (secrecy, illiteracy, guild closure), the loop breaks and invention plateaus, as it had after earlier efflorescences.

story.title: A brewery in Leeds and a pamphlet given away
story.hook: In 1767 Joseph Priestley, a Dissenting minister, moved into a house next to a brewery in Leeds and began experimenting with the 'fixed air' (carbon dioxide) lying over the fermenting vats. He found he could dissolve it in water to make a pleasant sparkling drink, and in 1772 he published a short pamphlet, Directions for Impregnating Water with Fixed Air, explaining exactly how. He took no patent, and the Royal Society awarded him its Copley Medal in 1773 for his work on airs. About a decade later in Geneva, Johann Jacob Schweppe, a German-born watchmaker and jeweller, worked out how to make carbonated water in quantity; his business moved to London in 1792 and still bears his name. Priestley, meanwhile, moved to Birmingham in 1780 and joined the Lunar Society of Matthew Boulton, James Watt, Josiah Wedgwood and Erasmus Darwin, who met on the Monday nearest the full moon so they could ride home by its light.
story.puzzle: Why would a man give away an invention that would found a company still selling drinks more than two centuries later, and how could a culture of giving knowledge away make a country richer rather than poorer?
story.payoff: In the Industrial Enlightenment, reputation in the Republic of Letters rather than patents was the main reward for natural knowledge, and publishing it lowered access costs for everyone, including a jeweller in Geneva. Mokyr's thesis is that this cheap circulation of useful knowledge between savants and makers kept British invention compounding instead of fizzling out.
sources: Joseph Priestley, Directions for Impregnating Water with Fixed Air (London, 1772)
Jenny Uglow, The Lunar Men: The Friends Who Made the Future (Faber, 2002)
Joel Mokyr, The Gifts of Athena (Princeton UP, 2002)

days.application: Squicciarini & Voigtländer, 'Human Capital and Industrialization: Evidence from the Age of Enlightenment' (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2015). French towns with more subscribers to the Encyclopédie (its 1770s quarto edition) grew faster and had more productive industry in the following century, while average literacy did not predict industrialization. This is evidence that the density of 'knowledge elites' (upper-tail human capital) mattered.

builds_on.why: Innovation as coupled loops between science and practice: Mokyr's Ω-λ feedback is the chain-linked model applied to a whole economy.
Printing made cheap circulation of knowledge possible; the Industrial Enlightenment is what a culture did with that capacity three centuries later.

across.link: Open-source software, such as Linux after Linus Torvalds's 1991 release (Day 115), runs on the mechanism Mokyr describes: reputation rewards and near-zero access costs let strangers build on each other's work. The analogy breaks where 18th-century techniques needed hands-on tacit skill to copy, while code copies perfectly.

days.apply_question: On 30 April 1993 CERN released the World Wide Web's software into the public domain. Using Mokyr's idea of access costs, explain why that decision may have mattered as much to the web's spread as the technology itself.
days.evidence_note: Settled: 18th-century Britain had dense institutions for sharing useful knowledge (scientific and philosophical societies, journals, lectures, instrument makers) that linked scientists with manufacturers. Debated: how much this culture caused industrialization compared with prices (Allen, Day 219) and institutions (Day 222). The thesis is hard to test directly, though Squicciarini & Voigtländer (2015) and Kelly, Mokyr & Ó Gráda (2014) offer quantitative support, and critics note that many early textile inventions came from artisans with little formal science. Value judgment: the 2025 Nobel recognizes the work but does not settle the debate.

resource.title: Popular science background to the 2025 Prize in Economic Sciences (Mokyr, Aghion and Howitt)
resource.creator: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (nobelprize.org, October 2025)
resource.why: The Academy's plain-language explanation of Mokyr's half of the 2025 prize: useful knowledge, its circulation and the feedback between science and technique, set beside Aghion and Howitt's model of growth through creative destruction.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: Bourgeois dignity: ideas that honoured innovation
days.headline_hint: Britain Raised a Colossal Statue of a Steam-Engine Maker Among Its Kings. Deirdre McCloskey Says That Kind of Honour Made Us Rich.
days.concept: Deirdre McCloskey's thesis: the Great Enrichment was caused chiefly by a change in ideas and rhetoric, in which society began to accord dignity and liberty to ordinary people who traded, improved and invented ('bourgeois dignity'), unleashing mass innovation.
days.focus: McCloskey argues that material explanations (capital accumulation, trade, exploitation, even institutions) were neither new enough nor big enough to explain a ten- to thirtyfold rise. What was new, first in the Netherlands and then in Britain after about 1700, was how people talked about and honoured commerce and betterment. Logan should leave able to state the thesis fairly, name its rhetorical evidence, and say what evidence would count against it, given that testability and reverse causation are its main problems.

story.title: A mechanic among kings, Westminster Abbey
story.hook: In 1824, five years after James Watt's death, the prime minister Lord Liverpool chaired a public meeting in London that launched a subscription for a national monument to him. The result was a colossal seated marble figure by Francis Chantrey, installed in Westminster Abbey among the tombs of kings, statesmen and poets (in 1834, according to the historian Christine MacLeod). Its inscription said it was raised 'to show that mankind have learnt to honour those who best deserve their gratitude'. It praised a man who 'enlarged the resources of his country, increased the power of man, and rose to an eminent place among the most illustrious followers of science and the real benefactors of the world.' A century earlier, Jonathan Swift had mocked 'projectors' (schemers with new machines and businesses) as fools.
story.puzzle: In a country still run by landed aristocrats, why would the political establishment raise a monument to an instrument-maker among its kings? And could a change in honour and talk really cause a twentyfold rise in income?
story.payoff: McCloskey reads monuments like Watt's as symptoms of a revaluation of bourgeois life: innovators were now honoured rather than sneered at, and she argues that change unleashed mass betterment. MacLeod's history adds a caution. The Watt cult was also a campaign by manufacturers and reformers for political recognition, so dignity may have followed industrial success as much as caused it. The statue shows that the change in rhetoric was real; whether it was the cause is the open question.
sources: Christine MacLeod, Heroes of Invention: Technology, Liberalism and British Identity, 1750-1914 (Cambridge UP, 2007)
Westminster Abbey, commemoration of James Watt (monument inscription)
Deirdre N. McCloskey, Bourgeois Dignity: Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World (University of Chicago Press, 2010)

days.application: The career of the word 'projector'. In Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), the projectors of the Academy of Lagado try to extract sunbeams from cucumbers. By the mid-19th century, inventors and engineers were the heroes of best-selling biography (Samuel Smiles, Self-Help, 1859; Lives of the Engineers, 1861-62). McCloskey treats such shifts in word use and esteem as her main evidence, and the lesson asks what that kind of evidence can and cannot show.

builds_on.why: Norms about what is honourable are self-enforcing expectations that can shift together, and bourgeois dignity is a claim about exactly such a shift.
Allen's wages-and-coal account is the material explanation McCloskey argues is too small to explain the Enrichment.

across.link: Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904-05) is the older cultural explanation of modern capitalism. McCloskey rejects its stress on thrift and accumulation and argues that the new thing was esteem for innovation, not saving. The two theses share the claim that ideas move economies and differ on which ideas.

days.apply_question: After 1978, Chinese official language moved from condemning private traders as 'capitalist roaders' to praising entrepreneurs. What evidence would distinguish McCloskey's claim that such a change in rhetoric drives growth from the rival claim that it merely followed reforms to prices and property rights?
days.evidence_note: Settled: attitudes to commerce and invention in north-west Europe changed markedly between about 1600 and 1850, and MacLeod documents the inventor's rise to national hero in Britain. Debated: whether that change caused the Great Enrichment. McCloskey says ideas were the prime mover. Economic historians who stress useful knowledge (Mokyr) or prices (Allen) see rhetoric as at most one factor, and critics say her claim is hard to test, rests on selected texts and may confuse effect with cause. Value judgment: McCloskey's case is also a moral argument that commercial life can be honourable and virtuous, which her The Bourgeois Virtues (2006) defends explicitly.

resource.title: Leave Me Alone and I'll Make You Rich: How the Bourgeois Deal Enriched the World (opening chapters)
resource.creator: Deirdre Nansen McCloskey and Art Carden (University of Chicago Press, 2020)
resource.why: McCloskey's own short, popular statement of the thesis, written with Art Carden to be argued with. Read it as the advocate's case.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: One Town, Split by a Line Drawn in 1853. On the Arizona Side, Households Earn About Three Times as Much.
days.concept: Acemoglu and Robinson's thesis: inclusive institutions (secure property, rule of law, open entry and broadly shared political power) give people incentives to invest and innovate, while extractive institutions concentrate power and wealth in a narrow elite and block sustained growth.
days.focus: Treats institutions as 'the rules of the game' (Douglass North) and teaches the inclusive/extractive distinction and why elites block the creative destruction that threatens them. It then shows how the thesis is tested: border comparisons, natural experiments and colonial origins (Day 229). The rival views are human capital first (Glaeser et al. 2004) and geography, along with weak identification in the classic studies. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson shared the 2024 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
key_concepts: institutions as rules of the game (North)
days.model_or_equation: A described pair of loops. Virtuous circle: inclusive political institutions protect inclusive economic institutions, which spread prosperity, which spreads power more widely, which sustains inclusive politics (reinforcing). Vicious circle: extractive politics enrich a narrow elite, which uses its wealth to keep power, which preserves extraction (reinforcing). Acemoglu and Robinson call the vicious circle's persistence through changes of ruler the 'iron law of oligarchy'.

story.title: A boundary drawn through one valley, 1853
story.hook: On 30 December 1853 in Mexico City, the American envoy James Gadsden signed a treaty buying about 30,000 square miles of what is now southern Arizona and New Mexico for $10 million. The new boundary ran across the dry valley of the Santa Cruz River. When the railway arrived in the 1880s, twin towns, both called Nogales, grew up on either side of the line. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson opened Why Nations Fail (2012) there, with the same climate, the same desert and many of the same families on both sides. Yet, they report, household income on the Arizona side is about three times that on the Sonora side, with better roads, health and schooling and far less crime and corruption.
story.puzzle: With geography, climate, ancestry and culture held roughly constant, why are the two halves of one town so different?
story.payoff: The line put the two halves under different rules: US property law, courts, elections and public services on one side, Mexico's on the other, with their different histories of extraction and accountability. That is the inclusive-versus-extractive contrast in miniature. The comparison is not perfectly clean, since the border itself shapes both economies and people choose which side to live on, which is why the thesis also needs other tests.
sources: Daron Acemoglu & James A. Robinson, Why Nations Fail (Crown, 2012), ch. 1
Gadsden Purchase Treaty (Treaty of La Mesilla), signed 30 December 1853, US National Archives
Douglass C. North, Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance (Cambridge UP, 1990)

days.application: North & Weingast, 'Constitutions and Commitment' (Journal of Economic History, 1989). After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, Parliament's control of taxation made the Crown's promises to repay believable, and English government borrowing became far larger and cheaper. Institutions made a commitment credible. Sussman & Yafeh (JEH 2006) found that interest rates did not fall for decades after 1688, so the timing, and with it the causal story, is disputed.

builds_on.why: A border splitting one town is a natural experiment, in effect a geographic regression discontinuity: almost everything but the rules is held constant.
Credible commitment is game theory: a ruler who can seize wealth cannot be believed when he promises not to, unless institutions bind him.

across.link: Botswana: in 'An African Success Story: Botswana' (2003), Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson credit its rapid growth after independence in 1966 to inclusive pre-colonial Tswana institutions, such as the kgotla assembly, and to leaders who preserved them. These state-capacity and legitimacy questions belong to the Government block.

days.apply_question: The Dominican Republic's income per head is now several times Haiti's, though they share one island. What evidence would let you tell whether institutions, rather than geography or the burden of Haiti's 1825 indemnity to France, explain most of that gap?
days.evidence_note: Settled: on average, countries with secure property and constrained rulers are much richer; the correlation is strong and many case studies fit it. Debated: how far institutions cause growth rather than follow it. Glaeser, La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes & Shleifer ('Do Institutions Cause Growth?', 2004) argue that human capital comes first; Jeffrey Sachs and others stress geography and disease; and the classic colonial-origins evidence has been challenged (Albouy 2012, Day 229). Value judgment: the label 'inclusive' carries a favourable judgment of pluralism, a value premise most readers share but which should be stated.

resource.title: Why Nations Fail, chapter 1, 'So Close and Yet So Different'
resource.creator: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson (Crown, 2012)
resource.why: The authors' own opening case, Nogales, with the inclusive/extractive framework in their words. It is the thesis's best statement; keep Glaeser's and Albouy's objections in mind while reading.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Great Divergence: why Europe, not China?
days.headline_hint: In 1793 China's Emperor Told Britain It Made Nothing China Needed. Historians Still Argue Whether He Was Right.
days.concept: The Great Divergence debate. Kenneth Pomeranz (2000) argued that China's most advanced regions, such as the Yangzi delta, matched England's living standards until about 1800, and that coal and colonial land let Europe break away. Newer wage and GDP reconstructions suggest the gap opened earlier, by the 1600s-1700s (Broadberry, Guan & Li 2018).
days.focus: Teaches how to compare like with like (regions, not whole empires) and contrasts the 'California school' (Pomeranz, R. Bin Wong) with the early-divergence view (Broadberry, Allen's wage studies). It also covers energy (coal near industry) and land (colonies and Atlantic trade, the 'ghost acres'). The key skill is seeing how a dating question decides which causes are even possible: a late divergence favours contingency such as coal and colonies, while an early one favours longer-run institutions and culture (Days 220-222).

story.title: An embassy at Chengde, September 1793
story.hook: In September 1793 George Macartney, Britain's first ambassador to China, was received by the Qianlong Emperor at his summer retreat at Chengde, north of Beijing, after a voyage of some ten months. He brought gifts chosen to show off British science and industry, including a planetarium, telescopes, globes and clocks, and he asked for a resident embassy and new trading rights. He declined the full kowtow, kneeling on one knee as he would to George III. The emperor's formal reply to the king, in the 1914 translation by Backhouse and Bland, said: 'we possess all things. I set no value on objects strange or ingenious, and have no use for your country's manufactures.' Macartney went home with nothing.
story.puzzle: Was the emperor right that in 1793 China needed nothing Britain made? And if China's richest regions were as prosperous as England then, why did the two diverge so dramatically over the next century?
story.payoff: On Pomeranz's account the emperor was roughly right about 1793: the Yangzi delta and England stood at similar levels, and only coal and colonies let Britain escape the land constraint after 1800. On Broadberry, Guan and Li's reconstruction, China's income per head had already fallen behind by the early 1700s, so the edict spoke for an economy that was being overtaken. Historians such as Henrietta Harrison add that the letter was a diplomatic formula drafted before Macartney's audience, and that it became famous as 'proof' of Chinese arrogance only in the 20th century.
sources: J. L. Cranmer-Byng (ed.), An Embassy to China: Lord Macartney's Journal, 1793-1794 (1962)
Henrietta Harrison, 'The Qianlong Emperor's Letter to George III and the Early-Twentieth-Century Origins of Ideas about Traditional China's Foreign Relations', American Historical Review 122:3 (2017)
Kenneth Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (Princeton UP, 2000)
Stephen Broadberry, Hanhui Guan & David Daokui Li, 'China, Europe, and the Great Divergence', Journal of Economic History 78:4 (2018)

days.application: China's convergence after 1978. With market reforms, China's output per head grew at very roughly 8-10% a year for three decades (World Bank data), among the fastest sustained catch-ups on record. It shows how quickly a follower can close a gap once it can adopt existing technology and its rules change, and why catch-up growth slows as the gap narrows.

builds_on.why: Power density: coal let Britain draw energy from underground instead of from scarce land, the heart of Pomeranz's 'ghost acres' argument.
The Columbian exchange and New World land are the other half of Pomeranz's escape from the land constraint.

across.link: E. A. Wrigley's 'organic versus mineral economy' (Energy and the English Industrial Revolution, 2010): an economy fuelled by photosynthesis on its own land faces a hard ceiling, and coal removed it, since Britain's coal by the early 1800s supplied energy that would have needed millions of acres of woodland. This is Pomeranz's argument in energy terms.

days.apply_question: Meiji Japan industrialized rapidly after 1868, largely by importing machines, engineers and methods from Britain and other Western countries rather than inventing them. Does a fast follower like Japan tell you anything about the causes of the original divergence, or only about how catch-up works?
days.evidence_note: Settled: by 1850-1900, north-west Europe's income per head was far above China's, and China's share of world output fell sharply in the 19th century. Debated: when the divergence began, and so which causes could have mattered. Pomeranz (2000) and the California school say around 1800. Broadberry, Guan & Li (2018) and the wage comparisons of Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata & van Zanden (Economic History Review 2011) put the Yangzi delta behind England by the 1700s. Value judgment: framing the question as 'why not China?' treats Europe's path as the norm, a framing Pomeranz himself criticized.

resource.title: The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy, Introduction
resource.creator: Kenneth Pomeranz (Princeton University Press, 2000)
resource.why: Pomeranz's own framing of the problem: why compare regions rather than nations, and why coal and colonies. Read it as one side, knowing that Broadberry and others now date the divergence earlier.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.headline_hint: A Professor Made Indigo in a Flask in 1880. It Took BASF Seventeen Years and a Fortune to Sell It, and an Indian Industry Died.
days.concept: In the late nineteenth century invention itself was industrialized: firms built research laboratories that employed trained scientists to search systematically, turning discovery and scale-up into a routine, budgeted activity rather than the work of lone inventors.
days.focus: Alfred North Whitehead wrote that the nineteenth century's greatest invention was 'the method of invention'. The lesson shows what that meant through the German dye industry and Edison's Menlo Park: why a laboratory synthesis is not yet a product (process development, raw materials, cost, scale), and how corporate laboratories, research universities and patents formed a system (Day 35). It ends with Robert Gordon's claim that this system powered an unrepeatable surge from 1870 to 1970, which is debated.

story.title: Blue from coal tar, Ludwigshafen, 1897
story.hook: In 1880 the Munich chemist Adolf von Baeyer found a way to make indigo, the world's most valuable natural dye, from coal-tar chemicals; it worked in a flask and was hopeless as a business. BASF of Ludwigshafen and its rival Hoechst acquired rights and set teams of chemists on the problem. It took BASF until 1897 to bring synthetic indigo to market, by a new route starting from naphthalene: some seventeen years and, by the company's own reckoning, about 18 million marks, a sum often said to exceed its share capital. Natural indigo then came mainly from plantations in Bengal and Bihar, worked by Indian tenant farmers, and within about fifteen years India's indigo exports had shrunk to a fraction of their former size.
story.puzzle: If the chemistry was solved in 1880, why did it take a company seventeen years and a fortune to make indigo, and what kind of organization could afford to wait that long?
story.payoff: A laboratory synthesis is not a product. Making indigo cheap by the tonne meant finding new raw materials, catalysts and plant, a systematic search that only a firm with a standing research laboratory, trained chemists and patient capital could run. BASF's indigo is the invention of invention in miniature: discovery made into a budgeted, organized routine, with consequences that reached tenant farmers in Bihar.
sources: BASF SE, corporate history of synthetic indigo
Anthony S. Travis, The Rainbow Makers: The Origins of the Synthetic Dyestuffs Industry in Western Europe (1993)
Johann Peter Murmann, Knowledge and Competitive Advantage: The Coevolution of Firms, Technology, and National Institutions (Cambridge UP, 2003)

days.application: Thomas Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey (1876) was the American version: a staff of machinists and scientists working to a promise, attributed to Edison, of 'a minor invention every ten days and a big thing every six months or so'. The phonograph (1877) and a practical incandescent lighting system (1879-80) followed. Robert Gordon (The Rise and Fall of American Growth, 2016) argues that the great inventions of this era drove a century of unusually fast growth in living standards that has since slowed.

builds_on.why: Innovation as a system, not a pipeline: the research lab is the institution that couples science, process engineering and markets in loops.
BASF's research organization later scaled up Haber-Bosch at Oppau, the same model of budgeted, team-based chemical development.

across.link: Bell Labs, AT&T's research laboratory founded in 1925, produced the transistor in December 1947 (Day 106). It was the 20th-century peak of the organized industrial lab that Menlo Park and the German dye firms began.

days.apply_question: Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine went from a published viral sequence in January 2020 to US emergency authorization in December 2020. Using the idea of organized invention, explain why the decades of earlier mRNA research mattered as much as those eleven months.
days.evidence_note: Settled: from the 1870s, German chemical firms and then American companies (GE, AT&T, DuPont) institutionalized research laboratories, which produced a large share of major 20th-century innovations. Debated: Gordon's claim that the inventions of 1870-1970 were uniquely powerful and that growth has slowed for good (Mokyr and Brynjolfsson, among others, expect new waves); and how much corporate labs mattered compared with universities and independent inventors, including why corporate research later declined (Arora, Belenzon & Patacconi, Strategic Management Journal 2018). Value judgment: whether synthetic indigo, which ruined Indian growers while cheapening dye for millions, counts as progress depends on whose gains and losses are weighed.

resource.title: The death of innovation, the end of growth
resource.creator: Robert J. Gordon, TED2013
resource.why: Gordon in his own words on why the inventions of 1870-1970 transformed daily life and why he thinks the pace has slowed. It is one side of a live debate; Erik Brynjolfsson gave the opposing view at the same conference.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: The Age of Revolutions: rights declared and denied
days.headline_hint: A Man Born in Africa and Once Enslaved Took His Seat in the French Convention. The Next Day France Abolished Slavery. Eight Years Later It Brought It Back.
days.concept: The Atlantic revolutions of 1776-1804 made universal rights the test of legitimate government while withholding them from most people, and the excluded used the declarations as levers to claim those rights. Where such rights talk came from is debated.
days.focus: Shows how a universal claim works as a ratchet: once a regime justifies itself by appeal to 'all men', every exclusion needs a reason and every excluded group gains an argument. It is taught through Saint-Domingue and Haiti, the only successful large-scale slave revolution, with the American and French declarations as the texts. The origins debate is a lesson in historiography: Tierney traces rights to medieval canon law and natural law, Hunt to 18th-century empathy, and Moyn to a movement of the 1970s, and each defines 'rights' differently. Christian contributions are presented among the others and attributed.

story.title: Three deputies from Saint-Domingue, Paris, 16 Pluviôse Year II
story.hook: On 3 February 1794, three deputies elected in Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, took their seats in the National Convention in Paris. They were Louis-Pierre Dufay, a white colonist; Jean-Baptiste Mills, a free man of colour; and Jean-Baptiste Belley, who said he had been born on Gorée, off the coast of West Africa, and had bought his own freedom. The next day, 16 Pluviôse Year II by the revolutionary calendar, after Dufay described the colony's situation, the Convention abolished slavery in all French colonies amid acclamation. That came four and a half years after the Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaimed that 'men are born and remain free and equal in rights', and two and a half years after the enslaved of Saint-Domingue's northern plain rose in revolt in August 1791. In 1802, under Napoleon, slavery was maintained in recovered colonies and reimposed in Guadeloupe and Guiana; Saint-Domingue fought on and declared independence as Haiti on 1 January 1804.
story.puzzle: Why did a revolution that declared all men free and equal in 1789 take five years and a slave uprising to apply that to enslaved people, and why could the decision be reversed in 1802?
story.payoff: Universal declarations do not apply themselves. They create a standard that excluded groups can invoke and opponents must argue around. The enslaved of Saint-Domingue, by revolt, made the contradiction impossible to ignore, and in 1794 a Convention at war over the colony found universalism useful. When the political balance shifted, Napoleon's government argued around it, and only Haiti's victory made freedom permanent there.
sources: Laurent Dubois, Avengers of the New World: The Story of the Haitian Revolution (Harvard UP, 2004)
Decree of 16 Pluviôse Year II (4 February 1794) abolishing slavery in the French colonies
Anne-Louis Girodet, Portrait of Jean-Baptiste Belley (1797), Château de Versailles

days.application: The Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (19-20 July 1848), drafted chiefly by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, copied the Declaration of Independence: 'We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal'. It listed grievances against men as the 1776 text had listed them against the king. Its resolution demanding the vote was the most controversial and passed only after Frederick Douglass spoke for it; one hundred people signed.

builds_on.why: Brian Tierney traces natural-rights language to the medieval canon lawyers whose Church institutions that lesson covered.
Saint-Domingue was the Atlantic plantation complex at its most intense, so the revolution happened inside the system that lesson described.

across.link: In Brom and Bett v. Ashley (Berkshire County, Massachusetts, 1781), Elizabeth Freeman ('Mum Bett'), an enslaved woman, sued for her freedom under the new state constitution's declaration that 'all men are born free and equal' and won. The Quock Walker cases (1781-83) followed: a declaration used as a lever in court.

days.apply_question: South Africa's Freedom Charter, adopted at Kliptown in June 1955, declared that 'South Africa belongs to all who live in it, black and white'. Using today's idea of declarations as levers, explain how such a document could matter politically for decades before it had any legal force.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the American and French declarations proclaimed universal rights while slavery, property qualifications and the exclusion of women continued. Saint-Domingue's revolt (from August 1791) preceded and pressed French abolition (1793-94); slavery was reimposed in Guadeloupe and Guiana in 1802 and abolished in the French colonies again only in 1848. Debated: where rights talk came from. Tierney (The Idea of Natural Rights, 1997) points to medieval canon law and Christian natural law, Hunt (Inventing Human Rights, 2007) to 18th-century empathy and print culture, and Moyn (The Last Utopia, 2010) to a movement of the 1970s. Historians also debate how much the 1794 decree owed to principle and how much to war strategy. Value judgment: that these exclusions were unjust is a near-universal moral judgment today.

resource.title: Inventing Human Rights: A History, chapter 4, "'There Will Be No End of It': The Consequences of Declaring"
resource.creator: Lynn Hunt (W. W. Norton, 2007)
resource.why: Hunt follows today's mechanism: how declaring rights in 1776 and 1789 drew Protestants, Jews, free Black men, the enslaved and women into claims the authors never intended. It represents her empathy-centred account, which Tierney and Moyn dispute.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: Slavery and capitalism: did profit end the trade?
days.headline_hint: Parliament Voted 283 to 16 to Kill a Trade That Was Still Making Money. Was It Conscience or Capitalism?
days.concept: The slavery-and-capitalism debate: Eric Williams (1944) argued that Britain abolished the slave trade and slavery once they had become economically obsolete; Seymour Drescher (1977) showed that abolition came while the British slave system was still growing and profitable ('econocide'); and historians still dispute how central slavery was to industrial capitalism.
days.focus: Teaches the argument as a test of evidence. Williams makes two claims: that slavery's profits financed industrialization, and that economic decline caused abolition. Drescher's trade data put the British West Indies near their peak around 1800. The 'new history of capitalism' (Baptist 2014; Beckert 2014) faces economic historians' critiques (Olmstead & Rhode 2018; earlier, Engerman 1972 and O'Brien 1982 on profits too small to finance industrial investment). Logan should end able to say what each side claims and which data decide it.

story.title: 283 to 16, House of Commons, February 1807
story.hook: On 23 February 1807, after a long debate, the House of Commons voted 283 to 16 to give a second reading to the bill abolishing Britain's slave trade. In 1791, William Wilberforce's first motion for abolition had lost by 163 votes to 88. During the 1807 debate the Solicitor-General, Sir Samuel Romilly, contrasted Napoleon on his throne with Wilberforce returning home to his family, and the House rose to cheer while Wilberforce sat, head in hands, in tears. The act received royal assent on 25 March 1807. Britain had been the largest slave-carrying nation of the 18th century, with more than three million Africans carried in its ships, and its Caribbean sugar colonies were among its most valuable possessions.
story.puzzle: If the trade was profitable and the planters' lobby powerful, why did the Commons vote 283 to 16 to destroy it? Was this conscience, or capitalism discarding a system it no longer needed?
story.payoff: Williams said the system was declining and capitalists no longer needed it. Drescher's trade figures show it was near its peak, so abolition destroyed value ('econocide') and needs a political and moral explanation: a mass petitioning movement, Quaker and evangelical conviction (Day 227), wartime politics and a shrewd 1806 measure that first cut the trade to foreign colonies. Today's dispute is narrower: not whether profit ended the trade, but how central slavery was to building industrial capitalism.
sources: Hansard, House of Commons debate on the Slave Trade Abolition Bill, 23 February 1807
Seymour Drescher, Econocide: British Slavery in the Era of Abolition (1977; 2nd ed., UNC Press, 2010)
Eric Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (UNC Press, 1944)
SlaveVoyages (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database)

days.application: Britain's Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 paid £20 million (commonly put at about 40% of annual government spending) to slave-owners, not to the enslaved, who were also bound to years of unpaid 'apprenticeship' that ended only in 1838. University College London's Legacies of British Slavery database traces the compensation claims and where the money went, a link between slavery and British wealth that historians can follow pound by pound.

builds_on.why: The scale and mechanics of the Atlantic trade are the data Williams and Drescher argue over.
British abolitionism is often counted among the first modern social movements: mass petitions, boycotts and organized lobbying, the organization-and-openings model of that lesson.

across.link: Gregson v Gilbert (1783), the Zong case: the owners of a Liverpool slave ship, whose crew had thrown well over a hundred captive Africans overboard in 1781, sued their insurers for the lost 'cargo', and Lord Mansfield's court treated it as an insurance dispute. Slavery was written into the commercial law of marine insurance, a link between slavery and British capitalism that Granville Sharp and other abolitionists publicized.

days.apply_question: Brazil, the largest single destination of enslaved Africans, ended its slave imports in 1850 under British naval pressure and abolished slavery only in 1888, while its coffee economy was booming. Does Brazil's case fit Williams's decline thesis or Drescher's econocide better?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Britain's slave trade was large and profitable up to 1807, and the British Caribbean was not in steep economic decline when the trade was abolished; most economic historians now side with Drescher against Williams's decline claim. Debated: how much slavery contributed to British and American industrialization. Williams and the 'new history of capitalism' (Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told, 2014; Beckert, Empire of Cotton, 2014) say centrally. Olmstead & Rhode (Explorations in Economic History 2018) dispute Baptist's evidence, and many estimates (Engerman 1972; O'Brien 1982) find slave-trade profits too small to finance industrial investment by themselves. Value judgment: that compensation went to owners and not to the enslaved was unjust is a moral judgment, now widely shared.

resource.title: Econocide: British Slavery in the Era of Abolition (introduction and opening chapter)
resource.creator: Seymour Drescher (1977; 2nd ed., University of North Carolina Press, 2010)
resource.length: about 30-40 pages; skim the tables (about 30 minutes)
resource.why: The book that overturned the decline thesis, with the trade data laid out. It answers Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) directly, so read it knowing which claim it targets.

days.phase: History II: The Great Enrichment and the Modern World
days.subject: History
days.topic: Abolition: Christian arguments on both sides
days.headline_hint: Nine of the Twelve Men Who Launched Britain's Campaign Against the Slave Trade Were Quakers. Slavery's Defenders Quoted the Same Bible.
days.concept: Christian conviction powered much of the antislavery movement, and Christian argument also defended slavery from scripture. An honest history counts both as Christian, then asks what else moved abolition: the enslaved's own resistance, Enlightenment critics, and the interests and self-image of a rising class.
days.focus: Lays out the evidence on both sides. On one side, Quaker and evangelical organizing (Anstey 1975; Christopher Leslie Brown, Moral Capital, 2006, on antislavery as a way for Britons to recover moral standing after the American war). On the other, the proslavery biblical case in the American South (Noll 2006). Alongside both sit David Brion Davis's argument about interests and ideology, and the enslaved's own agency: Haiti (Day 225) and Jamaica's 1831-32 Baptist War led by the Baptist deacon Samuel Sharpe. It names the No True Scotsman fallacy and shows how a historian defines 'Christian influence' before counting outcomes.

story.title: Twelve men in a Lombard Street print shop, 22 May 1787
story.hook: On 22 May 1787, twelve men met at 2 George Yard, Lombard Street, in the City of London, the premises of the Quaker printer and bookseller James Phillips, and formed the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. Nine were Quakers, members of a small sect that had already petitioned Parliament against the trade in 1783. The others included the veteran campaigner Granville Sharp and the young Anglican Thomas Clarkson, who would ride thousands of miles gathering evidence. That year the potter Josiah Wedgwood had his works produce a medallion of a kneeling, chained African under the words 'Am I Not a Man and a Brother?', which Clarkson recalled being worn on bracelets and hairpins. Across the Atlantic, over the following decades, many Southern ministers would preach from the same Bible that slavery was sanctioned by God.
story.puzzle: If Christian conviction drove the founders, how could equally devout Christians defend slavery from the same scriptures, and which side, if either, was the 'real' Christianity?
story.payoff: Both sides were Christian in the historian's sense: both drew sincerely on Christian scripture and churches. The historical question is which readings, traditions and circumstances produced which side. Quaker discipline and evangelical revival supplied conviction and organization; a literalist reading inside a slave society supplied the defence (Noll); and interests, self-image (Davis, Brown) and the resistance of the enslaved shaped when either side won. Whether antislavery was the truer reading of Christianity is a legitimate theological and moral judgment, but not one that historical counting can settle.
sources: Thomas Clarkson, The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade (1808)
Adam Hochschild, Bury the Chains (Houghton Mifflin, 2005)
Mark A. Noll, The Civil War as a Theological Crisis (UNC Press, 2006)

days.application: Frederick Douglass's Narrative (1845) ends with an appendix that distinguishes the slaveholding 'Christianity of this land', which he condemns, from 'the Christianity of Christ', which he embraces. It is an enslaved man's own theological answer to the No True Scotsman problem, and a test of how a historian should classify it: as a Christian argument about which reading is faithful, not as evidence that slaveholders were not Christians.

builds_on.why: Drescher's econocide leaves a political and moral explanation to be found, and this lesson examines its religious part.
Motivated reasoning: readers in a slave society found in scripture what their interests needed, and the same mechanism can operate on any side.

across.link: Antony Flew named the 'No True Scotsman' move in Thinking About Thinking (1975): rescuing a generalization by redefining the group to exclude counterexamples. Crediting Christianity with Wilberforce while declaring proslavery Christians not really Christian is that move, a hidden-premise problem of the kind Day 37 taught.

days.apply_question: In the US civil-rights movement of the 1950s-60s, Black churches and ministers such as Martin Luther King Jr. led the campaign, while many white Southern churches defended segregation, some from scripture. How would you define 'Christian influence' in advance so that you could fairly measure religion's net role in that movement?
days.evidence_note: Settled: Quakers and evangelicals were heavily over-represented among British and American abolitionists, and Christian ministers in the American South produced an extensive biblical defence of slavery (Noll 2006). Debated: how much religion caused abolition compared with economic change (Williams), the interests and self-image of a rising class (Davis, The Problem of Slavery in the Age of Revolution, 1975), the politics of moral capital (Brown 2006) and resistance by the enslaved; Anstey (1975) gives religion the leading role. Value judgment: whether antislavery was the faithful reading of Christianity is a theological claim, while that slavery was a grave wrong is a near-universal moral judgment.

resource.title: The Civil War as a Theological Crisis, chapter 3, 'The Crisis over the Bible'
resource.creator: Mark A. Noll (University of North Carolina Press, 2006)
resource.why: Noll, a leading evangelical historian, shows how proslavery and antislavery Americans argued from the same Bible and why a literal reading favoured slavery's defenders. It is the strongest short treatment of the side of the story that Christian accounts often leave out.
