days.model_or_equation: Levitsky and Ziblatt's four warning signs, as a <dl>: (1) rejection, in words or action, of the democratic rules of the game; (2) denial of the legitimacy of political opponents; (3) toleration or encouragement of violence; (4) readiness to curtail the civil liberties of opponents, including the media. Add their three moves of subversion: capture the referees, sideline the players, rewrite the rules.

story.title: A parliament votes in an opera house
story.hook: On Thursday 23 March 1933 the Reichstag met in Berlin's Kroll Opera House, because its own building had been gutted by fire four weeks earlier. A decree issued the day after the fire had suspended civil liberties. Most of the 81 Communist deputies had been arrested or had fled, some Social Democrats were missing too, and SA stormtroopers lined the hall. The Enabling Act before the deputies would let the government issue laws for four years without parliament, including laws that departed from the constitution. It needed a two-thirds majority. The Catholic Centre Party, promised protection for the Church, voted yes. Only the Social Democrats voted no. Their leader, Otto Wels, told the chamber: 'Freedom and life can be taken from us, but not our honour.' The result was 444 to 94, and President Hindenburg signed the Act the next day. Since 1930 Germany had already been governed largely by presidential emergency decrees under Article 48 of the Weimar constitution.
story.puzzle: No tanks surrounded the parliament. The Act passed by more than the supermajority the constitution demanded, and every step had a legal form. How can a democracy end by following its own rules?
story.payoff: Because rules are only as strong as the norms and referees behind them. By 1933 Weimar's referees had been captured: the president ruled by decree and appointed the chancellor. Its strongest opponents had been sidelined: Communist deputies were arrested under the fire decree, and the rules of procedure were reportedly altered so that unexcused absentees counted as present. Its conservative elites had made a 'fateful alliance', believing they could tame Hitler. Each step was legal; together they removed the guardrails. That is the pattern Levitsky and Ziblatt find again and again.
sources: Reichstag proceedings, 23 Mar 1933: the Enabling Act passed 444-94
Otto Wels's speech against the Enabling Act, 23 Mar 1933 (historical materials of the German Bundestag)
Richard J. Evans, The Coming of the Third Reich (2003)
Steven Levitsky & Daniel Ziblatt, How Democracies Die (2018)

days.application: Hungary since 2010. Fidesz won two-thirds of parliament's seats with about 53% of the party-list vote, then used that legal supermajority to write a new constitution (2011), enlarge and refill the Constitutional Court, centralize media regulation and redraw the electoral rules. V-Dem has classified Hungary as an 'electoral autocracy' since its 2020 report, and in 2022 the European Parliament described it as a 'hybrid regime of electoral autocracy'. Hungary's government rejects both judgments. Before writing about Hungary's present, the routine must check the outcome of the April 2026 parliamentary election and V-Dem's latest classification: an incumbent's defeat at the polls would itself be evidence in the measurement dispute.

builds_on.why: Forbearance and mutual toleration are social norms, self-enforcing expectations. Like the norms of Day 202, they can collapse quickly once enough players stop expecting others to keep them.

Motivated reasoning explains why voters excuse their own side's norm-breaking. In Graham and Svolik's experiments (APSR 2020), only a small minority of US voters punished a candidate for undemocratic positions when doing so meant voting against their own party.

across.link: Germany's Basic Law (1949) answered the Enabling Act with 'militant democracy'. Article 79(3), the 'eternity clause', puts human dignity, democracy and federalism beyond amendment. Article 21(2) lets the Federal Constitutional Court ban parties that seek to abolish the democratic order: it banned the SRP in 1952 and the KPD in 1956, and in 2017 it declined to ban the NPD as too insignificant to succeed.

days.apply_question: In 2004 Venezuela's National Assembly, controlled by Hugo Chávez's supporters, enlarged the Supreme Tribunal of Justice from 20 to 32 justices and filled the new seats with allies. In Levitsky and Ziblatt's framework, why can a step that was legal on its face still count as evidence of democratic erosion?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Weimar sequence (rule by Article 48 decree from 1930, the fire decree, the 444-94 vote) and Hungary's institutional changes after 2010 are documented. Debated: how much of Weimar's collapse came from institutional design (Article 48, proportional representation) rather than the Depression and elite choices. Also debated: whether expert-coded indices such as V-Dem overstate global backsliding. Little and Meng (PS: Political Science & Politics, 2024) find little decline in objective indicators, while Knutsen and colleagues (2024) defend expert coding. Check Hungary's April 2026 election result and V-Dem's current classification before describing Hungary's present. Value judgment: what counts as democracy at all, majority rule alone or majority rule bounded by rights and fair competition.

resource.title: How Democracies Die, Chapter 4: 'Subverting Democracy'
resource.creator: Steven Levitsky & Daniel Ziblatt (Crown, 2018)
resource.why: The chapter that sets out the three legal moves (capturing the referees, sidelining the players, changing the rules) with cases from Peru, Venezuela, Hungary and Turkey. It is the mainstream political-science account the brief summarizes; the 2024 measurement dispute questions it mainly at the global scale.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the book. The chapter number and title were not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: Switzerland Gave Women the Vote in 1971. One Canton Held Out Until Judges Ruled in 1990.
days.concept: Federalism divides authority between levels of government so that decisions can be made close to the people they affect and states can experiment. Subsidiarity, from Catholic social teaching, adds that a higher level should neither take over what a lower one can do well nor abandon it when it cannot, so the weight falls on the qualifier in 'the lowest competent level'.
days.focus: Teach the allocation question, who decides what, through federalism's benefits (local knowledge, fit to local preferences, experiments, the option to leave) and its costs (spillovers, races to the bottom, local majorities oppressing local minorities), together with Quadragesimo Anno's (1931) principle of subsidiarity, which runs in both directions. The angle: subsidiarity is often quoted as 'smaller is better', but its own text says the higher level exists to help (subsidium), which is how Swiss federal judges could rightly overrule a canton.
key_concepts: spillovers and races to the bottom

story.title: The last canton
story.hook: On Sunday 7 February 1971 Swiss men voted, by about two to one, to give women the vote in federal elections. Each canton still controlled its own franchise, and one by one they followed. The exception was Appenzell Innerrhoden, a small Catholic half-canton that still makes its laws at the Landsgemeinde, an open-air assembly where citizens vote by raising their hands in the square of the town of Appenzell. As late as April 1990 its men voted again to keep women out. Women of the canton, Theresa Rohner among them, took the case to the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne. On 27 November 1990 the judges ruled that the cantonal constitution violated the guarantee of equal rights for men and women that had been added to the federal constitution in 1981. In April 1991 the women of Appenzell Innerrhoden stood in the square and voted for the first time.
story.puzzle: Switzerland prizes local self-government and direct democracy more than almost any other country. Was the court defending democracy or overriding it? And who should decide which questions belong to the canton and which to the nation?
story.payoff: Federalism and subsidiarity say 'decide at the lowest level' only with a qualifier: the lowest competent level, within guarantees the higher level owes to everyone. Appenzell's assembly was competent to set its taxes and school calendar. But the federal constitution had made equal political rights a national guarantee, so a canton that denied them was not exercising autonomy; it was failing a duty. In subsidiarity's own terms, that is when the higher body steps in.
sources: Swiss Federal Supreme Court, judgment of 27 Nov 1990, BGE 116 Ia 359 (Rohner and others v. Appenzell Innerrhoden)
Federal popular vote of 7 Feb 1971 on women's suffrage (Swiss Federal Chancellery)
Pius XI, Quadragesimo Anno (15 May 1931), §79

days.application: US states' differing traffic-safety laws as Brandeis's 'laboratories'. Dissenting in New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann (1932), Brandeis wrote that 'a single courageous State may, if its citizens choose, serve as a laboratory'. New York passed the first mandatory seat-belt law in 1984; New Hampshire still has none for adults. Some states let police stop drivers for being unbelted (primary enforcement); others can cite it only after another offence. Because states adopted their laws at different times, researchers can compare them as natural experiments. Cohen and Einav (Review of Economics and Statistics, 2003) found that mandatory belt laws raised belt use and cut occupant deaths, with no measurable offsetting risk-taking. In Logan's chain this sits at the regulation link for the car.

builds_on.why: States that adopt a law at different times create natural experiments. Difference-in-differences across states is how 'laboratories of democracy' actually produce knowledge.
One of Ostrom's design principles is 'nested enterprises', governance in layers with each layer handling what it can. That is the commons version of federalism and subsidiarity.

across.link: The 'end-to-end argument' (Saltzer, Reed & Clark, ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, 1984) says a network's core should not perform functions that the endpoints can perform completely and correctly. It is a rule for where to place functions, with the same shape as subsidiarity. The analogy breaks because subsidiarity rests on the dignity and freedom of persons and communities, which packets do not have.

days.apply_question: Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union lets the EU act only where member states cannot sufficiently achieve an objective on their own. Using both directions of subsidiarity, should limits on power-plant carbon emissions be set in Brussels or by each member state, and why?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the Swiss dates and the court's ruling; the text of Quadragesimo Anno. Debated: whether competition between states produces useful experiments or races to the bottom, and how far successful policies actually spread from state 'laboratories' (the evidence is mixed by policy area). Value judgment: which questions are local and which are rights owed everywhere. Subsidiarity (Catholic social teaching), Kuyper's Protestant 'sphere sovereignty' and liberal federalism give different answers, and the Appenzell case shows the same principle of local self-rule being invoked on both sides.

resource.title: Federalism
resource.creator: Andreas Føllesdal, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (online entry, revised edition)
resource.length: about 30 minutes for the sections on the arguments for and against federal arrangements
resource.why: A philosopher's map of why authority is divided at all: the arguments from liberty, local knowledge, minority protection and experimentation, and the objections to each. Its author is a leading scholar of subsidiarity, and it gives the concept a structure the brief can only sketch.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the SEP entry and its author. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Bureaucracy and the merit civil service
days.headline_hint: A Man Who Wanted a Government Job Shot the President. Congress Answered With an Exam.
days.concept: A Weberian bureaucracy, with offices defined by written rules, files, expertise, and hiring and promotion on merit, all kept separate from the officeholder's private interests, replaced patronage. It bought competence and impartiality at the price of responsiveness, and the principal-agent problem of controlling officials never goes away.
days.focus: Teach why merit bureaucracy outperforms patronage, and why patronage's responsiveness keeps tempting reformers back, using Weber's ideal type, the principal-agent problem, and evidence from Evans and Rauch (1999) and Xu (2018). The angle: reform came when politicians had reasons to tie their own hands, and a bureaucracy's virtues (rules, impersonality, obedience to procedure) are also its pathologies.
key_concepts: Weberian bureaucracy (rules, files, expertise, merit, career)
tenure protection and political neutrality of the civil service
days.model_or_equation: The principal-agent problem in one line. The principal (the public, acting through elected leaders) wants outcome X. The agent (an official) knows more and has interests of her own. Patronage ties the agent to her patron; merit hiring and a protected career tie her to the rules and the job. Each solves one problem and opens another.

story.title: A disappointed office-seeker at the railroad station
story.hook: At about 9:30 on the morning of Saturday 2 July 1881, President James Garfield walked through the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station in Washington, on his way out of the city for the summer. Charles Guiteau had spent months pestering the White House and the State Department for a consulship in Paris. He shot the president twice from behind and reportedly declared, 'I am a Stalwart of the Stalwarts... Arthur is President now.' Garfield lingered for eleven weeks while his doctors probed the wound with unwashed fingers, and he died at Elberon, New Jersey, on 19 September. At the time almost every federal job, from postmaster to customs clerk to consul, was a party reward, handed out by the winners after each election. On 16 January 1883 President Chester Arthur, once the patronage boss of the New York Custom House, signed the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act. It required competitive examinations for about one federal job in ten.
story.puzzle: Patronage was the fuel of nineteenth-century party machines: it rewarded party workers and won elections. Why would the politicians who lived off it vote to give it up, and why did they start with only a tenth of the jobs?
story.payoff: Outrage at the assassination turned the spoils system into a national scandal, and the 1882 midterm elections punished the Republicans. With their hold on the presidency in doubt, they also had a reason to lock their own appointees into protected posts before a Democratic president could fire them. Historians weigh public pressure (Theriault 2003) against this partisan insurance. Either way, merit protection began small and spread as outgoing administrations 'blanketed in' their own people. Over time it built Weber's bureaucracy: officials chosen for competence and protected from the next election's spoils.
sources: Candice Millard, Destiny of the Republic (2011)
Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, 16 Jan 1883 (US Office of Personnel Management, history of the civil service)
Sean M. Theriault, 'Patronage, the Pendleton Act, and the Power of the People', Journal of Politics 65 (2003)

days.application: Governors in the British Empire. Guo Xu ('The Costs of Patronage: Evidence from the British Empire', American Economic Review, 2018) found that colonial governors with social ties to the Secretary of State for the Colonies received more lucrative postings and honours yet performed worse, notably in collecting revenue, and that these effects faded once their patrons left office and patronage was curbed. The costs of patronage show up in the accounts.

builds_on.why: Hilberg and Bauman showed that the machinery that makes bureaucracy competent, files, rules and divided labour, also made mass murder administrable. That is the dark side of Weber's ideal type.
Bureaucracies run on rules and measured targets, so Goodhart's law is a constant hazard: officials optimize the metric they are judged by, as with the NHS waiting-time targets of Day 23.

across.link: Robert K. Merton's 'Bureaucratic Structure and Personality' (Social Forces, 1940) named 'goal displacement': officials trained to follow rules come to treat the rules as ends in themselves. It is sociology's account of red tape, the counterpart to Weber's praise of rule-bound administration.

days.apply_question: For about 1,300 years, until 1905, imperial China recruited many of its officials through written civil-service examinations. Using the principal-agent problem, why might an emperor prefer officials chosen by examination to officials chosen by noble birth, even though the exam-chosen owed him no personal loyalty?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the facts of Garfield's assassination and the Pendleton Act. Debated: why Congress passed the Act (public outrage, as Theriault 2003 argues, or partisan insurance), and how large the performance gains from merit systems are. Cross-national evidence, such as Evans and Rauch (1999) on 'Weberian' bureaucracies and economic growth, is correlational; Xu (2018) comes closer to a causal estimate. Value judgment: the right balance between a neutral, protected civil service and elected leaders' control over the officials who carry out their policies.

resource.title: Political Order and Political Decay, chapters 9-10 (the American invention of clientelism and the end of the spoils system)
resource.creator: Francis Fukuyama (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2014)
resource.why: Places the Pendleton Act within a comparative history of how states moved from patronage to merit (Prussia, Britain, Greece, Italy and the US), and argues that clientelism is an early form of democratic politics rather than simply corruption.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge. The chapter numbers are recalled, not re-checked, because web search was unavailable for the rest of this session. No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: How regulation works: rules, prices and disclosure
days.headline_hint: The 1952 Smog Killed Perhaps 12,000 Londoners. The Smoke Came From Their Own Fireplaces. How Do You Regulate a Fireplace?
days.concept: Governments change behaviour with a small toolkit: commands (standards and bans), prices (taxes, subsidies and tradable permits) and information (disclosure). The right tool depends on what the regulator can observe, how many sources there are, and how much the cost of compliance differs among them.
days.focus: Teach the regulatory toolkit and how to choose among its instruments: technology versus performance standards, Pigouvian taxes and cap-and-trade (the economics is assumed at CFA level), subsidies, and disclosure such as restaurant hygiene grade cards, plus cost-benefit analysis as government's own test. The angle: Britain's 1956 Clean Air Act worked through zones, bans and grants because the polluters were millions of households, not a few smokestacks.
days.model_or_equation: A choice table rather than an equation, listing for each tool what the regulator must observe and when it works best. Standard: the technology or the emission rate; works with few, similar sources that are easy to inspect. Tax: emissions; fixes the price and leaves the quantity uncertain; suits cases where marginal damage is flat. Cap-and-trade: emissions; fixes the quantity and leaves the price uncertain; suits sources whose abatement costs differ widely. Disclosure: only that the information is true; works when buyers or neighbours can act on it. Weitzman's 'Prices vs. Quantities' (1974) formalizes the choice between tax and cap under uncertainty.

story.title: Five days when London could not see its feet
story.hook: On Friday 5 December 1952 a high-pressure system settled over London. Cold, windless air trapped smoke from power stations and from millions of household coal fires beneath a lid of fog. For five days visibility fell to a few metres. Buses crawled behind men carrying flares, a performance at Sadler's Wells was reportedly halted because the audience could no longer see the stage, and prize cattle at the Smithfield Show reportedly choked. Undertakers ran short of coffins. Officials first counted about 4,000 extra deaths; later re-analysis of the mortality records puts the toll at about 12,000. Londoners had complained about coal smoke at least since John Evelyn's Fumifugium of 1661. Even so, the government moved cautiously. It took a committee chaired by Sir Hugh Beaver, and a private member's bill pressed by the MP Gerald Nabarro, before Parliament passed the Clean Air Act in 1956.
story.puzzle: The smoke came from a vast number of small sources: ordinary families' grates, each one trivial, burning cheap coal to keep warm. A tax on smoke would need a meter on every chimney, and a simple ban would leave poor families cold. How do you regulate a fireplace?
story.payoff: You choose the tool that fits what you can observe. The 1956 Act let local councils declare smoke control areas, where burning smoky fuel was banned, which inspectors could enforce by sight. It also paid most of the cost of converting old grates to smokeless fuel, gas or electricity, so compliance did not fall on poor households alone. A command plus a subsidy worked where a price would not, because the regulator could see smoke but could not meter it.
sources: Met Office, 'The Great Smog of 1952'

Michelle L. Bell, Devra L. Davis & Tony Fletcher, 'A retrospective assessment of mortality from the London smog episode of 1952: the role of influenza and pollution', Environmental Health Perspectives 112 (2004)
Clean Air Act 1956 (UK)

days.application: The US Clean Air Act's own cost-benefit test. In 2011 the EPA's retrospective study, 'The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020', estimated benefits of about $2 trillion in 2020 against compliance costs of about $65 billion, roughly 30 to 1. Most of the benefit came from avoiding some 230,000 early deaths through lower fine-particle pollution. Critics question both the fine-particle mortality estimates and the dollar value placed on each statistical life. The example shows how regulation is justified, and where its numbers are softest.

builds_on.why: In Meadows's terms, a standard changes a parameter, while a tradable permit changes the rules and the information flows (the 1990 sulfur-dioxide market of Day 33). Choosing a tool means choosing a leverage point.
City air is an open-access commons. Each household's smoke harms everyone, which is why voluntary restraint failed and a rule or a price was needed.

across.link: Wang and colleagues ('Persistent sulfate formation from London Fog to Chinese haze', PNAS, 2016) reproduced the 1952 fog's chemistry: nitrogen dioxide in fog droplets rapidly turned coal's sulfur dioxide into sulfuric acid, the same pathway they found in Beijing's winter haze. Knowing the chemistry is what tells a regulator which pollutant, and which source, to target.

days.apply_question: Since 1998 Los Angeles County has required restaurants to display A, B or C hygiene grade cards in their windows. Using the regulatory toolkit, explain why disclosure can improve kitchen hygiene even though it adds no new rule or fine.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the smog's dates, the Clean Air Act 1956, and the basic properties of each instrument. Debated: the size of the 1952 death toll, between about 4,000 and 12,000; the higher figure comes from re-analysis that attributes deaths to pollution rather than influenza. Also debated: the EPA's roughly 30-to-1 ratio of benefits to costs, which rests heavily on fine-particle mortality estimates and on how statistical lives are valued. Value judgment: how to weigh lives against costs, and who should bear the costs; and whether a government should put a price on pollution (accepting some in exchange for money) or forbid it.

resource.title: Policy Evolution under the Clean Air Act
resource.creator: Richard Schmalensee & Robert N. Stavins, Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(4), Fall 2019
resource.length: about 40 minutes for the whole paper; the first half covers the choice of instruments
resource.why: Two leading environmental economists trace fifty years of the US Clean Air Act, showing where it used standards, where it used trading, and why the choice changed. It is the toolkit applied to a real statute, and it is free from the American Economic Association.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: A Railroad Lawyer Told a Railroad Boss to Keep His Regulator. It Could Be 'of Great Use to the Railroads.'
days.concept: Concentrated interests organize more easily than diffuse ones (Olson's logic of collective action), so regulators can drift toward serving the industries they oversee (Stigler's capture theory). But capture is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a law of nature, and institutions can be designed against it (Carpenter & Moss).
days.focus: Teach public choice's core move, treating officials and interest groups as self-interested actors, through Olson (1965) and Stigler (1971). Then teach the corrective: Carpenter and Moss insist on evidence and on degrees of capture (strong versus weak, plus 'cultural capture'). The angle: the 737 MAX shows how delegation, thin resources and close relationships can produce failures that look like capture with no bribes involved.
key_concepts: the logic of collective action (concentrated benefits, diffuse costs)
days.model_or_equation: Olson's asymmetry in numbers. A rule worth $100 million to 10 firms is worth $10 million to each, enough to hire lobbyists. If the same $100 million is spread across 100 million consumers, it costs each of them $1, not worth a phone call. Organized effort follows the concentrated stake, not the total.

story.title: A letter between railroad men
story.hook: In 1887 Congress created the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first major federal regulatory agency, in response to farmers' and shippers' fury at railroad rate discrimination. The courts soon began trimming its powers, and Charles E. Perkins, president of the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad, wanted it abolished altogether. He sought the advice of Richard Olney, a Boston lawyer long retained by railroads, who in March 1893 became Grover Cleveland's Attorney General. Olney's reply, usually dated 28 December 1892, advised against abolition. 'The Commission, as its functions have now been limited by the courts, is, or can be made, of great use to the railroads,' he wrote. 'It satisfies the popular clamor for a government supervision of railroads, at the same time that that supervision is almost entirely nominal.' And: 'the older such a commission gets to be, the more inclined it will be found to take the business and railroad view of things.' The ICC survived until 1995.
story.puzzle: The commission was created to restrain the railroads. Why would a railroad insider want to keep it? And what would have to be true for a regulator to end up serving the industry it was meant to police?
story.payoff: The railroads were few, highly organized, and had far more at stake in each of the commission's decisions than the scattered shippers and farmers did. So they could watch it, argue before it, staff it and shape it: Olson's logic. A commission that looked like protection but leaned the industry's way was more useful to them than no commission at all, because it absorbed public anger while the industry kept its influence. That is capture as Stigler later theorized it. Whether the ICC was in fact captured is still debated by historians.
sources: Richard Olney to Charles E. Perkins, 28 Dec 1892, quoted in Gabriel Kolko, Railroads and Regulation, 1877-1916 (1965)
Interstate Commerce Act (1887); ICC Termination Act (1995)
George J. Stigler, 'The Theory of Economic Regulation', Bell Journal of Economics and Management Science 2 (1971)

days.application: The Boeing 737 MAX. Under the FAA's Organization Designation Authorization program, Boeing employees did much of the certification work on the agency's behalf. The FAA was not fully informed of how much MCAS had changed, and two crashes killed 346 people (Day 93). The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's 2020 report found failures of FAA oversight and a 'culture of concealment' at Boeing, and Congress passed the Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act in December 2020. The live question is whether this was capture, chronic under-resourcing of the FAA (Congress had pushed delegation partly to save money), or both.

builds_on.why: The 737 MAX's MCAS design, which relied on a single sensor, is the engineering failure of Day 93. Today's lesson asks why the regulatory check that should have caught it was weak.
Olson's logic is an n-person prisoner's dilemma. Each diffuse consumer's best reply is to free-ride on others' lobbying, so the concentrated side wins by default.

across.link: James Kwak's chapter 'Cultural Capture and the Financial Crisis' (in Carpenter & Moss, eds., Preventing Regulatory Capture, 2014) argues that regulators can be captured without bribes, through shared identity, status and social networks with the people they regulate. It applies conformity and in-group psychology to the financial regulators before 2008.

days.apply_question: The US sugar program keeps domestic sugar prices well above world prices through import quotas and price supports, which benefit relatively few growers and processors while costing consumers more in total. Using Olson's logic, explain why the program has survived decades of criticism from economists across the political spectrum.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the arguments of Olson and Stigler, the text of the Olney letter, and the 737 MAX facts as found by investigators. Debated: how often capture actually happens. Stigler treated it as the rule; Carpenter and Moss (2014) find it is often asserted without evidence and comes in degrees. Historians still argue whether the ICC was captured (Kolko 1965) or merely weak, and analysts disagree whether the FAA's failures on the 737 MAX were capture or under-resourcing. Value judgment: how far to trust expert agencies at all. Public-choice scholars stress government failure as much as market failure; defenders of the administrative state stress the cost of leaving harms unregulated.

resource.title: Preventing Regulatory Capture: Special Interest Influence and How to Limit It (Introduction)
resource.creator: Daniel Carpenter & David A. Moss (eds.), Cambridge University Press / The Tobin Project, 2014 (open access)
resource.why: The best short corrective to 'capture is everywhere'. It defines capture precisely, distinguishes strong from weak capture, sets out what evidence would show it, and surveys how institutions can be designed to resist it.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge that the volume is open access from Cambridge University Press. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: Mexico's New President Kept His Rivals' Anti-Poverty Programme. A Randomized Trial Had Made It Hard to Kill.
days.concept: Governments can learn what works by testing policies with randomized and natural experiments. But a result shows what worked there and then; whether it transfers to another place, scale or time (external validity) is a separate question that needs its own evidence.
days.focus: Teach evidence-based policy as applied causal inference: internal versus external validity, the problem of scaling up, and the politics of evidence. The angle: PROGRESA's built-in randomized evaluation helped it survive Mexico's first opposition victory in 71 years, yet did not save it in 2019; and trials run by nudge units show that published effects shrink at scale (DellaVigna & Linos 2022).

story.title: An anti-poverty programme with a control group
story.hook: In 1997 Mexico's deputy finance minister, Santiago Levy, launched PROGRESA. It paid poor rural mothers cash every two months, on condition that their children attended school and the family kept up its clinic visits. Mexican governments had a habit: each new president replaced his predecessor's flagship anti-poverty programme with his own. Levy built in a defence. There was not enough money to start everywhere at once, so the first rollout was randomized. Of 506 eligible villages, about 320 began receiving payments and about 186 waited, while independent researchers at the International Food Policy Research Institute compared the two groups. In July 2000 Vicente Fox won the presidency, ending 71 years of rule by the PRI, the party that had created PROGRESA.
story.puzzle: Fox's new government had every political reason to scrap a PRI programme. Instead it kept PROGRESA, renamed it Oportunidades in 2002 and extended it to the cities, and many countries copied it. Then in 2019 a later government ended it anyway. What protected the programme for nearly two decades, and why was that protection not permanent?
story.payoff: Credible, public evidence. Because villages had been assigned at random, the evaluation could show that the transfers raised school enrolment, especially for girls in secondary school, and improved health, and that finding belonged to no party. The evidence raised the political cost of killing a programme that demonstrably worked. But evidence answers 'what works'. Whether to fund it is also a question of values and priorities, and a government that weighed them differently could still end it: Hume's gap between is and ought, in budget form.
sources: Santiago Levy, Progress Against Poverty: Sustaining Mexico's Progresa-Oportunidades Program (Brookings, 2006)
T. Paul Schultz, 'School subsidies for the poor: evaluating the Mexican Progresa poverty program', Journal of Development Economics 74 (2004)
International Food Policy Research Institute, PROGRESA evaluation reports (1998-2000)

days.application: The UK Behavioural Insights Team's 2011 tax-letter trial with HM Revenue and Customs. Letters telling late payers that nine out of ten people pay their tax on time, especially 'in your town', raised the share who paid within 23 days by several percentage points over the standard letter (Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe & Vlaev, Journal of Public Economics, 2017). The effect was cheap and real, and it also tests scaling: DellaVigna and Linos (Econometrica, 2022) found that trials run by government nudge units average an effect of about 1.4 percentage points, against about 8.7 points in published academic studies. They attribute the gap largely to publication bias and small samples.

builds_on.why: PROGRESA's phased rollout is a randomized controlled trial run by a government: chance, not officials, decided which villages went first, so the difference between groups estimates the programme's effect.
Nudge effects shrink between academic papers and nudge-unit trials because of publication bias, the same mechanism that inflated the published literatures of Day 22.

across.link: Evidence-based policy borrowed its methods from evidence-based medicine. Archie Cochrane's Effectiveness and Efficiency (1972) inspired the Cochrane Collaboration (1993), and the Campbell Collaboration (2000) carried its model of systematic reviews into education, crime and social welfare.

days.apply_question: In 2017-18 Finland ran a randomized basic-income experiment, paying 2,000 unemployed people €560 a month with no conditions. Using the idea of external validity, explain why its results could not settle what would happen if Finland paid a basic income to every adult.
days.evidence_note: Settled: random assignment gives credible estimates of effects in the population tested, and PROGRESA's evaluation is among the most cited in development economics. Debated: how far such results generalize. Deaton and Cartwright (2018) and Vivalt (2020) stress weak external validity; advocates such as Banerjee and Duflo (Nobel 2019) argue that repeated trials across settings build knowledge that transfers. Also debated: how large nudge effects are at scale (DellaVigna & Linos 2022). Value judgment: whether a programme that works should be funded is a separate question of priorities, and conditional transfers raise their own dispute between paternalism and unconditional aid.

resource.title: Social experiments to fight poverty
resource.creator: Esther Duflo, TED2010
resource.why: The future Nobel laureate makes the case for testing anti-poverty policies with randomized trials, using examples from health and education. It is an advocate's account, to set against the brief's critique based on external validity.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the TED talk. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.topic: Corruption and how countries escape it
days.headline_hint: A Hong Kong Police Chief Couldn't Explain HK$4 Million. He Fled, and the Colony Changed What Everyone Expected.
days.concept: Systemic corruption is an equilibrium of expectations: when everyone expects officials to take bribes, honesty does not pay for any one person. So lasting escapes usually come from 'big bang' changes that reset everyone's expectations at once, not from punishing a few individuals.
days.focus: Teach corruption as a collective-action and coordination problem (Persson, Rothstein & Teorell 2013), not only as a principal-agent problem, with Klitgaard's formula (monopoly plus discretion minus accountability) for the mechanics at the level of a single official. The angle: Hong Kong's ICAC, Georgia's police and nineteenth-century Sweden show that credible, simultaneous change can flip the equilibrium, and that an amnesty for the past may be part of the price.
key_concepts: systemic corruption as a coordination equilibrium
principal-agent versus collective-action views of corruption
days.model_or_equation: Klitgaard's formula, C = M + D − A. Corruption (C) grows with an official's monopoly over a decision (M) and with the discretion in making it (D), and shrinks with accountability (A). Read it as a heuristic, not an equation with units. The coordination view adds that A itself depends on what officials expect their colleagues to do.

story.title: Chief Superintendent Godber's flight
story.hook: In June 1973 Hong Kong's anti-corruption office, at the time a branch of the police force itself, gave Chief Superintendent Peter Godber a week to explain how he had accumulated more than HK$4 million, several times all the salary he had ever earned. On 8 June he used his airport pass to get past the checks at Kai Tak and flew to England. Hong Kong erupted, and students rallied under the slogan 'Fight Corruption, Catch Godber'. The bribery was not one officer's vice. Syndicates within the police collected regular payments from gambling dens, drug dealers and street hawkers and passed the money up the ranks. Governor Murray MacLehose appointed a commission of inquiry, and on 15 February 1974 created the Independent Commission Against Corruption, answerable to him alone. Godber was extradited in January 1975 and jailed for four years.
story.puzzle: Anti-corruption laws had existed for decades, and the police already had an anti-corruption branch. Why had nothing worked? And how did a colony whose police were among the most corrupt anywhere become, within a generation, one of Asia's cleanest administrations?
story.payoff: Because the problem was an equilibrium, not a few bad apples. Where everyone takes a cut, an honest officer gains nothing and risks his career, and an anti-corruption unit staffed by the same police is part of the system. The ICAC changed expectations all at once: it was independent of the police, well funded, and combined investigation, prevention and public education, so honesty became the safe strategy. When police protests in October 1977 threatened the whole effort, MacLehose granted a partial amnesty for most offences committed before 1977, pardoning the past to make the new expectations credible.
sources: Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong), official history of the ICAC
Leslie Palmier, The Control of Bureaucratic Corruption: Case Studies in Asia (1985)
Bo Rothstein, 'Anti-corruption: the indirect "big bang" approach', Review of International Political Economy 18 (2011)

days.application: Georgia after the Rose Revolution. In 2004 the new government dismissed the entire traffic police, a force notorious for roadside bribes (it is often reported at around 15,000 officers, though figures vary), and replaced it with a smaller, better-paid, newly trained patrol police. In later surveys the share of Georgians reporting bribes to public officials was among the lowest in the former Soviet Union. It is a textbook big bang, with a caution: petty bribery fell much more than concerns about elite corruption and political control, which persisted.

builds_on.why: Corruption is a norm in Day 202's sense, a self-enforcing expectation about what others do. Like footbinding or drunk driving, it changes when expectations shift together, not person by person.
Honest and corrupt administration are two equilibria of the same coordination game: each official's best reply depends on what the others do.

across.link: Gächter and Schulz ('Intrinsic honesty and the prevalence of rule violations across societies', Nature, 2016) gave the same die-rolling honesty test to 2,568 young people in 23 countries. They found more dishonest reporting where an index of corruption, tax evasion and electoral fraud was higher, evidence that institutional corruption shapes individual honesty.

days.apply_question: Since August 2016 Ukraine has required its public bodies to buy through ProZorro, an open online procurement system that publishes every government tender and bid. Using the equilibrium view of corruption, explain why making every contract public at once might work better than prosecuting a few corrupt procurement officials.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the reform sequences in Hong Kong and Georgia; corruption is strongly correlated with poverty and weak institutions. Debated: whether corruption is better modelled as a principal-agent problem (monitor and punish individuals) or a collective-action problem (Persson, Rothstein & Teorell 2013); whether gradual reform can work where a big bang is politically impossible; and how lasting Georgia's gains are. Indices such as Transparency International's measure perceptions, not bribes paid. Value judgment: whether an amnesty for past corruption is a fair price for future honesty.

resource.title: Fighting Corruption in Public Services: Chronicling Georgia's Reforms
resource.creator: World Bank (Directions in Development series, 2012)
resource.length: about 25 minutes for the chapter on the patrol police
resource.why: A detailed, sourced account of how Georgia dismissed and rebuilt its traffic police, cut red tape and changed expectations: the mechanics of a 'big bang' that the brief can only summarize. It is an official and largely sympathetic account, written before later concerns about elite corruption.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the World Bank report. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: She Held Up a 'No War' Sign on Russia's Evening News. The State's First Answer Was a Fine.
days.concept: Most modern autocrats survive less by mass terror than by manipulating information: selective censorship, propaganda that projects competence, co-opting elites and staging elections, with violence held in reserve. Guriev and Treisman (2022) call this 'spin dictatorship'.
days.focus: Teach the shift from 'fear dictators' to 'spin dictators' and their toolkit: censorship aimed at collective action rather than at criticism, co-optation, legitimacy earned by performance, and managed elections, together with the evidence for it (King, Pan & Roberts 2013). The angle: spin is a strategy, not a permanent condition. Under the strain of war, Russia moved back toward fear, criminalizing 'fakes' about its army in March 2022.

story.title: Live on Channel One
story.hook: On the evening of Monday 14 March 2022, less than three weeks into Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Marina Ovsyannikova, an editor at the state broadcaster Channel One, stepped behind the presenter of Vremya, the country's most-watched news programme. She held a hand-lettered sign: 'NO WAR. Stop the war. Don't believe the propaganda. They are lying to you here.' Ten days earlier Russia had made spreading 'knowingly false information' about its armed forces a crime punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Ovsyannikova was detained and questioned for about 14 hours, then fined 30,000 rubles, a few hundred dollars, for an online video calling for protests. Months later, after a one-woman street protest, she was charged under the new law and placed under house arrest. She escaped with her daughter, and in 2023 she was sentenced in absentia to eight and a half years.
story.puzzle: A regime that had just made criticism of its war a serious crime answered the most visible protest against that war, broadcast on its own flagship channel, with a fine. Why the light touch, and why did it not last?
story.payoff: Spin dictators prefer to avoid visible, dramatic repression, which creates martyrs and damages the image of a popular, competent government. They rely instead on controlling what most people see and on quiet, targeted pressure, and the fine fitted that playbook. The later criminal case fitted the other playbook. As the war raised the stakes, Russia moved back toward fear, with mass arrests and long sentences for dissent: a shift that many analysts, Guriev and Treisman among them, have described since the invasion.
sources: News reports of 14-15 Mar 2022 (for example BBC News and Reuters) on Ovsyannikova's protest and fine
Russian federal law of 4 Mar 2022 adding Article 207.3 to the Criminal Code
Sergei Guriev & Daniel Treisman, Spin Dictators: The Changing Face of Tyranny in the 21st Century (2022)

days.application: China's internet censorship. King, Pan and Roberts (American Political Science Review, 2013) collected millions of posts from Chinese social-media sites before the censors could act. Posts criticizing the state, its leaders and its policies were not especially likely to be deleted. Posts with collective-action potential, calling for or reporting on protests whatever their politics, were deleted far more often. A follow-up (APSR, 2017) estimated that the government fabricates about 448 million social-media posts a year, mostly cheerleading and distraction rather than argument.

builds_on.why: The Great Leap famine showed fear-based rule destroying the information its rulers needed. Spin dictators try to keep accurate information flowing to themselves while controlling what the public sees.

Granovetter's threshold model (Day 28) explains why censors target collective action. A protest can tip from a few people to many, so the regime suppresses the signals that let people see how many others would join.

across.link: China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, in force from 15 August 2023, require generated content to 'adhere to core socialist values'. The censorship apparatus now reaches from posts written by people to text written by models.

days.apply_question: Before Russia's 2024 presidential election, the authorities barred the anti-war candidate Boris Nadezhdin from the ballot over alleged flaws in his supporters' signatures, after long public queues had formed to sign for him. Using the spin-dictator toolkit, explain why a regime certain of winning would still keep him off the ballot rather than let him lose.
days.evidence_note: Settled: the facts of Ovsyannikova's case and of Russia's March 2022 law. King, Pan and Roberts's findings were supported by their later experimental work (Science, 2014). Debated: how large the shift from fear to spin really is (Guriev and Treisman's coding of regimes is contested); whether Russia since 2022 is best described as a spin dictatorship under strain or as a return to fear; and how much performance legitimacy explains in China. Value judgment: whether a regime that delivers growth and order but denies free expression can be legitimate. That is the gap between descriptive and normative legitimacy from Day 236.

resource.title: Informational Autocrats
resource.creator: Sergei Guriev & Daniel Treisman, Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(4), Fall 2019
resource.why: The authors' own compact statement of the spin-dictator model and the evidence for it: the falling share of autocrats who resort to mass killing, and the rise of co-optation and media manipulation. It is free from the American Economic Association; their book Spin Dictators (2022) expands it.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Government
days.headline_hint: On the Day Baptists Gave Jefferson a 1,235-Pound Cheese, He Wrote Baptists About a 'Wall of Separation.'
days.concept: States arrange their relation to religion along a spectrum: establishment, cooperation, separation and laïcité. The modern idea of religious liberty grew substantially from Christian dissenters' argument that coerced faith is not faith, an argument the Catholic Church formally adopted in Dignitatis Humanae (1965).
days.focus: Teach the church-state spectrum through real cases (England's established church, Germany's church tax, the US First Amendment, France's 1905 law) and the theology behind religious liberty, from Roger Williams's 'hedge or wall of separation' (1644) to Dignitatis Humanae. The angle: devout Baptists asked for the 'wall' to protect religion from the state, and its legal meaning in the US is still moving (Everson 1947, Lemon 1971, Kennedy v. Bremerton 2022).
key_concepts: incorporation (applying the First Amendment to the states)
Dignitatis Humanae (religious freedom as a right of the person)
days.model_or_equation: The spectrum as a <dl>. Establishment: an official state church (England, Denmark). Cooperation: the state recognizes churches and collects taxes for them, and the churches govern themselves (Germany). Separation, whether accommodating or strict: no established church, with free exercise protected (the US). Laïcité: the republic recognizes, pays and subsidizes no religion and keeps religion out of public institutions (France since 1905).

story.title: A cheese, a letter and a sermon
story.hook: On New Year's Day 1802 the Baptist preacher John Leland presented President Thomas Jefferson with a 'Mammoth Cheese' of about 1,235 pounds, made by the farmers of Cheshire, Massachusetts, in thanks for his defence of religious liberty. The same day Jefferson signed a reply to another group of Baptists, the Danbury Baptist Association of Connecticut. In October 1801 they had written to him as a persecuted minority. Connecticut still had an established Congregational church, and they complained that the religious privileges they enjoyed were treated 'as favors granted, and not as inalienable rights'. Jefferson answered that the First Amendment had built 'a wall of separation between Church & State'. Two days later, on Sunday 3 January, he attended a service in the chamber of the House of Representatives at which Leland preached.
story.puzzle: The 'wall of separation' is now quoted mostly to keep religion out of public life. Why did devout Baptists ask for it? Why did Connecticut keep its established church until 1818, decades after the First Amendment? And how could the man who coined the phrase go to church in the Capitol?
story.payoff: Because the wall was built to protect religion from the state as much as the state from religion. Dissenting Protestants, from Roger Williams to the Baptists and Quakers, argued that faith under compulsion is not faith, so a government that funds and polices one church wrongs all the others. The First Amendment originally bound only Congress, so state establishments survived (Massachusetts kept its church until 1833) until the Supreme Court applied the Amendment to the states in the 1940s. And separation never meant that officials must not worship. It meant the government may not establish or coerce religion; where that line falls is what the courts still argue about.
sources: Danbury Baptist Association to Thomas Jefferson, 7 Oct 1801, and Jefferson's reply, 1 Jan 1802 (Library of Congress)
James H. Hutson, ''A Wall of Separation': FBI Helps Restore Jefferson's Obliterated Draft', Library of Congress Information Bulletin (June 1998)
Library of Congress exhibition 'Religion and the Founding of the American Republic' (the Cheshire cheese and Leland's sermon)

days.application: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (27 June 2022). By 6 votes to 3, the Supreme Court held that a public-school football coach's brief prayer at midfield after games was protected by the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses. The Court said it had 'long ago abandoned' the Lemon test of 1971 (which asked about secular purpose, primary effect and excessive entanglement) in favour of reading the Establishment Clause by 'historical practices and understandings'. The dissent argued that the ruling let a school endorse prayer and pressure students. It is a live case of where the wall now stands.

builds_on.why: The wars of religion ended in settlements that slowly produced toleration. Roger Williams's Rhode Island and Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration (Day 198) are the direct ancestors of the Danbury Baptists' argument.

Religious-market theorists (Stark and Finke, Day 207) argue that America's disestablished churches competed and grew while state churches stagnated. That is a claim about the consequences of the church-state model itself.

across.link: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948) includes the freedom to change one's religion. Saudi Arabia, objecting partly to that clause, was among the eight states that abstained, so religious liberty became both an international norm and a fault line in the same text.

days.apply_question: Sweden's Lutheran church ceased to be the state church on 1 January 2000. Using the dissenters' argument for religious liberty, what case could a committed Swedish Lutheran make that disestablishment was good for the church itself?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the dates and texts (the Danbury exchange, the 1905 French law, Dignitatis Humanae, the holding in Kennedy v. Bremerton). Debated: what the Establishment Clause originally meant. Separationists, following Everson (1947), read the wall broadly; accommodationists argue it barred a national church and coercion, not public religious expression. Also debated: whether disestablishment strengthens religion (Stark and Finke) or simply accompanies its decline. Value judgment: how much public space religion should have. Christian traditions disagree among themselves, from established churches to the Baptist and Anabaptist insistence on separation, while Catholic teaching since 1965 grounds religious freedom in the dignity of the person.

resource.title: 'A Wall of Separation': FBI Helps Restore Jefferson's Obliterated Draft
resource.creator: James H. Hutson, Library of Congress Information Bulletin (June 1998)
resource.why: The Library of Congress's manuscripts chief uses the restored draft to show what Jefferson deleted from the Danbury letter and why, evidence that the 'wall' was also a political move. It sets the Baptists' letter and Jefferson's reply side by side.
resource.verified_how: From prior knowledge of the Library of Congress article. Not re-checked by web search this session (shared search budget exhausted). No URL.

days.phase: Government: Power, Legitimacy and the Administrative State
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 15: The FDA, drug regulation built by disasters
days.headline_hint: A Raspberry-Flavoured Medicine Killed More Than 100 People in 1937. The Law Could Only Charge a Misleading Word.
days.concept: How does a society decide when a medicine is safe and effective enough to sell? In the US the answer was written mostly by disasters and protests, each of which tightened or loosened the rules, so drug regulation behaves like a balancing loop with long delays.
days.focus: Walk the US drug-regulation system through the chain as a loop. A sulfa drug in a toxic solvent (1937) produced the 1938 safety law; thalidomide and Frances Kelsey (1961-62) produced the 1962 efficacy law; AIDS activists (1988) produced accelerated approval; user fees (1992) bought faster reviews; Vioxx (2004) tightened the rules after approval. The angle: the FDA is both gatekeeper and promoter, and its two kinds of error differ in visibility. The victims of a bad approval have names; the victims of a delayed good drug mostly do not.
key_concepts: two kinds of regulatory error (the 'invisible graveyard')
days.model_or_equation: The Loops. B1, the safety loop (balancing): a drug disaster brings public outrage, then stricter pre-market rules, so fewer harmful drugs reach patients and disasters become rarer. It acts with a delay of years. B2, the access loop (balancing in the opposite direction): stricter rules mean slower, costlier approvals; patients die waiting, mostly unseen; organized patients and industry push back; faster pathways follow (accelerated approval in 1992, breakthrough-therapy designation in 2012). R1, the funding loop (reinforcing, with capture risk): user fees pay for more reviewers and firm deadlines, approvals speed up, industry supports renewing the fees every five years, and the agency's budget comes to depend more on the industry it regulates. B1 and B2 together, with their delays, produce oscillation (Day 27): the rules tighten after each scandal and loosen after each era of frustration. Documented reversal: regulation followed disasters instead of anticipating them, and in 1937 the government could prosecute only under a labelling rule.

story.title: Taste of raspberries
story.hook: In September 1937 the S. E. Massengill Company of Bristol, Tennessee, began shipping 'Elixir Sulfanilamide', a liquid form of the new sulfa antibacterial that children could swallow. The company's chief chemist, Harold Cole Watkins, had found that the drug dissolved in diethylene glycol, a chemical cousin of antifreeze, and added raspberry flavouring. The firm tested the mixture for flavour, appearance and fragrance but not for toxicity, and no law required it to. Within weeks people in Tulsa and across the South were dying of kidney failure. FDA inspectors fanned out to trace every shipment and recovered most of the roughly 240 gallons, but more than 100 people died, many of them children. A Tulsa mother, Maise Nidiffer, wrote to President Roosevelt describing her daughter's death. Watkins later killed himself. The only charge the government could bring was misbranding: an 'elixir' was supposed to contain alcohol, and this one contained none.
story.puzzle: A company had sold a lethal medicine across the country, and the law could punish it only for a misleading word on the label. How does a society decide when a medicine is safe and effective enough to sell, and why were America's rules written, again and again, by disasters?
story.payoff: Because political attention follows visible catastrophe. Within a year Congress passed the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, signed on 25 June 1938, which required evidence of safety before a drug could be sold. Thalidomide did the same for efficacy in 1962, AIDS activists for speed in 1988-92, and Vioxx for monitoring after approval in 2007. Each disaster tightened one loop, and each period of delay loosened another. Today's rules are the residue of that oscillation, not the product of a single design.
sources: Carol Ballentine, 'Taste of Raspberries, Taste of Death: The 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide Incident', FDA Consumer (June 1981)
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 25 June 1938
Daniel Carpenter, Reputation and Power: Organizational Image and Pharmaceutical Regulation at the FDA (2010)

days.application: The system itself: US drug regulation from Elixir Sulfanilamide (1937) to the FDA's 2021 accelerated approval of aducanumab. For contrast, The Gambia in 2022, where cough syrups contaminated with diethylene glycol were linked to the deaths of about 70 children (WHO alert, October 2022): the 1937 chemistry recurring where testing capacity was thin.

builds_on.why: The 1962 amendments' demand for 'adequate and well-controlled investigations' made the randomized controlled trial the legal standard for proving efficacy.
How much evidence is enough before approval depends on the cost of each kind of error: inductive risk, which Day 42 applied to the FDA's 2021 approval of aducanumab.
Frances Kelsey's refusal to approve thalidomide is Weberian bureaucracy at its best: a protected, expert official applying the rules against company pressure.
Since 1992 user fees have made the agency's drug-review budget depend partly on the regulated industry, the structural setup capture theory warns about.

across.link: Product-liability litigation acts as a second regulator. Merck withdrew Vioxx in September 2004 and in November 2007 agreed to a $4.85 billion settlement of US claims: tort law putting a price on a risk the approval system had missed.

days.apply_question: Was the FDA's December 2020 emergency authorization of the first COVID-19 vaccines, after trials lasting months rather than years, a defensible move of the evidence bar? What would you need to know, and what would you need to value, to answer?
days.evidence_note: Settled: the disasters and the laws they produced (1937-38, 1961-62, 2004-07); the toxicity of diethylene glycol and thalidomide; PDUFA shortened review times. Debated: whether FDA stringency costs more lives through delay than it saves through screening, with Peltzman (1973) and later 'drug lag' critics on one side and defenders such as Carpenter, who credit the agency's reputation for the public trust that makes new drugs usable, on the other. Also debated: whether user fees compromise safety (Carpenter, Zucker & Avorn, NEJM 2008), and how much accelerated approval on surrogate endpoints actually helps patients. Value judgment: whose risk it is to take, patients' autonomy (the 2018 Right to Try Act) or protection of the vulnerable. Consequentialists count total lives, deontologists stress consent, and Christian traditions (natural law, Catholic social teaching's common good) emphasize protecting the weakest. Ask who gained (patients, firms), who paid (victims, taxpayers, those left waiting) and who consented. The counterfactual, how many would have died under looser or tighter rules, cannot be observed.

chain.point: Bacterial infections were leading killers. Sulfanilamide, from Gerhard Domagk's discovery that Prontosil fights bacteria (published 1935), was the first broadly useful antibacterial drug, and doctors wanted a liquid form for children with streptococcal infections.

Sulfanilamide dissolves poorly in water. Watkins chose diethylene glycol as the solvent because it dissolved the drug, without testing whether it was toxic; the body breaks it down into compounds that destroy the kidneys. The same chemistry has killed again wherever testing was weak, most recently in The Gambia in 2022 (about 70 children; WHO alert, October 2022).

Massengill's 'control laboratory' checked flavour, appearance and fragrance. Modern drug production runs under current Good Manufacturing Practice regulations (first issued in 1963), which apply statistical quality control to every batch and every ingredient.

The 1938 Act required evidence of safety before sale. In 1960-62 the FDA medical officer Frances Kelsey refused to clear thalidomide, which caused severe birth defects in perhaps 10,000 children abroad. The Kefauver-Harris Amendments of 10 October 1962 added proof of efficacy and a requirement of informed consent.

Efficacy must rest on 'substantial evidence' from 'adequate and well-controlled investigations', which in practice means randomized trials. Where to set the bar trades approving bad drugs against delaying good ones, as in the 2021 accelerated approval of aducanumab against its advisory committee's advice.

Under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (1992), firms pay fees that fund reviewers in return for review-time goals, and median review times fell sharply. Developing a new drug is estimated to cost from about $1 billion to $2.6 billion, counting failures and the cost of capital (Wouters et al. 2020; DiMasi et al. 2016), so the evidence standard is also a cost standard.

On 11 October 1988 ACT UP's 'Seize Control of the FDA' demonstration brought more than a thousand protesters to the agency's headquarters in Rockville, Maryland, to demand faster access to AIDS drugs. The FDA created expedited procedures (1988) and accelerated approval on surrogate endpoints (1992).

The two kinds of error differ in visibility: the victims of thalidomide and Vioxx had faces, while patients harmed by delay mostly did not. Sam Peltzman (Journal of Political Economy, 1973) estimated that the 1962 amendments cut new-drug introductions by more than half with no measurable gain in quality, a claim others dispute. Vioxx, withdrawn on 30 September 2004, was estimated by the FDA scientist David Graham to have caused tens of thousands of excess heart attacks and strokes.

Each disaster tightened the rules (1938, 1962, and the 2007 FDA Amendments Act after Vioxx), and each era of frustration loosened them (1992, the 2012 breakthrough-therapy designation, the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016): a balancing loop with long delays, so it oscillates. Carpenter, Zucker and Avorn (NEJM, 2008) found that drugs approved just before PDUFA deadlines had more safety problems later.

Courts are a second regulator. Product-liability suits (such as Merck's 2007 Vioxx settlement) and judicial review of agency rules shape what the FDA can do; the Law block teaches tort and product liability, and administrative law.

Medicines and their ingredients cross borders faster than any national regulator can reach (the Gambian syrups were made in India), which is why the WHO issues global alerts and regulators harmonize standards. The International Relations block takes up international institutions.
