days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: What is law? Positivism and natural law
days.focus: Concept: legal positivism says law is what is validly enacted (Hart); natural-law theory says a gravely unjust law is defective as law (Fuller's inner morality; Radbruch) (D48). Story: the postwar German 'grudge informer' case - a wife who had denounced her husband under Nazi law - at the centre of the Hart-Fuller exchange (Harvard Law Review 1958) - a case later shown to have been decided on narrower grounds than both men assumed (Pappe, Modern Law Review 1960). App: the Nuremberg tribunal's 'crimes against humanity' (1945-46).

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: common-law judges decide cases by precedent, extending principles case by case (stare decisis). Story: in August 1928 May Donoghue drank ginger beer with a decomposed snail in a Paisley café; Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) gave Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle', echoing the Good Samaritan. App: civil-law codes, from the Code Napoléon (1804), as the contrasting method.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: property is a bundle of rights the state enforces; rights tend to emerge when resources become valuable enough to fight over (Demsetz 1967). Story: Pierson v. Post (N.Y. 1805) - who owns a fox, the man chasing it or the man who killed it? App: Buenos Aires squatters who happened to get land titles invested more in their houses (Galiani & Schargrodsky 2010) (D21).

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: contract law makes promises enforceable so strangers can cooperate (D14); damages are limited to what was foreseeable. Story: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) - a Gloucester mill idled by a late-delivered crankshaft. App: 'code is law' tested - The DAO hack of 17 Jun 2016 drained about 3.6 million ether through a contract that ran exactly as written.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: negligence law imposes a duty of care, and strict product liability makes makers pay for defects - to compensate victims and deter carelessness. Story: MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co. (N.Y. 1916) - Cardozo held Buick liable to a driver for a collapsed wooden wheel despite no direct contract. App: Grimshaw v. Ford (1981) - a jury's $125 million Pinto punitive award, cut to $3.5 million (D45).

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: incorporation creates a legal person with limited liability and a separate pool of assets, which lets strangers combine capital; whom it serves is contested (shareholder primacy versus stakeholders) - finance itself assumed at CFA level. Story: Dodge v. Ford Motor Co. (Mich. 1919) - Henry Ford wanted to spend profits on employing more men; the court sided with the Dodge brothers as shareholders. App: the Business Roundtable's August 2019 statement on corporate purpose.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: patents trade a temporary monopoly for disclosure; copyright protects expression; both balance incentives against access. Story: George Selden's patent on the gasoline car (filed 1879, granted 1895) let a licensing association charge carmakers until Henry Ford won on appeal in 1911. App: Jonas Salk's 'Could you patent the sun?' (1955) and the 2022 WTO compromise on COVID-vaccine patents.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: a crime needs a guilty act and a guilty mind; punishment is justified by retribution, deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation (D45, D46). Story: R v Dudley and Stephens (1884) - shipwrecked sailors who killed and ate the cabin boy, Richard Parker; necessity was no defence. App: deterrence research finds the certainty of punishment matters more than its severity (Nagin 2013).

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Evidence, burdens of proof and due process
days.focus: Concept: standards of proof (preponderance, clear and convincing, beyond reasonable doubt) are moral choices about which errors to risk (D42, D15). Story: Clarence Earl Gideon's pencil-written petition led to Gideon v. Wainwright (18 Mar 1963) and the right to counsel; retried with a lawyer, he was acquitted. App: O.J. Simpson acquitted of murder (1995) but found liable in civil court (1997) - same facts, different burdens.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: courts can strike down laws as unconstitutional, which raises the counter-majoritarian difficulty (Bickel 1962) and the dispute between originalism and living constitutionalism. Story: Marbury v. Madison (24 Feb 1803). App: Brown v. Board of Education (17 May 1954) - and Gerald Rosenberg's argument (The Hollow Hope, 1991) that courts changed little until Congress acted.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Administrative law: who makes the rules?
days.focus: Concept: agencies make rules under delegated power, through notice-and-comment, subject to judicial review for being 'arbitrary and capricious'. Story: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (28 Jun 2024) - herring fishermen required to pay for federal monitors - overruled Chevron deference. App: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass'n v. State Farm (1983) - the Court struck down the rescission of the passive-restraint (airbag) rule.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.focus: Concept: international law comes from treaties, custom and general principles (ICJ Statute Art. 38); states mostly comply out of reciprocity and reputation - 'almost all nations observe almost all principles... almost all of the time' (Henkin 1968). Story: The Paquete Habana (1900) - the Supreme Court returned Cuban fishing boats seized in 1898: 'international law is part of our law'. App: the 2016 South China Sea arbitral award under UNCLOS, which China rejected.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Law
days.topic: Law and new technology: who is liable?
days.focus: Concept: intermediary liability decides who answers for harm through a platform or an autonomous system; law faces the Collingridge dilemma - easy to shape a technology early, when harms are unknown, hard later (Collingridge 1980). Story: Stratton Oakmont v. Prodigy (1995) prompted Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) - 'the 26 words that created the internet' (Kosseff 2019). App: the EU's 2024 Product Liability Directive extending liability to software.

days.phase: Law: The Rules That Make Cooperation Possible
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 16: Tobacco and manufactured doubt
days.focus: Story: on 4 Jan 1954 the tobacco companies run 'A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers' in 448 newspapers, promising research. Question: how did a product that kills up to half its long-term users stay legal and popular for so long - and what finally changed? Deep: epidemiology (D143); tort waves and burdens of proof (D254, D258); the corporation (D255); administrative and regulatory tools - warnings (1966), the TV-ad ban (1971), the FDA's 2009 authority (D260, D243); the 1998 Master Settlement (about $206 billion); the 2006 racketeering judgment (U.S. v. Philip Morris); nicotine and reward (D151). Preview: global treaty (FCTC 2003, International Relations). Loop: James Bonsack's 1881 rolling machine created the mass cigarette before the demand; science preceded regulation by decades; US adult smoking fell from about 42% (1965) to about 11% (2022), while the 'doubt' playbook spread to other fields (Oreskes & Conway 2010).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: with no world government, states must help themselves, and one state's security can be another's threat (the security dilemma; Herz 1950, Jervis 1978). Story: Thucydides' Melian Dialogue (416 BC): 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must'. App: the Anglo-German naval race after HMS Dreadnought (1906).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: liberal theories hold that institutions, trade and democracy make cooperation durable; the 'democratic peace' is a strong correlation with debated causes (D18). Story: Norman Angell's The Great Illusion (1909-10) argued war could not pay in an interdependent world; WWI came anyway (he never said war was impossible). App: the Schuman Declaration (9 May 1950) - pooling coal and steel to make war between France and Germany 'materially impossible'.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: threats and interests depend on identities and shared norms - 'anarchy is what states make of it' (Wendt 1992). Story: Alexander Wendt's example - 500 British nuclear weapons are less threatening to the US than 5 North Korean ones. App: the 'nuclear taboo' - no nuclear use in war since 1945 (Tannenwald).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: since war is costly, both sides should prefer a deal; wars happen through private information, commitment problems and indivisible stakes (Fearon 1995) (D14). Story: Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia (23 Jul 1914) with 48 hours to reply. App: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine read as a commitment problem and as misperception - competing accounts.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: deterrence works through a secure second strike and credible threats - 'the threat that leaves something to chance' (Schelling 1960). Story: on 27 Oct 1962 aboard Soviet submarine B-59, Vasili Arkhipov is reported to have refused consent to launch a nuclear torpedo (details debated). App: Stanislav Petrov's 26 Sep 1983 judgment that a satellite launch warning was false.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: whether a 'long peace' since 1945 is a trend or a lull is hard to tell when war sizes are fat-tailed (D12) - Pinker (2011) against Cirillo & Taleb (2016) and Braumoeller (2019). Story: Lewis Fry Richardson's Statistics of Deadly Quarrels (1960) - wars sized like earthquakes. App: battle deaths rose sharply in 2022 with Ukraine and Ethiopia (Uppsala Conflict Data Program).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: just war theory - just cause, legitimate authority, last resort; in war, discrimination and proportionality - runs from Augustine and Aquinas to Walzer (1977); double effect distinguishes intended from foreseen harm; Christian pacifists reject the whole frame (Yoder, The Politics of Jesus, 1972). Story: in 1956 Elizabeth Anscombe, a Catholic philosopher, opposed Oxford's honorary degree for Harry Truman, calling Hiroshima the murder of innocents ('Mr Truman's Degree'). App: NATO's 1999 Kosovo campaign, judged 'illegal but legitimate' by an independent commission (2000).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: interdependence creates chokepoints that states can weaponize - oil, finance, chips (Farrell & Newman 2019); the economics is assumed at CFA level. Story: the October 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled oil prices within months - and led to US fuel-economy rules and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. App: the US export controls on advanced chips of 7 Oct 2022 (D106).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: when a rising power approaches a ruling one, the risk of war may rise (power-transition theory); Graham Allison's 'Thucydides Trap' counted 12 of 16 cases ending in war - critics dispute the case selection. Story: Allison's 2015 essay and 2017 book. App: Taiwan and TSMC - the 'silicon shield' argument (D106).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: international organizations are designed by great powers to be useful but not binding on themselves - hence the Security Council veto. Story: in June 1950 the Security Council authorized defence of South Korea because the Soviet delegate was boycotting and could not veto. App: Security Council vetoes over Syria and Ukraine.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: human-rights norms spread through 'norm cascades' (Finnemore & Sikkink 1998) and are enforced weakly - through courts, universal jurisdiction and pressure; whether treaties change behaviour is debated (Hathaway 2002 against Simmons 2009) (D225). Story: Augusto Pinochet arrested in London on 16 Oct 1998 on a Spanish judge's warrant. App: the Responsibility to Protect (2005) and its use in Libya (2011).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.topic: Global commons: from ozone to climate
days.focus: Concept: states solve global collective-action problems when producers are few, substitutes exist and side payments and trade measures enforce the deal (D30); climate lacks most of these. Story: Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin's May 1985 Nature paper on the Antarctic ozone hole; the Montreal Protocol (16 Sep 1987) is the first treaty ratified by every UN member. App: the Paris Agreement's pledge-and-review design (2015) (D85).

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: International Relations
days.focus: Concept: outside powers can topple governments far more easily than they can build legitimate, capable states (D236, D237). Story: Kabul fell to the Taliban on 15 Aug 2021 after twenty years and over two trillion dollars of US war spending (Costs of War project). App: the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction's 'lessons learned' reports.

days.phase: International Relations: Power and Order Among States
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 17: Nuclear power - Atoms for Peace
days.focus: Story: on 8 Dec 1953 Eisenhower tells the UN General Assembly that atomic energy should serve peace ('Atoms for Peace'); in 1954 AEC chairman Lewis Strauss predicts electricity 'too cheap to meter'. Question: why did nuclear power stall in the West - and is it coming back? Deep: physics and reactors (D64, D65, D79); normal accidents - Three Mile Island (D94); risk perception (D158); negative learning curves (D97) - Vogtle 3 and 4 years late and about $35 billion; regulation - the AEC split into the NRC (1975) (D244, D260); nonproliferation - the IAEA (1957), the NPT (1968), India's 1974 test using a research reactor (D268). Preview: none - every link has been taught. Loop: the bomb came before the power plant; Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) reshaped politics, Germany closed its last reactors on 15 Apr 2023, and AI's power demand is reviving plants (D113).

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: explaining why there is something it is like to be a mind (the hard problem, Chalmers 1995) is different from explaining behaviour; functionalism and Searle's Chinese Room (1980) disagree about machines (D184). Story: in June 2022 Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed the LaMDA chatbot was sentient and was put on leave. App: the 2024 New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: compatibilists say freedom is acting from your own reasons even in a caused world; libertarians and hard determinists disagree - and theology has its own version (Augustine and Pelagius; Calvinists and Arminians). Story: Benjamin Libet (1983) found brain activity before people reported deciding to move - re-interpreted as background noise by Schurger et al. (2012). App: Roper v. Simmons (2005), which cited adolescent brain development in barring executions for crimes committed under 18.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: the main families - cosmological (Aquinas's Five Ways, the kalam), teleological and fine-tuning, ontological, moral - and their strongest objections (Hume, Kant, the multiverse, selection effects). Story: Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion, about 1078) and the monk Gaunilo's 'perfect island' reply. App: the fine-tuning argument from constants such as Hoyle's carbon resonance (D127) and the observation-selection objection (Sober).

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: the logical problem (Mackie 1955) and the evidential problem (Rowe 1979) against theism, and the replies - Plantinga's free-will defence (1974), soul-making (Hick 1966), sceptical theism. Story: the Lisbon earthquake on All Saints' Day, 1 Nov 1755 - churches full, tens of thousands dead - and Voltaire's poem against optimism. App: Rousseau's 1756 reply that people, not nature, had built seven-storey houses so close together - 'natural' disasters and human choices.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: evidentialism (believe only on sufficient evidence - Clifford 1877) against James's 'The Will to Believe' (1896) and Plantinga's Reformed epistemology (some beliefs are properly basic, 2000) (D41). Story: Clifford's shipowner who sends an unsound ship to sea, sincerely believing it safe. App: how believing scientists describe the relation (Francis Collins, The Language of God, 2006) - and how sceptics answer.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: Augustine's City of God holds that earthly goods are real but fragile and that no political order brings salvation - a lasting Christian scepticism about progress narratives; Reinhold Niebuhr's Christian realism carries it into politics. Story: the Visigoths sacked Rome on 24 Aug 410; pagans blamed Christianity and Augustine answered over thirteen years. App: Niebuhr's Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932) and his influence on Cold War statesmen.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle (1971) against Nozick's entitlement theory (1974), with utilitarian and Christian answers alongside. Story: Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument - fans freely pay to watch him play; is the resulting inequality unjust? App: Iran's regulated market in kidneys (since 1988) - how each theory, and the Catholic tradition, would judge it.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: human dignity, the common good, subsidiarity, solidarity, the preferential option for the poor and the universal destination of goods (Compendium 2004), developed from Rerum Novarum (1891) to Centesimus Annus (1991), Laudato si' (2015) and Antiqua et nova (2025). Story: Leo XIII issues Rerum Novarum on 15 May 1891 amid industrial strife. App: Fr John A. Ryan's A Living Wage (1906) and its influence on American labour policy - and Leo XIV's explanation (10 May 2025) that he took his name because Leo XIII answered the first industrial revolution and the Church must now answer AI (D184).

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: several traditions - Kuyper's sphere sovereignty, Niebuhr's realism, Hauerwas's church as a distinct community, O'Donovan's Resurrection and Moral Order (1986), Bonhoeffer's costly discipleship - that disagree with each other and with Catholic teaching. Story: Abraham Kuyper opening the Free University of Amsterdam on 20 Oct 1880: 'there is not a square inch... over which Christ... does not cry: Mine!'. App: Dutch 'pillarization' - Protestant, Catholic and secular institutions side by side in one welfare state.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Human dignity at the edges of life
days.focus: Concept: dignity grounds rights in Kantian, Christian (image of God) and secular forms; critics call it vague (Macklin 2003; Pinker 2008) - applied to IVF, embryo research and assisted dying. Story: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby, born 25 Jul 1978 in Oldham. App: Canada's medical assistance in dying - about 15,000 deaths in 2023, about 4.7% of all deaths - and the dispute over its expansion.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: whether moral progress is real, and what drives it - argument, an expanding circle of concern (Singer 1981; Buchanan & Powell 2018), honour and identity (Appiah 2010), or material change - with sceptics (Gray; MacIntyre) and the debunking challenge (D227, D44). Story: Frederick Douglass's 5 Jul 1852 speech 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'. App: the end of duelling in Britain and America, which Appiah attributes to a shift in honour codes.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: belief in progress is a historical idea - perhaps secularized Christian eschatology (Löwith 1949) or a genuinely modern achievement (Blumenberg 1966); Bury (1920), Nisbet (1980) and Lasch (1991) trace and criticise it (D185). Story: Condorcet wrote his Sketch for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind while hiding from the Terror, and died in prison in March 1794. App: Pinker's Enlightenment Now (2018) and its critics.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: are artifacts neutral tools, or do they embody politics and reshape us (Winner 1980; Ellul 1954; Borgmann 1984)? Technological determinism against social shaping. Story: Langdon Winner's claim that Robert Moses built Long Island parkway overpasses low to keep buses out - a story Bernward Joerges (1999) challenged. App: C.S. Lewis's The Abolition of Man (1943): 'man's power over Nature' turns out to be some men's power over others.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.focus: Concept: environmental ethics ranges from human-centred to stewardship to nature-centred; Lynn White's thesis that Christian dominion caused the ecological crisis meets mixed empirical tests. Story: Lynn White Jr.'s 'The Historical Roots of Our Ecologic Crisis' (Science, 10 Mar 1967). App: Laudato si' (2015), and the review by Taylor, Van Wieren & Zaleha (Conservation Biology 2016) finding little evidence of a 'greening' of Christian environmental behaviour.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Arguing fairly: steelmanning and the ideological Turing test
days.focus: Concept: to know your own case you must know the other side at its strongest - Mill's principle (On Liberty, 1859) and Bryan Caplan's ideological Turing test (2011); adversarial collaboration puts it into practice (D168, D163). Story: Mill: 'He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.' App: the Cogitate Consortium's adversarial test of two rival theories of consciousness, with predictions agreed by both camps in advance (Nature 2025) (D278) - the model for pre-registered theses in a book.

days.phase: Philosophy II: Persons, God, Progress and the Good
days.subject: Systems Case
days.topic: Systems Case 18: Car IV - the full loop: was the car progress?
days.focus: Story: on 17 Aug 1896 Bridget Driscoll is struck by a demonstration car at Crystal Palace, London - Britain's first pedestrian killed by a car; the coroner is reported to have said it must never happen again. Question: was the automobile, on balance, morally beneficial progress - and what would it take to answer? Deep, every link: need (D159); invention as combination (D35); constraints (D70, D54); engineering and production (D103); financing named at CFA level; regulation and liability (D254, D260, D49); adoption (D213); consequences (D216, D85); feedback and geopolitics (D271). Then the evaluation: measured goods and harms, the counterfactual that cannot be known, and how consequentialist, Kantian, virtue, natural-law and Catholic social teaching, Augustinian and philosophy-of-technology frameworks weigh them (D45, D285, D283, D290, D288), and whether 'beneficial' can be true at all (D44). Loop: regulation before the car (1865), roads before the car (cyclists' Good Roads movement, 1880), credit before demand - the chain Logan began with, redrawn as the loop it was.
